pericopes.text: And now it came to pass after I, Nephi, had made an end of teaching my brethren, our father, Lehi, also spake many things unto them: how great things the Lord had done for them, in bringing them out of the land of Jerusalem.

links.text: Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.

provenance.other: 'How great things the Lord' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 5:19. Luke 8:39 tells the same episode and reads 'how great things God hath done unto thee', which is not the wording here.
provenance.significance: The phrase re-enters in a different hand. At 1 Nephi 7:11 it is Nephi's rebuke to his brothers — 'how great things the Lord hath done for us' — and here it is the narrator's summary of what his father said to those same brothers. Mark's sentence is a commission: the man Jesus has just cleansed asks to follow him, is refused, and is sent home to tell his own people instead. Both Book of Mormon uses put it in the mouth of someone sent back to a hostile household to say what God has done, which is the one thing the source's context supplies and the phrase alone does not.

links.note: 'Lehi also spake many things unto them: how great things the Lord had done for them, in bringing them out of the land of Jerusalem.' The KJV has this formula once. The argument for it was made at 1 Nephi 7:11, where the run is eight words and the 1830 preserves 'how' against 1920's 'what' in the parallel at that verse; it is given again here because a new book is a new voice and a reader of 2 Nephi shown nothing at 1:1 has been told there is no borrowing here (ADJUDICATING §4). Note that the exposition Lehi is about to give — a deliverance recited as the warrant for present obedience — is the shape Mark 5:19 commissions.

pericopes.text: And he spake unto them concerning their rebellions upon the waters, and the mercies of God in sparing their lives, that they were not swallowed up in the sea.
And he also spake unto them concerning the land of promise, which they had obtained: how merciful the Lord had been in warning us that we should flee out of the land of Jerusalem.
For, Behold, saith he, I have seen a vision, in the which I know that Jerusalem is destroyed; and had we remained in Jerusalem, we should also have perished.

But, said he, notwithstanding our afflictions, we have obtained a land of promise, a land which is choice above all other lands; a land which the Lord God hath covenanted with me should be a land for the inheritance of my seed. Yea, the Lord hath covenanted this land unto me, and to my children forever; and also all they which should be led out of other countries, by the hand of the Lord.
Wherefore, I, Lehi, prohesy according to the workings of the spirit which is in me, that there shall be none come into this land, save they should be brought by the hand of the Lord.

Wherefore, this land is consecrated unto him whom he shall bring. And if it so be that they shall serve him according to the commandments which he hath given, it shall be a land of liberty unto them; wherefore, they shall never be brought down into captivity: if so, it shall be because of iniquity: for if iniquity shall abound, cursed shall be the land for their sakes; but unto the righteous, it shall be blessed forever.

links.text: And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.

provenance.other: 'Iniquity shall abound' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 24:12. The KJV's other 'abound' collocations are Pauline and positive — grace, hope, love, thanksgiving.
provenance.significance: The clause Lehi uses to state the condition on which the land is cursed is the clause the Olivet discourse uses to state the condition of the last days. In Matthew it is the third of the signs — false prophets, then iniquity abounding, then love waxing cold, then the end — so the words arrive already carrying a chronology of decline, which is exactly what verses 10-12 of this chapter then supply: the people receive the blessings, reject the Holy One, and are scattered as one generation passes to another. Lehi's conditional promise is worded out of an apocalypse.

links.note: 'If iniquity shall abound, cursed shall be the land for their sakes.' A KJV singleton, three words long and unmistakable, and it is doing the same work in both places: naming the point at which a promised condition tips into judgment. Well below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion, but the absolute rarity is what makes it worth having.

links.text: And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;

provenance.other: 'Cursed is the ground for thy sake' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:17; the only other curse-the-ground clause is Genesis 8:21's 'I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake'. 'For thy sake' by itself occurs in exactly nine KJV verses and cannot carry the link alone.
provenance.alternative: The Deuteronomic blessing-and-curse formularies (Deuteronomy 28:15-18) are the obvious background for a conditional land curse and share the vocabulary of cursing without the ground.
provenance.significance: Lehi has just called this a land of liberty and a land consecrated, and the sentence that states its liability is Eden's. Genesis 3:17 curses the ground because of what a man did, not because of what the ground is, and it is the KJV's founding statement that a place can be spoiled by the conduct of the people in it. That is the doctrine this chapter needs — the land is choice above all other lands and can nevertheless be cursed — and the Book of Mormon has taken it in the words of the sentence that first said it.

links.note: 'Cursed shall be the land for their sakes; but unto the righteous, it shall be blessed forever.' Against Genesis 3:17's 'cursed is the ground for thy sake', with 'ground' becoming 'land' and the singular becoming plural. What tells is the addition Lehi makes: Genesis has no answering blessing, and the Book of Mormon supplies one, which converts a sentence of expulsion into a conditional tenure. Proposed at moderate because the two content words that survive are 'cursed' and the 'for … sake' construction.

pericopes.text: And behold, it is wisdom that this land should be kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations: for behold, many nations would overrun the land, that there would be no place for an inheritance.

Wherefore, I, Lehi, have obtained a promise, that inasmuch as they which the Lord God shall bring out of the land of Jerusalem shall keep his commandments, they shall prosper upon the face of this land; and they shall be kept from all other nations, that they may possess this land unto themselves. And if it so be that they shall keep his commandments, they shall be blessed upon the face of this land, and there shall be none to molest them, nor to take away the land of their inheritance; and they shall dwell safely forever.

links.text: And they shall no more be a prey to the heathen, neither shall the beast of the land devour them; but they shall dwell safely, and none shall make them afraid.

provenance.other: 'Dwell safely' occurs in nine KJV verses and 'none shall make them afraid' in four; Ezekiel 34:28 is the one verse that holds both, together with the promise that they shall 'no more be a prey to the heathen'. 'Molest' occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Leviticus 26:5-6 gives the same two promises across two verses, and the whole cluster is standard covenant-blessing language that no single verse owns.
provenance.significance: Every element of the Book of Mormon's promise is in Ezekiel 34:28 and in the same order: safety from the nations, the absence of anyone to trouble them, and dwelling safely. The one substitution is the one that matters — Ezekiel's 'none shall make them afraid' becomes 'none to molest them', a word the KJV does not use at all. The borrowing has been paraphrased at exactly the point where the source is most formulaic, which is what a writer working from memory of the sense rather than the page produces.

links.note: 'They shall be kept from all other nations … there shall be none to molest them, nor to take away the land of their inheritance; and they shall dwell safely forever.' Proposed on the cluster rather than on any one phrase: only Ezekiel 34:28 assembles all three promises in a single verse. Recorded at moderate because 'dwell safely' is common and the distinctive word in the Book of Mormon's clause, 'molest', is not KJV English at all.
links.whyNot: Nothing here is a KJV singleton, and the sheep-shepherd frame that governs Ezekiel 34 is entirely absent from Lehi's blessing. A reader could take the whole verse as generic covenant idiom and would not be obviously wrong.

pericopes.text: But behold, when the time cometh that they shall dwindle in unbelief, after that they have received so great blessings from the hand of the Lord; having a knowledge of the creation of the earth, and all men knowing the great and marvellous works of the Lord from the creation of the world; having power given them to do all things by faith; having all the commandments from the beginning, and having been brought by his infinite goodness into this precious land of promise; behold, I say, if the day shall come that they will reject the Holy One of Israel, the true Messiah their Redeemer and their God, behold, the judgments of him that is just, shall rest upon them;

links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: 'Great and marvellous' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and only 15:3 attaches it to works: 'Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty.' The 1830 spells it 'marvellous', which is the KJV's spelling; 1920 modernized to 'marvelous' and in doing so erased the orthographic evidence of the borrowing (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: This is the fourth time in the corpus that Revelation 15:3 stands behind a Book of Mormon sentence, and Lehi takes the half of it that Nephi did not. 1 Nephi 1:14 borrowed the vocative — 'Great and marvellous are thy works, O Lord God Almighty' — from a verse Revelation itself labels 'the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb'. Here the same verse supplies the works, and nine verses later, at 1:19, Lehi finishes it: 'his ways are righteousness forever' answers Revelation 15:3's 'just and true are thy ways.' A dying man's last blessing runs on the song the redeemed sing in Revelation, and Revelation names that song after the man whose deathbed charge (Deuteronomy 33) this chapter is imitating.

links.note: 'All men knowing the great and marvellous works of the Lord from the creation of the world.' Two KJV verses have 'great and marvellous' and both are Revelation 15; only 15:3 has it of God's works, which is the form here. The link is not a fresh discovery of the verse — 1 Nephi 1:14 established it — but the distribution within this chapter is new: 1:10 takes the works and 1:19 takes the ways, which are the two halves of the same sentence in the source, split across nine verses of a single speech. Note also 'from the creation of the world', which is itself a KJV singleton at Romans 1:20 and is filed in the register.

pericopes.text: yea, he will bring other nations unto them, and he will give unto them power, and he will take away from them the lands of their possessions; and he will cause them to be scattered and smitten.

Yea, as one generation passeth to another, there shall be bloodsheds and great visitations among them; wherefore, my sons, I would that ye would remember; yea, I would that ye would hearken unto my words.

links.text: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever.

provenance.other: 'One generation passeth' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ecclesiastes 1:4 is also the KJV's only verse in which one generation passes and another comes as a single proposition.
provenance.significance: Recover the rest of Ecclesiastes 1:4 and the borrowing turns against the speaker: 'One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever.' The Preacher's point is that the land outlasts everyone who walks on it, which is a statement of futility. Lehi's point in this chapter is that the land is covenanted to his seed forever and will be blessed or cursed according to what the generations do on it. He has taken the Preacher's sentence about the permanence of the earth and used it to introduce bloodsheds and visitations — the same observation read as warning rather than as vanity.

links.note: 'As one generation passeth to another, there shall be bloodsheds and great visitations among them.' The KJV says 'One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh' once, and the Book of Mormon compresses it to a single subordinate clause. Ecclesiastes is not a book the Book of Mormon draws on often, which is part of why the singleton is worth recording; and the compression is the argument, since Ecclesiastes uses the sentence to say that nothing changes and Lehi uses it to say what will change.

pericopes.text: O that ye would awake, awake from a deep sleep, yea, even from the sleep of hell, and shake off the awful chains by which ye are bound, which are the chains which bind the children of men, that they are carried away captive down to the eternal gulf of misery and wo!

links.text: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, and sit down, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.

provenance.other: 'From the dust' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:2, and 'shake thyself from the dust' is that same singleton. 'Awake, awake' occurs at Isaiah 51:9, 51:17 and 52:1 and nowhere else in the KJV. The Book of Mormon phrase 'arise from the dust' occurs in no KJV verse at all: it is a recombination of Isaiah 52:2's two imperatives, which the KJV gives in the reverse order ('Shake thyself from the dust; arise').
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:1-2 is the engine of the whole blessing, and Lehi takes all four of its imperatives and redistributes them across his speech: awake (1:13, 1:23), shake off (1:13, 1:23), arise from the dust (1:14, 1:21, 1:23), and loose the bands of the neck, which becomes the chains by which his sons are bound. What Isaiah addresses to a city — 'O captive daughter of Zion' — Lehi addresses to four sons who are about to lose a birthright, and the captivity is transposed from political to spiritual in the same breath: the chains are hell's, the dust is the grave's. The transposition is what makes the borrowing interesting, and it is complete by the second imperative. Note that this book will later transcribe Isaiah 51:24-52:2 outright at 2 Nephi 8:24-25, seven chapters after Lehi has already spoken it as his own.

links.note: 'O that ye would awake, awake from a deep sleep … and shake off the awful chains by which ye are bound … that they are carried away captive.' Isaiah 52:1-2 in fragments: the doubled imperative of 52:1, the shaking and the dust of 52:2, the captivity of 52:2's closing vocative, the binding of its 'bands of thy neck'. Two of the phrases are KJV singletons. Mediation is straightforwardly direct-OT here, unlike at Jacob 3:11 where the transcription at 2 Nephi 8 already stood between the source and the allusion — 2 Nephi 1 precedes that transcription, so Isaiah is the only model available to the reader at this point in the book. Note that the imperative Lehi actually coins, 'arise from the dust', is in no KJV verse; he has fused Isaiah's 'from the dust' with Isaiah's 'arise' and produced the refrain that governs verses 14, 21 and 23.

pericopes.text: Awake! and arise from the dust, and hear the words of a trembling parent, whose limbs ye must soon lay down in the cold and silent grave, from whence no traveller can return: a few more days, and I go the way of all the earth.

links.text: I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man;

provenance.other: 'The way of all the earth' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joshua 23:14 and 1 Kings 2:2, and both are a leader's farewell. Only 1 Kings 2:2 has it in the first person present — 'I go the way of all the earth' — which is the form 2 Nephi 1:14 reproduces word for word, eight words in sequence.
provenance.alternative: Joshua 23:14 is the other candidate and shares the theme of a land promise kept; but Joshua reads 'this day I am going the way of all the earth', and the Book of Mormon has David's tense, not Joshua's.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 2:1-4 is the KJV's model deathbed charge and 2 Nephi 1 reproduces it whole, not in one phrase but in four: David says 'I go the way of all the earth' (2:2) and Lehi says it verbatim at 1:14; David says 'be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man' and Lehi says 'arise from the dust, my sons, and be men' at 1:21; David says 'keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments' and Lehi says 'observe the statutes and the judgments of the Lord' at 1:16; David says 'that thou mayest prosper' and Lehi says 'ye shall prosper in the land' at 1:20. The catalogue has already found 1 Kings 2:3 behind 1 Nephi 2:20, where Lehi first states the covenant formula. What 2 Nephi 1 does is complete the borrowing: having taken David's promise at the start of his journey, Lehi now takes David's death. And the metalepsis is exact — 1 Kings 2 is a dying father transferring a kingdom past the sons who would have had it by right, which is precisely what verses 28-29 of this chapter do to Laman.

links.note: 'A few more days, and I go the way of all the earth.' Eight words of 1 Kings 2:2 in sequence, from one of the KJV's two verses that contain the phrase and the only one in this tense. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because a complete clause is reproduced from an identifiable verse. The reason to read it as the whole charge rather than a tag is that three further elements of 1 Kings 2:2-4 turn up in the next seven verses of the same speech, in the source's order.

links.text: When a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return.

provenance.other: 'Shall not return' occurs in exactly thirteen KJV verses, but only Job 16:22 combines it with a few of something and with going a way: 'When a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return.' Job 10:21 is the same thought — 'Before I go whence I shall not return, even to the land of darkness'.
provenance.alternative: The famous English form of this sentiment is not biblical at all. Hamlet's 'undiscovered country, from whose bourn no traveller returns' is closer to the Book of Mormon's wording than any KJV verse is, and 'traveller' — the 1830's spelling, modernized to 'traveler' in 1920 — is Shakespeare's word here, not the King James translators'. The catalogue records the KJV candidate and flags the non-biblical one honestly rather than suppressing it.
provenance.significance: Job 16:22 sits immediately before Job's turn to the grave and the eye that shall no more see good, and its structure is the structure of this half-verse: a short reckoning of time, then a going, then a road with no return. The Book of Mormon has the same three elements in the same order and has interleaved them with 1 Kings 2:2, so that a single sentence carries a dying king's charge and a suffering man's arithmetic at once. What Job supplies that 1 Kings does not is the finality; what 1 Kings supplies that Job does not is the command.

links.note: 'From whence no traveller can return: a few more days, and I go the way of all the earth.' Read against Job 16:22, 'When a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return' — three elements shared (a few of a time-unit, going a way, no return) in the source's own sequence, with 'years' shortened to 'days'. Held at moderate because each element is ordinary on its own and because the nearest English parallel to the whole clause is Hamlet, not scripture; see provenance.alternative, which is a flag for Wilson rather than a settled judgment.

links.text: Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.

provenance.other: 'And arise from the' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:14, as does 'awake thou that sleepest'. It is the KJV's only verse pairing an imperative to awake with an imperative to arise, and 'Awake! and arise from the dust' differs from it by a single word. The Book of Mormon's own phrase 'arise from the dust' occurs in exactly no KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 52:1-2 supplies both verbs independently and is the chapter's demonstrable source (see 1:13); Ephesians may be doing nothing here that Isaiah is not already doing.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:14 is itself an unattributed scriptural citation — 'Wherefore he saith' — and what it is citing is generally taken to be Isaiah, which makes it the New Testament's own compression of the awake-and-arise material this chapter is working from. If the Book of Mormon has it, then the same fragment reaches 2 Nephi 1 twice, once through Isaiah 52 and once through Paul's condensation of it, and the tell is the word 'dead': Isaiah has dust and no death, Ephesians has death and no dust, and Lehi — speaking of the grave two clauses later — has both.

links.note: 'Awake! and arise from the dust.' One word away from Ephesians 5:14's 'Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead', which the machine stream caught as a four-word run. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because Isaiah 52:1-2 accounts for the same words and is independently demonstrated in the previous verse; what Ephesians adds is the imperative pairing itself, which Isaiah gives in the reverse order and across a clause boundary.
links.whyNot: Everything Ephesians 5:14 supplies, Isaiah 52:1-2 supplies as well, and Isaiah supplies the dust that Ephesians lacks. A reader who takes the whole refrain as Isaianic loses nothing except the neatness of the one-word substitution.

pericopes.text: But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell: I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.

links.text: The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them.

provenance.other: 'Everlasting arms' is a KJV singleton at Deuteronomy 33:27; the Book of Mormon's 'the arms of his love' occurs in no KJV verse, and 'in the arms of' occurs in none either.
provenance.alternative: 'Encircled about eternally in the arms of his love' may be Lehi's own figure and owe nothing to Deuteronomy; the shared element is one noun.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 33 is the KJV's one chapter that is a dying leader's blessing pronounced over sons tribe by tribe, which is the literary form of 2 Nephi 1-4 exactly: Lehi blesses Laman and Lemuel and Sam together, then Zoram, then Jacob, then Joseph, then the children of the sons. The verse that supplies the arms is the verse that closes the blessing of Israel as a whole, and its content is refuge — 'The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.' Lehi's line takes the same image and turns it from protection into embrace, and the adverb he uses, 'eternally', is Deuteronomy 33:27's 'eternal God' in adverbial form.

links.note: 'The Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell: I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.' The verbal contact is one noun and an adverb, so this is proposed on the genre rather than the wording: Deuteronomy 33 is the model final blessing, and this is the moment in Lehi's final blessing where he says what has become of him. 'Redeemed my soul' is itself a KJV phrase, at 2 Samuel 4:9 and 1 Kings 1:29, in both places David's oath formula — which is worth noting given that the next verse but one runs on David's deathbed charge.
links.whyNot: One noun. 'Arms' is not distinctive enough to establish dependence on its own, and Deuteronomy 33:27's arms are underneath as a support while Lehi's encircle as an embrace; the images are not the same image. Kept because the chapter's form is Deuteronomy 33's form and because the KJV has the phrase exactly once.

pericopes.text: And I desire that ye should remember to observe the statutes and the judgments of the Lord: behold, this hath been the anxiety of my soul, from the beginning.

links.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.other: 'The statutes and the judgments' in that exact article-bearing form occurs in exactly no KJV verse; 'his statutes and his judgments' occurs in exactly two, Deuteronomy 30:16 and Psalm 147:19. What identifies 1 Kings 2:3 is not the phrase in isolation but its position two verses after 'I go the way of all the earth', which 2 Nephi 1:14 has just quoted, and which occurs in exactly two KJV verses.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 30:16 has the same triad of commandments, statutes and judgments and is the source of the Deuteronomic formula generally; Psalm 19:9's 'the judgments of the LORD' is what the machine stream proposed and is filed in the register.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has already placed 1 Kings 2:3 behind 1 Nephi 2:20, the covenant promise Lehi receives on leaving Jerusalem. Its return here closes a bracket that runs the length of Lehi's life in the text: he begins with David's charge to Solomon as a promise and ends with it as a valediction. The choice of source is not neutral, because 1 Kings 2 is a succession narrative in which the charge is followed immediately by instructions to settle scores with Joab and Shimei — and 2 Nephi 1 likewise moves from the statutes and the judgments straight to what is to be done about Laman.

links.note: 'Remember to observe the statutes and the judgments of the Lord: behold, this hath been the anxiety of my soul, from the beginning.' The pairing is Deuteronomic and common; what makes 1 Kings 2:3 the source here is proximity in the source rather than rarity in the phrase. Two verses earlier the Book of Mormon quoted 1 Kings 2:2 verbatim, four verses later it will restate 1 Kings 2:3's 'that thou mayest prosper', and 1 Nephi 2:20 already drew the same verse. Three contacts with one short passage inside seven verses is the argument.

pericopes.text: My heart hath been weighed down with sorrow from time to time: for I have feared, lest for the hardness of your hearts, lest the Lord your God should come out in the fulness of his wrath, upon you, that ye be cut off and destroyed forever;

links.text: He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.

provenance.other: 'Hardness of your hearts' — second person plural, both nouns plural — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:8. Mark 10:5 has the singular 'the hardness of your heart' and Mark 3:5 has 'the hardness of their hearts', which is the form 1 Nephi uses of Laman and Lemuel in the third person. The Book of Mormon has the pronoun and the number right for a father addressing his sons to their faces.
provenance.significance: The pronoun is the finding. Three KJV verses carry this phrase and each is grammatically distinct, and the Book of Mormon has used each of them in its correct setting: Mark 3:5's 'their' in narration about the brothers, Matthew 19:8's 'your' here, where Lehi is speaking to them. In Matthew the phrase concedes something — Moses permitted divorce because of it, so the hardness is a fact the law accommodated rather than a fault it punished. Lehi's use is the opposite: he fears that the hardness will bring the wrath rather than a concession, which is what Jesus goes on to say in the same verse ('but from the beginning it was not so').

links.note: 'I have feared, lest for the hardness of your hearts, lest the Lord your God should come out in the fulness of his wrath.' A KJV singleton in the exact form used. The pronoun check is the point (ADJUDICATING §4): the KJV has three hardness-of-heart phrases distinguished only by pronoun and number, and this one is Matthew's. 'The fulness of his wrath' has no KJV source — the machine's proposal of Job 20:22 is filed in the register — so the borrowed material is the diagnosis, not the sentence.

pericopes.text: or, that a cursing should come upon you, for the space of many generations; and ye are visited by sword, and by famine, and are hated, and are led according to the will and captivity of the Devil.

links.text: And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.

provenance.other: The KJV states the devil's captivity of the will once: 'the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will'. 'Taken captive by him at his will' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 2:26; 'snare of the devil' occurs in exactly two, 1 Timothy 3:7 and 2 Timothy 2:26, and only the second adds the taking captive and the will. 'The will of the devil' occurs in exactly no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: 'Led according to the will and captivity of the Devil' is an odd English phrase — two abstract nouns coordinated where a reader expects one — and 2 Timothy 2:26 explains it: the source has both nouns, 'taken captive' and 'at his will', in one clause, and the Book of Mormon has compressed the clause into a pair. The context in 2 Timothy is instruction about how to correct those who oppose themselves, 'if God peradventure will give them repentance', which is the situation Lehi is in for the whole of this chapter: a man arguing with sons he still hopes will recover themselves. That is also where the chapter's chains come from, and it lets 1:13's captivity and 1:18's captivity be read as one figure.

links.note: 'Ye are visited by sword, and by famine, and are hated, and are led according to the will and captivity of the Devil.' The clause is a compression of the KJV's one statement that the devil takes men captive at his will. The first half of the verse — sword and famine — is Jeremiah's standing pair and identifies no source; the register records the machine's proposal there. What is not formulaic is the coordination of will and captivity, which exists in the KJV in a single verse.

pericopes.text: O my sons, that these things might not come upon you, but that ye might be a choice and a favored people of the Lord. But, behold, his will be done: for his ways are righteousness forever;
and he hath said, that inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land; but inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments, ye shall be cut off from my presence.

links.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.other: 'Prosper in the land' occurs in exactly no KJV verse; 1 Kings 2:3 has 'that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest', and 'the way of all the earth', quoted six verses earlier at 1:14, occurs in exactly two KJV verses of which 1 Kings 2:2 is one. See the full argument for the source at 1 Nephi 2:20.
provenance.significance: The verse announces its own mediation — 'and he hath said' — and what was said is 1 Nephi 2:20, the promise Lehi received in the wilderness. So the proximate model is the Book of Mormon's own earlier text and the ultimate model is David's charge to Solomon, which is exactly the layering the catalogue's mediation field exists to record. The second half is the interesting half: 1 Nephi 2:21 gave the sanction as being 'cut off from the presence of the Lord', and here it hardens into first-person divine speech, 'cut off from my presence' — which is a KJV singleton, and a priestly one.

links.note: 'He hath said, that inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land; but inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments, ye shall be cut off from my presence.' This is the Book of Mormon's covenant formula in its canonical form, and the verse presents it as a quotation of something already said. What it quotes is 1 Nephi 2:20-21, where the catalogue placed 1 Kings 2:3. Recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM for that reason rather than as a fresh contact with 1 Kings.

links.text: Say unto them, Whosoever he be of all your seed among your generations, that goeth unto the holy things, which the children of Israel hallow unto the LORD, having his uncleanness upon him, that soul shall be cut off from my presence: I am the LORD.

provenance.other: 'Cut off from my presence' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 22:3. The commoner biblical formula is 'cut off from among his people' or 'from the presence of the LORD' in the third person; the first-person possessive is Leviticus 22:3's alone.
provenance.alternative: 1 Nephi 2:21 already has 'cut off from the presence of the Lord', so the phrase may simply be that earlier Book of Mormon sentence recast into direct speech, with no fresh contact with Leviticus.
provenance.significance: Leviticus 22:3 is a purity statute: a priest who approaches the holy things while unclean is cut off from God's presence. It is the KJV's one use of the exact phrase, and it puts the sanction in the first person because it is God legislating about his own sanctuary. What the Book of Mormon does with it is to move the sanction from the sanctuary to a land — the uncleanness that severs a man from the presence is now disobedience on the land of promise — which is the same substitution the chapter has made twice already, at 1:7 where Eden's cursed ground becomes a cursed land and at 1:13 where Zion's captivity becomes hell's.

links.note: 'Ye shall be cut off from my presence.' A KJV singleton, and the shift into the first person is what identifies it: 1 Nephi 2:21 says 'cut off from the presence of the Lord', the ordinary form, and here Lehi reports God speaking, which is the form Leviticus 22:3 has. Recorded at moderate because the recasting could be the Book of Mormon's own and needs no source.

pericopes.text: And now that my soul might have joy in you, and that my heart might leave this world with gladness because of you; that I might not be brought down with grief and sorrow to the grave, arise from the dust, my sons, and be men, and be determined in one mind, and in one heart united in all things, that ye may not come down into captivity;

links.text: And he said, My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if mischief befall him by the way in the which ye go, then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.

provenance.other: 'With sorrow to the grave' occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Genesis 42:38, 44:29 and 44:31 — and all three are Jacob, or his sons quoting Jacob, about what his sons will do to him.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one formula for a father brought to the grave by grief over his sons belongs entirely to Jacob and the Joseph narrative, and it is spoken in each case about the loss of the youngest and best-loved. 2 Nephi 1 is Jacob's situation with the parts redistributed: an old man, sons who have already tried to kill the favoured brother once (1:24, 'ye sought to take away his life'), and a father who says in so many words that their conduct will decide whether he goes down in grief. Recovering the source makes the chapter's family plot legible — Lehi is speaking as Jacob, and the son he is defending will be renamed Joseph's line before the book is done.

links.note: 'That I might not be brought down with grief and sorrow to the grave, arise from the dust, my sons, and be men.' The KJV says 'bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave' three times and only ever of Jacob; the Book of Mormon drops the gray hairs and adds 'grief', keeping the verb and the prepositional phrase. Note what the same sentence then does: 'be men' answers 1 Kings 2:2's 'shew thyself a man', so a Jacob clause and a David clause stand in one sentence, which is what the whole chapter has been doing since verse 14.

pericopes.text: that ye may not be cursed with a sore cursing; and also, that ye may not incur the displeasure of a just God upon you, unto the destruction, yea, the eternal destruction of both soul and body.

links.text: And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

provenance.other: 'Both soul and body' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 10:18 and Matthew 10:28. Only Matthew makes it the object of destruction. 'A just God' is itself a KJV singleton, at Isaiah 45:21, 'a just God and a Saviour'.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 10:18 has the phrase and this book transcribes that verse at 2 Nephi 20:18, so a reader might reasonably look there first.
provenance.significance: The mediation is decided by one word and it is worth stating plainly. Both KJV verses that contain 'both soul and body' were available to this book, and one of them, Isaiah 10:18, is transcribed inside 2 Nephi itself at 20:18. But in Isaiah the phrase is a simile for the consuming of a forest and carries no threat of judgment on a person; in Matthew it is the thing God is able to do in hell, and it is set against what men can do, which is kill the body only. 2 Nephi 1:22 has 'unto the destruction, yea, the eternal destruction of both soul and body' — destruction, eternity, and both nouns as its object. That is Matthew's sentence and not Isaiah's, in a book that demonstrably had Isaiah's in front of it. tools/mediation-check.py declines the case because the two verses do not diverge at a point the Book of Mormon reproduces verbatim; the decision is made on which verse's predicate survives.

links.note: 'That ye may not incur the displeasure of a just God upon you, unto the destruction, yea, the eternal destruction of both soul and body.' Two KJV verses have the phrase and this one takes the New Testament's, on the evidence of the predicate: Matthew's God is 'able to destroy both soul and body in hell', Isaiah's fire merely consumes a forest 'both soul and body' as a figure. 'A just God' in the same sentence is a second KJV singleton, from Isaiah 45:21, where the point is that a just God is also a Saviour — the half Lehi does not quote.

pericopes.text: Awake, my sons; put on the armor of righteousness. Shake off the chains with which ye are bound, and come forth out of obscurity, and arise from the dust.

links.text: The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.

provenance.other: 'Awake out of sleep' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 13:11, and 'put on the armour' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 13:12 — consecutive verses, and the only place in the KJV where the two imperatives stand in that order. 'Works of darkness', the middle term Lehi replaces with chains, occurs in exactly two.
provenance.significance: The sequence is the finding. Romans 13:11-12 runs awake out of sleep, then cast off the works of darkness, then put on the armour; 2 Nephi 1 runs awake from a deep sleep (1:13), then shake off the chains (1:13 and again here), then put on the armour (1:23). Three steps, same order, ten verses apart, and each of the two outer steps is a KJV singleton in Romans. Paul's reason for the sequence is eschatological — the night is far spent — and Lehi's is that he is dying, which is the same argument scaled to one man. What the Book of Mormon substitutes is the middle term: Paul casts off works, Lehi shakes off chains, and the chains are Isaiah 52:2's bands, which is how the Isaiah refrain and the Romans sequence end up sharing a single sentence.

links.note: 'Awake, my sons; put on the armor of righteousness. Shake off the chains with which ye are bound, and come forth out of obscurity, and arise from the dust.' Two KJV singletons from consecutive verses of Romans 13, deployed in Romans' own order across this chapter. Note the 1830 spelling 'armor', which is American and not the KJV's 'armour' — the first edition here modernizes rather than preserving the source's orthography, which is the reverse of the usual case (CONVENTIONS §8) and means the borrowing is slightly less visible in every edition of the Book of Mormon than it is in the King James Bible.

links.text: By the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left,

provenance.other: 'Armour of righteousness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Romans 13:12 has 'the armour of light' and Ephesians 6:11 'the whole armour of God'; neither is the phrase used here.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has taken the imperative from Romans 13:12 and the genitive from 2 Corinthians 6:7, which are the KJV's two armour verses outside Ephesians, and fused them into a phrase that is in neither. What 2 Corinthians 6:7 supplies with the word is its setting: Paul is listing the credentials by which he commends himself as a minister — 'by the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness' — and three verses of this chapter later Lehi will defend Nephi's ministry in the same terms, 'the sharpness of the power of the word of God, which was in him' (1:26). Two of Paul's three phrases, from the same clause, turn up in Lehi's defence of his son.

links.note: 'Put on the armor of righteousness.' A KJV singleton supplies the noun phrase and Romans 13:12 supplies the verb; the composite is recorded as two rows because each half is separately a singleton and each carries its own context. The reason to keep 2 Corinthians 6:7 rather than fold it into the Romans row is 1:26, where the word of truth and the power of God from the same verse of 2 Corinthians reappear together.

links.text: And in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness.

provenance.other: 'Obscurity' occurs in exactly three KJV verses and all three are Isaiah: 29:18, 58:10, 59:9. Only 29:18 has anything coming out of obscurity.
provenance.alternative: 'Come forth out of obscurity' may be Lehi's own phrase; the word is rare in the KJV but not distinctive of any one of its three verses beyond the preposition.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:18 is the verse in which the deaf hear the words of the book and the blind see out of obscurity, and 2 Nephi 27 will expand that whole chapter into the book's central prophecy about its own coming forth — the sealed book, the words of the book delivered to one who is not learned. 2 Nephi 27:29 renders 29:18 directly. So when Lehi tells his sons to come forth out of obscurity, he is using, twenty-six chapters early, a word that the book will later claim for the emergence of the book itself.

links.note: 'Come forth out of obscurity, and arise from the dust.' The KJV uses 'obscurity' three times, all in Isaiah, and only 29:18 has sight coming out of it. Recorded as an echo because a single rare word in a different construction is all the contact there is; kept because of where the word goes later in this same book. The clause it stands in is Isaiah 52:2's, so the verse fuses two Isaiah passages the book will transcribe at 2 Nephi 8 and 2 Nephi 27 respectively.

pericopes.text: Rebel no more against your brother, whose views have been glorious, and who hath kept the commandments from the time that we left Jerusalem, and who hath been an instrument in the hands of God, in bringing us forth into the land of promise: for were it not for him, we must have perished with hunger in the wilderness; nevertheless, ye sought to take away his life; yea, and he hath suffered much sorrow because of you.

links.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!

provenance.other: 'Perish with hunger' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:17. The KJV's other famine language is 'die by famine', 'consumed by the famine', 'famished'.
provenance.alternative: Starving in a wilderness needs no source, and the phrase is short.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one 'perish with hunger' is the sentence in which the prodigal son comes to himself, and everything about its transposition is an inversion. In Luke the words are spoken by the younger son who took his portion and wasted it and who now returns to a father who will restore him over the elder brother's protest. Here they are spoken by the father, about the elder brothers, and what saves them from perishing is the younger son — the one whose birthright the elder brothers are about to lose to him four verses later. Luke's parable is the KJV's one story about which son gets the father's blessing at the end, which is the question 2 Nephi 1:28-29 exists to settle.

links.note: 'Were it not for him, we must have perished with hunger in the wilderness.' A three-word KJV singleton, and the case rests entirely on its rarity plus where it comes from. Held at moderate because the phrase is short and the situation is one a writer could describe in those words without a source; the reason for keeping it is that the chapter's business in the next five verses is a contested inheritance between an elder son and a younger, which is the parable's business too.

pericopes.text: And I exceedingly fear and tremble because of you, lest he shall suffer again: for behold, ye have accused him that he sought power and authority over you; but I know that he hath not sought for power nor authority over you; but he hath sought the glory of God, and your own eternal welfare.

And ye have murmured because he hath been plain unto you. Ye say that he hath used sharpness; ye say that he hath been angry with you. But behold, his sharpness was the sharpness of the power of the word of God, which was in him; and that which ye call anger, was the truth, according to that which is in God, which he could not constrain, manifesting boldly concerning your iniquities.

links.text: Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction.

provenance.other: 'Sharpness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse: 'lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction' (2 Corinthians 13:10). The Book of Mormon has the noun, the verb 'used', and the word 'power' in the same relation to it.
provenance.significance: The whole of Lehi's defence of Nephi is 2 Corinthians 13 in narrative. Paul's closing chapter is a defence of his own severity to a congregation that has accused him of being bold only at a distance: he writes sharply, he says, so that he need not use sharpness in person, and the sharpness is authorized by 'the power which the Lord hath given me'. Lehi's sons accuse Nephi of sharpness and of seeking power and authority; Lehi answers that the sharpness was 'the sharpness of the power of the word of God, which was in him', which is Paul's defence with Paul's two nouns. And the verse after Paul's is 'Finally, brethren, farewell … be of one mind', which 2 Nephi 1:21 has already used — 'be determined in one mind' — five verses earlier. Two consecutive verses of Paul's own valediction supply two clauses of Lehi's.

links.note: 'Ye say that he hath used sharpness … but behold, his sharpness was the sharpness of the power of the word of God, which was in him.' The KJV uses the word 'sharpness' once, and in that one place it is coupled to power and to a minister's authority to be severe — which is precisely the coupling the Book of Mormon makes and precisely the accusation Lehi is rebutting. This is as close to a certain link as an unquoted three-word contact gets; it is held at high rather than certain only because the noun is a natural English word for the thing being described. Note also that 2 Corinthians 6:7's 'word of truth … power of God … armour of righteousness' stands behind 1:23 and the phrase 'the power of the word of God' here.

pericopes.text: And it must needs be that the power of God must be with him, even unto his commanding you, that ye must obey. But behold, it was not him, but it was the spirit of the Lord which was in him, which opened his mouth to utterance, that he could not shut it.

links.text: And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel,

provenance.other: 'Open my mouth boldly' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 6:19; 'utterance' occurs in exactly five KJV verses, of which Ephesians 6:19 is the one that pairs it with an opened mouth. 'No man can shut it' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 3:8.
provenance.alternative: 'Opened his mouth' is common KJV narration, and 'utterance' could come from Acts 2:4, where the Spirit gives it — which is arguably closer to the theology of this verse than Ephesians is.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 6 supplies both ends of Lehi's defence of Nephi and it does so from the two halves of one paragraph. The armour of verse 23 is Ephesians 6:11-17's figure, even though the exact genitive came from 2 Corinthians 6:7; and the utterance of verse 27 is Ephesians 6:19-20, the request that closes the armour passage — 'that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly … that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.' Lehi's word for what his sons resented, at 1:26, is 'manifesting boldly'. So the chapter has put on Paul's armour and then asked for Paul's boldness of speech, in the source's own order, and has attributed both to the Spirit rather than to the man — which is the point Lehi needs to make to sons who have accused Nephi of seeking power for himself.

links.note: 'It was the spirit of the Lord which was in him, which opened his mouth to utterance, that he could not shut it.' Read against Ephesians 6:19: an opened mouth, an utterance given rather than possessed, and boldness — which is the word this speech uses one verse earlier. The closing clause is a second rare phrase, Revelation 3:8's 'no man can shut it', turned from a door into a mouth. Held at moderate because 'utterance' has five KJV homes and Acts 2:4's is a live alternative; the reason for preferring Ephesians is 1:23, where the same paragraph of Ephesians has already been in view.

pericopes.text: And now my son Laman, and also Lemuel and Sam, and also my sons which are the sons of Ishmael, behold, if ye will hearken unto the voice of Nephi, ye shall not perish. And if ye will hearken unto him, I leave unto you a blessing, yea, even my first blessing.
But if ye will not hearken unto him, I take away my first blessing, yea, even my blessing, and it shall rest upon him.

links.text: And he said, Is not he rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times: he took away my birthright; and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing. And he said, Hast thou not reserved a blessing for me?

provenance.other: 'Taken away my blessing' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 27:36 — Esau's protest that Jacob 'took away my birthright; and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing'. Genesis 49:3-4 is the other transfer, Reuben the firstborn told 'thou shalt not excel'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's family plot stated in its source's words, and the assignment of the words is the finding. In Genesis 27:36 it is the wronged elder brother who says a blessing has been taken away; in 2 Nephi 1:29 it is the father who says it, and he says it in advance, as a condition. That single change converts a theft into a judicial act — what Rebekah and Jacob accomplish by deceit at Isaac's bedside, Lehi announces openly from his own. The book has used Genesis 27 before, at 1 Nephi 4:21, where Nephi obtains the plates by wearing another man's clothes and answering to his name; a reader who holds both passages together sees the younger brother acquire the record by Jacob's method and then receive the blessing by Jacob's inheritance, with the father's consent supplied the second time.

links.note: 'If ye will not hearken unto him, I take away my first blessing, yea, even my blessing, and it shall rest upon him.' The KJV states the taking away of a blessing once, in Esau's mouth. Lehi transposes it into the first person of the man who gives the blessing and adds the birthright's technical term — 'my first blessing' — which pairs with Genesis 27:36's other clause, 'he took away my birthright'. Both halves of Esau's complaint are therefore present, redistributed. Genesis 49:3-4, Jacob demoting Reuben on his own deathbed, is the composite that supplies the setting.

pericopes.text: And now, Zoram, I speak unto you: Behold, thou art the servant of Laban; nevertheless, thou hast been brought out of the land of Jerusalem, and I know that thou art a true friend unto my son, Nephi, forever.

Wherefore, because thou hast been faithful, thy seed shall be blessed with his seed, that they dwell in prosperity long upon the face of this land; and nothing, save it shall be iniquity among them, shall harm or disturb their prosperity upon the face of this land forever.—
Wherefore, if ye shall keep the commandments of the Lord, the Lord hath consecrated this land for the security of thy seed with the seed of my son.

And now, Jacob, I speak unto you: Thou art my first born in the days of my tribulation in the wilderness. And behold, in thy childhood, thou hast suffered afflictions and much sorrow, because of the rudeness of thy brethren.
Nevertheles, Jacob, my first born in the wilderness, thou knowest the greatness of God; and he shall consecrate thine afflictions for thy gain.

Wherefore, thy soul shall be blessed, and thou shalt dwell safely with thy brother, Nephi; and thy days shall be spent in the service of thy God.—Wherefore, I know that thou art redeemed, because of the righteousness of thy Redeemer: for thou hast beheld, that in the fulness of time, he cometh to bring salvation unto men.

links.text: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,

provenance.other: Ephesians 1:10 is the only other KJV verse with the idiom, in the plural (“the fulness of times”). The Book of Mormon form recurs at 2 Nephi 2:26, adjudicated here at first use per ADJUDICATING §4.
provenance.significance: Recover Galatians 4:4's context and the borrowing acquires the next three verses of this chapter. Paul's sentence does not stop at the Son's coming: he is “made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.” Lehi's next two verses are the law's failure to justify (v. 5) and redemption through the Messiah (v. 6), and the whole discourse is addressed to a son. The phrase carries its own sequel into the chapter.

links.note: Lehi tells Jacob he has beheld that “in the fulness of time, he cometh to bring salvation unto men.” “The fulness of the time” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 4:4, and the only other place the idiom appears at all is Ephesians 1:10's “the dispensation of the fulness of times.” The Book of Mormon's “the fulness of time” matches neither exactly — it drops Galatians' second article and keeps its singular against Ephesians' plural — which is what a remembered phrase looks like rather than a copied one. What settles it is that Galatians' clause and Lehi's do the same work: both name the arrival of the Son as the moment redemption becomes available, and both immediately turn to the law.

pericopes.text: And thou hast beheld in thy youth, his glory; wherefore, thou art blessed even as they unto whom he shall minister in the flesh: for the spirit is the same, yesterday, to-day, and forever. And the way is prepared from the fall of man, and salvation is free.

links.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

provenance.other: 1830 “to-day” → 1920 “today”; 1830 “spirit” → current “Spirit”.
provenance.significance: Hebrews predicates the sameness of Jesus Christ; Lehi predicates it of the spirit, and uses it to license something Hebrews does not — access across a dispensation. Jacob is “blessed even as they unto whom he shall minister in the flesh” because what is the same yesterday and to-day cannot prefer one century to another. That is an argument from Hebrews 13:8 to a conclusion Hebrews never draws, and it is the load-bearing premise for a book in which people six hundred years early see Christ.

links.note: “The same yesterday” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Lehi reproduces the predicate whole — “the spirit is the same, yesterday, to-day, and forever” — dropping only the conjunction before “to-day.” It falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six, but a five-word run from a KJV singleton is not a coincidence of ordinary English. The 1830 reading is evidence twice over: it hyphenates “to-day,” which stands nearer the KJV's two-word “to day” than the modern text's “today,” and it sets “spirit” in lower case where the current edition capitalises it. Lower case makes the sentence a claim about the manner of Christ's ministering; upper case makes it a claim about the Holy Ghost. The first edition shows the borrowing, and the borrowed sentence in Hebrews is about Christ.

pericopes.text: And men are instructed sufficiently, that they know good from evil. And the law is given unto men. And by the law, no flesh is justified; or, by the law, men are cut off. Yea, by the temporal law, they were cut off; and also, by the spiritual law, they perish from that which is good, and become miserable forever.

links.text: Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.

provenance.mt: Psalm 143:2, “in thy sight shall no man living be justified” — “no man living be justified” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Galatians 2:16, the only other KJV verse with “no flesh be justified”; it lacks Romans' second clause.
provenance.significance: Romans 3:20b, “for by the law is the knowledge of sin,” is the sentence 2 Nephi 2:13 turns into a conditional: “if ye shall say there is no law, ye shall also say there is no sin.” Lehi takes Paul's two clauses and makes them the two ends of his discourse — the first at v. 5, the second inverted into a reductio eight verses later. Recovering the source verse whole is what shows that vv. 5 and 13 are one argument.

links.note: “No flesh be justified” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16, and both are Paul rewriting Psalm 143:2. tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive result: the Psalm reads “no man living be justified” and the New Testament reads “no flesh,” and Lehi has “no flesh.” The Old Testament verse behind this sentence reaches the Book of Mormon in its Pauline dress, not its own. Between the two Pauline forms, Romans is the better fit — Lehi writes bare “by the law,” which is Romans 3:20's second clause, not Galatians' “by the works of the law” — and Romans 3:20 alone supplies both halves of what Lehi goes on to argue.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, redemption cometh in and through the Holy Messiah: for he is full of grace and truth.

links.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

provenance.other: The chapter quarries the Johannine prologue at both ends: John 1:14 here, and John 1:13's “the will of the flesh” — itself a KJV singleton — at v. 29. Two consecutive verses of John, twenty-three verses apart in Lehi.
provenance.significance: John predicates the phrase of the Word made flesh and dwelt among us; Lehi predicates it of the Holy Messiah through whom “redemption cometh in and through.” The suppressed correspondence is the incarnation itself — John's grace and truth are full in a body, and Lehi's next sentence is that the Messiah “offereth himself a sacrifice.” The verse he takes the words from is the verse that makes the sacrifice possible.

links.note: “Full of grace and truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Five words reproduced without change from a singleton, applied to the same person the singleton applies them to. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: Behold, he offereth himself a sacrifice for sin, to answer the ends of the law, unto all those which have a broken heart and a contrite spirit; and unto none else can the ends of the law be answered.

links.text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

provenance.other: “Contrite spirit” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 66:2. Only Psalm 34:18 has both halves of Lehi's phrase, and only in the KJV's English — the noun assignment that makes the identification possible is a translator's choice, not the Hebrew's.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 51:17, excluded at this verse as better-source-identified.
provenance.significance: Psalm 34:18 is a promise about proximity: the LORD is *nigh unto* the broken-hearted. Lehi is arguing the opposite direction — that no flesh can dwell in God's presence except through the Messiah (v. 8) — and he grounds the exception on the one verse in the KJV where God comes near to precisely the people he has just named. The atonement in v. 7 answers the ends of the law for those to whom, in the source verse, God was already close.

links.note: The received identification of “a broken heart and a contrite spirit” is Psalm 51:17, and it is wrong on the KJV's own words. “Broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is Psalm 34:18 — which also contains “contrite spirit,” in that order, on either side of a clause boundary. Psalm 51:17 has “a broken spirit” and “a broken and a contrite heart”: the right adjectives attached to the wrong nouns. Lehi's pairing is Psalm 34:18's exactly, and it is invisible to a contiguous n-gram window by construction (CONVENTIONS §9), which is why the machine proposed nothing here.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, how great the importance to make these things known unto the inhabitants of the earth, that they may know that there is no flesh that can dwell in the presence of God, save it be through the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah, which layeth down his life according to the flesh, and taketh it again by the power of the spirit, that he may bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, being the first that should rise.

links.text: That Christ should suffer, and that he should be the first that should rise from the dead, and should shew light unto the people, and to the Gentiles.

provenance.significance: Recover the setting and the borrowing becomes an argument about Lehi's own position. Acts 26:23 is Paul before Agrippa, saying that he preaches “none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come” — that Christ should suffer and be the first that should rise. Paul's claim is that a pre-Christian prophet could have said this; Lehi is a pre-Christian prophet saying it, in Paul's words. The catalogue can only note the circularity: the verse that licenses the anachronism is the verse the anachronism borrows from.

links.note: “The first that should rise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Lehi reproduces it whole and stops where the source's next words are “from the dead,” which his own clause has already supplied as “the resurrection of the dead.” The n-gram stream ranked this verse first for 2:8 and was right, which is not the usual outcome.

links.text: No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment have I received of my Father.

provenance.other: The flesh/spirit antithesis Lehi builds around John's verbs is not John's; it is Romans 1:3-4's “according to the flesh … according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead.” The sentence fuses a Johannine saying with a Pauline frame.
provenance.significance: John's point in 10:18 is that no man takes Christ's life from him. Lehi's whole sentence is about what no flesh can do — dwell in God's presence — and he answers it with the one thing Christ can do that no man can do to him. The two impossibilities are made to answer each other, which neither text does alone.

links.note: “Layeth down his life according to the flesh, and taketh it again by the power of the spirit.” “Power to lay it down” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “take it again” in exactly two, John 10:17 and 10:18, both of the same saying. Lehi has all three of its elements — laying down, taking again, and the power by which it is done — in John's order.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, he is the first fruits unto God, inasmuch as he shall make intercession for all the children of men; and they that believe in him, shall be saved.

links.text: These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. These were redeemed from among men, being the firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb.

provenance.other: 1830 “first fruits” → 1920 “firstfruits”. “First fruits unto God” as two words occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:4 calls the hundred and forty and four thousand the firstfruits, redeemed from among men. Lehi transfers the title to the one who redeems them, and does it in the next breath after saying he is “the first that should rise.” Recovering the source inverts the referent: in Revelation the firstfruits are the saved, in Lehi they are the saviour, and the phrase carries the crowd of the redeemed silently along with it into a verse about intercession “for all the children of men.”

links.note: “Firstfruits unto God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The doctrine Lehi is stating — Christ the firstfruits of the resurrection — is 1 Corinthians 15:20-23's, but 1 Corinthians never writes the phrase this way; Revelation does, once. So the argument comes from one book and the words from another. The 1830 reading is the evidence for the borrowing being verbal at all: it prints “first fruits” as two words, and 1920 closed it to “firstfruits,” which is the KJV's own form — a later edition moving the text toward its source (CONVENTIONS §8).

links.text: Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 53:12, “and made intercession for the transgressors”.
provenance.other: The two other KJV verses with “make intercession”, Jeremiah 7:16 and 27:18, both read “make intercession *to*” and mean praying to God rather than for men — the opposed sense.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 7:25 grounds the intercession in Christ's not dying: he ever liveth, therefore he ever intercedes. Lehi has just made him “the first that should rise” and “the first fruits unto God”; the suppressed premise that lets v. 9 follow v. 8 is exactly Hebrews' — the resurrection is what makes the intercession permanent.

links.note: “Make intercession for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Old Testament locus for a redeemer's intercession is Isaiah 53:12, but it reads “made intercession for the transgressors” — past tense, of a completed act — while Lehi has “shall make intercession,” which is Hebrews' continuous form and Hebrews' whole point (“he ever liveth to make intercession”). tools/mediation-check.py found no decisive divergence between Isaiah 53:12 and Hebrews 7:25 at any point Lehi reproduces, because it ignores single common words; the verb form is the discrimination, and it is caught by eye, so the mediation call here is weaker than the one at v. 5.
links.whyNot: The mediation-check tool returns no decisive divergence here, and the case for Hebrews over Isaiah 53:12 rests on a single verb form (“make” against “made”) that the tool is built to ignore. A reader who thinks Lehi is simply generalising Isaiah's servant would not be refuted by anything in this verse.

pericopes.text: And because of the intercession for all, all men cometh unto God; wherefore, they stand in the presence of Him, to be judged of Him, according to the truth and holiness which is in Him. Wherefore, the ends of the law which the Holy One hath given, unto the inflicting of the punishment which is affixed, which punishment that is affixed is in opposition to that of the happiness which is affixed, to answer the ends of the atonement;

for it must needs be, that there is an opposition in all things. If not so, my first born in the wilderness, righteousness could not be brought to pass; neither wickedness; neither holiness nor misery; neither good nor bad. Wherefore, all things must needs be a compound in one; wherefore, if it should be one body, it must neeeds remain as dead, having no life, neither death nor corruption, nor incorruption, happiness nor misery, neither sense nor insensibility.

Wherefore, it must needs have been created for a thing of nought; wherefore, there would have been no purpose in the end of its creation. Wherefore, this thing must needs destroy the wisdom of God, and his eternal purposes; and also, the power, and the mercy, and the justice of God.

And if ye shall say there is no law, ye shall also say there is no sin. If ye shall say there is no sin, ye shall also say there is no righteousness.— And if there be no righteousness, there be no happiness. And if there be no righteousness nor happiness, there be no punishment nor misery. And if these things are not, there is no God. And if there is no God, we are not, neither the earth: for there could have been no creation of things, neither to act nor to be acted upon; wherefore, all things must have vanished away.

links.text: But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen:

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 15:13-19 → KJV → Book of Mormon (form, not wording)
provenance.other: Romans 3:20's second clause, “by the law is the knowledge of sin,” supplies the chain's first link and is catalogued at v. 5.
provenance.significance: Paul's reductio defends one doctrine by showing that its denial takes everything else down with it. Lehi runs the identical machine on the denial of law, and gets a conclusion Paul never draws — not that preaching is vain but that nothing exists. Read the two together and the Book of Mormon's argument for agency turns out to be built on the shape of Paul's argument for the resurrection, which is also the doctrine Lehi has just asserted in vv. 8-9. The form is borrowed from the passage whose content he has already used.

links.note: Verse 13 is a sorites: seven conditionals chained head to tail — no law, no sin; no sin, no righteousness; no righteousness, no happiness; and so down to “we are not, neither the earth.” The KJV has one passage of that shape, 1 Corinthians 15:13-19, where Paul runs the same figure from the same kind of premise (“if there be no resurrection of the dead”) through the same escalating consequences to the same terminal absurdity, and lands on the word Lehi's chain also lands on: Paul's “we are of all men most miserable,” Lehi's “no punishment nor misery.” The verbal contact is almost nil and the structural contact is exact, which is what the figural type is for.
links.whyNot: No clause and no distinctive phrase is shared; the case is entirely one of argumentative form, and reductio by chained conditionals is not a figure the KJV invented. A reader could hold that Lehi arrived at it independently and lose nothing.

pericopes.text: And now, my sons, I speak unto you these things, for your profit and learning: for there is a God, and he hath created all things, both the heavens and the earth, and all things that in them is; both things to act, and things to be acted upon;

links.text: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.

provenance.route: Exodus 20:11 or Acts 4:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 1830 “all things that in them is” → 1920 “are”.
provenance.alternative: Acts 4:24 reproduces Exodus 20:11's clause verbatim; tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence at any point Lehi reproduces, so this verse cannot settle its own mediation and the field is recorded as uncertain rather than guessed (CONVENTIONS §7).
provenance.significance: Exodus 20:11 is the sabbath commandment's reason clause — God made all that in them is, and rested. Lehi uses it to establish that God “hath created all things” in order to divide those things into “things to act, and things to be acted upon,” which is a distinction the source text does not contain and which the whole doctrine of agency in this chapter rests on. The creation formula is being made to carry a metaphysics.

links.note: “All that in them is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24, which is a creation formula and its New Testament citation. The 1830 text is what makes this a link rather than a coincidence: it reads “all things that in them **is**,” preserving the KJV's singular verb after a plural subject — a concord no one writes by accident in 1830 — and 1920 corrected it to “are.” The borrowing is plain in the first edition and invisible in the modern one, which is the 1 Nephi 1:20 pattern running the other way (CONVENTIONS §8). The “all things that” Lehi adds is Nehemiah 9:6's, from the same family of creation doxologies.

links.text: For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.

provenance.significance: Romans 15:4 is the verse that authorises reading old scripture as addressed to oneself. Lehi applies it in the opposite direction — not to a reader receiving what was written aforetime, but to a writer producing what will be read afterward — and the chapter he is writing is one that quotes, by this catalogue's count, from Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah, John, Romans, Galatians, Hebrews, Luke and Revelation. The verse about scripture's afterlife is being used at the moment scripture is being made.

links.note: “For our learning” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; Lehi writes “for your profit and learning,” which is that phrase with the pronoun turned outward and “profit” added. The phrase “profit and learning” occurs in no KJV verse. What supports the echo is not the two words but their office: Romans 15:4 is a statement about why written scripture is preserved for later readers, and Lehi is a writer telling his sons why he is telling them this, three verses before he says he speaks “according to the things which I have read … according to that which is written.”
links.whyNot: Two words, one of them added. “Learning” in this construction is ordinary enough English that a reader could decline the echo without straining, and 1 Corinthians 10:11 (“written for our admonition”) is the same idea in different words.

pericopes.text: and to bring about his eternal purposes in the end of man, after that he had created our first parents, and the beasts of the field, and the fowls of the air, and in fine, all things which are created, it must needs be that there was an opposition; even the forbidden fruit in opposition to the tree of life; the one being sweet and the other bitter;

links.text: And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.

provenance.other: “Beasts of the field, and the fowls of the air” in the plural occurs in no KJV verse. Daniel 2:38 has the plural pairing but reads “fowls of the heaven”, and is excluded at this verse.
provenance.significance: Everything Lehi's Eden is made of comes from Genesis 2 and 3, never from Genesis 1: the beasts of the field and fowls of the air from 2:19, the tree of life from 2:9, the serpent's words from 3:4-5, the expulsion from 3:23-24. That is the J account, not the P account — the garden narrative rather than the six days — and it is the account in which a command is given, broken, and punished. A chapter arguing that opposition must exist could not have been built on Genesis 1, where nothing is forbidden.

links.note: “Beast of the field, and every fowl of the air” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is not in Genesis 1. This is worth stating flatly, because it is the chapter's cleanest test of which creation account Lehi is working from: Genesis 1 pairs “fowl of the air” with “beast of the earth” (1:30) and “beast of the earth after his kind” (1:25), and never with “beast of the field.” Genesis 2:19 is the only verse in the Bible that pairs the two Lehi pairs, and it is a creation verse — God forms them out of the ground and brings them to Adam. Lehi's plural (“the beasts … the fowls”) occurs in no KJV verse; he has generalised the source's distributive singulars.

links.text: And out of the ground made the LORD God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.

provenance.other: “Forbidden fruit” occurs in no KJV verse. It is one of two phrases in this chapter's Eden and demonology that have no scriptural warrant at all; the other is “the father of all lies” at v. 18.
provenance.significance: Lehi's opposition is “the forbidden fruit in opposition to the tree of life” — but in Genesis 2:9 the two trees in the midst of the garden are the tree of life and the tree of *knowledge of good and evil*, and it is knowledge, not prohibition, that names the second one. Substituting “forbidden” for “knowledge of good and evil” moves the antithesis from what the tree gives to what the law says about it, which is precisely the move the chapter needs: v. 5's law, v. 13's “if ye shall say there is no law.” The unscriptural adjective is doing the argument's work.

links.note: “The tree of life” occurs in exactly six KJV verses and cannot identify a source on its own, but the frame decides it: Lehi is naming what God created in Eden, and Genesis 2:9 is the verse that plants it there. The interesting half of this verse is the other term of Lehi's antithesis. “Forbidden fruit” occurs in no KJV verse — none. The KJV's serpent speaks of “the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden” (Genesis 3:3) and God of “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (2:17); the adjective “forbidden” is nowhere applied to it.
