The psalm of Nephi answers Lamentations 3 in Lamentations 3's own grammar — and then at 4:33 it goes back for the one clause it has not yet used, “he hath hedged me about, that I cannot get out” (3:7), and turns it into a petition: “hedge not up my way, but the ways of mine enemy.” This is the chapter's largest single borrowing and no word of it is more than four words long.

links.note: “My God hath been my support; he hath led me through mine afflictions in the wilderness.” The opening formula is a KJV singleton and its source is the great lament, where the same words mean the opposite — “He hath led me, and brought me into darkness, but not into light.” The following five verses continue the anaphora, and each turns the affliction into mercy. Recorded at 4:20 as the first instance of a structural borrowing that runs to 4:25 and returns at 4:33; the individual verses are registered in recurrenceRefs rather than given rows of their own, except 4:21, where the second KJV singleton makes an independent case.

links.text: Art thou not it which hath dried the sea, the waters of the great deep; that hath made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over?

provenance.other: “The waters of the great deep” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 51:10.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 51:10 asks whether it was not the arm of the LORD that dried the sea and made the depths a way for the ransomed to pass over — an Exodus verse used to argue that the ransomed will come again. Nephi, who crossed an ocean, claims it as autobiography: the waters of the great deep are not a figure for him. And the chapter he is quoting is one he will transcribe entire four chapters later, at 2 Nephi 8:10. The catalogue can therefore watch the same verse enter the book twice — once as Nephi's own words about his own voyage, and once as Isaiah's, quoted as Isaiah's.

links.note: “He hath preserved me upon the waters of the great deep.” The phrase is a KJV singleton and the source is Isaiah 51, which 2 Nephi 8 transcribes in full; recurrenceRefs points there. The borrowing is not a repetition of the transcription — it comes first in the book — but the reverse: Nephi speaks in Isaiah's words before he sets down Isaiah's chapter, which is what a writer does with a text he has by heart rather than one he is copying.

pericopes.text: He hath filled me with his love, even unto the consuming of my flesh.

links.text: He hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood.

provenance.other: “He hath filled me with” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 3:15, where the object is bitterness.
provenance.significance: The substitution is a single word and it reverses the passage: he hath filled me with bitterness becomes he hath filled me with his love. And the consequence Nephi draws — “even unto the consuming of my flesh” — is Lamentations 3:4's, “my flesh and my skin hath he made old”. The love does to Nephi's body what the wrath did to the poet's. That is not a softening of Lamentations; it is a claim that the same experience, physically, can be read either way, which is precisely the argument 4:26-29 goes on to have with itself.

links.note: “He hath filled me with his love, even unto the consuming of my flesh.” The formula is a KJV singleton with one word changed, and the change is from bitterness to love. Given a row of its own rather than folded into the Lamentations 3 structural link at 4:20 because the singleton makes it independently demonstrable, and because the wasting of the flesh in the second clause reaches back to a different verse of the same passage.

pericopes.text: He hath confounded mine enemies, unto the causing of them to quake before me.
Behold, he hath heard my cry by day, and he hath given me knowledge by visions in the night time.

links.text: I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry.

provenance.other: “Heard my cry” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 40:1. The night half of Nephi's antithesis is closer to Job 4:13 and Genesis 46:2, where “visions of the night” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses; Nephi has “visions in the night time”, and “in the night time” occurs in exactly 0.
provenance.significance: Nephi's antithesis is day and night, cry and vision: heard my cry by day, gave me knowledge by visions in the night. The KJV's own day-and-night lament is Psalm 22:2 — “O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent” — where both halves fail. Nephi's verse is that structure with both halves answered. Whether or not Psalm 22 is in view, Psalm 40:1's “he inclined unto me, and heard my cry” is the KJV's one sentence for a cry that got through, and it is the sentence Nephi has.

links.note: “He hath heard my cry by day, and he hath given me knowledge by visions in the night time.” Recorded on the strength of the singleton alone, and kept at echo because the rest of the verse has no KJV wording behind it — the night clause is Nephi's own, formed on the KJV's “visions of the night” but not reproducing it. The verse belongs to the “He hath” sequence begun at 4:20 out of Lamentations 3, so what is borrowed here is a psalm's answer set inside a lament's grammar.

pericopes.text: And by day have I waxed bold in mighty prayer before him; yea, my voice have I sent upon high; and angels came down and ministered unto me.

links.text: Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.

provenance.other: “Angels came and ministered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 4:11; Mark 1:13's parallel reads “the angels ministered unto him”, without the verb of arrival. “Waxed bold” in the first clause occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:46.
provenance.significance: Matthew 4:11 is the last verse of the temptation: “Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.” The next verse of Nephi's psalm takes the exceeding high mountain from Matthew 4:8, and four verses later he asks why he should “give way to temptations, that the evil one have place in my heart” (4:27). The psalm of Nephi describes its author's spiritual life in the vocabulary of Christ's temptation in the wilderness — the mountain, the tempter, the ministering angels — and does so in reverse order, taking the consolation first and the mountain second, which is how a man remembers a trial he has survived rather than how an evangelist narrates one.

links.note: “And by day have I waxed bold in mighty prayer before him; yea, my voice have I sent upon high; and angels came down and ministered unto me.” Two KJV singletons in one sentence. “Waxed bold” is Paul and Barnabas turning to the Gentiles; “angels came and ministered” is the end of the temptation narrative, with “down” inserted and “him” made “me”. Note that the 1830 “sent upon high” was repunctuated to “sent up on high” in 1920 — the first edition's reading is the harder one and the modern text has smoothed it.

pericopes.text: And upon the wings of his spirit hath my body been carried away upon exceeding high mountains. And mine eyes hath beheld great things; yea, even too great for man; therefore I was bidden that I should not write them.

links.text: Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them;

provenance.other: “Exceeding high mountain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 4:8. “Carried me away in the spirit” occurs in exactly 2, Revelation 17:3 and 21:10, both of them John being taken to see something. Nephi's sentence fuses the two: carried away in the spirit, to an exceeding high mountain.
provenance.significance: The two sources pull in opposite directions and the verse holds both. In Matthew the exceeding high mountain is where the devil takes Jesus to show him the kingdoms of the world; in Revelation the spirit carries John to a great and high mountain to show him the holy city. Nephi's own mountain vision at 1 Nephi 11 was a revelation, so the Revelation sense governs — but the phrase he reaches for is Matthew's, from the temptation whose ministering angels he has just borrowed in the previous verse. The result is a mountain that is simultaneously the tempter's and the angel's, in a psalm whose subject is exactly that ambiguity.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 40:2, “brought me … and set me upon a very high mountain”, is the OT analogue and could stand behind the vision-taking; it lacks the KJV's “exceeding”.

links.note: “Upon the wings of his spirit hath my body been carried away upon exceeding high mountains.” The mountain phrase is a KJV singleton from Matthew 4:8, the being-carried phrase belongs to Revelation's two verses, and the wings are the Psalter's (“the wings of the wind”, three KJV verses). Note the 1830 “mine eyes hath beheld”, a plural subject with a singular verb, corrected to “have” in 1920 — the kind of KJV-adjacent grammar the first edition preserves and later editions tidy.

links.text: How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.

provenance.other: “Not lawful for a man to utter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:4. Nephi does not reproduce the clause; he reproduces its content — “too great for man; therefore I was bidden that I should not write them”.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 12:2-4 is the KJV's one first-person account of being taken up and forbidden to report it, and it is also the KJV's one passage that worries about the body during such a taking: “whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell.” Nephi settles that question in the affirmative and in the same breath — “hath MY BODY been carried away” — and then, like Paul, declines to say what he saw. The psalm's boast and its refusal to boast are Paul's, from the passage where boasting is the explicit problem.

links.note: “Mine eyes hath beheld great things; yea, even too great for man; therefore I was bidden that I should not write them.” No clause is reproduced, which is why this is not catalogued as a quotation; what is reproduced is a distinctive and rare configuration — rapture, uncertainty about the body, and an express prohibition on reporting the content — which the KJV has in one place. Set beside the Matthew 4:8 link on the same verse, this is the second New Testament vision-narrative in a single sentence.

pericopes.text: O then, if I have seen so great things; if the Lord in his condescension unto the children of men, hath visited men in so much mercy, why should my heart weep, and my soul linger in the valley of sorrow, and my flesh waste away, and my strength slacken, because of mine afflictions?

And why should I yield to sin, because of my flesh? Yea, why should I give way to temptations, that the evil one have place in my heart, to destroy my peace and afflict my soul? Why am I angry because of mine enemy?
Awake, my soul! No longer droop in sin. Rejoice O my heart, and give place no more for the enemy of my soul.

links.text: Neither give place to the devil.

provenance.other: “Give place to the devil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:27; the bare verb “give place” occurs in exactly 4, of which the other three are spatial or concessive (Isaiah 49:20, Matthew 9:24, Romans 12:19).
provenance.significance: Ephesians 4:26-27 is the KJV's one command against nursing anger: let not the sun go down upon your wrath, neither give place to the devil. Both halves are in Nephi's two verses. 4:27 ends “Why am I angry because of mine enemy?” and 4:29 begins “Do not anger again”; between them stands “give place no more for the enemy of my soul”. The Book of Mormon has taken the Ephesians pairing of anger with the devil's foothold and made a psalm-stanza of it, which is what it also does to Hebrews 12 and Lamentations 3 in this chapter.

links.note: “Rejoice O my heart, and give place no more for the enemy of my soul.” The KJV's idiom for yielding ground to the adversary is Ephesians 4:27's and no other verse's, and the previous verse has already used it in the other direction — “that the evil one HAVE PLACE in my heart”. Adjudicated at 4:28 where the verb matches; 4:27's noun phrase is the same borrowing anticipated and is registered in recurrenceRefs.

links.text: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.

provenance.other: “Put on thy strength” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:1. Nephi does not reproduce it; what he shares with Isaiah is the imperative “Awake” addressed to a self or a city, and the strength that follows it in the next verse (“Do not slacken my strength”, 4:29).
provenance.significance: Isaiah 51:9 and 52:1 are the double summons — Awake, awake, put on strength — and 2 Nephi 8 transcribes both, at 8:9 and 8:24, four chapters after this verse. Nephi's “Awake, my soul!” is the same imperative turned inward: he addresses to himself what Isaiah addresses to the arm of the LORD and to Zion. That inward turn is the psalm's whole method, and this is where it is most visible.

links.note: “Awake, my soul! No longer droop in sin.” The KJV has no “awake, my soul”; the nearest is Psalm 57:8, “Awake up, my glory”. What makes Isaiah the likelier background is that Nephi is a writer who transcribes Isaiah 51-52 in this same book and whose next verse asks not to have his strength slackened, against Isaiah's “put on thy strength”.
links.whyNot: No clause is shared. The imperative “awake” is common enough in the KJV that a self-address could be formed without any particular source, and the strength language is separated by a verse. Recorded because the specific Isaiah chapters are demonstrably in this author's hands, not because the wording compels it.

pericopes.text: Do not anger again, because of mine enemies. Do not slacken my strength, because of mine afflictions.
Rejoice, O my heart, and cry unto the Lord, and say, O Lord, I will praise thee forever; yea, my soul will rejoice in thee, my God, and the rock of my salvation.

links.text: He shall cry unto me, Thou art my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation.

provenance.other: “Rock of my salvation” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 2 Samuel 22:47 and Psalm 89:26. Only Psalm 89:26 has the full eight-word run the Book of Mormon has — “my God, and the rock of my salvation” — 2 Samuel reading “the God of the rock of my salvation”. The choice between the two is therefore decidable, and it falls to the Psalm.
provenance.significance: Psalm 89:26 is God speaking about David: “He shall cry unto me, Thou art my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation.” Nephi's verse is the cry the Psalm predicts, delivered — “cry unto the Lord, and say … my God, and the rock of my salvation” — including the verb “cry” that Psalm 89:26 uses to introduce it. He has taken a third-person prophecy about what the anointed son will say and performed it in the first person.

links.note: Eight consecutive words of Psalm 89:26, and the two-verse rarity of the core phrase is resolved by the full run: 2 Samuel 22:47 has “the God of the rock”, which is not what Nephi has. The verse's other half is Isaiah 12:1's (separate row). At 4:35 the same formula returns as “the rock of my righteousness”, which occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses — Nephi varying a borrowed phrase once he has established it, which is how the catalogue distinguishes a source from a habit.

links.text: And in that day thou shalt say, O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me.

provenance.other: “O LORD, I will praise thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 12:1.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 12 is the song sung after the deliverance of Isaiah 11, and 2 Nephi transcribes it at chapter 22 — eighteen chapters after Nephi uses its opening line as his own. The catalogue can watch the same words function twice in one book: here as Nephi's private vow of praise in the middle of a lament, there as Isaiah's public song quoted as scripture. The first use is the more interesting one, because Isaiah 12:1 continues “though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away” — and Nephi's psalm is at this exact point turning away from its own anger (4:27, “Why am I angry because of mine enemy?”; 4:29, “Do not anger again”).

links.note: “Cry unto the Lord, and say, O Lord, I will praise thee forever.” The five-word run is a KJV singleton and it arrives with its formula of address intact, including the “and say” that introduces it in Isaiah. The word “forever” is Nephi's addition. recurrenceRefs points to 2 Nephi 22:1, where the same verse is transcribed in full as part of the Isaiah block — later in the book, so this is not a repetition of the transcription but its anticipation.

pericopes.text: O Lord, wilt thou redeem my soul? Wilt thou deliver me out of the hands of mine enemies? Wilt thou make me that I may shake at the appearance of sin?

links.text: My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.

provenance.other: “Hand of mine enemies” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 31:15; the Book of Mormon has the plural, “hands of mine enemies”, which occurs in exactly 0. “Deliver me out of the hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 17:37 (David and Goliath), which supplies the “out of” the Psalm lacks. “Redeem my soul” in the same sentence occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 49:15.
provenance.significance: The verse is a three-part fusion and each part comes from a different kind of deliverance: Psalm 49:15 redeems a soul from the power of the grave, Psalm 31:15 delivers a body from persecutors, 1 Samuel 17:37 delivers a boy from a giant. Nephi's enemies in this chapter are his brothers (4:13), and the David verse is the one where a younger brother is about to fight a battle his elder brothers would not. Note too that Psalm 31:14, the verse immediately before the one borrowed, reads “I trusted in thee, O LORD: I said, Thou art my God” — which is 2 Nephi 4:34's opening almost exactly. The psalm is being read, not remembered in fragments.

links.note: “O Lord, wilt thou redeem my soul? Wilt thou deliver me out of the hands of mine enemies?” Two KJV singletons in two clauses, from two different Psalms, with the preposition of a third verse. The plural “hands” is the only departure and it is the sort of change a writer makes without noticing. Catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation because no single source verse survives whole.

pericopes.text: May the gates of hell be shut continually before me, because that my heart is broken and my spirit is contrite? O Lord, wilt thou not shut the gates of thy righteousness before me, that I may walk in the path of the low valley, that I may be strict in the plain road?

links.text: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

provenance.other: “Gates of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 16:18. The Old Testament's nearest equivalent is Isaiah 38:10's “gates of the grave”, which is a different image — death's door, not hell's.
provenance.significance: Matthew 16:18 promises that the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church. Nephi asks for something narrower and stranger: that they be shut continually BEFORE ME, personally, and he gives as the ground of the request his own broken heart. The public promise made to Peter is being claimed as a private one, and in the same breath the petitioner asks that the other gate — righteousness's — not be shut. Two gates, one verse, from two different scriptures, and the whole prayer is about which of them is open.

links.note: “May the gates of hell be shut continually before me.” A KJV singleton, and one that on the text's own chronology could not have been available: the phrase belongs to a promise made at Caesarea Philippi in the first century AD. The 1830 punctuation makes the whole verse a question; 1920 changed the first mark to an exclamation and the second to an exclamation as well, which converts a plea into an assertion. The first edition's reading is the anxious one and is the running text here.

links.text: Open to me the gates of righteousness: I will go into them, and I will praise the LORD:

provenance.other: “Gates of righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 118:19.
provenance.significance: Psalm 118:19 is a petition to have the gates opened — “Open to me the gates of righteousness: I will go into them, and I will praise the LORD” — and its next verse says who may enter: “This gate of the LORD, into which the righteous shall enter.” Nephi's request is the same petition put negatively, which is the request of a man who has just called himself wretched: not open them to me, but do not shut them against me. And the Psalm's promised response, “I will praise the LORD”, is what he has already said two verses earlier at 4:30. He has taken Psalm 118's vow of praise first and made its condition into a plea afterwards.

links.note: “O Lord, wilt thou not shut the gates of thy righteousness before me?” The phrase is a KJV singleton, with “thy” inserted so that the gates are God's rather than the abstract quality's. Paired in a single sentence with the gates of hell from Matthew 16:18 — one gate asked to stay shut and one asked to stay open — which is a construction neither source supplies and which is the verse's own contribution.

links.text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

provenance.other: This is decidable and it does not go the way a reader expects. “Broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 34:18. “Contrite spirit” occurs in exactly 2, Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 66:2. “Contrite heart” occurs in exactly one, Psalm 51:17 — and Psalm 51:17 assigns the adjectives the other way round: “a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart”. The Book of Mormon reads “my heart is broken and my spirit is contrite”, which is Psalm 34:18's assignment and not Psalm 51:17's.
provenance.significance: The famous verse is Psalm 51:17 and the commonplace phrase in later devotional English is “a broken and a contrite heart”, which is Psalm 51's. Nephi does not have it. He has the pairing exactly as Psalm 34:18 distributes it, in Psalm 34:18's order, and Psalm 34:18 is a verse of consolation rather than of sacrifice — the LORD is NIGH unto them that are of a broken heart. That is why the clause functions in 2 Nephi 4:32 as a ground of confidence (“because that my heart is broken”) rather than as an offering, which is how Psalm 51 uses it. The catalogue's usual finding is that the Book of Mormon has the more famous verse; here it has the less famous one, and correctly.

links.note: “Because that my heart is broken and my spirit is contrite.” Two nouns, two adjectives, and the whole question is which goes with which. Psalm 51:17 pairs broken with spirit and contrite with heart; Psalm 34:18 pairs broken with heart and contrite with spirit; 2 Nephi 4:32 has Psalm 34:18's arrangement. The choice is not stylistic — it decides which Psalm is in view, and with it whether the clause is an offering made or a promise claimed. Psalm 51:17 is filed in the exclusion register at this verse as a better-source-identified displacement.

pericopes.text: O Lord, wilt thou encircle me around in the robe of thy righteousness? O Lord, wilt thou make a way for mine escape before mine enemies? Wilt thou make my path straight before me? Wilt thou not place a stumbling block in my way? But that thou wouldst clear my way before me, and hedge not up my way, but the ways of mine enemy.

links.text: I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.

provenance.other: “Robe of righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 61:10.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 61:10 is a verse of completed joy: “I will greatly rejoice in the LORD … for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself.” It is in the past tense and it is a boast. Nephi turns it into a question — wilt thou encircle me around in the robe of thy righteousness? — and asks for it as a man who has just described himself as encompassed about by sin (4:18). The two encirclings are the psalm's argument in miniature: he is surrounded by one thing and asks to be surrounded by another, and the second word is the KJV's, from the chapter Isaiah's servant reads in the synagogue at Luke 4:18.

links.note: “O Lord, wilt thou encircle me around in the robe of thy righteousness?” The phrase is a KJV singleton and is the only borrowed element; “encircle me around” is the Book of Mormon's own and has no KJV counterpart. Note the deliberate answer to 4:18's “I am encompassed about” — the psalm asks to be re-clothed in the same figure that names its problem.

links.text: There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.

provenance.other: “A way to escape” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 10:13; “make a way” occurs in exactly 2, of which the other is Isaiah 43:19's way in the wilderness. The Book of Mormon has both halves of the singleton, redistributed: “wilt thou make a way for mine escape”.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 10:13 is the KJV's one promise about temptation: God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able, but will with the temptation also make a way to escape. It is the answer to the question 2 Nephi 4:27 asks — “why should I give way to temptations?” — and it is the answer 2 Nephi 4:18 needs, since Nephi is there “encompassed about, because of the temptations and the sins”. Nephi asks for the escape in Paul's words six verses after naming the problem in Hebrews'. The interesting alteration is “before mine enemies”: Paul's escape is from a temptation, Nephi's is from persons, and the psalm has been sliding between the two since 4:27 paired “temptations” with “mine enemy” in one breath.

links.note: “O Lord, wilt thou make a way for mine escape before mine enemies?” The one KJV verse that puts making, way and escape together is 1 Corinthians 10:13, and it is the verse about temptation, which is the psalm's declared subject at 4:18 and 4:27. That the machine streams proposed nothing at all for this verse is worth noting — CONVENTIONS §9's point about contiguous windows: the source's words are here but redistributed across a clause boundary, and an n-gram cannot see it.

links.text: Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths.

provenance.other: “Hedge up thy way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hosea 2:6. The verb in this sense occurs in only three KJV verses at all — Job 3:23, Lamentations 3:7 and Matthew 21:33 — and Lamentations 3:7's “he hath hedged me about, that I cannot get out” belongs to the passage already standing behind 2 Nephi 4:20-25.
provenance.significance: Both KJV sources hedge a way as a punishment. Hosea 2:6 is God blocking the adulterous wife's road so that “she shall not find her paths”; Lamentations 3:7 is the same act done to the man of sorrows. 2 Nephi 4:33 asks God to do it — but to somebody else: “hedge not up my way, but the ways of mine enemy.” This is the psalm's most exact reversal of a source, and it closes the Lamentations 3 borrowing that opened at 4:20. Having spent six verses turning Lamentations' catalogue of divine affliction into a catalogue of mercy, Nephi comes to the one clause he cannot convert, and disposes of it by redirecting it.

links.note: “Hedge not up my way, but the ways of mine enemy.” The KJV's idiom for divinely obstructing a road is Hosea 2:6's, and the Book of Mormon has it verb, particle and noun. What the verse does with it is the finding: it is a prayer that a punishment scripture pronounces on the speaker's own type — an unfaithful spouse in Hosea, an afflicted penitent in Lamentations — be applied instead to his enemies. Read with the Lamentations 3 link at 4:20, the psalm has now used four separate verses of Lamentations 3:1-16, all of them inverted.

links.text: And make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed.

provenance.other: “Make straight paths” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 12:13; “make his paths straight” occurs in exactly 3, all of them the Isaiah 40:3 citation in the Gospels. The Book of Mormon has the singular, “make my path straight”, which occurs in exactly 0.
provenance.significance: This is the third and last stop on a route through one chapter. Hebrews 12:1's sin that so easily besets is 2 Nephi 4:18; Hebrews 12:12's hands that hang down and feeble knees are 2 Nephi 4:28-29's “no longer droop” and “do not slacken my strength”; Hebrews 12:13's make straight paths is 2 Nephi 4:33. Three verses of Hebrews 12 in the source's order across fifteen verses of the psalm, tracking the same movement Hebrews makes — from the weight of sin, through exhaustion, to a straightened path. The catalogue found the identical habit with Hebrews 11 behind 1 Nephi 2 and 1 Nephi 4: a chapter of Hebrews used as an index and worked down.

links.note: “Wilt thou make my path straight before me?” Taken alone the clause is unremarkable and would belong in the exclusion register — the words are common and the Gospels' Isaiah citation is the more famous phrasing. What makes it a link is position. Hebrews 12:1 is quoted at 4:18 on the strength of a KJV singleton, and Hebrews 12:12's two images of exhaustion appear at 4:28-29 in the same order; a third contact eleven verses further on, from the very next verse of the source, is not independent evidence but it is not coincidence either.
links.whyNot: No rare wording. The claim rests entirely on the sequence, and a reader who thinks the 4:28-29 correspondence with Hebrews 12:12 is generic — drooping and slackening are natural enough figures for discouragement — will reasonably decline the whole chain and read this clause as psalm-idiom.

pericopes.text: O Lord, I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever. I will not put my trust in the arm of flesh; for I know that cursed is he that putteth his trust in the arm of flesh.— Yea, cursed is he that putteth his trust in man, or maketh flesh his arm.

links.text: Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.

provenance.other: “Maketh flesh his arm” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 17:5, and is reproduced here word for word. “Trusteth in man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The other half of Nephi's sentence, “the arm of flesh”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 32:8 — Hezekiah on the wall telling Judah that Sennacherib has an arm of flesh and they have the LORD. The formula that replaces Jeremiah's “cursed be the man that trusteth” is “he that putteth his trust in”, which is the KJV's own idiom at Proverbs 28:25 and Isaiah 57:13.
provenance.significance: Recover Jeremiah 17 and the verse Nephi has NOT quoted is the one he has just performed. Jeremiah 17:5 curses the man who trusts in man; 17:7 blesses “the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is”. 2 Nephi 4:34 opens with the blessing — “O Lord, I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever” — and then quotes the curse. Nephi supplies both halves of the Jeremiah oracle, in reverse order, with himself standing in the blessed half. And the sentence is made possible by the two KJV singletons for an arm of flesh being fused: Jeremiah's man who makes flesh his arm, and Hezekiah's enemy who has one.

links.note: The final clause is Jeremiah 17:5 verbatim in its rarest element — “maketh flesh his arm” — with the curse formula reworded from “cursed be the man that trusteth in man” to “cursed is he that putteth his trust in man”, which substitutes the KJV's own commonest trust-idiom (Proverbs 28:25, Isaiah 57:13) for Jeremiah's participle. The doubling in the verse is worth noting: the sentence is said once with “the arm of flesh” from 2 Chronicles 32:8 and then again with Jeremiah's own “maketh flesh his arm”, as though the writer reached the second and better wording on the second attempt and kept both. The 1830 dash after the first “arm of flesh” marks the seam; 1920 removed it.

pericopes.text: Yea, I know that God will give liberally to him that asketh. Yea, my God will give me, if I ask not amiss: therefore I will lift up my voice unto thee; yea, I will cry unto thee, my God, the rock of my righteousness. Behold, my voice shall forever ascend up unto thee, my rock and mine everlasting God. Amen.

links.text: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.

provenance.other: “Let him ask of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 1:5, and “give to all men liberally” occurs in exactly 0 — the KJV reads “that giveth to all men liberally”, which the Book of Mormon compresses to “God will give liberally to him that asketh”, folding in Matthew 7:7's “ask, and it shall be given you”.
provenance.significance: James 1:5 is not a neutral choice of proof text. It is the verse the 1838 history names as the occasion of Joseph Smith's first prayer — “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God” — and here it stands at the close of the psalm of Nephi, paired with James 4:3 on asking amiss. Whatever one makes of that, the catalogue's job is to record that the Book of Mormon's most personal chapter ends by quoting the two James verses on prayer that frame its own account of its origin, and that it quotes them together, from opposite ends of a short epistle.

links.note: “I know that God will give liberally to him that asketh.” The three elements — God, giving liberally, and the asker — occur together in one KJV verse. Nephi rearranges rather than reproduces, which is why this is catalogued as allusion; the giveaway is “liberally”, a KJV adverb that appears in this sense only in James 1:5.

links.text: Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.

provenance.other: “Ask amiss” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:3. The construction “if I ask not amiss” is the Book of Mormon's negation of it.
provenance.significance: James 4:3 supplies the condition James 1:5 omits: ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts. Nephi has put the two together and made the second into a proviso on the first — “my God will give me, if I ask not amiss” — which is a piece of exegesis, not a borrowing. Two verses three chapters apart in James, one about the generosity of God and one about the corruption of the asker, are here reconciled into a single sentence, and the reconciliation is exactly the psalm's problem: a man who has just called himself wretched asking for something and doubting his own motive in asking.
provenance.alternative: “Amiss” is not a rare word in itself, but in the sense of a defective request the KJV has it only here.

links.note: “My God will give me, if I ask not amiss.” The clause is James 4:3 with the negative supplied, and it sits in the same sentence as James 1:5. The close of the psalm then returns to the rock of 4:30 with the noun changed — “the rock of my righteousness”, which occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses, and “mine everlasting God”, whose KJV form “the everlasting God” occurs in exactly 3. Nephi ends on a phrase he has made rather than one he has taken, which after thirty-five verses of borrowing is itself worth recording.

pericopes.text: Behold, it came to pass that I, Nephi, did cry much unto the Lord my God, because of the anger of my brethren.
But behold, their anger did increase against me, insomuch that they did seek to take away my life.

provenance.other: “to take away my life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 31:13. The near neighbours are 1 Kings 19:4, where Elijah asks God to take away his own life, and 1 Kings 19:10 and 19:14, where the clause is inverted — “they seek my life, to take it away.” Only the Psalm has the Book of Mormon's word order, and only the Psalm has it as the design of many against one.
provenance.significance: Psalm 31:13 is a conspiracy verse: “I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.” Recover that context and the three elements of 2 Nephi 5:2-4 are already assembled in it — the slander (Nephi's “all the words which they murmured against me”, which he declines to write down), the taking of counsel together (5:3's speech in the brothers' own mouths), and the design on the life. The Psalm continues, at 31:22, “I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes”, which is the sentence the chapter passes on the brothers at 5:20 in the KJV's other idiom. The catalogue does not press that second contact into a link, but the Psalm is plainly in the room.

links.note: “Insomuch that they did seek to take away my life.” Five words verbatim from the KJV's only occurrence of the clause, repeated at 5:4 and again at 5:19 — three times in one chapter, which is the pattern of a phrase the writer has to hand rather than one he reaches for. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations. The clause entered the corpus at 1 Nephi 7:16 and 7:19, where it was adjudicated to Genesis 37:20 on the strength of the plot rather than the words; the words are Psalm 31:13's, and this is the first place in a new book where they carry the sentence on their own.
links.text: For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.

pericopes.text: Yea, they did murmur against me, saying: Our younger brother thinketh to rule over us; and we have had much trial because of him; wherefore, now let us slay him, that we may not be afflicted more because of his words. For behold, we will not that he shall be our ruler: for it belongeth unto us, which are the elder brethren, to rule over this people.

provenance.other: “let us slay him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 37:20. Genesis 37:8 supplies the other half of the sentence in the KJV's own idiom — “Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?” — though the Book of Mormon's verb is “rule”, which is not Genesis's word here.
provenance.significance: The Joseph cycle has been running since 1 Nephi 3:2 and was made a genealogy at 1 Nephi 5:14; 2 Nephi 3 has just spent a whole chapter on Joseph who was sold into Egypt. Here the cycle reaches the pit, and the Book of Mormon does what Genesis does not: it puts the two speeches together. Genesis 37:8 is the brothers' objection to the dream, thirteen verses before Genesis 37:20 is their plan for the dreamer; 2 Nephi 5:3 runs them into a single sentence, resentment of rule and resolution to kill, with the grievance Genesis leaves to the narrator — “it belongeth unto us, which are the elder brethren” — stated by the brothers themselves.

links.note: “Our younger brother thinketh to rule over us … wherefore, now let us slay him.” Four words verbatim from the KJV's sole occurrence, and in the setting that produced them: elder brothers, a younger brother who presumes to rule, a resolution to kill. 1 Nephi 7:16 gave the plan of Genesis 37:20 without reproducing any of its wording; this verse reproduces the wording, which is why it is catalogued as a quotation despite running to only four words and falling far below Skousen's threshold.
links.text: Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into some pit, and we will say, Some evil beast hath devoured him: and we shall see what will become of his dreams.

provenance.mt: Exodus 2:14 — “Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?”
provenance.route: Exodus 2:14 → Acts 7:27, 7:35 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “a ruler and a judge” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 7:27 and Acts 7:35; “a prince and a judge” occurs in exactly one, Exodus 2:14, which is the same question in the KJV's Old Testament form. The Book of Mormon's noun has been “ruler” at 1 Nephi 2:22, 3:29 and 16:37, and is “ruler” twice more in this chapter, at 5:3 and 5:19.
provenance.significance: The formula crosses a book boundary here and does so in the mouths that Stephen wrote it for. 1 Nephi 16:37 was the sneer as a capital charge — “our brother Nephi, who hath taken it upon him to be our ruler and our teacher” — and 2 Nephi 5:3 is the same charge with the clause Acts leaves implicit made explicit: not merely that he is not their ruler but that the office belongs by right to the elder. That is the exact grievance of Acts 7:27's “he that did his neighbour wrong thrust him away”, and the whole point of Stephen's speech is that the refused man was the appointed one, which 5:19 goes on to say in as many words.

links.note: “For behold, we will not that he shall be our ruler.” The noun identifies the New Testament form of a question the Old Testament asks with “prince” (Exodus 2:14). Not a reproduced clause but a redeployment, and the fourth in the corpus; the argument for the mediation was made at 1 Nephi 2:22 and is not restated here. What is new is that the sneer and its answer are now split across one chapter, 5:3 against 5:19, which is Acts 7:27 against Acts 7:35.
links.text: But he that did his neighbour wrong thrust him away, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?

pericopes.text: Now I do not write upon these plates, all the words which they murmured against me. But it sufficeth me to say, that they did seek to take away my life.
And it came to pass that the Lord did warn me, that I, Nephi, should depart from them, and flee into the wilderness, and all they which would go with me.

provenance.other: “flee into” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Exodus 9:20, Matthew 2:13 and Matthew 24:16. “warned of God” occurs in exactly three, Matthew 2:12, Matthew 2:22 and Hebrews 11:7. Matthew 2 is the only chapter in the Bible that holds both.
provenance.significance: The sequence is Matthew's and not the Old Testament's: a divine warning, a departure from those who mean to kill, a flight, and the taking of a household along. Matthew 2:13 gives the reason as “Herod will seek the young child to destroy him”, which is what 5:2 and 5:4 have just said twice. The Exodus frame the book usually reaches for supplies a flight from Egypt; Matthew supplies a flight of one family out of a hostile kindred, which is the shape of this chapter.

links.note: “The Lord did warn me, that I, Nephi, should depart from them, and flee into the wilderness.” Warn, depart, flee, take the family: four verbs in Matthew's order, and the KJV keeps “warned of God” and “flee into” to three verses each, two of the first and one of the second being Matthew 2. 1 Nephi 2:2-4 told the same story of Lehi without any of this vocabulary, which is what makes the wording here worth noticing.
links.whyNot: No clause is reproduced, and each of the four verbs is ordinary English. The case rests on the sequence and on two moderately rare collocations, not on verbal volume; a reader who declines it is declining a pattern, not a quotation.
links.text: And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, it came to pass that I, Nephi, did take my family, and also Zoram and his family, and Sam, mine elder brother, and his family, and Jacob and Joseph, my younger brethren, and also my sisters, and all they which would go with me. And all they which would go with me, were they which believed in the warnings and the revelations of God; wherefore, they did hearken unto my words.

And we did take our tents and whatsoever things were possible for us, and did journey in the wilderness for the space of many days. And after that we had journied for the space of many days, we did pitch our tents.
And my people would that we should call the name of the place Nephi; wherefore, we did call it Nephi.
And all they which were with me, did take it upon them to call themselves the people of Nephi.
And we did observe to keep the judgments, and the statutes, and the commandments of the Lord, in all things, according to the law of Moses.

provenance.other: 1 Kings 2:3 is the only KJV verse that holds statutes, commandments, judgments and the law of Moses together, and the only KJV verse that holds the law of Moses and prospering together. “all things according to the law” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 2:39, which supplies the Book of Mormon's “in all things, according to the law of Moses” in the KJV's own words with a different genitive.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's hinge, and it decides 5:16. 1 Kings 2:3 is David's dying charge to Solomon: keep the statutes and the commandments and the judgments as it is written in the law of Moses, “that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest.” 2 Nephi 5:10-11 keeps them and prospers, in that order and in that causal relation, and six verses later builds a temple after the manner of Solomon's. The Solomon of 5:16 is not fetched from 1 Kings 6; he is already present at 5:10, in the verse where a founder is told what to keep in order to prosper and to build. Recover the rest of the charge and the fit is closer still: what David is preparing Solomon for at 1 Kings 2:3 is the throne and the house, and what 2 Nephi 5 is narrating is a man who takes the second and refuses the first (5:18).

links.note: “And we did observe to keep the judgments, and the statutes, and the commandments of the Lord, in all things, according to the law of Moses.” Three of the four nouns of 1 Kings 2:3 and its concluding appeal to the law of Moses, followed immediately by its promised outcome — the KJV's clause is “that thou mayest prosper”, and 5:11 is “we did prosper exceedingly.” Deuteronomy supplies the same triad repeatedly but never with the law of Moses attached, and Deuteronomy 28:15's “to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes” is the source of the Book of Mormon's verb “observe” rather than of the list; that verse returns at 5:20-21 for the other half of its sentence.
links.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

pericopes.text: And the Lord was with us; and we did prosper exceedingly: for we did sow seed, and we did reap again in abundance. And we began to raise flocks, and herds, and animals of every kind.

provenance.other: “made it to prosper” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 39:23. “The LORD was with” occurs in eighteen and cannot identify a source on its own; what narrows it is the pairing with prospering, which the KJV makes four times and three of them in Genesis 39. Genesis 26:12 offers the other candidate frame — Isaac sows in the land of those who envied him and receives a hundredfold — but its wording (“sowed in that land”) is not the Book of Mormon's.
provenance.significance: Genesis 39 is what happens to Joseph after the pit. The Book of Mormon quoted the pit four verses earlier at 5:3 and now takes the sequel from eleven verses on in the same story: the brothers plot, the younger brother is separated from them, and the refrain of the separated life is that the LORD was with him and made what he did prosper. Nephi's people are named at 5:9 and prosper at 5:11 in Joseph's formula; the brothers are named Lamanites at 5:14 and cursed at 5:21. Genesis never says the two halves belong together — it simply narrates them in order, which is what this chapter does.

links.note: “And the Lord was with us; and we did prosper exceedingly: for we did sow seed, and we did reap again in abundance.” The KJV's collocation of the LORD's presence with prospering is concentrated in Genesis 39, where it is the whole account of Joseph in exile, and “made it to prosper” is that chapter's own singleton. The 1830 text has “prosper exceedingly” twice in three verses (5:11, 5:13), which is the refrain doing what a refrain does.
links.text: The keeper of the prison looked not to any thing that was under his hand; because the LORD was with him, and that which he did, the LORD made it to prosper.

pericopes.text: And I, Nephi, had also brought the records which were engraven upon the plates of brass; and also the ball, or compass, which was prepared for my father, by the hand of the Lord, according to that which is written.
And it came to pass that we began to prosper exceedingly, and to multiply in the land.

And I, Nephi, did take the sword of Laban, and after the manner of it did make many swords, lest by any means the people which were now called Lamanites, should come upon us and destroy us: for I knew their hatred towards me and my children, and they which were called my people.

And I did teach my people, that they should build buildings; and that they should work in all manner of wood, and of iron, and of copper, and of brass, and of steel, and of gold, and of silver, and of precious ores, which were in great abundance.

provenance.other: “work in all manner of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 31:5. “in all manner of workmanship” occurs in exactly three, Exodus 31:3, 31:5 and 35:31, all of them the commissioning of Bezalel. Exodus 31:4's list — “to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass” — is the KJV's other contribution; 2 Chronicles 2:14's longer list of the same metals for Solomon's temple has none of the Book of Mormon's syntax.
provenance.significance: This is the finding the temple verse depends on. 5:15 and 5:16 are one movement — teach the people to work in metals, then build a sanctuary — and the KJV passage that moves that way is Exodus 31, where the spirit of God fills a craftsman with wisdom and knowledge and all manner of workmanship so that the tabernacle can be made. So the sanctuary of 5:16 is named for Solomon and worded from Moses: the label comes from 1 Kings and the language comes from the tabernacle texts. That is a coherent thing for this book to do — 5:10 has just said the people keep the law of Moses — but it is not what a reader of 5:16 would predict.

links.note: “And that they should work in all manner of wood, and of iron, and of copper, and of brass, and of steel, and of gold, and of silver.” The five-word run is a KJV singleton and belongs to Bezalel, whose commission is to work in gold and silver and brass, to cut stones and carve timber, in all manner of workmanship. The Book of Mormon's list adds copper and steel, neither of which the KJV names as a worked metal in a sanctuary context, and reverses the KJV's order by putting wood first — which is Exodus 31:5's order of operations rather than 31:4's list.
links.text: And in cutting of stones, to set them, and in carving of timber, to work in all manner of workmanship.

pericopes.text: And I, Nephi, did build a temple; and I did construct it after the manner of the temple of Solomon, save it were not built of so many precious things: for they were not to be found upon the land; wherefore, it could not be built like unto Solomon’s temple. But the manner of the construction was like unto the temple of Solomon; and the workmanship thereof was exceeding fine.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 6 → (as a named referent, not a quoted text) → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Neither “the temple of Solomon” nor “after the manner of the temple” occurs in any KJV verse. The KJV's own designation is “the house which king Solomon built for the LORD” (1 Kings 6:2) and “the house of the LORD”; “Solomon's temple” is the phrase of later English usage, not of the translation the rest of this chapter is following. 1 Chronicles 29:2's “all manner of precious stones … in abundance” is the closest KJV wording to 5:16's “so many precious things”, and shares no distinctive run with it.
provenance.significance: The verse names its source instead of using it, and that is the observation worth publishing. Everything verbal in the temple-building movement comes from Exodus 31 (see 5:15); 1 Kings 6-7 contributes the proper noun and nothing else — no cubits, no cedar, no cherubim, no “house of the LORD”. What the verse does with the name is argue from it in the negative: the temple is like Solomon's in manner of construction and unlike it in materials, which is a comparison a reader could only make from the outside of 1 Kings, from the general reputation of Solomon's temple for gold and precious stones rather than from its text.

links.note: “I did construct it after the manner of the temple of Solomon, save it were not built of so many precious things.” Catalogued as figural because there is nothing here to test: the KJV does not use the phrase “the temple of Solomon”, and the verse borrows no clause, measurement or furnishing from 1 Kings 6-7. What it borrows is a reputation. The link is recorded so that a reader who comes to this verse expecting 1 Kings is told plainly where the chapter's temple language actually comes from, which is Exodus 31 one verse earlier.
links.whyNot: No verbal contact of any kind with 1 Kings 6-7, and the designation the verse uses is not the KJV's. If the standard is dependence on a text rather than reference to a building, this row does not meet it, and it would be withdrawn if the catalogue decided that a named referent without wording is not a link.
links.text: And the house which king Solomon built for the LORD, the length thereof was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof twenty cubits, and the height thereof thirty cubits.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I, Nephi, did cause my people that they should be industrious, and that they should labor with their hands.
And it came to pass that they would that I should be their King. But I, Nephi, was desirous that they should have no King; nevertheless, I did do for them according to that which was in my power.

provenance.other: “Rule thou over us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 8:22, and “I will not rule over you” in exactly one, Judges 8:23. “make us a king” occurs in exactly one, 1 Samuel 8:5. Those three verses are the whole KJV inventory of a people offering rule to a deliverer and of a deliverer or prophet resisting it.
provenance.significance: Two episodes stand behind the verse and they say opposite things, which is why the Book of Mormon's version is worth reading closely. Gideon refuses because “the LORD shall rule over you”, and the refusal is honoured; Israel demands a king in 1 Samuel 8 and the demand is a rejection of God, granted in anger. 2 Nephi 5:18 takes Gideon's answer and 1 Samuel's grammar — the people “would that I should be their King”, as Israel would — and then does what neither passage does: Nephi neither rules as king nor stands aside, but “did do for them according to that which was in my power.” Read against 5:3, the refusal is also an answer to the brothers: the office they killed for is the office he declines.

links.note: “And it came to pass that they would that I should be their King. But I, Nephi, was desirous that they should have no King.” The KJV has exactly one scene of a people pressing rule on the man who delivered them and exactly one refusal of it, and they are adjacent verses. The Book of Mormon reproduces no clause from either, but the shape — offer, refusal, continued rule in fact if not in name — is Judges 8:22-23's and nothing else in the KJV's. The 1830 text capitalizes “King” at both occurrences, as the KJV does not; 1920 lowercases it.
links.text: And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you.

pericopes.text: And behold, the words of the Lord had been fulfilled unto my brethren, which he spake concerning them, that I should be their ruler and their teacher; wherefore, I had been their ruler and their teacher, according to the commandments of the Lord, until the time that they sought to take away my life.

provenance.mt: Exodus 2:14 — “Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?”
provenance.route: Exodus 2:14 → Acts 7:35 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “a ruler and a judge” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 7:27 and Acts 7:35, against exactly one for the Old Testament's “a prince and a judge” at Exodus 2:14; and Acts 7:35 is the only KJV verse in which the refused man is said to have been sent as ruler nonetheless. The Book of Mormon's noun has been “ruler” at every occurrence since 1 Nephi 2:22.
provenance.significance: This is metalepsis of a strict kind, and it runs across sixteen verses. Acts 7:35 is Stephen's answer to Acts 7:27: “This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer.” 2 Nephi 5:3 is the refusal, in the brothers' mouths and with the elder-brother grievance stated; 2 Nephi 5:19 is the answer, in the same terms and the same order — the man they refused had been their ruler all along, by the Lord's word, “until the time that they sought to take away my life.” Neither text says the Lamanite separation is the Exodus rejection of Moses. The pairing says it, and it says it in the noun.

links.note: “The words of the Lord had been fulfilled unto my brethren, which he spake concerning them, that I should be their ruler and their teacher.” The promise of 1 Nephi 2:22 declared fulfilled, and the mediation argued there governs here: the KJV Old Testament asks the question with “prince”, Acts with “ruler”, and the Book of Mormon has read “ruler” throughout. What this verse adds is Acts 7:35's structure — refusal answered by vindication — laid over 5:3 and 5:19 as the frame of the whole separation. The verse ends with the chapter's third use of Psalm 31:13's clause (see 5:2).
links.text: This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, the word of the Lord was fulfilled which he spake unto me, saying: That inasmuch as they will not hearken unto thy words, they shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord. And behold, they were cut off from his presence.

provenance.other: “hearken unto thy words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 1:18, and this is its first appearance anywhere in the Book of Mormon. Deuteronomy 28:15 supplies the same condition in the covenant's own formula — “if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God” — with the second person pointed at God rather than at a man.
provenance.significance: Joshua 1:18 is the oath the tribes swear to Moses's successor: whoever rebels against thy commandment and will not hearken unto thy words shall be put to death. The Book of Mormon takes that sentence and changes only the penalty — not death but being cut off from the presence of the Lord — which is precisely the substitution the covenant curse makes at Deuteronomy 28. Note what this does to the succession question the chapter is arguing: 1 Nephi 2:21 conditioned the sentence on rebellion against Nephi, and 5:20 restates it as failure to hearken to his words, which is Joshua's wording for the authority of the man who takes the prophet's place.

links.note: “That inasmuch as they will not hearken unto thy words, they shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord.” The chapter presents this as a quotation of what the Lord had said to Nephi, and the 1 Nephi wording it points back to (2:21) reads “rebel against thee”, not “hearken unto thy words”. The new clause is a KJV singleton, and its verse contains “rebel against thy commandment” as well — so the restatement is not a slip of memory but a second borrowing from the same verse of Joshua. The n-gram stream ranked Joshua 1:18 first here, which is one of the few places in this chapter where it was right.
links.text: Whosoever he be that doth rebel against thy commandment, and will not hearken unto thy words in all that thou commandest him, he shall be put to death: only be strong and of a good courage.

provenance.other: “From the presence of the LORD/Lord” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses; Genesis 4:16 is the only one where the departure is a sentence passed on a brother. The argument was made at 1 Nephi 2:21 and is not remade here.
provenance.significance: The mediation is the point of the row. 2 Nephi 5:20 is not reaching for Genesis; it is declaring a Book of Mormon prophecy fulfilled, and the words it repeats are the words 1 Nephi 2:21 had already taken from Cain. What follows in the next verse — a curse, and a mark set on the cursed so that others may know them — is the rest of Genesis 4, arriving in the Book of Mormon's own vocabulary rather than the KJV's. So the Cain frame reaches this chapter through the corpus, not through the Bible, and the chapter's most consequential sentence sits inside it.

links.note: “And behold, they were cut off from his presence.” The clause is quoted from 1 Nephi 2:21 rather than from Genesis, which is what the fulfilment formula around it says it is doing: “the word of the Lord was fulfilled which he spake unto me.” Recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM for that reason, with the Genesis 4:16 case argued at its first occurrence.
links.text: And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden.

pericopes.text: And he had caused the cursing to come upon them, yea, even a sore cursing, because of their iniquity. For behold, they had hardened their hearts against him, that they had become like unto a flint; wherefore, as they were white, and exceeding fair and delightsome, that they might not be enticing unto my people, therefore the Lord God did cause a skin of blackness to come upon them.

provenance.other: “The LORD shall send upon thee cursing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 28:20, which is also the KJV's only use of “cursing” as the thing sent upon a people. “curses shall come upon thee” occurs in exactly two, Deuteronomy 28:15 and 28:45, both conditioned on not hearkening — which is the condition 5:20 has just stated. “a sore curse” and “a sore cursing” occur in no KJV verse; the phrase is 1 Nephi 2:23's.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 28 is the chapter's silent structure, and it is present in both directions. 5:10 keeps the statutes and the commandments and prospers, which is Deuteronomy 28:1-14; 5:20-21 will not hearken and the cursing comes, which is Deuteronomy 28:15-68. The Book of Mormon's innovation is not the curse but its medium: Deuteronomy's curses are botch and blindness and madness, agricultural failure and exile, and none of them is a change of appearance.

links.note: “And he had caused the cursing to come upon them, yea, even a sore cursing, because of their iniquity.” The noun “cursing”, the causal “because of”, and the coming-upon are Deuteronomy 28's, and the condition attached in 5:20 is Deuteronomy 28:15's. But the intensifier is the corpus's own: “a sore curse” is 1 Nephi 2:23, not a KJV phrase, and this verse inflects it to “a sore cursing” to match Deuteronomy's noun. Recorded as mediated through 1 Nephi 2:23 for that reason.
links.text: The LORD shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke, in all that thou settest thine hand unto for to do, until thou be destroyed, and until thou perish quickly; because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast forsaken me.

provenance.route: Zechariah 7:12 (sense) + Isaiah 50:7 (wording) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “like a flint” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 50:7. “as an adamant” occurs in exactly two, Ezekiel 3:9 and Zechariah 7:12, and only Zechariah's is a hardened heart. “hardened their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 6:6, of the Egyptians and Pharaoh.
provenance.significance: The verse is built from two KJV places that mean opposite things, and the second is one the Book of Mormon transcribes in full two chapters later. Isaiah 50:7 is the servant's steadfastness — “therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed” — and 2 Nephi 7:7 reproduces it verbatim. Here the same simile is turned into the figure for a heart that will not hear, which is Zechariah 7:12's adamant. So the chapter's curse verse borrows the resolve of the servant and assigns it to the rebels; a reader who has the whole book in view meets the phrase again, sixty verses on, doing the opposite work. Whether that is design or reuse the catalogue cannot say, but the collision is exact and the KJV offers the simile nowhere else.

links.note: “They had hardened their hearts against him, that they had become like unto a flint.” Two rare KJV collocations in one clause. The hardened heart made mineral is Zechariah 7:12's “they made their hearts as an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the LORD of hosts hath sent … by the former prophets”, which is the sense exactly, down to the refusal being of a prophet's words (5:20). The mineral itself is Isaiah 50:7's flint, the KJV's only one, and Ezekiel 3:9 is the verse that joins flint to adamant. “Hardened their hearts” is itself a singleton, and it is Pharaoh's.
links.text: Yea, they made their hearts as an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the LORD of hosts hath sent in his spirit by the former prophets: therefore came a great wrath from the LORD of hosts.
In which time Moses was born, and was exceeding fair, and nourished up in his father’s house three months:

provenance.other: “exceeding fair” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:20, of the infant Moses. “delightsome” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Malachi 3:12, and 2 Nephi 5:21 is the word's first appearance in the Book of Mormon. The first is visible only in the earlier editions: 1830 and 1920 both read “exceeding fair and delightsome”, and the current text reads “exceedingly”, which breaks the phrase — no KJV verse has “exceedingly fair”. Against that, no KJV verse contains “skin of blackness”, or “a skin of” in any form, or any phrase making blackness of skin a thing God causes — see the exclusions filed at this verse.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons meet in one clause, and one of them belongs to a speech this chapter has already used twice. Acts 7:20 is the third borrowing from Stephen in 2 Nephi 5, after Acts 7:27 at 5:3 and Acts 7:35 at 5:19, and it is the verse where Moses is born “exceeding fair” — the beauty that moves Pharaoh's daughter to save him, in the KJV's only use of the phrase. 2 Nephi 5:21 takes it for the appearance that is about to be removed. So the chapter's most consequential sentence is built, at the level of its adjectives, out of the same Acts 7 that supplies its account of rejected leadership; and Malachi's “delightsome”, the KJV's only occurrence, is a promise of restoration (“all nations shall call you blessed”) borrowed to name what a curse takes away. The verbs of the curse itself borrow nothing. That is the honest result of the search on this verse: where readers most want to know whether the Book of Mormon is following the KJV's English, the answer is that it is, for the condition being lost, and is not, for the thing imposed.

links.note: “As they were white, and exceeding fair and delightsome.” Two adjectival phrases, each a KJV singleton, in eight words; the odds of that pairing arising without the KJV are poor. The link rests on the running text and is invisible in the current edition, which reads “exceedingly” and so breaks the contact with Acts 7:20; 1830 and 1920 both read “exceeding”, so this is a modern correction away from the KJV rather than the 1920 revision — the sort of case CONVENTIONS §8 exists for. Nothing else in the clause is traceable: the KJV joins skin to blackness only at Job 30:30 and Lamentations 4:8 and 5:10, in none of which it is inflicted (Leviticus 13:31 has both words, of hair in a plague-spot), and Jeremiah 13:23's Ethiopian is an emblem of what cannot be changed rather than of what God changes.
links.whyNot: “Exceeding” as an intensifier is ordinary KJV usage and “fair” is a common word; the singleton is a collocation, not a distinctive lexeme, and a reader may hold that the two words met by accident. The Acts 7 context (an infant's beauty) has no relation to a people's complexion except through the metalepsis argued above.

pericopes.text: And thus saith the Lord God, I will cause that they shall be loathsome unto thy people, save they shall repent of their iniquities.
And cursed shall be the seed of him that mixeth with their seed: for they shall be cursed even with the same cursing. And the Lord spake it, and it was done.

provenance.other: “mingled themselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezra 9:2, where “the holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands”; “mingle themselves with the seed” occurs in exactly one, Daniel 2:43. “Cursed shall be” occurs in exactly two, Deuteronomy 28:17 and 28:18, both of them covenant curses on what a body and a land produce. The Book of Mormon's verb, “mixeth”, occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: Ezra 9 is the KJV's one passage in which intermarriage defiles a seed rather than merely a household, and it is a priest's confession, not a divine oracle; Daniel 2:43 is the one place where mingled seed is prophesied and its result is that “they shall not cleave one to another.” 2 Nephi 5:23 does what neither does: it extends the curse of 5:21 forward by descent, so that the mark is inherited through marriage. Deuteronomy 28's “cursed shall be the fruit of thy body” is the formula for that, and this verse is its application to a specific other people.

links.note: “And cursed shall be the seed of him that mixeth with their seed: for they shall be cursed even with the same cursing.” The formula is Deuteronomy 28:17-18's, the seed-mingling is Ezra 9:2's, and the verb belongs to neither — the KJV never writes “mixeth”, and where it mixes seed at all (Leviticus 19:19's mingled seed of a field) the subject is agriculture. Recorded at moderate: the sense is Ezra's and the wording is only partly the KJV's.
links.whyNot: No clause is reproduced from any of the three candidates, and the idea of a curse passing by intermarriage is common enough in English religious usage that it need not come from a particular verse.
links.text: For they have taken of their daughters for themselves, and for their sons: so that the holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands: yea, the hand of the princes and rulers hath been chief in this trespass.

pericopes.text: And because of their cursing which was upon them, they did become an idle people, full of mischief and subtlety, and did seek in the wilderness for beasts of prey.

provenance.other: “full of all subtilty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “subtilty and all mischief” in exactly one, both of them Acts 13:10. The KJV pairs the two nouns nowhere else: “mischief” is spread over forty-nine KJV verses and “subtilty” over six, and they meet only here. The 1830 text spells the second word “subtlety”, which is not the KJV's spelling in this verse; 1 Nephi 13:27 took its clause from the other end of the same verse.
provenance.significance: Acts 13:10 is Paul's sentence on Elymas the sorcerer, and what follows it is a curse of darkness: “thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness.” 2 Nephi 5:24 stands three verses after a divine darkening of a people, and reaches for the KJV verse whose sequel is exactly that — an opposer of the Lord's messengers, named full of subtilty and mischief, struck in the body so that others may see it. The metalepsis is uncomfortable and it is the point: the chapter's account of the curse is worded, at its last stage, out of the New Testament's one story of a man cursed with darkness for resisting a missionary. Note that Acts 13:11 supplies “a mist and a darkness”, which is the phrase 1 Nephi's “mist of darkness” has already drawn on from 2 Peter 2:17.

links.note: “They did become an idle people, full of mischief and subtlety, and did seek in the wilderness for beasts of prey.” The pairing is a KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon has been to this verse before, taking “pervert the right ways of the Lord” at 1 Nephi 13:27. Across a book boundary the row is written again rather than cross-referenced, because the clause borrowed is a different one. The rest of the verse has no KJV wording: “beasts of prey” is in no KJV verse, and the idleness that hunts rather than sows is the chapter's own inversion of 5:11 — the two peoples divide as Genesis 25:27 divides Esau, “a cunning hunter, a man of the field”, from Jacob dwelling in tents, though not a word of that verse is here.
links.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

pericopes.text: And the Lord God said unto me, they shall be a scourge unto thy seed, to stir them up in remembrance of me; and inasmuch as they will not remember me, and hearken unto my words, they shall scourge them even unto destruction.

provenance.other: “Scourges in your sides” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 23:13, and the argument for it was made at 1 Nephi 2:24. “stir you up by putting you in remembrance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 1:13; 2 Peter 3:1 has the same idiom again. The Book of Mormon's purpose clause has moved between its two occurrences: 1 Nephi 2:24 reads “to stir them up in the ways of remembrance”, and 2 Nephi 5:25 reads “to stir them up in remembrance of me”, which is 2 Peter's construction rather than the first version's.
provenance.significance: The verse is a fulfilment quotation, and the interesting thing is what changed in the quoting. Everything else is 1 Nephi 2:24 repeated — a scourge unto thy seed, stirring up, the condition of not remembering — but the awkward “in the ways of remembrance” has been smoothed into the KJV's own idiom for the purpose of a reminder, which the KJV has only in 2 Peter. A prophecy is being reported as fulfilled and is quietly improved in transmission, toward the New Testament.

links.note: “They shall be a scourge unto thy seed, to stir them up in remembrance of me.” Joshua 23:13's doctrine of the useful enemy, taken not from Joshua but from 1 Nephi 2:24, where it was given to Lehi as a prophecy and is here reported as the Lord's word to Nephi. Recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM for that reason. The one departure from 1 Nephi 2:24 is the purpose clause, which now runs in 2 Peter 1:13's construction.
links.text: Know for a certainty that the LORD your God will no more drive out any of these nations from before you; but they shall be snares and traps unto you, and scourges in your sides, and thorns in your eyes, until ye perish from off this good land which the LORD your God hath given you.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I, Nephi, did consecrate Jacob and Joseph, that they should be priests and teachers over the land of my people.
And it came to pass that we lived after the manner of happiness.
And thirty years had passed away from the time we left Jerusalem.
And I, Nephi, had kept the records upon my plates, which I had made of my people thus far.
And it came to pass that the Lord God said unto me, Make other plates; and thou shalt engraven many things upon them which are good in my sight, for the profit of thy people.—
Wherefore, I, Nephi, to be obedient to the commandments of the Lord, went and made these plates upon which I have engraven these things.
And I engravened that which is pleasing unto God. And if my people be pleased with the things of God, they be pleased with mine engravings which are upon these plates.
And if my people desire to know the more particular part of the history of my people, they must search mine other plates.
And it sufficeth me to say, that forty years had passed away, and we had already had wars and contentions with our brethren.
The words of Jacob, the brother of Nephi, which he spake unto the people of Nephi:

Behold, my beloved brethren, that I, Jacob, having been called of God, and ordained after the manner of his holy order, and having been consecrated by my brother, Nephi, unto whom ye look as a king or a protector, and on whom ye depend for safety, behold, ye know that I have spoken unto you exceeding many things;

provenance.other: 'Called of God' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hebrews 5:4 and 5:10, and they are eight verses apart in one argument about priestly appointment. The second of the two is the one that couples the phrase with an order: 'Called of God an high priest after the order of Melchisedec.' 'His holy order' as such is in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Jacob opens by stating his credentials in the only KJV vocabulary that exists for stating them. Recover the context and Hebrews 5 is arguing that no man takes the honour to himself — 'no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron' — which is precisely the disclaimer Jacob needs, since his commission came through his brother Nephi, the man the same sentence goes on to describe as the one 'unto whom ye look as a king'. The KJV passage that supplies his warrant is the passage that separates a called priesthood from a royal one, and Jacob's sentence has both a priest and a king in it.

links.note: 'Having been called of God, and ordained after the manner of his holy order, and having been consecrated by my brother, Nephi.' Two of the three verbs are Hebrews 5's. The phrase 'called of God' is a KJV rarity — two verses, both in this one argument — and the second of them attaches it to an order ('after the order of Melchisedec'), which is what Jacob's next clause does with 'after the manner of his holy order'. The substitution is worth noting: Hebrews names the order after a man, Melchizedek, and Jacob names it after God ('his holy order'), which is the move Alma 13 will later make explicit. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages.
links.text: And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron.

pericopes.text: nevertheless, I speak unto you again: for I am desirous for the welfare of your souls. Yea, mine anxiety is great for you; and ye yourselves know that it ever has been. For I have exhorted you with all diligence; and I have taught you the words of my father; and I have spoken unto you concerning all things which are written from the creation of the world.

provenance.route: Acts 20:18-35 (Paul at Miletus) → KJV → Book of Mormon
