provenance.other: 'Ye yourselves know' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:34. The rest of the contact is with the same speech: 'Ye know, from the first day' (20:18), 'have taught you publickly, and from house to house' (20:20), 'I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears' (20:31).
provenance.significance: The genre is the finding as much as the wording. Acts 20 is the KJV's one full-dress farewell address by a minister to a congregation he has taught at length and is anxious for, and every structural beat of it is in 2 Nephi 6:2-3: the speaker's credentials, the appeal to what the hearers themselves already know, the record of tireless past teaching, and the anxiety for their souls going forward. Jacob is not quoting Paul; he is delivering Paul's speech. The same template runs again at Jacob 2:2-3, which is what makes it a habit of this speaker rather than an accident of one sentence.

links.note: 'Ye yourselves know that it ever has been. For I have exhorted you with all diligence; and I have taught you the words of my father.' 'Ye yourselves know' is a KJV singleton and it sits at Miletus, in the middle of Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders — a speech Jacob's exordium reproduces beat for beat, down to 'I have taught you' (Acts 20:20) and the ceaseless warning of 20:31 behind 'exhorted you with all diligence'. The n-gram stream found the singleton and could not see the speech around it, which is the ordinary case (CONVENTIONS §9).
links.text: Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.

provenance.other: 'From the creation of the world' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 1:20. The near neighbours read differently — 'since the beginning of the world' (John 9:32), 'from the foundation of the world' (Matthew 13:35 and eight others).
provenance.significance: Paul's clause is about what has been legible without a text since the world was made; Jacob's is about what has been written since then — 'all things which are written from the creation of the world'. The borrowing turns Romans' argument from general revelation into an inventory of scripture, which is the move the whole chapter needs, since Jacob is about to read Isaiah and claim it can be likened to a people who were not in it.

links.note: 'I have spoken unto you concerning all things which are written from the creation of the world.' A KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon's phrase is Paul's exactly; but it is five words and the sense has been reversed from the unwritten to the written, so this is recorded as an echo rather than an allusion.
links.whyNot: Five words, and 'from the creation of the world' is unremarkable English for 'since the beginning'. Nothing else in 6:3 has any contact with Romans 1, and the sense Paul gives the phrase — knowledge available without scripture — is the opposite of Jacob's.
links.text: For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:

pericopes.text: And now, behold, I would speak unto you concerning things which are, and which are to come; wherefore, I will read you the words of Isaiah. And they are the words which my brother hath desired me that I should speak unto you. And I speak them unto you for your sakes, that ye may learn and glorify the name of your God.

And now, the words which I shall read, are they which Isaiah spake concerning all the House of Israel; wherefore, they may be likened unto you: for ye are of the House of Israel. And there are many things which have been spoken by Isaiah, which may be likened unto you, because that ye are of the House of Israel.

And now, these are the words: Thus saith the Lord God: Behold, I will lift up mine hand to the Gentiles, and set up my standard to the people; and they shall bring thy sons in their arms, and thy daughters shall be carried upon their shoulders.

provenance.other: 'Set up my standard' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does 'carried upon their shoulders'; both are this one. Word-for-word identical to the KJV apart from Jacob's own framing clause 'And now, these are the words'. It is also word-for-word identical to 1 Nephi 21:22, where the same verse stands inside a continuous transcription of Isaiah 49.
provenance.significance: This is Isaiah 49 entering the book a second time, and in a different voice. 1 Nephi 21 transcribes the chapter; here Jacob reads out five of its verses in order to argue from them, announces that he is doing so ('I will read you the words of Isaiah', 6:4), and then glosses them for eleven verses. The catalogue records the second entry as a link rather than a repeat because a new book is a new hand and the reader page is per-book (ADJUDICATING §4).

links.note: Jacob's quotation of Isaiah 49:22 is verbatim, with only 'And now, these are the words' prefixed as the citation formula — an explicit quotation in the strict sense, announced as such two verses earlier. The interest of the block is not that it is accurate but that its five verses are accurate in slightly different directions: see 6:7, 6:16 and 6:18, where the departures from the KJV and the departures from 1 Nephi 21 do not line up.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 2 Ne 6.7 (Isaiah 49:22-23, keyed to the second verse of the pair)
links.text: Thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I will lift up mine hand to the Gentiles, and set up my standard to the people: and they shall bring thy sons in their arms, and thy daughters shall be carried upon their shoulders.

pericopes.text: And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their faces towards the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the Lord: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.

provenance.other: Two departures from the KJV. KJV 'with their face toward the earth' → 'with their faces towards the earth'. 1 Nephi 21:23 has already changed 'toward' to 'towards' but keeps the singular 'face', so 2 Nephi 6:7 agrees with the earlier Book of Mormon reading in one word and departs from both texts in the other. 'Nursing fathers' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, this one.
provenance.significance: The pluralised 'faces' is a small thing that does exactly what Jacob's gloss will do at 6:13: it distributes a singular collective image across a plurality of individual actors. Isaiah's kings and queens bow with one face; Jacob's do it with their own faces each, and eleven verses later the dust of Isaiah's promise is being licked by named opponents. The verse is being prepared for the use it is about to be put to.

links.note: Verbatim from the KJV except 'faces towards' for 'face toward'. Worth holding beside 6:13, where Jacob quotes this same verse back in his own exposition and reverses it — 'lick up the dust of thy feet', said to Zion about her attendants, becomes 'they that fight against Zion... shall lick up the dust of their feet'.
links.text: And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.

pericopes.text: And now I, Jacob, would speak somewhat concerning these words: For behold, the Lord hath shewn me that they which were at Jerusalem, from whence we came, have been slain and carried away captive;

nevertheless, the Lord hath shewn unto me that they should return again. And he also hath shewn unto me, that the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, should manifest himself unto them in the flesh; and after that he should manifest himself, they should scourge him and crucify him, according to the words of the angel, which spake it unto me.

provenance.other: 'Manifest in the flesh' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:16 — 'God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.' The 1830 keeps the KJV's 'shewn' three times in this verse, which 1920 modernized to 'shown'.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one sentence for incarnation is a creedal formula, and Jacob uses it of 'the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel' — Isaiah's title, from the chapter he has just read — rather than of 'God' flatly. Recover 1 Timothy's context and the six clauses that follow the borrowed one are a précis of the rest of Jacob's paragraph: seen of angels (6:9, 'according to the words of the angel'), preached unto the Gentiles (6:12), believed on in the world (6:14, 'when they shall believe in him'). The verse Jacob takes four words from is the outline of what he says next.

links.note: 'That the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, should manifest himself unto them in the flesh.' The phrase is a KJV singleton and the doctrinal weight of the sentence rests on it. What Jacob changes is the voice: 1 Timothy has the passive 'God was manifest in the flesh', and Jacob makes it reflexive and volitional — the Holy One 'should manifest himself' — and then repeats the reflexive twice more in the same verse and again at 6:14. That is not the KJV's grammar, and it is the chapter's characteristic move (compare 6:14, where Isaiah's 'the Lord shall set his hand' becomes 'the Messiah will set himself').
links.text: And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.

provenance.other: 'To scourge, and to crucify' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:19: it is the only place in the Bible where scourging and crucifixion stand in a single clause as a pair of announced future acts. The synoptic parallels break the pair — Mark 10:34 has 'shall scourge him... and shall kill him', Luke 18:33 'shall scourge him, and put him to death'. mediation-check.py reports 'scourge' as decisive for Mark against Matthew's 'deliver', but that is an alignment artifact: Matthew has 'scourge' too, four words later, and it is the pairing with 'crucify' that only Matthew supplies.
provenance.significance: Matthew 20:19 is the passion prediction that specifies who does the scourging: 'shall deliver him to the Gentiles to mock, and to scourge, and to crucify him.' Jacob is in the middle of a gloss on a prophecy about the Gentiles — the verse he has just read promises that kings and queens will nurse Israel — and three verses later he will bless the Gentiles who repent. The KJV verse he reaches for to describe the crucifixion is the one that hands Jesus to the Gentiles to be crucified, which is the tension the whole exposition is managing.

links.note: 'They should scourge him and crucify him.' The two verbs occur together in exactly one KJV verse and Jacob has them in Matthew's order, with the pronoun distributed to each verb in the manner of Mark 10:34 and Luke 18:33 ('shall scourge him... and shall'). So the pairing is Matthew's and the syntax is the other two synoptics'; the composite records both. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages.
links.text: And shall deliver him to the Gentiles to mock, and to scourge, and to crucify him: and the third day he shall rise again.

pericopes.text: And after that they have hardened their hearts and stiffened their necks against the Holy One of Israel, behold, the judgments of the Holy One of Israel shall come upon them. And the day cometh that they shall be smitten and afflicted.

provenance.other: 'Stiffened' occurs in exactly one KJV verse in any form — 2 Chronicles 36:13, of Zedekiah: 'but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart from turning unto the LORD God of Israel.' It is a KJV hapax. 'Hardened their hearts' is likewise a singleton (1 Samuel 6:6, of Pharaoh and the Egyptians), but only 2 Chronicles 36:13 has the two verbs together, and only it has 'stiffened' at all. The KJV's usual idiom is 'hardened their necks' (2 Kings 17:14, Nehemiah 9:16-17, Jeremiah 19:15) or 'stiffnecked' (nine verses); Jacob has neither.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's strongest find and it is a matter of one word. The only man in the King James Bible who stiffens his neck is Zedekiah, in whose first year Lehi's family left Jerusalem (1 Nephi 1:4), and the verses immediately after his are the content of Jacob's preceding sentence: 36:17, the Chaldees who 'slew their young men with the sword', and 36:20, 'them that had escaped from the sword carried he away to Babylon' — which is 6:8's 'have been slain and carried away captive' — followed at 36:22-23 by Cyrus's decree, which is 6:9's 'they should return again'. Jacob is glossing Isaiah, but the paragraph he glosses it with is walking down 2 Chronicles 36: the slaying, the captivity, the return, and then the hardened heart and stiffened neck that caused all three. The metalepsis is that the words the KJV uses for the last king of Judah refusing Jeremiah are the words Jacob uses for Jerusalem refusing the Messiah. The same verse the same way — twice, six centuries apart, in the vocabulary of one hapax.

links.note: 'After that they have hardened their hearts and stiffened their necks against the Holy One of Israel.' 'Stiffened' is a King James hapax legomenon and it belongs to Zedekiah at 2 Chronicles 36:13, where it stands beside 'hardened his heart' in the same clause — the same pair Jacob has, pluralised from one king to a people. The KJV has an ordinary idiom available for this ('hardened their necks', four verses; 'stiffnecked', nine) and Jacob does not use it. Read the surrounding paragraph and the borrowing is not isolated: 6:8-9's slaying, captivity and return are 2 Chronicles 36:17, 36:20 and 36:22-23 in order. Invisible to the n-gram stream, which proposed only Jeremiah 46:21's 'come upon them and' for this verse.
links.text: And he also rebelled against king Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God: but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart from turning unto the LORD God of Israel.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, after they are driven to and fro, for thus saith the angel, many shall be afflicted in the flesh and shall not be suffered to perish, because of the prayers of the faithful: wherefore, they shall be scattered, and smitten, and hated; nevertheless, the Lord will be merciful unto them, that when they shall come to the knowledge of their Redeemer, they shall be gathered together again to the lands of their inheritance.

And blessed are the Gentiles, they of whom the prophet hath written: for behold, if it so be that they shall repent and fight not against Zion, and do not unite themselves to that great and abominable church, they shall be saved: for the Lord God will fulfil his covenants which he hath made unto his children; and for this cause, the prophet hath written these things.

Wherefore, they that fight against Zion and the covenant people of the Lord, shall lick up the dust of their feet; and the people of the Lord shall not be ashamed. For the people of the Lord are they which wait for him: for they still wait for the coming of the Messiah.

provenance.route: Isaiah 49:23, quoted at 2 Nephi 6:7 and re-applied → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Lick up the dust' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 49:23. Separately, 'the dust of their feet' — the third-person form Jacob substitutes for Isaiah's 'thy feet' — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:51, where Paul and Barnabas shake it off against those who rejected them and turn to the Gentiles.
provenance.significance: This is what an exposition does that a transcription cannot, and it is why the chapter was adjudicated by hand. Isaiah's promise is addressed to Zion in the second person and is unambiguously a blessing: your attendants will bow so low that they lick the dust at your feet. Jacob keeps the KJV's singular idiom and changes one pronoun, and it becomes a curse on a third party — 'they that fight against Zion... shall lick up the dust of their feet'. Grammatically 'their feet' now most naturally means the enemies' own feet, so the humiliation is reflexive: they eat their own dust. Whether the shift is deliberate or a slip of the pronoun, the sentence Jacob produces is not the sentence he read out six verses earlier, and the same operation is run on the second half of the verse ('they shall not be ashamed that wait for me' becomes 'the people of the Lord shall not be ashamed. For the people of the Lord are they which wait for him'), where second-person address is converted to third-person definition.

links.note: Jacob quotes Isaiah 49:23 at 6:7 and takes it apart at 6:13. Both of its distinctive clauses come back — the KJV singleton 'lick up the dust' and 'they shall not be ashamed... that wait for me' — and both are turned from address into exposition, with 'thy feet' becoming 'their feet' and 'me' becoming 'him'. The 1830's 'they which wait for him' preserves the relative pronoun of the KJV's 'they... that wait for me'; 1920 changed 'which' to 'who', which is the direction of travel through most of this chapter. Recorded as an allusion rather than a quotation because nothing is reproduced as a clause; the whole point is that the clauses have been rebuilt.
links.text: And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.

pericopes.text: And behold, according to the words of the prophet, the Messiah will set himself again the second time, to recover them; wherefore, he will manifest himself unto them in power and great glory, unto the destruction of their enemies, when that day cometh when they shall believe in him; and none will he destroy that believeth in him.

provenance.other: 'Second time to recover' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11. The bare 'again the second time' occurs in six, and is unremarkable; it is the infinitive that makes the count absolute. 2 Nephi 21:11 transcribes Isaiah 11:11 in full later in this same book.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Isaiah 11:11 has 'the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people'; Jacob has 'the Messiah will set himself again the second time, to recover them'. The hand becomes the person. In Isaiah the second recovery is an act God performs; in Jacob it is a second coming God undergoes, and the verse is immediately continued with 'he will manifest himself unto them in power and great glory' — which is the synoptic parousia, not Isaiah's regathering from Assyria and Egypt. A restoration oracle has been read as an advent oracle by deleting one noun.

links.note: 'The Messiah will set himself again the second time, to recover them.' Hardy cross-references Isaiah 11:11 here, and the wording bears him out: 'second time to recover' is a KJV singleton. What the catalogue adds is the shape of the change — 'set his hand' → 'set himself' — which is the same reflexive move the chapter makes at 6:9 with 1 Timothy 3:16's passive. Note that Isaiah 11 is transcribed in full at 2 Nephi 21, so this is the chapter re-entering as argument in the same book that will later reproduce it as text; recurrenceRefs points there.
links.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

provenance.route: Matthew 24:30 / Luke 21:27 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Power and great glory' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:30 and Luke 21:27, and both are the parousia of the Son of man in the synoptic apocalypse. Nothing in Jacob's clause discriminates between them, since the four words are identical in both and he keeps neither the cloud nor the sign.
provenance.significance: Jacob has just rewritten Isaiah 11:11's second recovery as the Messiah's second coming, and the phrase he completes the sentence with is the KJV's phrase for exactly that event. The two halves of 6:14 are an Isaiah restoration oracle and a synoptic advent oracle welded at the caesura, and the weld is what makes the reading possible: 'again the second time, to recover them; wherefore, he will manifest himself unto them in power and great glory.' The next clause — 'unto the destruction of their enemies' — belongs to neither and is Jacob's own.

links.note: 'He will manifest himself unto them in power and great glory.' Four words shared with the two KJV verses that have them, both describing the coming of the Son of man; the immediately preceding clause is Isaiah 11:11 (see the link above), so the composite is doing real work here rather than hedging. Recorded as an allusion, not a quotation — four words is short, and Jacob keeps none of the surrounding apocalyptic furniture.
links.text: And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.

pericopes.text: And they that believe not in him, shall be destroyed, both by fire, and by tempest, and by earthquakes, and by bloodsheds, and by pestilence, and by famine. And they shall know that the Lord is God, the Holy One of Israel:

provenance.route: Luke 21:11 / Matthew 24:7 (the earthquakes, famines and pestilences) + Isaiah 29:6 (the fire and tempest) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Famines, and pestilences' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:7 and Luke 21:11, and both list them beside earthquakes — which is Jacob's triad. 'Great earthquakes' is a Luke 21:11 singleton. Isaiah 29:6 supplies the other half: 'with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with storm and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire.' Isaiah 29:6 is itself transcribed later in this book, at 2 Nephi 27:2.
provenance.significance: Jacob's six-item list is welded from the two KJV catalogues of eschatological disaster, and it keeps the item each of them has that the other does not: fire and tempest from Isaiah 29, famine and pestilence from the synoptic apocalypse, earthquake from both. The sixth item, 'bloodsheds', is in no KJV list at all. Having just quoted a synoptic advent at 6:14, he supplies its judgments from Isaiah as well as from Luke — which is the chapter's method throughout: Isaiah read through the Gospels and the Gospels supplied from Isaiah.

links.note: 'Both by fire, and by tempest, and by earthquakes, and by bloodsheds, and by pestilence, and by famine.' No single KJV verse has this list, and the machine stream proposed nothing at all for the verse. The two verses that come closest are Luke 21:11 and Isaiah 29:6, and between them they account for five of the six items; the pairing 'famines, and pestilences' is a two-verse KJV rarity and both of those verses are the synoptic apocalypse. Proposed under CONVENTIONS §0a: the individual words are common and the case rests on the composition of the list rather than on any string.
links.whyNot: Every item in the list is ordinary KJV disaster vocabulary, and lists of judgments are a biblical commonplace — Ezekiel's 'sword, famine, pestilence' triad alone recurs more than a dozen times. Nothing here is a verbal run, and a reader who declined the whole row would be within their rights.
links.text: And great earthquakes shall be in divers places, and famines, and pestilences; and fearful sights and great signs shall there be from heaven.

pericopes.text: for shall the prey be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captive delivered?

provenance.route: Isaiah 49:24, by way of the reading already at 1 Nephi 21:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Lawful captive' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, this one. Two departures, pulling opposite ways: the KJV's 'Shall the prey be taken' is prefixed with 'For' in both Book of Mormon passages and in no English Bible, which is a shared non-KJV reading; but 1 Nephi 21:24 reads 'the lawful captives delivered' in the plural, and 2 Nephi 6:16 has the KJV's singular 'captive'.
provenance.significance: This is the one verse of the block where mediation can be argued rather than guessed, and the answer is mixed. The prefixed 'For' is an agreement in error — a reading neither text could have got from the KJV — which is the classic signature of one Book of Mormon passage standing behind another, so mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM. But the singular 'captive' is an agreement with the KJV against 1 Nephi 21, which the same hypothesis cannot explain. Two verses later, at 6:18, the pattern reverses again. Whatever the relation between the two Isaiah 49 passages is, it is not simple copying in either direction.

links.note: Isaiah 49:24 quoted with one added word. 'For shall the prey be taken from the mighty' agrees with 1 Nephi 21:24 against every English Bible; 'the lawful captive delivered' agrees with the KJV against 1 Nephi 21:24's plural. The mediation field records the first of those and the note records the second, because the two cannot both be right and the catalogue should say so rather than pick.

pericopes.text: But thus saith the Lord: Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and the prey of the terrible shall be delivered: for the Mighty God shall deliver his covenant people. For thus saith the Lord: I will contend with them that contendeth with thee,

provenance.other: 'Captives of the mighty' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so do 'the prey of the terrible' and 'contendeth with thee'; all three are this one. Three departures: an interpolation of thirteen words — 'for the Mighty God shall deliver his covenant people. For thus saith the Lord' — in place of the KJV's single 'for'; 'him that contendeth' → 'them that contendeth', which leaves a plural subject with a singular verb; and the omission of the KJV's closing clause 'and I will save thy children', which 1 Nephi 21:25 keeps. 'The mighty God' is not this verse's phrase: it occurs in seven KJV verses, of which Isaiah 9:6 ('his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God') and Isaiah 10:21 ('the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God') are the two in Isaiah, and both are transcribed later in this book at 2 Nephi 19:6 and 20:21.
provenance.significance: The interpolation is the whole finding, and it does two things at once. It supplies a subject — the KJV's 'for' leaves the deliverance to the bare first person, and Jacob names the deliverer 'the Mighty God', which is the messianic title of Isaiah 9:6 imported into Isaiah 49. And it re-opens the quotation formula: 'For thus saith the Lord' is inserted mid-verse, so that the second half of Isaiah 49:25 is re-announced as a fresh oracle. Set that beside the omission of 'and I will save thy children' and the shape of the edit is clear: the children of Zion have been replaced by 'his covenant people', which is the term Jacob has been using since 6:13, and the verse has been re-aimed from a mother's family to a covenant body.

links.note: Isaiah 49:25 with the largest departure in the chapter. Where the KJV reads 'shall be delivered: for I will contend with him that contendeth with thee, and I will save thy children', Jacob reads 'shall be delivered: for the Mighty God shall deliver his covenant people. For thus saith the Lord: I will contend with them that contendeth with thee' — thirteen words interpolated, the KJV's final clause dropped, and 'him' pluralised to 'them' while the verb stays singular. 1 Nephi 21:25 has none of this and reproduces the KJV exactly, so the two Book of Mormon witnesses to Isaiah 49:25 are not the same text. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 49:25 at this verse.
links.text: But thus saith the LORD, Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and the prey of the terrible shall be delivered: for I will contend with him that contendeth with thee, and I will save thy children.

pericopes.text: and I will feed them that oppress thee, with their own flesh; and they shall be drunken with their own blood, as with sweet wine; and all flesh shall know that I the Lord am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.

provenance.other: 'With their own blood' and 'all flesh shall know' are each KJV singletons, both in this verse. 'The mighty One of Jacob' occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 49:26 and Isaiah 60:16, whose second half is verbally identical to this one's. The significant reading is a small conjunction: the KJV has 'with their own flesh; AND they shall be drunken', 1 Nephi 21:26 drops the 'and', and 2 Nephi 6:18 restores it — an agreement with the KJV against the earlier Book of Mormon passage. The 1830's 'Saviour' is the KJV spelling; 1920 changed it to 'Savior'.
provenance.significance: Two verses after 6:16, where the shared 'For' argued that 1 Nephi 21 stood behind this quotation, the conjunction argues the other way: 2 Nephi 6:18 has a KJV reading that 1 Nephi 21:26 does not have, so it cannot have been copied from it here. Taken with 6:7's 'faces', which departs from both, the block's five verses agree with the KJV, with 1 Nephi 21, and with neither, in no consistent pattern. That is a real result about the two Isaiah 49 passages and it is only visible because the catalogue collates the second one against the first rather than treating it as a repeat.

links.note: Isaiah 49:26 essentially verbatim, and the closing title — 'the Mighty One of Jacob' — is capitalised in the 1830 where the KJV has 'the mighty One'. The verse carries three of the chapter's KJV singletons in eighteen words. Its interest is textual rather than exegetical: it restores a conjunction that 1 Nephi 21:26 had dropped, which is the counter-evidence to the mediation argued at 6:16, and the provenance note sets the two side by side.

pericopes.text: And now, my beloved brethren, I have read these things that ye might know concerning the covenants of the Lord; that he hath covenanted with all the House of Israel;

that he hath spoken unto the Jews, by the mouth of his holy prophets, even from the beginning down, from generation to generation, until the time cometh that they shall be restored to the true Church and fold of God; when they shall be gathered home to the lands of their inheritance, and shall be established in all their lands of promise.

links.text: As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began:

provenance.other: “by the mouth of his holy prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:70. The one near neighbour is Acts 3:21, which reads “by the mouth of all his holy prophets”; Jacob has no “all”.
provenance.alternative: Acts 3:21, on the subject matter rather than the wording.
provenance.significance: The two verses divide the sentence between them. Jacob's wording is Zacharias's — the seven-word run without Peter's “all” — while Jacob's subject is Peter's: the restoration of Israel to its own. Acts 3:21 is “the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets”, and Jacob's clause runs on to “until the time cometh that they shall be restored”. Recovering the Acts context also recovers what stands two verses later at Acts 3:22-23, the Deuteronomy 18 prophet-like-Moses oracle that 1 Nephi 22:20 takes in its Acts form. The seam between the two verses is where the interest is: the phrasing of the one, the argument of the other.

links.note: Jacob's summary of prophetic testimony — “he hath spoken unto the Jews, by the mouth of his holy prophets, even from the beginning down” — reproduces seven consecutive words of Luke 1:70 exactly. This is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is catalogued as an allusion, but the run is verbatim and the phrase is a KJV singleton, and the Benedictus is the KJV's one place where prophetic speech, the covenant with the fathers and Israel's deliverance stand in a single sentence — which is precisely the three-part subject of 2 Nephi 9:1-2. Note also the tail: Luke has “which have been since the world began”, Acts 3:21 “since the world began”, and Jacob “even from the beginning down, from generation to generation”, which paraphrases the same idea in the KJV's own register without taking either wording.

pericopes.text: Behold, my beloved brethren, I speak unto you these things that ye may rejoice, and lift up your heads forever, because of the blessings which the Lord God shall bestow upon your children.
For I know that thou hast searched much, many of you, to know of things to come; wherefore I know that ye know that our flesh must waste away and die; nevertheless, in our bodies, we shall see God.

links.text: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:

provenance.other: “in my flesh shall I see God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 19:26.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing acquires its argument. Job 19:25-26 is the KJV's locus classicus for bodily resurrection — “I know that my redeemer liveth … yet in my flesh shall I see God” — and it is spoken by a man insisting on vindication against friends who have told him he is wrong. Jacob is two days into a temple sermon to a divided people and is about to spend fifty verses on the resurrection of the body; he opens the argument by putting Job's certainty into the first person plural. The turn from Job's “my flesh” to “our bodies” is the whole rhetorical move: the one man's private hope of seeing God in his own flesh becomes a congregation's.

links.note: “Our flesh must waste away and die; nevertheless, in our bodies, we shall see God.” Both halves of Job 19:26 are here in order — the body destroyed, and then God seen in the body — and the second half is a KJV singleton. Jacob's substitution of “bodies” for “flesh” is not a weakening of the link but a consequence of his own first clause, which has already spent “flesh” on the corpse (“our flesh must waste away”); having used the KJV's word for what dies, he needs another for what sees. The 1830 reads “thou hast searched much” at the head of the verse, second person singular against the plural “many of you” that follows, and 1920 regularised it to “ye”; the 1830's awkwardness is the older reading.

pericopes.text: Yea, and I know that ye know, that in the body he shall shew himself unto they at Jerusalem, from whence we came; for it is expedient that it should be among them; for it behoveth the Great Creator that he suffereth himself to become subject unto man, in the flesh, and die for all men, that all men might become subject unto him.

For as death hath passed upon all men, to fulfil the merciful plan of the Great Creator, there must needs be a power of resurrection, and the resurrection must needs come unto man by reason of the fall; and the fall came by reason of transgression; and because man became fallen, they were cut off from the presence of the Lord;

links.text: Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:

provenance.other: “death passed upon all men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 5:12.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis of the plainest kind. Romans 5:12 is a protasis with no apodosis — Paul's “as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men” breaks off and is not completed until 5:18-19, and the completion is that by one man's righteousness the free gift came upon all men. Jacob borrows the broken protasis and supplies his own apodosis on the spot: “as death hath passed upon all men … there must needs be a power of resurrection.” The suspended sentence in Romans is finished in 2 Nephi, and finished with the Adam-Christ symmetry that Paul finishes it with. Whatever else it is, this is a reader of Romans 5 who knows where the sentence is going.

links.note: Five words verbatim, and the one KJV verse they come from. Jacob's clause reads “For as death hath passed upon all men, to fulfil the merciful plan of the Great Creator, there must needs be a power of resurrection” — Paul's “so” becomes “as”, which converts a conclusion into a premise, and the rest of the verse then argues from the fall to the resurrection exactly as Romans 5:12-21 does. The run is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and this is not one of his passages; it is catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the singleton rather than the length, per CONVENTIONS §2. The chapter's whole atonement argument is built on the Pauline pair Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, and this is where the first of them enters.

pericopes.text: wherefore it must needs be an infinite atonement; save it should be an infinite atonement, this corruption could not put on incorruption. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man, must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.

links.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “corruptible must put on incorruption” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:53; “put on incorruption” occurs in exactly two, 15:53 and 15:54.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 15:53-54 is the verse on which Paul's resurrection chapter turns from argument to triumph — the putting on of incorruption is what makes “Death is swallowed up in victory” sayable. Jacob takes the clause and negates it: “save it should be an infinite atonement, this corruption could not put on incorruption.” The borrowed words are used to state the condition under which Paul's sentence would have been false. Recovering the context recovers what 15:54 goes on to promise, and Jacob's next three verses (8-13) are that promise: the flesh rises, hell delivers up its captives, all men become incorruptible and immortal.

links.note: The one substitution carries the argument. Paul writes “this corruptible must put on incorruption”, an adjective naming the perishable body; the 1830 reads “this corruption could not put on incorruption”, an abstract noun naming the state, which is what lets the sentence be about the atonement rather than about a body. The 1830 already has “corruption” — this is not a later editorial drift — and “incorruptible, and immortal” returns at 9:13 to complete the pair 1 Corinthians 15:53 makes (incorruption and immortality). Note that Romans 5:12 entered one verse earlier at 9:6: the two Pauline resurrection chapters arrive together and in the order in which a reader working from a Bible would meet them.

pericopes.text: O the wisdom of God! his mercy and grace! For behold, if the flesh should rise no more, our spirits must become subject to that Angel which fell from before the presence of the Eternal God, and became the Devil, to rise no more.

links.text: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!

provenance.other: “O the depth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — a genuine singleton, not merely the best of three. Psalm 107:26 and Micah 7:19 read “the depths” (plural, of literal water), not “the depth”; only Romans 11:33 has the exact singular noun in this exclamation.
provenance.significance: Romans 11:33 is where Paul breaks off an argument about Israel's rejection and restoration to exclaim at the wisdom of God, and 2 Nephi 9 is an argument about Israel's restoration (9:1-2) punctuated by exactly such exclamations — six of them, at 9:8, 9:10, 9:13, 9:17, 9:19 and 9:20. The doxology is not decoration in either place: it is what an argument about covenant reversal does when it reaches a point it cannot argue past.

links.note: “O the wisdom of God! his mercy and grace!” The KJV has one exclamation of this construction — vocative O, an abstract attribute, of God — and it is Romans 11:33's “O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” Jacob's is not a verbal reproduction; the shared material is the syntax and the pairing of God's wisdom with his mercy, which Romans 11:30-32 has just spent three verses on (“that he might have mercy upon all”). The link is recorded at the first of the six exclamations and the rest are listed as recurrences rather than given rows of their own.
links.whyNot: No content word is shared beyond “God” and “wisdom”, both far too common to point anywhere. The form could as easily be Jacob's own, and the exclamatory O is available from the Psalms in bulk. This is graded moderate as a formal echo, and a reader who declines it loses nothing else in the chapter.

pericopes.text: And our spirits must have become like unto him, and we become Devils, Angels to a Devil, to be shut out from the presence of our God, and to remain with the father of lies, in misery, like unto himself; yea, to that being who beguiled our first parents; who transformeth himself nigh unto an angel of light, and stirreth up the children of men unto secret combinations of murder, and all manner of secret works of darkness.

links.text: And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.

provenance.other: “an angel of light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 11:14.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about false apostles: the transformation into an angel of light is offered as the reason “his ministers also be transformed as the ministers of righteousness” (11:15). Jacob is warning a congregation against a being who “stirreth up the children of men unto secret combinations of murder”, and he reaches for the KJV's one verse about Satan disguised as a messenger of God. The suppressed half of the source is the half about the disguised ministers, which is the danger a sermon delivered from a temple would have most reason to name and does not.

links.note: “Who transformeth himself nigh unto an angel of light.” The phrase is a KJV singleton and the subject is the same being. Two departures are worth recording. Paul's verb is passive — “Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” — where Jacob's is active and reflexive, which makes the disguise a thing the devil does rather than a thing done to him; and Jacob's “nigh unto” is a hedge with no counterpart in the KJV, conceding that the resemblance is not complete. Both changes push in the same direction, toward an agent who counterfeits and does not quite succeed.

links.text: Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.

provenance.other: “father of it”, the KJV's phrase for the devil as author of lying, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:44.
provenance.significance: John 8:44 holds in one sentence the two things Jacob's verse holds: “He was a murderer from the beginning … he is a liar, and the father of it.” Jacob's clause runs “to remain with the father of lies, in misery … and stirreth up the children of men unto secret combinations of murder”, and the pairing of the lie with the murder is not a general association — it is John's, in John's order, from the verse where Jesus tells his hearers whose children they are. The metalepsis is in the address: John 8:44 is spoken to covenant Israelites who have claimed Abraham as their father, which is exactly Jacob's audience.

links.note: The KJV has no phrase “father of lies”; it has John 8:44's “he is a liar, and the father of it”, which the Book of Mormon compresses into the noun phrase later English would settle on. Two independent contacts sit in one verse of John and one verse of Jacob — the lie and its fatherhood, and the murder from the beginning — and the same chapter of John returns at 2 Nephi 9:38 (“wo unto all they that die in their sins”, John 8:21, 24). A chapter that touches John 8 twice, thirty verses apart, at its two most distinctive phrases, is reading John 8.

pericopes.text: O how great the goodness of our God, who prepareth a way for our escape from the grasp of this awful monster; yea, that monster, death and hell, which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit.
And because of the way of deliverance of our God, the Holy One of Israel, this death, of which I have spoken, which is the temporal, shall deliver up its dead; which death is the grave.

And this death of which I have spoken, which is the spiritual death, shall deliver up its dead; which spiritual death is hell; wherefore, death and hell must deliver up its dead, and hell must deliver up its captive spirits, and the grave must deliver up its captive bodies, and the bodies and the spirits of men will be restored, one to the other: and it is by the power of the resurrection of the Holy One of Israel.

links.text: And the sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works.

provenance.other: “death and hell delivered up the dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:13.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's structural borrowing and it explains a puzzle. Revelation 20:13-14 runs: death and hell deliver up their dead, they are judged, and then “death and hell were cast into the lake of fire”. 2 Nephi 9 does the same three things in the same order — death and hell deliver up their dead here at 9:12, the judgment follows at 9:15, and the lake of fire and brimstone arrives at 9:16 and again at 9:19 and 9:26. So the “awful monster, death and hell” that Jacob names at 9:10 and cannot stop naming is not a free-standing image: it is John's paired personification, borrowed with the plot it belongs to. Recovering Revelation 20 recovers the reason the lake of fire has to come three verses later.

links.note: Jacob's “death and hell must deliver up its dead” reproduces the KJV's clause with one change of number, and the surrounding sentences unpack it: “hell must deliver up its captive spirits, and the grave must deliver up its captive bodies”. The 1830's singular “its dead” against a plural subject was corrected to “their” in 1920 — the sort of grammatical roughness the first edition preserves and later editions smooth, and here the direction of the change is away from the source, since the KJV reads “the dead which were in them”. The link is placed at 9:12, where the wording is, rather than at 9:10 where the monster is first named.

pericopes.text: O how great the plan of our God! For on the other hand, the paradise of God must deliver up the spirits of the righteous, and the grave deliver up the body of the righteous; and the spirit and the body is restored to itself again, and all men become incorruptible, and immortal, and they are living souls, having a perfect knowledge like unto us, in the flesh; save it be that our knowledge shall be perfect;

links.text: He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.

provenance.other: “paradise of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 2:7.
provenance.significance: In Revelation 2:7 the paradise of God is where the tree of life stands and is promised to him that overcometh; in 2 Nephi 9:13 it is a holding place that “must deliver up the spirits of the righteous” at the resurrection. The borrowing has moved the phrase from a destination to a waiting room, and the sense it takes is Luke 23:43's rather than John's — the paradise a dying man enters today. The two-word phrase carries the geography of one text and the doctrine of another.

links.note: The disembodied-spirits paradise of 2 Nephi 9:13 is named with the KJV's one occurrence of “paradise of God”, from the letter to Ephesus. This is graded moderate because two words, however rare their combination, are thin evidence, and because the chapter has already shown it will take an eschatological furnishing from Revelation and use it structurally (Revelation 20:13 one verse earlier). That prior borrowing is the reason to take this one seriously: the paradise arrives in a sentence built out of the same book's twentieth chapter.
links.whyNot: Two words. “Paradise” alone appears in three KJV verses and any of them would license the idea; only the genitive construction is distinctive, and a writer with Luke 23:43 in mind could arrive at “paradise of God” without Revelation.

links.text: And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.

provenance.route: Genesis 2:7 → 1 Corinthians 15:45 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “living soul” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Genesis 2:7, 1 Corinthians 15:45 and Revelation 16:3. tools/mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between Genesis 2:7 and 1 Corinthians 15:45 at any point 2 Nephi 9:13 reproduces, so the mediation is argued from context rather than from wording.
provenance.significance: The phrase has been inverted in transit. For Paul, “the first man Adam was made a living soul” is the *low* term of the contrast: the living soul is the natural body that dies, set against “the last Adam … a quickening spirit”. Jacob applies it to the resurrected — “all men become incorruptible, and immortal, and they are living souls” — which is Paul's own vocabulary used for Paul's opposite. That is not a misreading so much as a collapse of the antithesis, and it is the kind of thing that shows a source being used rather than merely shared.

links.note: The mediation is the finding here, and the tool cannot settle it: Genesis 2:7 and 1 Corinthians 15:45 do not differ at “living soul”, so the wording is neutral between them. The context is not. The sentence around the phrase is 1 Corinthians 15's and nowhere else's — “incorruptible, and immortal” is 15:53's pair, the resurrection body is 15's subject, and 15:53 has already been used at 2 Nephi 9:7 six verses earlier. Genesis 2:7 supplies the phrase to Paul; Paul supplies it to Jacob. Recorded as OT-via-NT on that argument, and a reader who prefers direct-OT is disagreeing with an inference, not with a word count.

pericopes.text: wherefore, we shall have a perfect knowledge of all our guilt, and our uncleanness, and our nakedness; and the righteous shall have a perfect knowledge of their enjoyment, and their righteousness, being clothed with purity, yea, even with the robe of righteousness.

links.text: I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.

provenance.other: “robe of righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 61:10.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 61:10 is a garment verse in a chapter about reversal — the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness are given to those who had ashes and mourning. Jacob has just built the same reversal out of clothing: the wicked receive “a perfect knowledge of all our guilt, and our uncleanness, and our nakedness”, and the righteous “their enjoyment, and their righteousness, being clothed with purity”. The nakedness the borrowing implies is Isaiah's unspoken opposite, and the resurrection-judgment scene in which Jacob sets it makes the clothing an eschatological verdict rather than a festal ornament.

links.note: A KJV singleton, taken with its verb of clothing intact and set against a nakedness the source does not mention. This is the machine stream's one solid proposal in the chapter's first half (it scored Isaiah 61:10 at 9:14 on a five-word run), and it is right: nothing else in the KJV pairs a robe with righteousness. Note that Jacob does not take Isaiah's other garment, the “garments of salvation” of the same verse — a selective borrower, not a copyist.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass, that when all men shall have passed from this first death unto life, insomuch as they have become immortal, they must appear before the judgment seat of the Holy One of Israel; and then cometh the judgment, and then must they be judged according to the holy judgment of God.

links.text: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.

provenance.other: “appear before the judgment seat” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 5:10; “judgment seat” alone occurs in eleven, most of them Roman magistrates in Acts. Romans 14:10, the near neighbour, reads “stand before the judgment seat”.
provenance.significance: Paul's judgment seat is Christ's, and the clause that follows it — “that every one may receive the things done in his body” — is a judgment on embodied deeds. Jacob has spent nine verses arguing that the body must be restored to the spirit before judgment can occur, and he reaches the judgment seat only once every man has been made immortal: “when all men shall have passed from this first death unto life, insomuch as they have become immortal, they must appear before the judgment seat.” The borrowed phrase arrives with Paul's reason for it already supplied by the argument.

links.note: The verb decides between the two Pauline judgment-seat verses. Romans 14:10 has men *stand* before it, 2 Corinthians 5:10 has them *appear* before it, and Jacob's “must appear before the judgment seat” takes the second — and takes “must all” with it (“all men … they must appear”). The 1830 prints “judgment seat” as two words and 1920 hyphenates it to “judgment-seat”, which is a small piece of evidence for the direction of transmission: the first edition has the KJV's typography, and the later edition has the nineteenth-century compound.

pericopes.text: And assuredly, as the Lord liveth, for the Lord God hath spoken it, and it is his eternal word, which cannot pass away, that they which are righteous, shall be righteous still, and they which are filthy, shall be filthy still; wherefore, they which are filthy, are the Devil and his angels; and they shall go away into everlasting fire, prepared for them; and their torment is a lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever, and hath no end.

links.text: He that is unjust, let him be unjust still: and he which is filthy, let him be filthy still: and he that is righteous, let him be righteous still: and he that is holy, let him be holy still.

provenance.other: “filthy still” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 22:11, which also supplies “righteous still”.
provenance.significance: Revelation 22:11 stands eleven verses from the end of the Bible and is the sealing-up of moral destiny: after it there is nothing but the invitation and the curse on adders. Jacob quotes it as the ground of an appeal to men who can still change — “that they which are righteous, shall be righteous still, and they which are filthy, shall be filthy still” — and then spends thirty-five verses urging repentance. The borrowed verse says the door is shut; the sermon it is quoted in is the door being held open, and the tension is not resolved.

links.note: Both halves of Revelation 22:11's second pair, in the KJV's own words and in the KJV's own antithetical construction, introduced by “it is his eternal word, which cannot pass away”. The KJV has jussives (“let him be righteous still”) and Jacob has futures (“shall be righteous still”), which converts John's permission into a prediction — the difference between a decree ratifying what men have become and a law about what they will be. The 1830's “they which are righteous” was modernised to “those who” in 1920; the first edition keeps the KJV's relative pronoun and shows the borrowing more plainly.

links.text: Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

provenance.other: “the devil and his angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:41.
provenance.significance: The finding is the division of labour with 9:18. Matthew 25:31-46 is one judgment scene with two halves, a curse on the left hand (25:41, “Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels”) and a blessing on the right (25:34, “inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”). Jacob takes the curse here and the blessing two verses later, keeps the shared word “prepared” in both, and reverses Matthew's order so that his own sermon ends on the blessing. The sheep-and-goats scene has been dismantled and reassembled around Jacob's antithesis, and neither half is quoted without the other.

links.note: Two runs from Matthew 25:41 — “the devil and his angels” and “into everlasting fire, prepared for” — and a third from 25:46, “shall go away into everlasting”, whose noun Jacob replaces (Matthew's “everlasting punishment” for Matthew's own “everlasting fire”). The changed word in 25:41 is the beneficiary: Matthew's fire is prepared *for the devil and his angels*, and Jacob's is prepared “for them”, the filthy, having identified them with the devil and his angels in the preceding clause. That identification is Jacob's contribution and it is what lets one verse of Matthew do the work of two.

links.text: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

provenance.route: Revelation 14:10-11 and 20:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “ascendeth up for ever and ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:11. Revelation 14:10 supplies “tormented with fire and brimstone”; Revelation 20:10 supplies “the lake of fire and brimstone”.
provenance.significance: Jacob's sentence — “their torment is a lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever” — fuses two verses that the KJV keeps six chapters apart, and takes from each what the other lacks. Revelation 14:10-11 has the torment and the ascending, but its column is smoke and its fire is not a lake; Revelation 20:10 has the lake of fire and brimstone, but nothing ascends from it. What ascends in the Book of Mormon is flames, which is in neither. The composite is the evidence: a writer working from one verse does not produce a phrase that requires two.

links.note: The 1830 reads “whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever”, with a plural subject and a singular verb that 1920 tidied to “flame”. The verb is the borrowed word — the KJV's one “ascendeth up for ever and ever” has smoke for its subject, and substituting flames for smoke is what forced the grammatical roughness the first edition preserves and the later edition removed. This is 1830 evidence of the useful kind: the awkwardness is a fingerprint of the substitution.

pericopes.text: O the greatness and the justice of our God! For he executeth all his words, and they have gone forth out of his mouth, and his law must be fulfilled.

But, behold, the righteous, the saints of the Holy One of Israel, they which have believed in the Holy One of Israel; they which have endured the crosses of the world, and despised the shame of it; they shall inherit the Kingdom of God, which was prepared for them from the foundation of the world: and their joy shall be full forever.

links.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.

provenance.other: “despising the shame” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 12:2.
provenance.significance: In Hebrews the one who endures the cross and despises the shame is Jesus, and the saints are told to look at him; in 2 Nephi it is the saints themselves who “have endured the crosses of the world, and despised the shame of it”. The transfer is the point, and it is the transfer Hebrews 12:1-3 is arguing for — the cloud of witnesses, the race set before us, the author and finisher of faith held up as the pattern. Jacob has taken the conclusion Hebrews draws and stated it as though it were the premise.

links.note: Two clauses of Hebrews 12:2 in Hebrews' order — the cross endured, the shame despised — with each term pluralised or possessed: “the crosses of the world”, “the shame of it”. The pluralised cross is the departure that matters, since it converts a single historical execution into a class of hardships, which is precisely what a sermon exhorting a congregation needs it to be. Jacob is not quoting a christological verse about Christ; he is quoting it about his hearers, and the KJV singleton is what shows the verse is in view at all.

links.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

provenance.other: “prepared for you from the foundation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:34; “from the foundation of the world” alone occurs in six.
provenance.significance: See the note at 9:16. The two halves of Matthew's judgment scene are distributed across Jacob's antithesis: the fire prepared for the devil and his angels at 9:16, the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world at 9:18, with “prepared” standing in both as it does in Matthew. What Jacob adds is the reason the righteous inherit — “they which have endured the crosses of the world” — which Matthew gives as feeding the hungry and visiting the prisoner. The frame is Matthew's and the criterion is not.

links.note: Seven words of Matthew 25:34 with one pronoun changed: “inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” becomes “they shall inherit the Kingdom of God, which was prepared for them from the foundation of the world”. The shift from second to third person follows from Jacob's syntax — Matthew's King is addressing the blessed, Jacob is describing them — and the inserted “of God” is his, since Matthew's King says only “the kingdom”. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages, catalogued as a quotation on the singleton and the verbatim run.

pericopes.text: O the greatness of the mercy of our God, the Holy One of Israel! For he delivereth his saints from that awful monster, the Devil, and death and hell, and that lake of fire and brimstone, which is endless torment.
O how great the holiness of our God! For he knoweth all things, and there is not any thing, save he know it.

And he cometh into the world that he may save all men, if they will hearken unto his voice: for behold, he suffereth the pains of all men; yea, the pains of every living creature, both men women and children, which belong to the family of Adam.—
And he suffereth this, that the resurrection might pass upon all men, that all might stand before him, at the great and judgment day.
And he commandeth all men that they must repent, and be baptised in his name, having perfect faith in the Holy One of Israel, or they cannot be saved in the Kingdom of God.

links.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “be baptized every one of you in the name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:38. Frederick observes that the exact phrase “baptized in his name”, which is Jacob's form here and at 9:24, is unique to Mormon scripture and is not found in the Bible — a real qualification to any claim of verbal dependence, and one that should be recorded against this row rather than argued away.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:38 is Peter's answer to “what shall we do?” on the day of Pentecost, and it is the KJV's one place where repentance and baptism are commanded together in a single imperative to a crowd. Jacob's “he commandeth all men that they must repent, and be baptised in his name” is that imperative turned into a report of a standing commandment. Recovering the context recovers what makes the borrowing anachronistic in an interesting rather than a trivial way: the model is not a prophecy of baptism but the first Christian administration of it.

links.note: The wording is Peter's minus the possessive: Acts 2:38 has “in the name of Jesus Christ” where Jacob has “in his name”, the referent having been supplied by the preceding verses. That difference is not incidental, and Frederick makes something of it — his discussion of 2 Nephi 9:23-24 notes that “baptized in his name” as such occurs nowhere in the Bible and is a phrase peculiar to Mormon scripture. So the case here rests on the pairing (repent + be baptized + a name) rather than on a reproduced string, which is why this is graded high rather than certain. The chapter's own next verse extends the list, and the John 1:12 row at 9:24 is where Frederick's argument properly sits.

pericopes.text: And if they will not repent and believe in his name, and be baptised in his name, and endure to the end, they must be damned; for the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, hath spoken it;

links.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: The shared material is “believe … on/in his name”. Frederick treats the phrase at 2 Nephi 9:24 as an allusion to John 1:12, notes that the pairing of “repent” with “believe in his name” occurs seven times in Mormon scripture and nowhere in the Bible, and concludes that the allusion serves a rhetorical rather than an interpretive function — echoing an authoritative text for a nineteenth-century audience rather than engaging John's argument.
provenance.significance: The interest is in what the borrowing does to the source. In John 1:12 belief on his name is sufficient and binary — those who receive him are given power to become the sons of God, and that is the whole condition. In 2 Nephi 9:24 believing in his name is one item in a list of four (repent, believe, be baptised, endure to the end), any of which can be failed. Frederick's reading is that Jacob expands John's condition into a set of requirements and thereby loses John's polarity; on that reading the echo is doing rhetorical rather than exegetical work, which is a claim about the whole Book of Mormon's use of John and not only about this verse.

links.note: This is the one row in the chapter where a scholar we hold has actually treated the passage. Frederick's chapter on the Book of Mormon's Johannine language discusses 2 Nephi 9:23-24 at length, identifies “believe in his name” as reaching back to John 1:11-12, and argues that its function is rhetorical. The catalogue records the link on his evidence and grades it moderate on ours: the shared words are four common ones in a common order, and the case rests on the Johannine formula rather than on rarity. Note that his conclusion is a deflationary one — he finds no attempt to engage John beyond the repetition of its language — so citing him here is citing an argument about the *kind* of borrowing, not a claim that John 1:12 is the only possible source.
bibliography: Frederick 2016: ch. 4, on 2 Nephi 9:23-24 and John 1:11-12

links.text: He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.

provenance.route: Mark 16:16 and Matthew 10:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “shall be damned” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:16; “endureth to the end” occurs in exactly one, Matthew 10:22.
provenance.significance: Mark 16:16 is the KJV's one sentence holding belief, baptism, salvation and damnation together, and it is a conditional with two arms. Jacob keeps both terms and collapses the arms into one: “if they will not repent and believe in his name, and be baptised in his name, and endure to the end, they must be damned.” Matthew 10:22's endurance clause is spliced in from a persecution discourse where enduring to the end is surviving betrayal by one's family — which is a harder thing than the list Jacob has made it the last item of, and the harder sense is the one his sermon has been arguing for since 9:18's crosses of the world.

links.note: Two KJV singletons in one sentence, from two Gospels, in the order Mark gives them: believe, be baptised, and then the damnation that is Mark's alternative. Jacob's verb is “must be damned”, a necessity, against Mark's simple future — consistent with the chapter's argument that the law's demands are met or not met and that justice, not caprice, decides. The single word “damned” is what makes the verse identifiable at all; “believe” and “baptised” between them fill hundreds of KJV verses, and the row would not stand on them.

pericopes.text: wherefore he hath given a law; and where there is no law given, there is no punishment; and where there is no punishment, there is no condemnation; and where there is no condemnation, the mercies of the Holy One of Israel hath claim upon them, because of the atonement: for they are delivered by the power of him:

links.text: Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression.

provenance.route: Romans 4:15 and 5:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “where no law is” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 4:15. Romans 5:13 states the same principle in different words: “sin is not imputed when there is no law”.
provenance.significance: Both Pauline verses stand inside the argument 2 Nephi 9 has been running since 9:6, and 5:13 is four verses past the “death passed upon all men” that Jacob quoted there. Paul uses the no-law principle to explain how death reigned from Adam to Moses; Jacob uses it to exempt those who never received the law from the demands of justice. The premise is Paul's and the conclusion is not — Romans is explaining a fact about history, 2 Nephi is granting a class of persons a claim on mercy.

links.note: “Where there is no law given, there is no punishment; and where there is no punishment, there is no condemnation.” The construction is Romans 4:15's — a conditional of the form *where no X, no Y*, which the KJV uses of law in that one verse — and Jacob extends it into a chain of three, each link taking the previous consequent as its antecedent. The chain is a piece of scholastic reasoning built on a Pauline formula, and the word Jacob adds at the head is “given”, which does the exempting: it is not that no law exists but that none was given to them. Graded moderate because no distinctive string is reproduced; what is borrowed is a sentence shape and a doctrine.
links.whyNot: The wording is not reproduced. Paul's terms are law and transgression; Jacob's are law, punishment and condemnation, and only “law” is shared. A reader could hold that this is common eighteenth-century covenant theology reaching Jacob by way of the pulpit rather than by way of Romans 4.

pericopes.text: for the atonement satisfieth the demands of his justice upon all those who have not the law given to them, that they are delivered from that awful monster, death and hell, and the Devil, and the lake of fire and brimstone, which is endless torment; and they are restored to that God who gave them breath, which is the Holy One of Israel.

links.text: Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.

provenance.other: “unto God who gave it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 12:7.
provenance.significance: Ecclesiastes 12:7 is a death verse — “then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” — and the return is a dissolution, the undoing of Genesis 2:7 in Genesis 2:7's own vocabulary. Jacob turns the same clause into a verse about deliverance: those without the law “are restored to that God who gave them breath”. Restored, not returned; and the breath rather than the spirit, which pulls Genesis 2:7's “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” back into a sentence Ecclesiastes had built out of it.

links.note: The distinctive material is the relative clause: God characterised as the one who gave what is now being given back. The KJV does this once. Jacob's two changes both raise the temperature — “restored” for “return”, which makes the movement a gift rather than a forfeiture, and “breath” for “it”, which names what Ecclesiastes leaves as a pronoun and names it with Genesis 2:7's word. Graded moderate: the clause is short, and a writer could reach it independently from Genesis, though not with the KJV's exact relative construction.

pericopes.text: But wo unto him that hath the law given; yea, that hath all the commandments of God, like unto us, and that transgresseth them, and that wasteth the days of his probation: for awful is his state!

O that cunning plan of the evil one! O the vainness, and the frailties, and the foolishness of men! When they are learned, they think they are wise, and they hearken not unto the counsel of God, for they set it aside, supposing they know of themselves. Wherefore, their wisdom is foolishness, and it profiteth them not. Wherefore they shall perish.

links.text: For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.

provenance.other: “the wisdom of this world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 1:20, 2:6 and 3:19 — every one of them in the same letter and the same argument.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 1-3 is a sustained attack on human wisdom as a qualification for the gospel, and 2 Nephi 9:28-29, 42-43 is the same attack with the same moves in the same order: the learned think they are wise (1 Cor 1:20, 3:18), their wisdom is foolishness with God (3:19), and the remedy is to become a fool in order to be wise (3:18). Recovering the Corinthian context recovers a qualification Jacob then supplies himself at 9:29 — “to be learned is good, if it so be that they hearken unto the counsels of God” — which is a concession Paul does not make in those chapters and which reads like a reader correcting the source's excess.

links.note: “When they are learned, they think they are wise … Wherefore, their wisdom is foolishness, and it profiteth them not.” The predicate is Paul's, from the one KJV verse that says the wisdom of this world is foolishness, and the reasoning around it is Paul's too: those who suppose they know of themselves, set against the counsel of God. The chapter returns to the same three chapters of 1 Corinthians twice more, at 9:42 (become a fool, puffed up) and by implication at 9:43, which is the signal that this is a source being worked rather than a proverb in the air. Note that Jacob has stated as a conclusion (“their wisdom is foolishness”) what Paul states as a fact about God's estimate (“foolishness with God”), dropping the qualifier that made Paul's claim bearable.

pericopes.text: But to be learned is good, if it so be that they hearken unto the counsels of God.

But wo unto the rich, which are rich as to the things of the world. For because that they are rich, they despise the poor, and they persecute the meek, and their hearts are upon their treasures; wherefore their treasure is their God. And behold, their treasure shall perish with them also.

links.text: But ye have despised the poor. Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats?

provenance.route: James 2:5-6 and 5:1, with Luke 6:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “despised the poor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 2:6; “woe unto you that are rich” occurs in exactly one, Luke 6:24; “ye rich men” occurs in exactly one, James 5:1.
provenance.significance: Jacob's woe to the rich reproduces the three elements the New Testament keeps in three different places: the woe itself (Luke 6:24), the despising of the poor (James 2:6), and the perishing of the treasure (James 5:1-3, where the rich men's gold is cankered). James 2:6 is the sharpest of them because its next clause is “do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats?” — and Jacob's chapter has stood the rich before a judgment seat fifteen verses earlier at 9:15. The suppressed half of the source is the courtroom, which the sermon has already supplied.

links.note: Three KJV singletons converge on one sentence: “wo unto the rich, which are rich as to the things of the world. For because that they are rich, they despise the poor, and they persecute the meek.” The woe-formula is Luke's, the despising of the poor is James's, and the persecution is James 2:6's oppression. Jacob's added qualification — rich “as to the things of the world” — is the same move he makes at 9:29 about learning: the condemnation is narrowed to a disposition, not the condition. James 2:5, “hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith”, supplies the terms of that narrowing.

links.text: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

provenance.other: “where your treasure is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:21 and Luke 12:34, which are verbally identical; the wording cannot decide between them.
provenance.significance: Matthew 6:21 sits between the treasures laid up in heaven and the impossibility of serving God and mammon, and Jacob's sentence draws the conclusion Matthew leaves implicit: “their hearts are upon their treasures; wherefore their treasure is their God.” The heart following the treasure becomes the treasure being the God, which is Matthew 6:24 four verses on. The borrowing has read to the end of the paragraph.

links.note: Matthew's aphorism is inverted rather than quoted — the KJV moves from treasure to heart, and Jacob from heart to treasure — but the pairing is Matthew's and it arrives with Matthew 6:24's conclusion attached. The choice of Matthew over the identical Luke 12:34 cannot be made on wording; it is made on the chapter's own habits, since 2 Nephi 9:41-42 goes on to use Matthew 7:14 and Matthew 7:8, from the same sermon and a page later in the same Gospel. That is an argument from company, not from words, and it is offered as such.

links.text: But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.

provenance.other: “money perish with thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:20.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most interesting suppressed context if it holds. Acts 8:20 is Peter to Simon Magus — “thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” — the KJV's one rebuke to a man who tried to buy what is not for sale. Twenty verses later Jacob closes his sermon with Isaiah 55:1-2, the KJV's one invitation to buy without money: “he that hath no money, come buy and eat.” A chapter that condemns the rich with the words spoken over Simon's silver and then offers wine and milk without price has arranged its own two ends around the same question, and neither Isaiah nor Acts says so.

links.note: “Their treasure shall perish with them also.” The construction is Acts 8:20's — a possession commanded to perish along with its owner — and the KJV says this once.
