The link is graded moderate and typed as an echo because Jacob's noun is “treasure” where Peter's is “money”, and because the sentence would be intelligible without the source; what recommends it is the shape (perish *with them*, not merely perish) and the chapter's return to money at 9:50-51.
links.whyNot: Only three words are shared and one of them is a preposition. “Perish” is common in the KJV and Jacob has used it three times in this passage already (9:28, 9:31, 9:32), so the verb may simply be his. A reader who declines this row loses the Simon Magus reading and nothing else.

pericopes.text: And wo unto the deaf, that will not hear: for they shall perish.
Wo unto the blind, that will not see: for they shall perish also.
Wo unto the uncircumcised of heart: for a knowledge of their iniquities shall smite them at the last day.

links.text: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that are in the utmost corners, that dwell in the wilderness: for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 9:26 / Ezekiel 44:7 / Acts 7:51 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “uncircumcised in heart” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Ezekiel 44:7, Ezekiel 44:9 and Acts 7:51; Jeremiah 9:26 has “uncircumcised in the heart”. The Book of Mormon reads “uncircumcised of heart”, which matches none of them exactly. tools/mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between Ezekiel 44:7 and Acts 7:51 at any point 2 Nephi 9:33 reproduces, so the mediation is recorded as uncertain rather than guessed.
provenance.significance: Each candidate brings a different audience. Jeremiah 9:26 is the one that says “all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart”, which is Jacob's congregation exactly; Ezekiel 44:7 uses the phrase to bar strangers from the sanctuary, which is the wrong audience for a temple sermon addressed to the covenant people themselves; Acts 7:51 is Stephen before the council, an indictment delivered by a man about to be killed for delivering it, which is the closest in rhetorical situation to a preacher who ends by shaking his garments and declaring himself rid of his hearers' blood (9:44). The phrase is one of the few in the KJV whose every occurrence is an accusation from inside the covenant.

links.note: “Wo unto the uncircumcised of heart: for a knowledge of their iniquities shall smite them at the last day.” The preposition is the problem and the reason this is graded moderate: the KJV never says “of heart”, and the three verses that say “in heart” or “in the heart” do not differ from one another at any word Jacob reproduces, so nothing in the wording can adjudicate between them. Jeremiah 9:26 is listed as the source because it alone applies the charge to the whole house of Israel, which is what Jacob is doing; Acts 7:51 and Ezekiel 44:7 are recorded as composites, and a reader who prefers either is not contradicted by any evidence this catalogue can produce.
links.whyNot: No exact string is shared. The idea of an uncircumcised heart is available from Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6 as well, in different words, and “uncircumcised” is common enough in the KJV that the collocation with heart is the only distinctive thing here.

pericopes.text: Wo unto the liar: for he shall be thrust down to hell.

links.text: And thou, Capernaum, which art exalted to heaven, shalt be thrust down to hell.

provenance.other: “thrust down to hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 10:15. The Matthean parallel at 11:23 reads “brought down to hell”, so the verb decides the source.
provenance.significance: Luke 10:15 is the woe on Capernaum: “thou, Capernaum, which art exalted to heaven, shalt be thrust down to hell.” It belongs to a series of woes on cities, which is the form Jacob is in the middle of — ten woes running from 9:27 to 9:38. And the same chapter of Luke returns at 9:43, where the things hidden from the wise and prudent are Luke 10:21's. Two of the chapter's borrowings come from a single page of Luke, and both come from the sayings the woes are made of.

links.note: A KJV singleton, taken with its verb intact, and the machine stream's best find in this chapter — the n-gram run flagged it at both 9:34 and 9:36. Matthew's parallel says “brought down to hell” and Jacob says “thrust down to hell”, so this is one of the cases where a single word settles which Gospel is in view, in the manner of the mediation tests at 1 Nephi 22:20. The phrase is used twice within four verses (of the liar at 9:34 and of the whoremonger at 9:36); the second is Jacob using his own formula and is registered as a recurrence rather than a second borrowing.

pericopes.text: Wo unto the murderer, who deliberately killeth: for he shall die.
Wo unto them who commit whoredoms: for they shall be thrust down to hell.
Yea, wo unto they that worship Idols: for the Devil of all Devils delighteth in them.
And, in fine, wo unto all they that die in their sins: for they shall return to God, and behold his face, and remain in their sins.

links.text: Then said Jesus again unto them, I go my way, and ye shall seek me, and shall die in your sins: whither I go, ye cannot come.

provenance.other: “die in your sins” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 8:21 and John 8:24, and John 8:24 has it twice.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis inverts the source. John 8:21 runs: “ye shall die in your sins: whither I go, ye cannot come” — dying in one's sins means being unable to come where Christ is. Jacob's version is the opposite: “they shall return to God, and behold his face, and remain in their sins.” They do come; they see him; and the sins are still there. The horror is relocated from exclusion to presence, which is exactly the doctrine the chapter has been building since 9:15, where every man without exception must appear before the judgment seat. Recovering John 8 shows what Jacob had to change to make his own eschatology work.

links.note: The last and heaviest of the ten woes takes its wording from John 8, whose 44th verse supplied the father of lies at 9:9 — the chapter's two Johannine borrowings sit twenty-nine verses apart and both come from the same discourse. Jacob's “die in their sins” is the third person of John's second person, addressed to a congregation rather than to opponents. The phrase is a near-singleton confined to one chapter of one Gospel, which is what makes the identification safe; “sins” and “die” separately would prove nothing.

pericopes.text: O, my beloved brethren, remember the awfulness in transgressing against that holy God, and also the awfulness of yielding to the enticings of that cunning one. Remember, to be carnally minded, is death, and to be spiritually minded, is life eternal.

links.text: For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.

provenance.other: “carnally minded” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:6. “life eternal” occurs in exactly four, of which Matthew 25:46 is the one this chapter has already used, at 9:16.
provenance.significance: Romans 8:6's second half is “life and peace”, and peace is what Jacob drops. He replaces it with “life eternal”, and the phrase comes from Matthew 25:46 — the verse whose first half (“shall go away into everlasting punishment”) he had already taken at 9:16 for the everlasting fire. So the substitution is not a lapse of memory but a splice: the Pauline antithesis is completed out of the Matthean judgment scene the chapter has been quarrying since its middle. Paul's contrast is between two present dispositions and their present fruits; Jacob's is between two eternal destinations, and the changed word is what performs the change.

links.note: The clearest quotation in the chapter and one of the clearest in the book: “Remember, to be carnally minded, is death, and to be spiritually minded, is life eternal” against “For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.” Fourteen words in sequence with one substitution, from the KJV's one verse containing “carnally minded”. Still below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and not one of his passages. The 1830 prints “carnally minded” and “spiritually minded” open, as the KJV does; 1920 hyphenated both, so the first edition again preserves the source's typography where the modern text obscures it.

pericopes.text: O, my beloved brethren, give ear to my words. Remember the greatness of the Holy One of Israel. Do not say that I have spoken hard things against you: for if ye do, ye will revile against the truth: for I have spoken the words of your Maker. I know that the words of truth are hard against all uncleanness; but the righteous fear it not, for they love the truth, and are not shaken.

links.text: Give ear to my words, O LORD, consider my meditation.

provenance.other: “give ear to my words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 5:1.
provenance.significance: Psalm 5:1 is a man asking God to listen — “Give ear to my words, O LORD, consider my meditation” — and Jacob has reversed the direction of the appeal, asking a congregation to listen to him. The reversal is licensed by what he says next: “I have spoken the words of your Maker.” The words the people are asked to give ear to are not his, so the psalm's construction, in which the words given ear to are God's business, survives the change of addressee. The psalm continues “my King, and my God: for unto thee will I pray”, and Jacob's sermon ends at 9:52 telling them to “pray unto him continually”.

links.note: A five-word KJV singleton in a verse otherwise made of Jacob's own idiom. The identification is safe on the phrase and the argument is about what the reversal does; graded moderate rather than high because the words are all common in themselves and because an exhortation to hear is the most predictable thing a preacher can say. What is not predictable is that the KJV's one instance of this exact formula is a prayer, and that Jacob's use of it is immediately defended by the claim that the words are God's.

pericopes.text: O then, my beloved brethren, come unto the Lord, the Holy One. Remember that his paths are righteousness. Behold, the way for man is narrow, but it lieth in a straight course before him, and the keeper of the gate is the Holy One of Israel: and he employeth no servant there; and there is none other way, save it be by the gate, for he cannot be deceived; for the Lord God is his name.

links.text: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

provenance.other: “narrow is the way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:14; “none other name” occurs in exactly one, Acts 4:12.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:13-14 gives a gate and a way, and says the gate is strait and the way narrow. Jacob keeps both and adds what Matthew does not have: a keeper. “The keeper of the gate is the Holy One of Israel; and he employeth no servant there.” The addition is a denial — no servant — and it is the sort of denial that answers something. What it answers is not in Matthew; the porter who opens the gate belongs to John 10:3. Whether the denial is aimed there is beyond what the wording will support, but the sentence is constructed as a correction of somebody.

links.note: Two elements of Matthew 7:13-14, gate and narrow way, with a philological curiosity between them. The KJV's gate is *strait*, meaning narrow, and its way is *narrow*; the 1830 keeps “narrow” for the way and then writes that it “lieth in a straight course before him”, which is the homophone with its geometric sense. Whether that is a compositor's spelling or the text's own reading, the effect is that the KJV's two words for narrowness have become one word for narrowness and one for directness. The verse closes on Acts 4:12's exclusivity formula — “there is none other way, save it be by the gate” against “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” — the KJV's one such construction about salvation, and the chapter's argument at 9:23-24 has just been about a name.

pericopes.text: And whoso knocketh, to him will he open, and the wise, and the learned, and they that are rich, which are puffed up because of their learning, and their wisdom, and their riches; yea, they are they, whom he despiseth; and save they shall cast these things away, and consider themselves fools before God, and come down in the depths of humility, he will not open unto them.

links.text: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.

provenance.other: “knocketh it shall be opened” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:8 and Luke 11:10, which are verbally identical at this point.
provenance.significance: Matthew's promise is unconditional — every one that asketh receiveth, and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. Jacob quotes the promise and then withdraws it from a named class: “And whoso knocketh, to him will he open, and the wise, and the learned, and they that are rich … he will not open unto them”, unless they cast these things away. The suppressed context is that Matthew's saying stands six verses before the strait gate Jacob has just used at 9:41; he has taken two consecutive paragraphs of the Sermon on the Mount and set the second against the first, so that the door which opens to all opens to nobody who arrives puffed up.

links.note: The Matthew/Luke pair cannot be separated on wording — the two verses are identical where Jacob touches them — so the source is argued from the immediate company: 9:41 has just used Matthew 7:14, which has no Lucan counterpart in that form. That is the same kind of argument made at 9:30 for Matthew 6:21 over Luke 12:34, and it should be weighed once rather than twice. Jacob's construction reverses the KJV's voice, “to him will he open” for “it shall be opened”, which supplies the agent Matthew leaves in the passive — and the agent, per 9:41, is the keeper of the gate who employs no servant.

links.text: Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise.

provenance.other: “let him become a fool” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 3:18. “Puffed up” occurs in six KJV verses, five of them in 1 Corinthians (4:6, 4:18, 4:19, 5:2, 13:4) and one in Colossians — so both of this verse's distinctive terms come from the same letter.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 3:18 is the verse immediately before 3:19, which 2 Nephi 9:28 has already used. Jacob's chapter therefore takes two consecutive verses of 1 Corinthians 3 and separates them by fourteen verses of his own sermon, using the second first: the wisdom that is foolishness at 9:28, the becoming a fool in order to be wise at 9:42. Reading the source's context restores the sequence and shows that the two passages of 2 Nephi 9 that concern learning are one borrowing, split.

links.note: “Save they shall cast these things away, and consider themselves fools before God, and come down in the depths of humility, he will not open unto them.” Paul's imperative — if any man seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise — is here a condition of entry, and Jacob's “puffed up because of their learning” takes the other half of Paul's Corinthian vocabulary for the same fault. The two terms are not a general pair in the KJV; they belong to one letter, and to the four chapters of it that argue about wisdom.

pericopes.text: But the things of the wise and the prudent, shall be hid from them forever; yea, that happiness which is prepared for the Saints.

links.text: In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit, and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes: even so, Father; for so it seemed good in thy sight.

provenance.other: “wise and prudent” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 11:25 and Luke 10:21. tools/mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between them at any point 2 Nephi 9:43 reproduces — the two Gospels differ at the frame (“At that time … answered” against “In that hour … rejoiced in spirit”) and not at the saying — so the choice is argued from elsewhere.
provenance.significance: In both Gospels the things hidden from the wise and prudent are revealed unto babes, and the hiding is a matter for thanksgiving. Jacob keeps the hiding, drops the babes, and substitutes what is hidden: not the revelation but “that happiness which is prepared for the Saints”. The consequence is severe in a way neither Gospel is — in Matthew and Luke the wise merely fail to receive; in 2 Nephi 9:43 the happiness prepared for others is withheld from them for ever, which turns a saying about revelation into a sentence about damnation, and lands it in the middle of the passage on learning that runs from 9:28 to 9:43.

links.note: Luke is named as the source rather than Matthew on a chapter-level argument: 2 Nephi 9:34's “thrust down to hell” is a Luke 10:15 singleton whose Matthean parallel reads “brought down to hell”, so this chapter demonstrably has Luke 10 in hand, and Luke 10:21 stands six verses from Luke 10:15. The wording itself cannot decide, and Matthew 11:25 is recorded as a composite rather than dismissed. This is the mediation case in the chapter I am least able to close, and it is offered as an argument from company, which is weaker than a word test and should be read as such.

pericopes.text: O my beloved brethren, remember my words: Behold, I take off my garments, and I shake them before you: I pray the God of my salvation that he view me with his All-searching eye; wherefore, ye shall know at the last day, when all men shall be judged of their works, that the God of Israel did witness that I shook your iniquities from my soul, and that I stand with brightness before him, and am rid of your blood.

links.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

provenance.other: “shook his raiment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 18:6; “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one, Acts 20:26.
provenance.significance: Acts 18:6 is the whole of Jacob's gesture in one sentence: “he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean.” Paul does it at the moment he abandons a synagogue for the Gentiles, and Acts 20:26 repeats the formula at Miletus in his farewell — “I am pure from the blood of all men” — which is the setting Jacob's verse actually occupies, the last address of a preacher who will not have another chance. The metalepsis is the transfer of a missionary's disclaimer to a man addressing his own people in their own temple: Paul shakes his raiment at those who reject him, and Jacob shakes his garments at a congregation he is still trying to save.

links.note: Three elements in Acts 18:6's order — the garments shaken, the hearers' blood, the speaker's innocence — recast as a first-person ritual: “I take off my garments, and I shake them before you … that I stand with brightness before him, and am rid of your blood.” Jacob adds an act the KJV does not have, the taking off before the shaking, which converts a gesture of dust-shaking into something closer to Nehemiah 5:13's shaking out of the lap as an oath, and adds the judgment-day frame the source lacks. The link is the chapter's clearest borrowing from Acts, and it is placed where it is because “shook his raiment” is a KJV singleton and no other verse pairs it with blood.

pericopes.text: O my beloved brethren, turn away from your sins; shake off the chains of him that would bind you fast; come unto that God which is the rock of your salvation.

links.text: O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.

provenance.other: “rock of our salvation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 95:1; “the rock of my salvation” occurs in exactly two, 2 Samuel 22:47 and Psalm 89:26; Deuteronomy 32:15 has “the Rock of his salvation”. The Book of Mormon's “the rock of your salvation” is the one person of the formula the KJV never uses.
provenance.significance: Every KJV form of the phrase is spoken by the worshipper about his own God — our rock, my rock, or, in Deuteronomy 32:15, Jeshurun's rock forsaken. Jacob turns it to the second person and hands it to his hearers: “come unto that God which is the rock of your salvation.” The nearest source, Psalm 95:1, opens the psalm whose second half is the wilderness warning (“harden not your heart, as in the provocation”) that Hebrews 3-4 makes the type of apostasy — which is what Jacob's verse is about, men bound by chains who must turn away from their sins.

links.note: The paradigm is filled out in a person no KJV verse uses, which is evidence of a formula being handled rather than a verse being copied. Psalm 95:1 is named as the source because it is the closest form and because its psalm is the one about hardening the heart, but Deuteronomy 32:15 has a claim too: Jeshurun waxes fat and forsakes the Rock of his salvation, and Jacob's next breath at 9:51 is “let your soul delight in fatness”, the same figure turned to good. Graded moderate on the person shift and the plurality of candidates.
links.whyNot: Four words, one of them a possessive that matches nothing in the KJV, and the rock-of-salvation figure is spread across Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel and the Psalms. No single verse can be pinned.

pericopes.text: Prepare your souls for that glorious day, when justice shall be administered unto the righteous; even the day of judgment, that ye may not shrink with awful fear; that ye may not remember your awful guilt in perfectness, and be constrained to exclaim, Holy, holy are thy judgments, O Lord God Almighty. But I know my guilt; I transgressed thy law, and my transgressions are mine; and the Devil hath obtained me, that I am a prey to his awful misery.

links.text: And I heard another out of the altar say, Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are thy judgments.

provenance.route: Revelation 16:7 and 4:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “true and righteous are thy judgments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:7; “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 4:8.
provenance.significance: Jacob's damned man cries “Holy, holy are thy judgments, O Lord God Almighty”, which is not a KJV sentence but is exactly two KJV sentences fused. Revelation 16:7 supplies the frame — an acclamation of God's judgments addressed to the Lord God Almighty, spoken out of the altar as the vials are poured out — and Revelation 4:8 supplies the substituted predicate, the trisagion of the four beasts. The fusion is doctrinally loaded: the vindication of God's justice in Revelation 16 is sung by the altar, and in 2 Nephi 9:46 it is put in the mouth of the man being judged, who goes on to say “I know my guilt; I transgressed thy law”. Note that Revelation 15:3-4 is the immediate context of both, and 1 Nephi 1:14 already borrowed six words from Revelation 15:3.

links.note: Two Revelation verses spliced at the point where they share “Lord God Almighty”. Jacob has the shorter double “Holy, holy” rather than the trisagion — the third repetition is dropped, as it is nowhere else in the KJV — and has moved the adjective from God to God's judgments, where Revelation 16:7 has “true and righteous”. The result says something neither source says: that the judgments themselves are holy, conceded by the man they fall on. This is the third distinct borrowing from Revelation in the chapter (20:13 at 9:12, 14:11 and 20:10 at 9:16), and the fourth if the paradise of God at 9:13 holds.

pericopes.text: But behold, my brethren, is it expedient that I should awake you to an awful reality of these things? Would I harrow up your souls, if your minds were pure? Would I be plain unto you according to the plainness of the truth, if ye were freed from sin?
Behold, if ye were holy, I would speak unto you of holiness; but as ye are not holy, and ye look upon me as a teacher, it must needs be expedient that I teach you the consequences of sin.
Behold, my soul abhorreth sin, and my heart delighteth in righteousness; and I will praise the holy name of my God.
Come, my brethren, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters; and he that hath no money, come buy and eat; yea, come buy wine and milk without money and without price.

links.text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

provenance.other: “he that hath no money” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 55:1. The machine stream scored a sixteen-word contiguous run here, the longest in the chapter by a wide margin.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 55 opens the last movement of Second Isaiah, immediately after the barren woman's song of Isaiah 54 — and Jacob has been expounding Isaiah 49-52 since 2 Nephi 6, with Isaiah 50 and 51:1-52:2 transcribed in the two chapters that follow this one. So the invitation he ends his day's preaching with is the passage that stands just past the block he is working through: he closes with the text his exposition is heading toward. The suppressed context is Isaiah 55:3, “I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David”, which is the covenant language 9:1 opened the sermon with.

links.note: Sixteen consecutive words of Isaiah 55:1 with one substitution and one deletion: the KJV's “Ho, every one that thirsteth” becomes “Come, my brethren, every one that thirsteth”, replacing the prophetic hail with a preacher's address, and the second “come ye” before “buy” is dropped. This is at Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is one of the few passages in the chapter that would meet it, but it is not among his thirty-six and no claim is made that it is. The verse is quoted, not transcribed — it sits inside Jacob's own sermon and is introduced by his own vocative — which is why it is adjudicated by hand rather than collated with tools/collate-isaiah.py.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, do not spend money for that which is of no worth, nor your labor for that which cannot satisfy. Hearken diligently unto me, and remember the words which I have spoken; and come unto the Holy One of Israel, and feast upon that which perisheth not, neither can be corrupted, and let your soul delight in fatness.

links.text: Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.

provenance.other: “let your soul delight itself in fatness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 55:2.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's question — why spend money for that which is not bread? — is rhetorical, and Jacob converts it into a command: “do not spend money for that which is of no worth.” The change of mood is the whole of his exposition. Isaiah asks the exiles why they do a foolish thing; Jacob forbids a congregation to do it, and then replaces Isaiah's “eat ye that which is good” with “feast upon that which perisheth not, neither can be corrupted”, which imports the chapter's own resurrection vocabulary (9:7's incorruption, 9:13's incorruptible) into the prophet's meal. The Isaiah invitation has been made an invitation to the incorruptible body.

links.note: Isaiah 55:2 in sequence with three departures, each of which does work. The interrogative becomes an imperative; “that which is not bread” becomes “that which is of no worth” and “satisfieth not” becomes “cannot satisfy”, both flattening a concrete figure into a valuation; and the reflexive drops out of the final clause, so that the KJV's “let your soul delight itself in fatness” becomes “let your soul delight in fatness”. The 1830 has the shorter form, so this is not a later modernisation. Between the two departures Jacob inserts a sentence of his own — “remember the words which I have spoken; and come unto the Holy One of Israel” — which is how the chapter has handled every long borrowing: the source is carried, and Jacob's own title for God is set inside it.

pericopes.text: Behold, my beloved brethren, remember the words of your God; pray unto him continually by day, and give thanks unto his holy name by night. Let your hearts rejoice,

and behold how great the covenants of the Lord, and how great his condescensions unto the children of men; and because of his greatness, and his grace and mercy, he hath promised unto us that our seed shall not utterly be destroyed, according to the flesh, but that he would preserve them; and in future generations, they shall become a righteous branch unto the House of Israel.

links.text: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.

provenance.other: “righteous Branch” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15 has “the Branch of righteousness”.
provenance.significance: In Jeremiah the righteous Branch is a single messianic king raised unto David, and in 2 Nephi 9:53 it is a surviving remnant: “our seed shall not utterly be destroyed … in future generations, they shall become a righteous branch unto the House of Israel.” The figure has been transposed from one person to a people, which is the same transposition the Book of Mormon's whole covenant argument depends on — the Lehite seed as the branch broken off and preserved. Jacob's sermon opened at 9:1 on the covenants with all the house of Israel; it closes with the house of Israel receiving a branch back.

links.note: A KJV singleton in an unexpected sense. Jeremiah's Branch is Davidic and royal; Jacob's is genealogical, a preserved seed rather than a coming king, and “unto the House of Israel” takes the place of Jeremiah's “unto David”. Graded moderate because two words are all that is shared and “branch” is common in the KJV; what makes the row worth having is that the one verse pairing branch with righteous is a promise of preservation to a people about to be scattered, which is exactly what Jacob is promising.

pericopes.text: And now, my brethren, I would speak unto you more; but on the morrow I will declare unto you the remainder of my words. Amen.
And now I, Jacob, speak unto you again, my beloved brethren, concerning this righteous branch of which I have spoken.

For behold, the promises which we have obtained, are promises unto us according to the flesh; wherefore, as it hath been shown unto me that many of our children shall perish in the flesh, because of unbelief, nevertheless, God will be merciful unto many; and our children shall be restored, that they may come to that which will give them the true knowledge of their Redeemer.

provenance.other: “because of unbelief” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Romans 11:20, Hebrews 3:19 and Hebrews 4:6. The two Hebrews verses are about the wilderness generation failing to enter the rest; only Romans 11:20 makes unbelief the cause of a branch being broken off from Israel, which is the figure Jacob has been running since 10:1.
provenance.significance: Jacob opens the chapter 'concerning this righteous branch', and the first thing he says about it is that children will perish 'because of unbelief' and then 'be restored'. That is the shape of Romans 11 in two clauses: broken off because of unbelief (11:20), graffed in again if they abide not still in unbelief (11:23). Recover the context and the metalepsis is sharp — Paul's warning is addressed to the Gentile branch not to boast over the natural one, and Jacob's chapter goes on to promise the land to Gentiles who are 'numbered among the house of Israel' (10:18). The suppressed premise of Romans 11 is exactly the premise of Jacob's sermon.

links.note: 'Many of our children shall perish in the flesh, because of unbelief... and our children shall be restored.' The verbal contact is three words, but they are the three words of Romans 11:20 and they arrive attached to the branch of 10:1 and the breaking-off of 10:22 — the two other load-bearing terms of the same Pauline paragraph. Below any quotation threshold, Skousen's included; the case rests on the co-occurrence, not the length.
links.text: Well; because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear:

pericopes.text: Wherefore, as I said unto you, it must needs be expedient that Christ, (for in the last night the Angel spake unto me that this should be his name,) should come among the Jews, among they which are the more wicked part of the world; and they shall crucify him: For thus it behooveth our God; and there is none other nation on earth that would crucify their God.

provenance.alternative: The bare 'they shall crucify him' is Jacob's own, adjudicated at 2 Nephi 6:9 against Matthew 20:19; nothing here requires a second source.
provenance.significance: 'There is none other nation on earth that would crucify their God' is a claim about counterfactual national responses to a divine visitor, and the KJV has one verse that makes such a claim: 'had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.' Paul excuses the crucifiers by ignorance; Jacob incriminates them by election, arguing that Jerusalem alone was wicked enough to do it. The two verses answer the same question in opposite directions, which is why the echo is worth recording even though the shared vocabulary is one word.

links.note: Written under CONVENTIONS 0a as a link worth putting on the table. The argument is structural, not verbal: 1 Corinthians 2:8 is the only KJV verse that asks what a nation would have done had it known whom it was crucifying, and 2 Nephi 10:3-4 is a sustained answer to that question, continued in 10:4's counterfactual about the other nations.
links.whyNot: One shared word, 'crucify', and it is the unavoidable word for the event. A reader who declines this link loses nothing from the chapter; the surrounding argument runs on Matthew 11:21 (10:4), which has real verbal contact.
links.text: Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

pericopes.text: For should the mighty miracles be wrought among other nations, they would repent, and know that he be their God;

provenance.other: “they would have repented” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 11:21. Luke's parallel at 10:13 recasts it as 'they had a great while ago repented', so the Book of Mormon's counterfactual has Matthew's form of the verb, not Luke's. 'Mighty works' (10 KJV verses) becomes 'mighty miracles', which is in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:21-23 is the KJV's one sustained argument that a city which saw the miracles is guiltier than the pagan cities that did not: Tyre and Sidon would have repented, Sodom would have remained. 2 Nephi 10:4-5 reproduces that argument entire and then names its target — 'they at Jerusalem will stiffen their necks against him' — putting Jerusalem in Capernaum's place. Recover Matthew's context and the substitution is the point: the oracle Jesus pronounced against the towns of Galilee is here pronounced against the city that crucified him.

links.note: 'For should the mighty miracles be wrought among other nations, they would repent, and know that he be their God; but because of priest-crafts and iniquities, they at Jerusalem will stiffen their necks.' The counterfactual, the comparison class of other nations, and the verdict against the city that actually saw the works are all Matthew 11:21-23, and the singleton 'they would have repented' anchors the wording. The machine stream proposed nothing at all for this verse, which is CONVENTIONS 9 in miniature: no contiguous window survives the substitution of 'mighty miracles' for 'mighty works'.
links.text: Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.

pericopes.text: but because of priest-crafts and iniquities, they at Jerusalem will stiffen their necks against him, that he be crucified.
Wherefore, because of their iniquities, destructions, famines, pestilences, and bloodsheds, shall come upon them; and they which shall not be destroyed, shall be scattered among all nations.

provenance.route: Luke 21:11, 21:24 / Matthew 24:7 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon (via Jacob's own list at 2 Nephi 6:15)
provenance.other: “famines, and pestilences” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:7 and Luke 21:11, in that order in both. mediation-check.py reports one 'decisive' point for Matthew, but it is an absence — the Book of Mormon lacks Luke's 'in divers places' — and an absence cannot decide between two verses that agree on everything the Book of Mormon reproduces. The mediation is left uncertain on the evidence of this verse.
provenance.significance: Jacob has already given this list once, at 2 Nephi 6:15, in the reverse order and with 'bloodsheds' added to the synoptic set. Here it returns compressed and forward-ordered. The interesting half of the verse is the second: 'they which shall not be destroyed shall be scattered among all nations' is the fate Luke 21:24 assigns to Jerusalem after the same catalogue of signs, and Jacob applies it to the same city.

links.note: A repeat of Jacob's own formula rather than a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING 4): the link is written because the discourse is continuous and the second half of the verse adds Luke 21:24, but the argument for the synoptic catalogue itself was made at 2 Nephi 6:15 and is not restated here.
links.text: And great earthquakes shall be in divers places, and famines, and pestilences; and fearful sights and great signs shall there be from heaven.

pericopes.text: But behold, thus saith the Lord God: When the day cometh that they shall believe in me, that I am Christ, then have I covenanted with their fathers that they shall be restored in the flesh, upon the earth, unto the lands of their inheritance.

And it shall come to pass that they shall be gathered in from their long dispersion, from the isles of the sea, and from the four parts of the earth; and the nations of the Gentiles shall be great in the eyes of me, saith God, in carrying them forth to the lands of their inheritance.

provenance.other: “islands of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11, and “four corners of the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 11:12 and Revelation 7:1. The Book of Mormon has 'isles of the sea' and 'four parts of the earth' — neither is the KJV's word, and both departures are consistent (see 10:21, where 'isles' is made to carry an argument).
provenance.significance: Isaiah 11:11-12 is the KJV's one place where a gathering of the dispersed from the islands of the sea and from the four corners of the earth stand in adjacent verses, and 2 Nephi 10:8 fuses them into a single clause. Jacob has already invoked the first of the two at 6:14 ('set himself again the second time'), and his own book transcribes the whole chapter at 2 Nephi 21.

links.note: 'Gathered in from their long dispersion, from the isles of the sea, and from the four parts of the earth.' Two rare Isaiah 11 phrases in one sentence, each altered in the same direction — toward a commoner English word. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 11:11 at 10:21 rather than here; the fuller verbal contact is at 10:8 and the link is placed accordingly (CONVENTIONS 6a).
links.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

pericopes.text: Yea, the kings of the Gentiles shall be nursing fathers unto them, and their queens shall become nursing mothers; wherefore, the promises of the Lord are great unto the Gentiles: for he hath spoken it, and who can dispute.

provenance.other: “nursing fathers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “nursing mothers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Isaiah 49:23; the singular “nursing father” is Numbers 11:12. Jacob transcribed the verse at 2 Nephi 6:7 and here returns to it as his own text.
provenance.significance: The clause is re-quoted with one substitution that carries the chapter: Isaiah's 'kings shall be THY nursing fathers' becomes 'the kings of the GENTILES shall be nursing fathers unto them'. Isaiah's second person is the daughter of Zion; Jacob has resolved the pronoun into a specific reading of who the kings are, and the rest of the chapter (10:10-11, 10:18-19) is built on that resolution.

links.note: A re-quotation inside an exposition, not a fresh borrowing: the transcription is at 2 Nephi 6:7 and the argument for it was made there. What is new here is the gloss — the identification of Isaiah's kings and queens as Gentiles, which the Isaiah verse does not make and which the whole land-promise of 10:10-19 depends on. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 49:22-23 at this verse.
links.text: And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.

pericopes.text: But behold, This land, saith God, shall be a land of thine inheritance; and the Gentiles shall be blessed upon the land.
And this land shall be a land of liberty unto the Gentiles; and there shall be no kings upon the land, which shall raise up unto the Gentiles.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 8:7 and 12:12 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: 'There shall be no kings upon the land' is a promise, and 10:14 gives the reason: 'he that raiseth up a king against me shall perish. For I the Lord, the King of Heaven, will be their king.' That is the theology of 1 Samuel 8 exactly — a human king is a rejection of the divine one, 'they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them' — and 1 Samuel 12:12 states the antithesis in the same terms Jacob does, 'a king shall reign over us: when the LORD your God was your king.' Nephi refused the crown at 2 Nephi 5:18 on Gideon's grounds; Jacob now makes the refusal a standing condition of the land.

links.note: No verbal borrowing to speak of — 'king' and 'reign' are the only shared words — so this is filed as a conceptual allusion, on the strength of a whole argument reproduced rather than a phrase. It matters because it is the scriptural warrant behind the chapter's most-quoted sentence, 'this land shall be a land of liberty', a phrase that is in no KJV verse at all.
links.whyNot: A reader may reasonably say that a monarchy-refusing land promise needs no source, and that 1 Samuel 8 is where any such argument in English would land by gravity rather than by borrowing.
links.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

pericopes.text: And I will fortify this land against all other nations;
and he that fighteth against Zion, shall perish, saith God:

provenance.other: “against mount Zion” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:8. The preceding verse, Isaiah 29:7, has 'fight against Ariel' where the Book of Mormon's own expansion of the chapter at 2 Nephi 27:3 reads 'fight against Zion' — so the Book of Mormon replaces Ariel with Zion at exactly the point where Jacob's formula needs it.
provenance.significance: Jacob's refrain 'he that fighteth against Zion shall perish' agrees with the Book of Mormon's Isaiah rather than with the KJV's. Isaiah 29:7-8 fights against Ariel and then against mount Zion; 2 Nephi 27:3 fights against Zion in both places; Jacob has the second form. The finding is internal: the phrase he treats as scriptural is the reading his own book will give of Isaiah 29 fifteen chapters later, not the reading a KJV reader would find at Isaiah 29:7.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:8 here and the singleton 'against mount Zion' justifies it. The reason to keep the link at 10:13 rather than move it forward to the transcription is that Jacob is using the phrase as a fixed formula — he repeats it verbatim at 10:16 — which is what makes its agreement with 2 Nephi 27:3 worth recording. Flagged for Wilson: this is a within-book agreement pointing FORWARD to a chapter not yet adjudicated in this run, so the mediation is recorded as direct-OT rather than OT-via-earlier-BoM, which would be false about the order of the book.
links.text: It shall even be as when an hungry man dreameth, and, behold, he eateth; but he awaketh, and his soul is empty: or as when a thirsty man dreameth, and, behold, he drinketh; but he awaketh, and, behold, he is faint, and his soul hath appetite: so shall the multitude of all the nations be, that fight against mount Zion.

pericopes.text: for he that raiseth up a king against me, shall perish. For I the Lord, the King of Heaven, will be their king; and I will be a light unto them forever, that hear my words.

provenance.other: “the King of heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 4:37. “be a light unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 7:8 ('when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me'); the everlasting-light promise itself is Isaiah 60:19-20.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest piece of metalepsis. The KJV uses the title 'the King of heaven' once, and it is Nebuchadnezzar's confession after seven years of madness, ending 'and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.' Jacob's sentence is about kings: no king shall be raised up in this land, he that raiseth up a king shall perish, and the Lord will be their king instead. The one KJV verse that names God 'the King of heaven' is the verse in which the greatest king in scripture is abased for pride and made to say so. Neither text says this; the borrowed title says it.

links.note: 'For I the Lord, the King of Heaven, will be their king.' A three-word title, but an absolute singleton, and it lands in the one sentence of the chapter where a human king is being disposed of. The second half of the verse, 'I will be a light unto them forever', pairs a second singleton (Micah 7:8) with the everlasting light of Isaiah 60:19-20; the composite is recorded rather than split into separate rows because the sentence is one movement.
links.text: Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, for this cause, that my covenants may be fulfilled, which I have made unto the children of men, that I will do unto them while they are in the flesh, I must needs destroy the secret works of darkness, and of murders, and of abominations;

provenance.other: “works of darkness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 13:12 and Ephesians 5:11. Romans 13:12 was the source adjudicated at 2 Nephi 1:23 ('put on the armour'), and it has nothing about secrecy; Ephesians 5:12 supplies it in the next breath — 'those things which are done of them in secret.' The Book of Mormon's 'secret works of darkness' fuses the two adjacent Ephesians verses, and the choice between the two 'works of darkness' verses is decided by the adjective.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:11-12 also supplies the company the phrase keeps here. Jacob's triad is 'the secret works of darkness, and of murders, and of abominations'; Ephesians 5:3-5 lists fornication, uncleanness and covetousness as the things not to be named, and 5:12 makes their secrecy the shameful part. What Jacob adds is murder, which turns a moral catalogue into a description of conspiracy — the reading the rest of the Book of Mormon will build on.

links.note: The discriminating evidence is the word 'secret'. Of the KJV's two 'works of darkness' verses only Ephesians has secrecy attached, and it is attached in the immediately following verse. Below any quotation threshold; the case is a two-verse fusion, not a reproduced clause.
links.text: And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.

pericopes.text: wherefore, he that fighteth against Zion, both Jew and Gentile, both bond and free, both male and female, shall perish: for they are they which are the whore of all the earth; for they which are not for me, are against me, saith our God.

provenance.route: Galatians 3:28, with 1 Corinthians 12:13's wording in the first pair -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “male nor female” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 3:28, and “bond nor free” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11. Only Galatians has all three pairs, and the Book of Mormon has them in Galatians' order. But Galatians reads 'neither Jew nor Greek', and the Book of Mormon reads 'both Jew and Gentile' — which is 1 Corinthians 12:13's pairing, 'whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free'. mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for this verse, because the two candidates do not differ at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces word for word; the discrimination has to be made from the singleton and the substituted pair instead.
provenance.significance: Paul's triad abolishes the distinctions inside Christ; Jacob's triad abolishes them inside a threat. 'Both Jew and Gentile, both bond and free, both male and female, shall perish' takes the KJV's one formula for the irrelevance of human categories and applies it to the categories of the damned. Recover Galatians 3:28's context — 'for ye are all one in Christ Jesus' — and the borrowing reads as a deliberate inversion: the same universality, opposite sign.

links.note: Three pairs, in one KJV verse's order, with one pair reworded toward a second KJV verse's vocabulary. The strength is the singleton 'male nor female'; the interest is that 'Jew and Gentile' is not Galatians' phrase and is 1 Corinthians'. The machine stream proposed Numbers 5:3 here on 'both male and female', which is excluded.
links.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.

provenance.route: Matthew 12:30 / Luke 11:23, with Luke 9:50's preposition -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “is not with me is against me” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 12:30 and Luke 11:23, and both read 'with me'. The Book of Mormon reads 'they which are not FOR me, are against me'. The KJV has one verse with the polarity stated that way round — Luke 9:50, 'he that is not against us is for us' — and it is the saying's mirror image, not this one.
provenance.significance: The two logia are famously opposite: Matthew 12:30 and Luke 11:23 exclude the neutral, Mark 9:40 and Luke 9:50 include them. The Book of Mormon has the exclusive saying's polarity with the inclusive saying's preposition, which is the sort of cross-contamination that happens when a formula is remembered rather than copied. It is worth recording precisely because it cannot be got from any single KJV verse.

links.note: 'They which are not for me, are against me, saith our God.' A short clause, but it is a KJV rarity and the one-word departure from it is the finding: 'for' where both source verses have 'with'. Flagged as the kind of case ADJUDICATING 4 warns about in reverse — here the window does not close early, it closes on a substituted preposition that only the other member of the pair uses.
links.text: He that is not with me is against me; and he that gathereth not with me scattereth abroad.

provenance.other: “whore” occurs in exactly 15 KJV verses, almost all of them prophetic-adultery language in the Hebrew Bible. The great whore who is a corporate entity spanning the earth, rather than a figure for apostate Israel, is Revelation's: 17:5's 'MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH' and 19:2's 'the great whore, which did corrupt the earth'.
provenance.significance: 'The whore of all the earth' is a Book of Mormon coinage, but its two components are Revelation 17:5's genitive of scope and 19:2's earth-corrupting subject. What the borrowing does is make the whore a category rather than a city: Jacob's whore is not Babylon but everyone, of either nation and either sex, who fights against Zion.

links.note: Recorded at moderate because no clause is reproduced; the case is that the specific idea of a whore whose scope is the whole earth exists in the KJV only in Revelation 17-19. Below any quotation threshold and offered under CONVENTIONS 0a.
links.whyNot: 'Whore' is one of the commonest prophetic insults in the KJV and 'all the earth' is not rare; a reader who thinks Jacob has fused two ordinary biblical words without reference to Revelation is not obviously wrong.
links.text: And upon her forehead was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.

pericopes.text: For I will fulfil my promises which I have made unto the children of men, that I will do unto them while they are in the flesh.

Wherefore, my beloved brethren, thus saith our God: I will afflict thy seed by the hand of the Gentiles; nevertheless, I will soften the hearts of the Gentiles, that they shall be like unto a father to them; wherefore, the Gentiles shall be blessed and numbered among the House of Israel.—

Wherefore, I will consecrate this land unto thy seed and they which shall be numbered among thy seed, forever, for the land of their inheritance: For it is a choice land, saith God unto me, above all other lands; wherefore, I will have all men that dwell thereon, that they shall worship me, saith God.

provenance.other: “dwell upon the earth shall worship” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 13:8. The Book of Mormon has 'I will have all men that dwell thereon, that they shall worship me'.
provenance.significance: If the echo is real it is an inversion: the KJV's one sentence about all the earth's inhabitants worshipping is about the beast, and the names not written in the book of life. Jacob's land is consecrated on the same condition with the opposite object.

links.note: Proposed under CONVENTIONS 0a as a rarity worth putting on the table, and no more than that. The shared string is a singleton, but it is a singleton made of five of the commonest words in the KJV, which is exactly the profile of a coincidence.
links.whyNot: 'Dwell' and 'worship' are unavoidable words for the thought, and the Book of Mormon breaks the phrase across a relative clause ('that dwell thereon, that they shall worship me') rather than reproducing it. Nothing else in 10:19 has any contact with Revelation 13.
links.text: And all that dwell upon the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.

pericopes.text: And now, my beloved brethren, seeing that our merciful God hath given us so great knowledge concerning these things, let us remember him, and lay aside our sins, and not hang down our heads, for we are not cast off; nevertheless, we have been driven out of the land of our inheritance; but we have been led to a better land: for the Lord hath made the sea our path, and we are upon an isle of the sea.

provenance.route: Psalm 77:19 and Isaiah 43:16 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “path in the” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and they are the same verse twice over: Psalm 77:19, 'Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters', and Isaiah 43:16, 'which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters'. Both pair 'way' with 'path' and both are about the Red Sea.
provenance.significance: 'The Lord hath made the sea our path' is the family's ocean crossing described in the only two KJV verses that put a path in the sea, and both of them mean the Exodus. The metalepsis is the Book of Mormon's standing one: recover the context of Psalm 77 and it is a psalm about remembering the years of the right hand of the most High, which ends 'Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.' Jacob's sentence — driven out of the land of our inheritance, led to a better land, the sea made our path — is the Exodus reused as the charter of a colony.

links.note: Two words of contact, but they are 'path' and 'sea' in the KJV's only two verses that join them, and the sentence they sit in is doing the Exodus typology the whole book runs on. The preceding clause, 'we are not cast off', is the language of Psalm 94:14 and Romans 11:1-2 and belongs with the Romans 11 argument at 10:2 rather than with this link.
links.text: Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known.

pericopes.text: But great is the promises of the Lord unto they which are upon the isles of the sea; wherefore, as it sayeth isles, there must needs be more than this; and they are inhabited also by our brethren.

provenance.route: Isaiah 24:15 (and Isaiah 49:1) -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “isles of the sea” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Esther 10:1, where it is the extent of Ahasuerus's tribute, and Isaiah 24:15, where it is where the LORD's name is to be glorified. Isaiah 11:11 — the verse Hardy cross-references here, and the verse Jacob is expounding — reads 'islands of the sea', and so does the Book of Mormon's own transcription of it at 2 Nephi 21:11.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most interesting textual fact and it is an internal one. Jacob makes an exegetical argument out of a plural: 'as it sayeth ISLES, there must needs be more than this.' But the passage he is expounding does not say isles. It says islands — in the KJV at Isaiah 11:11, and in the Book of Mormon's own Isaiah at 2 Nephi 21:11. The word he exegetes is the word of Isaiah 24:15 and Isaiah 49:1 ('Listen, O isles, unto me'), the latter being the chapter Jacob had transcribed four chapters earlier at 2 Nephi 6.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 11:11 at this verse, which is right about what Jacob is expounding and wrong about where the wording comes from; the fuller Isaiah 11:11 link is therefore placed at 10:8 and this row records the 'isles' crux (CONVENTIONS 6a). Flagged for Wilson: the observation that a Book of Mormon exegesis turns on a word its own transcription of the source does not contain is a finding about the book, not just about this verse, and may deserve a place in the front matter rather than a chapter row.
links.text: Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.

pericopes.text: For behold, the Lord God hath led away from time to time from the House of Israel, according to his will and pleasure. And now, behold, the Lord remembereth all they which have been broken off; wherefore, he remembereth us also.

provenance.other: “broken off” occurs in exactly five KJV verses: Job 17:11 (purposes), Isaiah 27:11 (withered boughs), and Romans 11:17, 11:19 and 11:20, all of the olive-tree allegory. Three of the five are one paragraph of Romans, and it is the only KJV place where what is broken off is a part of Israel.
provenance.significance: The chapter closes its argument where it opened it. 10:1 announced 'this righteous branch'; 10:2 gave the reason for breaking off, 'because of unbelief'; 10:22 gives the remedy, 'the Lord remembereth all they which have been broken off.' Paul's point in Romans 11 is that the breaking-off is not final, and Jacob's application is that it is not even local — the branches broken off from the house of Israel 'from time to time' include his own family, 'wherefore, he remembereth us also.'

links.note: Adjudicated as a link rather than a bare recurrence because the phrase does work here that it did not do at 10:2 or at 2 Nephi 3:5: this is where the Romans 11 figure is applied to the Lehites themselves. The argument for the source was made at 10:2 and is not restated.
links.text: And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;

pericopes.text: Therefore cheer up your hearts, and remember that ye are free to act for yourselves: to choose the way of everlasting death, or the way of eternal life.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 21:8, with Deuteronomy 30:19's framing -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the way of life, and the way of death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 21:8. Deuteronomy 30:19 sets life and death before the people but does not call them ways; the Book of Mormon has Jeremiah's noun and Deuteronomy's imperative to choose.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 21:8 is spoken to a Jerusalem under siege, and the way of life it offers is surrender to Babylon — a way of life that looks like defeat. Jacob's audience is a colony that has been 'driven out of the land of our inheritance' (10:20), and he offers them the same choice in the same words, having just told them the exile was not abandonment. The metalepsis fits the chapter: the KJV verse that phrases the choice this way is addressed to people about to lose their land.

links.note: Hardy cross-references both Deuteronomy 30:19 and Jeremiah 21:8 here, and the two do different work: Deuteronomy gives 'choose', Jeremiah gives 'the way of ... and the way of ...'. Deuteronomy 30:19 as the source of Lehi's agency language was adjudicated at 2 Nephi 2:27; this row is placed on Jeremiah, which is where the wording of THIS verse is.
links.text: And unto this people thou shalt say, Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, reconcile yourselves to the will of God, and not to the will of the Devil and the flesh; and remember that after ye are reconciled unto God, that it is only in and through the grace of God that ye are saved.

provenance.other: “reconciled to God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 5:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:20. Only 2 Corinthians has it as an imperative addressed to an audience — 'we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God' — which is the form 2 Nephi 10:24 takes.
provenance.significance: Paul's imperative is spoken by an ambassador standing in Christ's stead; Jacob's is spoken by a consecrated priest at the temple, at the end of a two-chapter sermon, and it is the sentence the whole sermon has been driving at. The reflexive is the departure: Paul says 'be ye reconciled', a passive, and Jacob says 'reconcile YOURSELVES', which puts the act on the hearer — and then immediately takes it back with 'it is only in and through the grace of God that ye are saved.'

links.note: The single most quoted line of the chapter, and its wording is 2 Corinthians 5:20's with the voice changed from passive to reflexive. That change is the argument of the verse, not an accident of paraphrase: the second half of the verse exists to qualify it.
links.text: Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.

provenance.other: “by grace are ye saved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 2:8 (the shorter 'by grace ye are saved' is Ephesians 2:5). The machine stream proposed Titus 2:11 for this verse on 'the grace of God that'; Titus has grace appearing, not grace saving, and is excluded.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 2:8-9 is the KJV's flat denial that salvation is 'of yourselves'. 2 Nephi 10:24 has just told its hearers to reconcile THEMSELVES to the will of God, and then answers the objection the imperative raises by quoting the one verse that forecloses it. The two halves of the verse are a reflexive command and its Pauline corrective, in that order.

links.note: 'It is only in and through the grace of God that ye are saved.' The adverbial 'only in and through' is not KJV, but 'the grace of God' and 'ye are saved' are Ephesians 2:8's, and the sentence performs the same argumentative move Ephesians 2:8-9 does. Split from the 2 Corinthians link because the two halves of the verse have different sources and the tension between them is the point.
links.text: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:

pericopes.text: Wherefore, may God raise you from death, by the power of the resurrection; and also from everlasting death, by the power of the atonement, that ye may be received into the Eternal Kingdom of God, that ye may praise him through Grace Divine. Amen.

provenance.other: “the power of his resurrection” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 3:10. 2 Nephi 10:25 has 'by the power of the resurrection', changing only the pronoun.
provenance.significance: Philippians 3:10-11 wants to know the power of his resurrection in order to 'attain unto the resurrection of the dead'. Jacob's closing benediction turns the phrase from an object of knowledge into an instrument of a blessing: 'may God raise you from death, by the power of the resurrection'.

links.note: One KJV verse in the whole Bible speaks of resurrection as a power; Jacob's benediction uses it as one. The parallel clause, 'and also from everlasting death, by the power of the atonement', builds a second phrase on the same pattern out of a word ('atonement') that the KJV never joins to 'power' — a good example of the book coining on a borrowed template.
links.text: That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death;

provenance.other: “everlasting kingdom” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Psalm 145:13, Daniel 4:3, Daniel 7:27, 2 Peter 1:11); only 2 Peter 1:11 is about a person being received into it. 'Divine' as an adjective is rare in the KJV — Proverbs 16:10, Hebrews 9:1, and 2 Peter 1:3 ('his divine power') and 1:4 ('the divine nature'); the other nineteen occurrences of the string are the verb, diviners and divination.
provenance.significance: The closing sentence takes three things from one short passage of 2 Peter: the entrance ministered into the everlasting kingdom (1:11), a power that is divine (1:3), and the adjective itself. 'Grace Divine', capitalized in the 1830 running text, is not a KJV phrase — but its adjective belongs, in this sense, almost solely to the passage the rest of the sentence comes from.

links.note: The Book of Mormon's 'received into the Eternal Kingdom of God' answers 2 Peter 1:11's 'an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom'; the substitution of 'eternal' for 'everlasting' is the departure. The n-gram stream proposed 2 Samuel 21:3 here on 'the atonement, that ye may' — the Gibeonite blood-price — which is excluded as wrong-sense.
links.text: For so an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

pericopes.text: And now Jacob spake many more things to my people at that time; nevertheless, only these things have I caused to be written: for the things which I have written, sufficeth me.

provenance.other: “sufficeth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 14:8. The 1830 reads “for the things which I have written, sufficeth me”, with the singular verb after a plural subject; the modern text keeps it.
provenance.significance: If the echo is real, the metalepsis is exact. The KJV's one “sufficeth” is Philip asking to be shown the Father — “shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us” — and being told that having seen the Son is having seen him. Nephi's next two verses are entirely about who has seen: Isaiah “verily saw my Redeemer, even as I have seen him”, and Jacob “also hath seen him as I have seen him.” The word that closes the record of Jacob's sermon is, in the KJV, the word of a disciple asking whether seeing is enough.

links.note: Proposed under CONVENTIONS 0a on the strength of an absolute rarity and nothing else. The interest is the company the word keeps: a chapter about a sufficiency of eyewitnesses opens with the KJV's only sufficiency word, and closes the thought at 11:3 with the number of witnesses required to establish a matter.
links.whyNot: One word, and it is a perfectly ordinary word of the period that needs no biblical source. The syntax is unrelated — Philip's “it sufficeth us” is a clause, Nephi's is a predicate on “the things which I have written” — and John 14 has no other contact with the chapter. A reader who declines this loses nothing.
links.text: Philip saith unto him, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us.

pericopes.text: And now I, Nephi, write more of the words of Isaiah: for my soul delighteth in his words. For I will liken his words unto my people; and I will send them forth unto all my children: for he verily saw my Redeemer, even as I have seen him.

provenance.other: “my soul delighteth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 42:1: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him.” The phrase is Nephi's refrain — four times in this eight-verse chapter (11:2, 11:4, 11:5 twice, 11:6) and earlier at 2 Nephi 4:15-16.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's principal finding and it is a piece of metalepsis in the strict sense. The one KJV verse in which a soul delights is the first Servant Song, and the soul that delights is God's, and what it delights in is the Servant. Nephi announces at 11:2 that he is about to write more of the words of Isaiah, and he announces it in the phrase Isaiah gives to God about the Servant. Then at 11:4 he says what his soul delights in: “proving unto my people the truth of the coming of Christ” — that is, the Servant. The refrain and its object come from the same verse, and neither text says so.

links.note: Nephi's signature formula, and it is a KJV singleton lifted from the verse that opens the Servant Songs — the body of Isaiah he is about to transcribe from chapter 12 onward. The machine stream proposed nothing for this verse, and could not: the phrase is four common words and the argument is entirely in the rarity of their combination. Flagged for Wilson: the refrain's first occurrence in the book is at 2 Nephi 4:15-16, adjudicated by another agent in this run without this source, so by ADJUDICATING 4 the row arguably belongs there and this one should be the recurrence. The link is written here because this is the chapter where the phrase does its work.
links.text: Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.

pericopes.text: And my brother Jacob also hath seen him as I have seen him; wherefore, I will send their words forth unto my children, to prove unto them that my words are true. Wherefore, by the words of three, God hath said, I will establish my word. Nevertheless, God sendeth more witnesses; and he proveth all his words.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 19:15 via 2 Corinthians 13:1 / Matthew 18:16 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The two forms differ on one noun. Deuteronomy 19:15 ends “shall the MATTER be established”; the New Testament citations end “every WORD be established” — “every word be established” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 13:1, with Matthew 18:16's “every word may be established” beside it. 2 Nephi 11:3 reads “I will establish my WORD.” The Book of Mormon has the New Testament's noun. Against that, “three” standing alone as a sufficient number is Deuteronomy's — the New Testament always has “two or three”, which occurs in exactly four KJV verses, and Nephi has “by the words of three”. Note that mediation-check.py reports one decisive point for Deuteronomy on the word “witnesses”; that is an artifact of the alignment, which matched “witnesses” from Nephi's following sentence (“God sendeth more witnesses”) against a gap. The real divergence is matter/word, and it goes the other way.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 19:15 is a rule of criminal evidence: no man is convicted on one witness. The New Testament keeps the rule but changes what is being established from a matter to a word, and Nephi takes the New Testament's version and applies it to a text — his own. He has just named exactly three seers of the Redeemer (Isaiah at 11:2, Jacob and himself at 11:3), which is Deuteronomy's number; and then he exceeds his own rule in the next clause, “Nevertheless, God sendeth more witnesses.” The 1830 volume opens with a page headed The Testimony of Three Witnesses, which is the same rule put to the same use.

links.note: The chapter's one Hardy row, and it is a mediation case that turns on a single word. Deuteronomy supplies the three witnesses, the New Testament supplies “establish my word” against Deuteronomy's “establish the matter”, and the Book of Mormon has both. Hardy cross-references all three verses here — Deuteronomy 19:15, Matthew 18:16 and 2 Corinthians 13:1 — without adjudicating between them; the finding is that the sentence does not have to choose, because it has taken the number from one and the object from the other.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 2 Ne 11.3 (Deut 19.15; Matt 18.16; 2 Cor 13.1)
links.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.

pericopes.text: Behold, my soul delighteth in proving unto my people the truth of the coming of Christ: for, for this end hath the law of Moses been given; and all things which have been given of God from the beginning of the world, unto man, are the typifying of him.

provenance.route: Hebrews 10:1 / Colossians 2:17, with Romans 5:14's construction -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV has no word “type” and no verb “typify”. Where the Book of Mormon says “the typifying of him”, the KJV says “a shadow of good things to come” (Hebrews 10:1), “a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Colossians 2:17), and “the figure of him that was to come” (Romans 5:14). Romans 5:14 is the only one with the genitive of the person, which is the construction 2 Nephi 11:4 uses.
provenance.significance: The claim of 11:4 — that the law of Moses was given for the purpose of proving Christ, and that everything given from the beginning of the world typifies him — is Hebrews' argument about the law compressed into one sentence, with Colossians' body/shadow and Romans' figure/fulfilment behind it. What is not from the KJV is the vocabulary. The Book of Mormon reaches for a technical term of Christian typology that the KJV does not contain, in a verse whose whole business is naming the practice, and the term it reaches for is the post-biblical one.

links.note: Filed as an echo and no higher, because the wording is not the KJV's — that is the point of the row. The concept is Hebrews 10:1 and Colossians 2:17 exactly; the word is not, and the mismatch is evidence worth cataloguing about how the book's theological vocabulary relates to its scriptural one.
links.whyNot: No distinctive shared phrase at all. A reader may fairly say that a book arguing the law points to Christ needs no particular verse behind it, and that “typifying” is nineteenth-century theological English rather than a rendering of anything in Hebrews.
links.text: For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.

pericopes.text: And also, my soul delighteth in the covenants of the Lord which he hath made to our fathers; yea, my soul delighteth in his grace, and his justice, and power, and mercy, in the great and eternal plan of deliverance from death.
And my soul delighteth in proving unto my people, that save Christ should come, all men must perish.

For if there be no Christ, there be no God; and if there be no God, we are not, for there could have been no creation.— But there is a God, and he is Christ; and he cometh in the fulness of his own time.

provenance.other: “if there be no” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: 1 Samuel 11:3, 1 Corinthians 14:28 and 1 Corinthians 15:13 (Acts 25:11 reads “if there be none”, a different word, not a fourth instance). Only 1 Corinthians 15 uses it to open a chain of consequences — “if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen: and if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain” — which is the form 2 Nephi 11:7 takes twice over. The closing clause, “he cometh in the fulness of his own time”, rests on “the fulness of the time”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 4:4, adjudicated at 2 Nephi 2:3.
provenance.significance: Paul reasons from the denial of the resurrection down to the collapse of the preaching; Nephi reasons from the denial of Christ down to the collapse of creation itself — “if there be no God, we are not, for there could have been no creation.” Lehi had already run the same figure at 2 Nephi 2:13, and this is the son doing the father's argument in the father's borrowed form. Recover 1 Corinthians 15's context and the borrowing is apt: Paul's chain exists to establish that Christ is risen, and Nephi's exists to establish that Christ will come.

links.note: A structural allusion rather than a verbal one: the shared material is a chained conditional, the KJV's four “if there be no” verses, and the reductio that ends by asserting the antecedent (“But there is a God, and he is Christ” answers Paul's “But now is Christ risen”). The n-gram stream proposed Daniel 2:28 and 1 Samuel 17:46 here on “but there is a God”; both are excluded.
links.text: But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen:

pericopes.text: Now I, Nephi, do speak somewhat concerning the words which I have written, which have been spoken by the mouth of Isaiah. For behold, Isaiah spake many things which were hard for many of my people to understand: for they know not concerning the manner of prophesying among the Jews.
For I, Nephi, have not taught them many things concerning the manner of the Jews; for their works were works of darkness, and their doings were doings of abominations.

provenance.other: “manner of the Jews” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 19:40. The near neighbours are Galatians 2:14's “manner of the Gentiles” and Esther's “manner of the women”, neither of which supplies this collocation.
provenance.significance: The one place the King James Bible speaks of the manner of the Jews, it is speaking of how they bury a body: 'as the manner of the Jews is to bury'. Nephi uses the phrase four times in six verses of a manner he refuses to teach his children, and eleven verses later he reaches the sepulchre himself — 'after that he is laid in a Sepulcher for the space of three days'. Recovering John's context turns the chapter's refrain into an anticipation of its climax: the manner of the Jews that Nephi will not teach is, in the KJV, the manner in which they buried Jesus.

links.note: The chapter's governing phrase, repeated at 25:1 ('the manner of prophesying among the Jews'), 25:2, 25:5 and 25:6.
