Graded moderate because the phrase is short and because the next clause drops it — 'that the Gentiles be convinced also, that Jesus is the Christ, the Eternal God' — which suggests the writer is not holding a source open in front of him.
links.text: But Saul increased the more in strength, and confounded the Jews which dwelt at Damascus, proving that this is very Christ.

pericopes.text: and that he manifesteth himself unto all they that believe in him, by the power of the Holy Ghost; yea, unto every nation, kindred, tongue, and people, working mighty miracles, signs and wonders, among the children of men, according to their faith.

provenance.other: “every nation, and kindred, and tongue” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:6. The fourfold formula appears elsewhere in Revelation with 'people' first or 'kindreds' plural (5:9, 7:9, 11:9, 13:7); only 14:6 has this order with 'every' governing.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:6's four nouns belong to the angel with the everlasting gospel to preach to them that dwell on the earth. Nephi's sentence is about Christ manifesting himself 'unto every nation, kindred, tongue, and people, working mighty miracles, signs and wonders' — the same universality and the same commission, with Christ himself in the angel's place. The verse would become the Latter-day Saint proof-text for the restoration; here it is doing the plainer work of saying that the gospel has no ethnic boundary, which is 26:33's conclusion.

links.note: A four-term list in a KJV singleton's order, with the conjunctions dropped as the Book of Mormon habitually drops them. 'Signs and wonders' in the same clause occurs in thirteen KJV verses and cannot be sourced; it is not counted toward this row.
links.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

pericopes.text: But behold I prophesy unto you concerning the last days; concerning the days when the Lord God shall bring these things forth unto the children of men.

After that my seed and the seed of my brethren shall have dwindled in unbelief, and shall have been smitten by the Gentiles; yea, after that the Lord God shall have camped against them round about, and shall have laid siege against them with a mount, and raised forts against them; and after that they shall have been brought down low into the dust, even that they are not, yet the words of the righteous shall be written, and the prayers of the faithful shall be heard, and all they which have dwindled in unbelief, shall not be forgotten;

provenance.other: Isaiah 29:3 reads 'And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee.' 2 Nephi 26:15 reads 'the Lord God shall have camped against them round about, and shall have laid siege against them with a mount, and raised forts against them'. Every content word is Isaiah's; only person and tense change. “lay siege against thee with a mount” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:3.
provenance.significance: This is the structural fact that governs 2 Nephi 26 and 27 together, and it is worth stating once. Isaiah 29 enters the Book of Mormon twice and in two pieces. Verses 3-5 — the siege, the voice from the dust, the chaff — are used here at 26:15-18 and applied to the destruction of Nephi's own seed. Verses 6-24 are expanded at 2 Nephi 27 and applied to the last days and the coming forth of a book. Verses 1-2, the only part naming Ariel and 'the city where David dwelt', are used nowhere: the one section that ties the oracle to Jerusalem is the section that is dropped. So the chapter is not simply quoted, it is dismembered along a line that removes its geography and distributes its two halves to two different peoples and two different centuries.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:3-5 at 26:14, one verse before the wording begins; CONVENTIONS §6a puts the link where the wording is and the register at 26:14 sends the reader here. Three clauses reproduced in Isaiah's order with the subject changed from God speaking in the first person to God reported in the third, which is what an expositor does and a transcriber does not.
links.text: And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee.

pericopes.text: for they which shall be destroyed shall speak unto them out of the ground, and their speech shall be low out of the dust, and their voice shall be as one that hath a familiar spirit; for the Lord God will give unto him power, that he may whisper concerning them, even as it were out of the ground; and their speech shall whisper out of the dust.

provenance.other: “whisper out of the dust” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:4, and the machine's rarity score for this pairing, 10.02 on a nine-word run, is the second highest in the chapter. Isaiah's four elements all appear: speaking out of the ground, speech low out of the dust, a voice as of one that hath a familiar spirit, and a whisper out of the dust.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:4 is a threat: the besieged city is brought so low that its voice comes from underground like a necromancer's ghost, and the simile is contemptuous — a familiar spirit is what Leviticus 20:27 says to stone a person for consulting. The Book of Mormon reverses the valuation entirely. The voice from the dust is its own voice, the record of a destroyed people speaking to a later one, and 'the Lord God will give unto him power, that he may whisper concerning them' turns the ghost into an authorised messenger. This is the verse the book uses to describe itself — Moroni will return to it, and 2 Nephi 33:13 speaks 'as the voice of one crying from the dust' — so an oracle of humiliation has been made the Book of Mormon's account of its own mode of existence.
provenance.alternative: None; the wording has no other KJV home.

links.note: The chapter's densest borrowing after Malachi 4:1, and its most consequential. Isaiah's second person becomes third and the passive becomes an act of divine enabling, but the four clauses stand in Isaiah's order. Note the added agent: Isaiah has no one giving power to whisper. Hardy's cross-reference to Isaiah 29:4 is keyed to 2 Nephi 27:13, where the wording is only a paraphrase ('speak as if it were from the dead'); the verbal link belongs here.
links.text: And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.

pericopes.text: For thus saith the Lord God: They shall write the things which shall be done among them, and they shall be written and sealed up in a book, and they that have dwindled in unbelief, shall not have them, for they seek to destroy the things of God:

wherefore, as they which have been destroyed, have been destroyed speedily; and the multitude of their terrible ones, shall be as chaff that passeth away. Yea, thus saith the Lord God: It shall be at an instant, suddenly.

provenance.other: “chaff that passeth away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:5, and “at an instant” in exactly two, Isaiah 29:5 and 30:13. The Book of Mormon has both, in Isaiah's order, with 'suddenly' following: 'It shall be at an instant, suddenly.'
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:5's first half — 'the multitude of thy strangers shall be like small dust' — is dropped, and the second half kept. That is consistent with what 26:15-18 is doing to the whole oracle: the strangers besieging a city have no place in a prophecy about a people destroying itself, so the besiegers go and the suddenness stays. The Book of Mormon also reads 'their terrible ones' where the KJV has 'the terrible ones', which attaches the multitude to the destroyed people rather than to their attackers, completing the transfer.

links.note: Two KJV rarities in one clause, one of them a singleton, and the second sentence — 'Yea, thus saith the Lord God: It shall be at an instant, suddenly' — reproduces Isaiah's closing words with a messenger formula prefixed. The pronoun change from 'the' to 'their' is the interpretive move and it is worth recording as such.
links.text: Moreover the multitude of thy strangers shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the terrible ones shall be as chaff that passeth away: yea, it shall be at an instant suddenly.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass, that they which have dwindled in unbelief, shall be smitten by the hand of the Gentiles.

And the Gentiles are lifted up in the pride of their eyes, and have stumbled, because of the greatness of their stumbling block, that they have built up many Churches; nevertheless they put down the power and the miracles of God, and preach up unto themselves, their own wisdom, and their own learning, that they may get gain, and grind upon the face of the poor;

provenance.other: “grind the faces of the poor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 3:15, and this book transcribes it at 2 Nephi 13:15. The Book of Mormon's exposition alters the preposition — 'grind upon the face of the poor' — and the singular 'face'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 3:15 is addressed to 'the ancients of his people, and the princes thereof': the grinders are the rulers of Judah. Nephi transfers the charge to Gentile churchmen who 'preach up unto themselves, their own wisdom, and their own learning, that they may get gain'. The oracle against a native ruling class is redirected at a foreign religious one, and the mechanism of the oppression changes from judicial to commercial.

links.note: One of three Isaiah phrases fused in this verse — with Isaiah 2:11's lofty looks and Isaiah 8:14's stone of stumbling, both catalogued below — and all three come from chapters this book has already transcribed. Hardy cross-references all three at this verse and the reference is exact in each case. The catalogue splits them into separate rows because they come from three different oracles and are doing three different things.
links.text: What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor? saith the Lord GOD of hosts.

provenance.other: “stone of stumbling” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 8:14 and 1 Peter 2:8, which quotes it. This book transcribes Isaiah 8:14 at 2 Nephi 18:14.
provenance.significance: In Isaiah the stone of stumbling is the Lord of hosts himself, a sanctuary to some and a snare to others; in Romans 9:32 and 1 Peter 2:8 it is Christ, and men stumble at the word. Nephi's Gentiles 'have stumbled, because of the greatness of their stumbling block' — and the stumbling block turns out to be their own churches, 'that they have built up many Churches'. The Christological stone has been replaced by the institutions built in its name, which is a sharper reading of Isaiah than either Paul's or Peter's and is made out of their vocabulary.

links.note: 'Stumbling block' rather than 'stone of stumbling' is the Book of Mormon's form, and it is a KJV phrase in its own right (Leviticus 19:14, Romans 14:13 and elsewhere), so the row rests on the collocation with 'stumbled' and on Hardy's grouping of this verse with Isaiah 8:14-15. Mediation is set to OT-via-earlier-BoM: the transcription at 2 Nephi 18:14 is in this book and is the nearer model, and the New Testament reapplications are recorded as composite because Nephi's use is Christological in the way theirs are and Isaiah's is not.
links.text: And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “lofty looks” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 2:11, and this book transcribes it at 2 Nephi 12:11. Isaiah 2:12 supplies 'every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 2:11-12 is the day of the Lord against everything high, and its refrain is that the lofty are brought low. Nephi's 'the Gentiles are lifted up in the pride of their eyes' compresses Isaiah's two verses into one clause — the lifting up from v. 12, the eyes from v. 11's lofty looks — and the day of the Lord that follows in Isaiah has already been announced in this chapter at 26:4-6.

links.note: Graded moderate: 'lifted up in the pride of' is not a KJV string, and the case is that the two ideas Isaiah 2:11-12 pairs are the two Nephi pairs. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 2:12-14 here, which is right and slightly wide; v. 11 supplies the eyes.
links.text: The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.

provenance.other: “get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:13: 'ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain'.
provenance.significance: James's traders are rebuked not for trading but for presuming on a future they do not own — 'ye know not what shall be on the morrow' — and the phrase in the KJV belongs to them alone. The Book of Mormon makes it the motive of priestcraft. It uses the phrase three times in two chapters: here of churchmen who preach their own learning, at 26:29 in the definition of priestcraft itself, and at 27:16 of the learned man who asks for the sealed book 'because of the glory of the world, and to get gain'. A commercial idiom with one biblical home has become this section's standing term for religion practised for money.

links.note: Two words, and they carry a row because the KJV has them once and the Book of Mormon builds a doctrine on them. The link is placed at the first of the three occurrences and the other two are recorded as recurrences (ADJUDICATING §4). Graded moderate because 'get gain' is ordinary enough English that a nineteenth-century writer might reach it without James.
links.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:

pericopes.text: and there are many churches built up which causeth envyings, and strifes, and malice;

and there are also secret combinations, even as in times of old, according to the combinations of the Devil, for he is the founder of all these things; yea, the founder of murder, and works of darkness; yea, and he leadeth them by the neck with a flaxen cord, until he bindeth them with his strong cords forever.

provenance.other: “cords of vanity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 5:18 — 'Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope' — transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 15:18. The Book of Mormon shares only the noun: 'a flaxen cord', 'his strong cords'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's woe is on people who haul their own sin about like a cart; the cords are theirs and the pulling is theirs. Nephi reverses the agency completely — the devil 'leadeth them by the neck with a flaxen cord, until he bindeth them with his strong cords forever' — so the rope that was a figure for self-inflicted guilt becomes a leash held by someone else, and the woe becomes a captivity. The image also acquires a progression Isaiah has no room for: a flaxen cord first, strong cords afterwards.
provenance.alternative: Proverbs 5:22, 'he shall be holden with the cords of his sins', is nearer to Isaiah's sense and further from Nephi's wording; Hosea 11:4's 'cords of a man' and 'bands of love' are the KJV's other leading-cords.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 5:18 here, and this is a case where his row is worth having and worth qualifying. The verbal contact is one common noun; what justifies the row is that Isaiah 5 is transcribed in this same book, that Nephi has already drawn on Isaiah 5:24-25 at 26:6, and that the image of iniquity drawn with cords has no other biblical home. Graded moderate, and typed conceptual rather than verbal, because the wording is not reproduced and the sense is inverted.
links.text: Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope:

pericopes.text: For behold, my beloved brethren, I say unto you, that the Lord God worketh not in darkness.

He doeth not any thing, save it be for the benefit of the world; for he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life, that he may draw all men unto him. Wherefore, he commandeth none that they shall not partake of his salvation.

provenance.other: “draw all men unto me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:32: 'And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.' “lay down my life” occurs in three, John 10:15, 10:17 and 13:37.
provenance.significance: John 12:32's drawing is conditional on the lifting up, and John 12:33 glosses the lifting up as the manner of his death. The Book of Mormon states the same causal chain without the metaphor: 'he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life, that he may draw all men unto him'. The crucifixion has been named rather than figured, and John's 'if I be lifted up' has become a plain purpose clause. That is a decision about how to read John 12:32, and the verse makes it silently.

links.note: A Johannine sentence assembled from three of John's own: 'he loveth the world' from 3:16, 'layeth down his own life' from 10:17, 'draw all men unto him' from 12:32, with the last a KJV singleton. The argument the sentence is making — that God does nothing except for the benefit of the world — is the chapter's, not John's.
links.text: And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.

pericopes.text: Behold, doth he cry unto any, saying, Depart from me? Behold, I say unto you, nay; but he saith, Come unto me all ye ends of the earth, buy milk and honey, without money, and without price.

provenance.other: “without money and without price” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 55:1, which reads 'come, buy wine and milk without money and without price'. The Book of Mormon reads 'buy milk and honey, without money, and without price'.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Isaiah's pair is wine and milk; the Book of Mormon's is milk and honey, which is the KJV's standing formula for the land of promise — 'a land flowing with milk and honey', some twenty times from Exodus 3:8 onward. So the invitation to buy without money is answered not with Isaiah's drink but with the promised land itself, offered free. Whether the change is deliberate or a memory sliding from one fixed phrase to another, it converts an invitation to a meal into an invitation to an inheritance, which is what 2 Nephi has been promising since chapter 1. Note also that this verse retrieves the half of Isaiah 52:3 that 26:10 suppressed: 'ye shall be redeemed without money'.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 55:1 here and the reference is exact. Two further sources are fused into the same sentence: 'Come unto me all' is Matthew 11:28's opening and 'all ye ends of the earth' answers Isaiah 45:22's 'Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth'. The rhetorical frame — 'doth he cry unto any, saying, Depart from me? … nay; but he saith, Come unto me' — sets Matthew 7:23's dismissal against Matthew 11:28's invitation, which is a use of the gospels against each other rather than a borrowing from either. Matthew 11 has now supplied this section three times (25:18, 25:28, here).
links.text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

pericopes.text: Behold, hath he commanded any that they should depart out of the synagogues, or out of the houses of worship? Behold, I say unto you, nay.

Hath he commanded any that they should not partake of his salvation? Behold, I say unto you, nay; but he hath given it free for all men; and he hath commanded his people that they should persuade all men unto repentance.
Behold, hath the Lord commanded any that they should not partake of his goodness? Behold, I say unto you, nay; but all men are privileged the one like unto the other, and none are forbidden.

He commandeth that there shall be no priestcrafts; for, behold, priest-crafts are that men preach and set themselves up for a light unto the world, that they may get gain, and praise of the world; but they seek not the welfare of Zion.

Behold, the Lord hath forbidden this thing; wherefore, the Lord God hath given a commandment, that all men should have charity, which charity is love. And except they should have charity, they were nothing: wherefore, if they should have charity, they would not suffer the laborer in Zion to perish.

provenance.other: “have not charity” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 13:1, 2 and 3, the refrain of the chapter. 'Charity' as the KJV's rendering of ἀγάπη is itself a version-specific choice: Geneva has 'love' at 1 Corinthians 13 and modern versions almost all read 'love'.
provenance.significance: Paul's refrain is that gifts without charity leave the possessor as nothing — 'I am nothing'. Nephi turns the first person into the third and makes it a condition of a commandment: 'the Lord God hath given a commandment, that all men should have charity, which charity is love. And except they should have charity, they were nothing.' Paul does not command charity in 1 Corinthians 13; he measures the gifts against it. The Book of Mormon converts a measure into a law, and then applies the law to a labour dispute — 'they would not suffer the laborer in Zion to perish'.

links.note: The gloss 'which charity is love' is the interesting half of the row. It is an explanation the KJV needs and the Greek does not, and it is the sort of thing a nineteenth-century reader of the King James Bible would supply for a word whose ordinary English sense had drifted to almsgiving — which is, as it happens, exactly the sense the surrounding verses about the labourer in Zion are about to require. The dependence on 1 Corinthians 13 is not in doubt; what is worth recording is that the verse translates its source for its reader.
links.text: And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.

pericopes.text: But the laborer in Zion, shall labor for Zion; for if they labor for money, they shall perish.

And, again, the Lord God hath commanded that men should not murder; that that they should not lie; that they should not steal; that they should not take the name of the Lord their God in vain; that they should not envy; that they should not have malice; that they should not contend one with another; that they should not commit whoredoms; and that they should do none of these things; for whoso doeth them, shall perish;

provenance.other: Nephi's list runs: not murder, not lie, not steal, not take the name of the Lord their God in vain, not envy, not have malice, not contend, not commit whoredoms. Four are Decalogue commandments in the KJV's own wording, and 'take the name of the LORD thy God in vain' is Exodus 20:7 almost verbatim with the pronoun changed. “take the name of the LORD thy God in vain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:7 and its Deuteronomy 5:11 double, so the Decalogue's two recensions cannot be distinguished here.
provenance.significance: The order is the finding. The Decalogue's sequence is name, sabbath, parents, murder, adultery, theft, false witness, coveting; Nephi's is murder, lying, theft, the name, envy, malice, contention, whoredoms. The commandment against taking the name in vain has fallen from third to fourth, the sabbath and the honouring of parents are absent, and four items with no Decalogue equivalent — envy, malice, contention, whoredoms — have been appended. What emerges is not the Decalogue but a vice-list of the sort the New Testament epistles produce (Galatians 5:19-21, Colossians 3:8), built out of the Decalogue's raw material and finished with the sins the preceding verses have been describing: envy and strife at 26:21, priestcraft and gain at 26:29.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Exodus 20:7-17 here, which is the right range, and the interest of the row is in what the range does not cover. This is also where 26:9's allusion to Exodus 20:5's 'third and fourth generation' pays off: the same chapter of Exodus supplies the measure of the Nephite reprieve and the terms of the law they break.
links.text: Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

pericopes.text: for none of these iniquities come of the Lord; for he doeth that which is good among the children of men; and he doeth nothing save it be plain unto the children of men; and he inviteth them all to come unto him, and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female; and he remembereth the heathen, and all are alike unto God, both Jew and Gentile.

provenance.other: “bond nor free” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11. Only Galatians 3:28 has the three pairs together and in this order — Jew/Greek, bond/free, male/female — and Nephi's list keeps two of them in Galatians' sequence and closes on the third: 'bond and free, male and female … both Jew and Gentile'.
provenance.significance: Galatians 3:28's point is that the distinctions are abolished in Christ; Nephi's is that they are irrelevant to invitation — 'he denieth none that come unto him'. The added pair is the one Paul does not have: 'black and white'. That is not a biblical antithesis at all, and its insertion at the head of Paul's list is the most consequential single word-choice in the chapter, since 2 Nephi 5:21 has already made skin colour a mark of curse. The catalogue records the borrowing and notes that the added term sits uneasily with the source's logic and with the book's own earlier use of it.
provenance.alternative: Colossians 3:11 shares 'bond nor free' and adds Barbarian and Scythian, but lacks male and female.

links.note: The chapter's last sentence and its best-known one. Three Pauline pairs, one interpolated pair, and a closing 'both Jew and Gentile' that returns to the head of Galatians' list — so the verse both opens and closes on Paul's first antithesis. 'He inviteth them all to come unto him' is Matthew 11:28's verb again and 'he denieth none that come unto him' answers John 6:37, which was adjudicated at 2 Nephi 25:29; both are recorded as composite rather than given their own rows.
links.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.

pericopes.text: But, behold, in the last days, or in the days of the Gentiles; yea, behold all the nations of the Gentiles, and also the Jews, both they which shall come upon this land, and they which shall be upon other lands; yea, even upon all the lands of the earth; behold, they will be drunken with iniquity, and all manner of abominations;
and when that day shall come, they shall be visited of the Lord of hosts, with thunder and with earthquake, and with a great noise, and with storm and tempest, and with the flame of devouring fire;

provenance.other: “flame of devouring fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:6; Isaiah 30:30 has 'the flame of a devouring fire' with the article. Isaiah 29:6 reads 'Thou shalt be visited of the LORD of hosts with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with storm and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire.'
provenance.significance: The expansion of Isaiah 29 begins here, at v. 6, and not at v. 1 — verses 1-5 have already been used in the previous chapter, and vv. 1-2, the only ones naming Ariel and the city where David dwelt, are used nowhere. So the first thing 2 Nephi 27 does with Isaiah 29 is start in the middle of it, at the point where the oracle stops being about a named city and becomes about a day.

links.note: Every content word is Isaiah's. The two departures are grammatical and both are the same kind: 'Thou shalt be visited' becomes 'they shall be visited', and 'with' is supplied before 'a great noise' and before 'storm' where the KJV omits it. The first shifts an address into a report, which is what 27:1's new framing requires; the second regularises Isaiah's asyndeton. Note the 1830 verse division: the Book of Mormon's chapter 27 opens with an entirely non-biblical verse before the quotation starts.
links.text: Thou shalt be visited of the LORD of hosts with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with storm and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire.

pericopes.text: and all the nations that fight against Zion, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision; yea, it shall be unto them, even as unto a hungry man, which dreameth, and behold he eateth, but he awaketh and his soul is empty; or like unto a thirsty man, which dreameth, and behold he drinketh, but he awaketh, and behold he is faint, and his soul hath appetite; yea, even so shall the multitude of all the nations be that fight against mount Zion:

provenance.other: Two whole verses of Isaiah in one verse of the Book of Mormon, and the machine's longest run in the chapter, eighteen words, falls here. Isaiah 29:7-8: 'the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision. It shall even be as when an hungry man dreameth …' “a dream of a night vision” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:7.
provenance.significance: The one substitution is the whole point. Isaiah's besieged city is Ariel — a cult-name for Jerusalem, glossed by v. 1 as 'the city where David dwelt' — and the Book of Mormon replaces it with Zion: 'all the nations that fight against Zion, and that distress her'. Isaiah's own v. 8 already ends on 'mount Zion', so the substitution can be read as harmonisation; but it is also the move that lets the oracle be about a city that does not yet exist rather than one that has already fallen. The dropped clause, 'and her munition', goes with the fortification: a Zion without walls has none.
provenance.alternative: None; the passage has no other source.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:7 here. Besides Ariel/Zion, the departures are all of the same kind — Isaiah's similes are turned into second comparisons ('even as unto a hungry man, which dreameth' for 'as when an hungry man dreameth'), and the relative 'which' replaces 'when' twice. Everything else, including 'his soul hath appetite' and 'the multitude of all the nations', stands verbatim.
links.text: And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision.

pericopes.text: for behold, all ye that do iniquity, stay yourselves and wonder, for ye shall cry out, and cry; yea, ye shall be drunken, but not with wine; ye shall stagger, but not with strong drink:

provenance.other: “drunken, but not with wine” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 29:9 and 51:21 — and the second of those is transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 8:21, so the phrase has already appeared in 2 Nephi once before this chapter reaches it.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:9 describes a condition in the third person — 'they are drunken, but not with wine' — after two second-person imperatives. The Book of Mormon makes the whole verse second person: 'ye shall be drunken, but not with wine; ye shall stagger'. That change turns a description into an accusation, and the added opening, 'for behold, all ye that do iniquity', supplies the addressee Isaiah leaves unnamed. The tense also moves from present to future, which is required by 27:1's relocation of the whole oracle to the last days.

links.note: Isaiah's four imperatives — stay yourselves, wonder, cry ye out, cry — survive as 'stay yourselves and wonder, for ye shall cry out, and cry'. The only added material is the vocative. This is the clearest short example in the chapter of what the expansion does: it does not paraphrase Isaiah, it re-points him, changing person and tense while leaving the words alone.
links.text: Stay yourselves, and wonder; cry ye out, and cry: they are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.

pericopes.text: for behold, the Lord hath poured out upon you, the spirit of deep sleep. For behold, ye have closed your eyes, and ye have rejected the Prophets, and your rulers, and the seers hath he covered because of your iniquities.

provenance.other: “spirit of deep sleep” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:10: 'For the LORD hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes: the prophets and your rulers, the seers hath he covered.'
provenance.significance: This is the most consequential single departure in the chapter and it is one clause long. In Isaiah, God closes their eyes and covers the prophets, the rulers and the seers: three objects of one divine verb, and the blinding is God's act. The Book of Mormon keeps the pouring out of the spirit of deep sleep and keeps the covering of the seers, but between them it substitutes 'For behold, ye have closed your eyes, and ye have rejected the Prophets, and your rulers' — the people close their own eyes and reject their own prophets, and only the covering of the seers is left to God, now with a stated cause, 'because of your iniquities'. Isaiah's hardening is transferred from God to the hardened, and the divine act is made a consequence rather than a cause. The theology of 2 Nephi 2 — that men are free to act and not to be acted upon — is being written back into Isaiah's sentence.
provenance.alternative: None. The wording is Isaiah's throughout; only the syntax of agency changes.

links.note: The catalogue treats this as a quotation because every phrase is Isaiah's, but the row's value is the departure rather than the borrowing. Note that the change is invisible to any measure of verbal overlap: the shared vocabulary is nearly total and the sense is reversed, which is the mirror image of the wrong-sense exclusions in the register. It is also the reason a chapter like this cannot be run through collate-isaiah.py — a word-level collation would report 'closed your eyes' as agreement.
links.text: For the LORD hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes: the prophets and your rulers, the seers hath he covered.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass, that the Lord God shall bring forth unto you, the words of a book, and they shall be the words of them which have slumbered.

provenance.other: “the words of a book that is sealed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:11. The Book of Mormon divides the phrase across two verses: 'the words of a book' here, 'the book shall be sealed' at 27:7.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:11 is a simile — the vision has become to you AS the words of a sealed book — and the Book of Mormon deletes the comparison. What was a figure for incomprehension becomes an actual book that God 'shall bring forth unto you', and the next twenty verses are about its physical delivery, its witnesses, and the man who will read it. The single most important thing 2 Nephi 27 does to Isaiah 29 is to literalise its metaphor. The second half of the verse, 'they shall be the words of them which have slumbered', has no counterpart in v. 11 at all; it reaches back to v. 10's spirit of deep sleep and forward to 26:16's voice out of the dust, and identifies the sleepers as the dead whose record the book is.
provenance.alternative: Daniel 12:4 and 12:9 supply a sealed book of the end from the other direction and are catalogued at 27:22.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:11-12 at this verse. That is a chapter-level pointer at the head of the passage: v. 11's simile is here, but the dialogue of vv. 11-12 — 'Read this, I pray thee', 'I cannot; for it is sealed', 'I am not learned' — is at 27:15-19, and those rows carry the verbal links (CONVENTIONS §6a). The compound 'them which have slumbered' is the Book of Mormon's own and is one of the passages where the expansion adds rather than re-points.
links.text: And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I cannot; for it is sealed:

pericopes.text: And behold, the book shall be sealed; and in the book shall be a revelation from God, from the beginning of the world, to the ending thereof.

Wherefore, because of the things which are sealed up, the things which are sealed, shall not be delivered in the day of the wickedness and abominations of the people. Wherefore the book shall be kept from them.
But the book shall be delivered unto a Man, and he shall deliver the words of the book, which are the words of they which have slumbered in the dust; and he shall deliver these words unto another;

but the words which are sealed, he shall not deliver, neither shall he deliver the book. For the book shall be sealed by the power of God, and the revelation which was sealed, shall be kept in the book until the own due time of the Lord, that they may come forth: for, behold, they reveal all things from the foundation of the world, unto the end thereof.

And the day cometh that the words of the book which were sealed, shall be read upon the house-tops; and they shall be read by the power of Christ: and all things shall be revealed unto the children of men which ever hath been among the children of men, and which ever will be, even unto the end of the earth.

provenance.other: “upon the housetops” occurs in exactly four KJV verses; two are the saying about secrets made public, Matthew 10:27 ('preach ye upon the housetops') and Luke 12:3 ('shall be proclaimed upon the housetops'). Neither uses the verb 'read', which is the Book of Mormon's.
provenance.significance: Luke 12:3's saying is precisely about the reversal of concealment: what was spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light, what was said in closets proclaimed on the housetops. 2 Nephi 27 is a chapter about a book that is sealed, hidden, kept from the eyes of the world, and then read; the housetop is the image the gospels use for the end of that concealment, and the Book of Mormon supplies it at the exact point where the sealed words are finally unsealed. The verb changes from proclaiming to reading because the thing revealed is a text.

links.note: 27:7-14 is the part of this chapter with no Isaiah counterpart at all, and this is one of the few clauses in it that has any biblical wording. Graded moderate: two words, and the source cannot be narrowed between Matthew and Luke — though Luke's 'proclaimed' is nearer the passive construction than Matthew's imperative 'preach ye'.
links.text: Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, at that day when the book shall be delivered unto the man of whom I have spoken, the book shall be hid from the eyes of the world, that the eyes of none shall behold it, save it be that three witnesses shall behold it, by the power of God, besides him to whom the book shall be delivered; and they shall testify to the truth of the book, and the things therein.

And there is none other which shall view it, save it be a few, according to the will of God, to bear testimony of his word unto the children of men: for the Lord God hath said, that the words of the faithful should speak as if it were from the dead.

Wherefore, the Lord God will proceed to bring forth the words of the book; and in the mouth of as many witnesses as seemeth him good, will he establish his word: and wo be unto him that rejecteth the word of God.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 19:15 → Matthew 18:16 / 2 Corinthians 13:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “mouth of two or three witnesses” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 18:16 and 2 Corinthians 13:1, both quoting Deuteronomy 19:15. The three differ in two words that decide this case: Deuteronomy has 'AT the mouth of two witnesses … shall THE MATTER be established'; the New Testament pair has 'IN the mouth of two or three witnesses … every WORD be established'.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon reads 'in the mouth of as many witnesses as seemeth him good, will he establish his word', and it has the New Testament form on both discriminating points: the preposition is 'in', not 'at', and the thing established is a word, not a matter. This is the chapter's mediation result and it matters beyond the verse, because the three witnesses of 27:12 are the doctrine the whole passage exists to install — so the law of witnesses enters the Book of Mormon in the form Paul and Matthew give it rather than the form Deuteronomy gives it.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 19:15 alone, which is where mediation-check.py's single decisive point falls; but the word it finds decisive is 'witnesses', which all three verses share, and the tool's alignment does not reach the preposition or the object. The reading here is by eye and the discriminants are named above.

links.note: The replacement of 'two or three' by 'as many witnesses as seemeth him good' is the Book of Mormon's own, and it does work: it licenses the three witnesses of 27:12 and the eight who would follow, without binding the number. Note that the borrowing sits in the stretch of this chapter — vv. 7 to 14 — that has no Isaiah 29 counterpart, so where the expansion leaves Isaiah it reaches for the New Testament.
links.text: This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.

pericopes.text: But behold, it shall come to pass that the Lord God shall say unto him to whom he shall deliver the book, Take these words which are not sealed, and deliver them to another, that he may shew them unto the learned, saying: Read this, I pray thee. And the learned shall say, Bring hither the book, and I will read them:

provenance.other: “Read this, I pray thee” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 29:11 and 29:12, where it is said twice — once to the learned man and once to the unlearned. 2 Nephi 27:15 keeps it in the first of the two positions.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's 'which men deliver to one that is learned' is a passive impersonal; the Book of Mormon supplies a chain of named agents — the Lord God says to the man to whom he delivers the book, take these words and deliver them to another, that HE may shew them to the learned. Two deliveries where Isaiah has one, and the words that go to the learned are specifically 'these words which are not sealed'. Isaiah's scene is a figure for a nation that cannot read its own vision; the Book of Mormon's is a procedure, with a custodian, an intermediary, and a restriction on what may be shown.
provenance.alternative: None.

links.note: The added reply is the largest single expansion in the chapter: Isaiah's learned man says only 'I cannot; for it is sealed', and the Book of Mormon has him first say 'Bring hither the book, and I will read them' — a demand Isaiah does not record and which 27:16 then motivates as being made 'because of the glory of the world, and to get gain'. So a refusal has become a negotiation, and a motive has been assigned to it.
links.text: And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I cannot; for it is sealed:

provenance.other: “get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:13. This is its third occurrence in two chapters of 2 Nephi.
provenance.significance: The phrase was adjudicated at 2 Nephi 26:20, where it names the motive of churchmen who preach their own learning. Its reappearance here, in 27:16, attaches the same motive to the learned man of Isaiah 29:11 — so the figure Isaiah uses for incapacity is re-read as a figure for venality, and the section's standing term for religion practised for money is what performs the re-reading.

links.note: The occurrence is in 27:16, which is a continuation of the sentence begun here and has no independent biblical content; the row is filed at 27:15 with the Isaiah quotation it comments on. The argument for James 4:13 as the source is made at 26:20 and is not restated.
links.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:

pericopes.text: and now, because of the glory of the world, and to get gain, will they say this, and not for the glory of God.
And the man shall say, I cannot bring the book, for it is sealed.

provenance.other: Isaiah 29:11 ends 'and he saith, I cannot; for it is sealed'. 2 Nephi 27:17 reads 'And the man shall say, I cannot bring the book, for it is sealed.' “I cannot; for it is sealed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:11.
provenance.significance: The speaker has changed. In Isaiah the words 'I cannot; for it is sealed' are the learned man's refusal to read; in the Book of Mormon they are the unlearned custodian's refusal to hand the book over, and the learned man's 'I cannot read it' is given a verse of its own at 27:18. So Isaiah's one refusal has been split into two, redistributed between two speakers, and given two different reasons — the book cannot be brought because it is sealed, and it cannot be read because the reader is not able. Everything the expansion adds to this passage follows from that split.

links.note: A three-word clause reproduced exactly ('for it is sealed') with a new object supplied for the verb. The row is worth separating from 27:15's because the reassignment of the line is the interpretive act, and a reader collating the two chapters by eye will otherwise see only that the words are Isaiah's.
links.text: And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I cannot; for it is sealed:

pericopes.text: Then shall the learned say, I cannot read it.
Wherefore it shall come to pass, that the Lord God will deliver again the book and the words thereof, to him that is not learned; and the man that is not learned, shall say, I am not learned.

provenance.other: “I am not learned” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:12: 'And the book is delivered to him that is not learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I am not learned.' The Book of Mormon has both of the verse's distinctive phrases, 'him that is not learned' and 'I am not learned'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:11-12 is a pair of failures: the learned man cannot read because the book is sealed, the unlearned man cannot read because he is unlearned, and the point is that the vision reaches nobody. The Book of Mormon accepts the second failure and then overturns it — 27:20 has God answer 'thou shalt read the words which I shall give unto thee'. The unlearned man's disqualification becomes his qualification, and Isaiah's closed circle is opened at the one place the KJV leaves an opening: Isaiah records the unlearned man's objection but not, as with the learned man, a reason why the reading is impossible.
provenance.alternative: None.

links.note: The chapter's most consequential quotation, and the one that carries the Book of Mormon's account of its own translator. Two of Isaiah 29:12's clauses stand verbatim; the delivery is redirected — 'the Lord God will deliver again the book' rather than 'the book is delivered' — so that God, not 'men', is the agent throughout the scene.
links.text: And the book is delivered to him that is not learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I am not learned.

pericopes.text: Then shall the Lord God say unto him, The learned shall not read them, for they have rejected them, and I am able to do mine own work; wherefore, thou shalt read the words which I shall give unto thee.

provenance.other: “I am able to do” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 9:28: 'and Jesus saith unto them, Believe ye that I am able to do this? They said unto him, Yea, Lord.' The Book of Mormon completes it as 'mine own work', a phrase that occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The verse Matthew puts those words in is the healing of two blind men — 'the blind men came to him: and Jesus saith unto them, Believe ye that I am able to do this?' — and nine verses later this chapter arrives at Isaiah 29:18, 'the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity and out of darkness'. So the one place in the King James Bible where Christ says 'I am able to do' is a restoration of sight, quoted twice inside an expansion of the one chapter of Isaiah that ends in the restoration of sight. Neither text says this. The catalogue proposes that the sentence God speaks over the unlearned reader at 27:20-21 is Christ's question to the blind, answered.

links.note: 'I am able to do mine own work' is the hinge of the chapter's central scene — it is what disqualifies the learned and licenses the unlearned — and it is said twice, here and at 27:21. The n-gram stream found the string and ranked it low; nothing in the dossier connects it to the blindness that the chapter is heading toward, and that connection is this catalogue's. Graded high rather than certain because the completion of the clause is not Matthew's and the four shared words are common individually.
links.text: And when he was come into the house, the blind men came to him: and Jesus saith unto them, Believe ye that I am able to do this? They said unto him, Yea, Lord.

pericopes.text: Touch not the things which are sealed, for I will bring them forth in mine own due time: for I will shew unto the children of men, that I am able to do mine own work.

Wherefore, when thou hast read the words which I have commanded thee, and obtained the witnesses which I have promised unto thee, then shalt thou seal up the book again, and hide it up unto me, that I may preserve the words which thou hast not read, until I shall see fit in mine own wisdom, to reveal all things unto the children of men.

provenance.other: “seal the book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 12:4 — 'shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end' — and “sealed till the time of the end” in exactly one, Daniel 12:9. Isaiah 29:11 has a book that IS sealed but no instruction to seal one.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29 supplies this chapter's sealed book but not the act of sealing it, and not the reserving of its contents to an appointed time. Those are Daniel's: 'seal up the book again, and hide it up unto me, that I may preserve the words which thou hast not read, until I shall see fit in mine own wisdom, to reveal all things unto the children of men' is Daniel 12:4 and 12:9 in substance — words closed up and sealed till the time of the end — expressed without a phrase of Daniel's being reproduced. The chapter takes its book from Isaiah and its eschatology of sealing from Daniel.

links.note: Typed conceptual and graded moderate because there is almost no shared wording: 'seal' and 'book' are the whole verbal contact, and the Book of Mormon's 'mine own due time' at 27:21 is not Daniel's 'the time of the end'. The row is proposed on the strength of the whole apparatus arriving together — a book sealed by command, a portion withheld, a fixed time of disclosure — which the KJV assembles nowhere else. Flagged as a deliberate risk under CONVENTIONS §0a.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal survives. A writer with Isaiah 29:11's sealed book in front of him and any general knowledge of apocalyptic could produce this sentence without Daniel; and Revelation 5:1-5, with its book sealed and none worthy to open it, is an equally good conceptual home.
links.text: But thou, O Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end: many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.

pericopes.text: For behold, I am God; and I am a God of miracles; and I will shew unto the world that I am the same yesterday, to-day, and forever; and I work not among the children of men, save it be according to their faith.

provenance.other: “the same yesterday” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 13:8: 'Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.' The 1830 prints 'the same yesterday, to-day, and forever', hyphenating what the KJV sets as two words and closing up 'for ever'.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 13:8 is a statement about Christ's constancy set among practical exhortations; the Book of Mormon makes it a premise in an argument about miracles — 'I am God; and I am a God of miracles; and I will shew unto the world that I am the same yesterday, to-day, and forever'. The inference the verse wants is that a God who worked miracles anciently must work them now, which is Moroni 7:22 and Mormon 9:9's argument in full. Hebrews' unchangeableness has been made an argument for continuing revelation, which is the doctrine this whole chapter exists to establish.

links.note: A KJV singleton reproduced with the name removed, because in the Book of Mormon's sentence the speaker is the one Hebrews names. The orthographic detail cuts against CONVENTIONS §8's usual direction: here the 1830 modernises the KJV's spacing rather than preserving it, as it does with 'marvelous' at 25:17 and 'rumors' at 25:12. The first edition is not uniformly closer to the King James text than later ones.
links.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

pericopes.text: And again it shall come to pass, that the Lord shall say unto him that shall read the words that shall be delivered him,
For asmuch as this people draw near unto me with their mouth, and with their lips do honor me, but have removed their hearts far from me, and their fear towards me is taught by the precepts of men,

provenance.other: “precept of men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:13. The verse is quoted in the New Testament at Matthew 15:8-9 and Mark 7:6-7 in a markedly different form: 'This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me … teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.'
provenance.significance: The mediation test settles cleanly and in Isaiah's favour. The Book of Mormon reads 'this people draw near unto me with their mouth, and with their lips do honor me, but have removed their hearts far from me, and their fear towards me is taught by the precepts of men'. Three of its clauses exist only in the Old Testament form: 'draw near' rather than the gospels' 'draweth nigh'; 'have removed their heart[s] far from me', which the gospels reduce to 'their heart is far from me'; and the whole final clause about fear taught by precept, which the gospels replace with worship taught for doctrine. This matters because Isaiah 29:13 is one of the most familiar Old Testament verses in the New, and the Book of Mormon does not have the familiar form. It has the Hebrew Bible's.

links.note: mediation-check.py reports divergences pointing both ways and flags the verse as a possible composite; one of its two Isaiah points and its single Matthew point should both be discounted. The 'Matthew' point is an artifact — the tool records the Book of Mormon as lacking 'do honour me' when the 1830 reads 'do honor me', an American spelling the normalizer does not fold. Corrected, every discriminating clause favours Isaiah. The Book of Mormon's departures from Isaiah are the plural 'hearts', the plural 'precepts', 'towards' for 'toward', and the omission of Isaiah's 'Wherefore the Lord said' — none of which is a synoptic reading. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:13 here.
links.text: Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:

pericopes.text: therefore, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people; yea, a marvellous work, and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise and learned shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent shall be hid.

provenance.other: “marvellous work and a wonder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:14. The 1830 spells it with the KJV's double l here — 'a marvellous work among this people; yea, a marvellous work, and a wonder' — where at 2 Nephi 25:17, in Nephi's own exposition, the same 1830 prints 'marvelous'.
provenance.significance: The clause has now entered the book twice, and the two entries differ in exactly the ways one would expect of quotation and paraphrase. At 25:17 it is third person ('he will proceed to do'), the KJV's 'even' is replaced by 'and', the spelling is modernised, and it is applied to the restoration of Israel. Here it is first person as Isaiah has it, the spelling is the KJV's, and it is applied to the book. The catalogue can therefore exhibit a single KJV verse being handled two ways within two chapters by the same writer, which is a better piece of evidence about method than either occurrence alone.
provenance.alternative: None.

links.note: Two departures from Isaiah beyond 'yea' for 'even': 'their wise and learned' for 'their wise men', and 'their prudent' for 'their prudent men'. Both drop the KJV's 'men', and the first substitutes 'learned' — which is the word the preceding ten verses have been about, the learned man who could not read the sealed book. The quotation has been edited to point at the scene the expansion built.
links.text: Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, even a marvellous work and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid.

pericopes.text: And wo unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord. And their works are in the dark; and they say, Who seeth us; and who knoweth us? And they also say, Surely, your turning of things upside down, shall be esteemed as the potter’s clay. But behold, I will shew unto them, saith the Lord of Hosts, that I know all their works. For shall the work say of him that made it, He made me not? Or, shall the thing framed say of him that framed it, He had no understanding?

provenance.other: “esteemed as the potter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:16. Two whole verses of Isaiah stand here, and the machine's rarity scores for both, 22.23 and 36.50 on runs of twenty-nine words, are the highest in the chapter.
provenance.significance: The one substantive insertion is a repair. Isaiah 29:15-16 runs the mockers' speech and the prophet's rebuttal together without marking the transition — 'they say, Who seeth us? and who knoweth us? Surely your turning of things upside down shall be esteemed as the potter's clay' — so that the KJV's 'Surely' is ambiguous between the two voices. The Book of Mormon inserts 'And they also say' before it, assigning the clause to the mockers, and then adds 'But behold, I will shew unto them, saith the Lord of Hosts, that I know all their works' to mark the answer. An obscurity in the King James English has been resolved by adding a speech tag, which is a reading of the KJV and not of the Hebrew.

links.note: Apart from the two insertions, the passage is verbatim across nearly sixty words, including the two rhetorical questions about the work and the thing framed. This is the longest continuous agreement in the chapter and is well above Skousen's threshold, though the passage is not one of his 36.
links.text: Woe unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the LORD, and their works are in the dark, and they say, Who seeth us? and who knoweth us?

pericopes.text: But behold, saith the Lord of Hosts, I will shew unto the children of men, that it is not yet a very little while, and Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field; and the fruitful field shall be esteemed as a forest.

provenance.other: “a very little while” with Lebanon and the fruitful field occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:17; Isaiah 32:15 has the fruitful field and the forest in a different frame ('counted for a forest'). The machine's longest run here is twenty-five words.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:17 is a rhetorical question — 'Is it not yet a very little while …?' — whose force is that the reversal is imminent. The Book of Mormon turns it into a negated statement inside a divine speech: 'I will shew unto the children of men, that it is not yet a very little while, and Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field'. Read as English the sense is nearly inverted: Isaiah asks whether the time is not short, and the Book of Mormon asserts that it is not yet short. The words are the same and the grammar has done something to them, which is the most instructive small departure in the chapter.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:17 here. Whether the change is deliberate is not decidable from the text: turning a KJV rhetorical question into a statement is what this chapter does at 27:4 and 27:5 as well, and in those places the sense survives. Here it does not obviously survive, and the catalogue records that rather than smoothing it. 1830 and 1920 agree; there is no variant to appeal to.
links.text: Is it not yet a very little while, and Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be esteemed as a forest?

pericopes.text: And in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book; and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity and out of darknesss;

provenance.other: “out of obscurity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:18. The verse stands here verbatim apart from the 1830's misprint 'darknesss'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:18's 'the words of the book' is a figure completed by v. 11's simile; in the Book of Mormon it has a referent, because vv. 6-22 of this chapter have spent sixteen verses producing an actual book for the deaf to hear. And the blindness healed here is what makes sense of 27:20's borrowing from Matthew 9:28: the one KJV verse in which Christ says 'I am able to do' is a healing of blind men, and it is quoted eleven verses before Isaiah promises that the eyes of the blind shall see.

links.note: A whole verse reproduced with no departure of substance. It is catalogued rather than passed over because it is the terminus of the chapter's argument — the book that could not be read is now read, and the eyes that were closed at 27:5 are opened here — and because the closing of those eyes at 27:5 was the chapter's largest departure from Isaiah. The 1830's trebled s in 'darknesss' is a compositor's error corrected by 1920.
links.text: And in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness.

pericopes.text: and the meek also shall increase, and their joy shall be in the Lord; and the poor among men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.

provenance.other: Isaiah 29:19 reads 'The meek also shall increase their joy in the LORD'. 2 Nephi 27:30 reads 'and the meek also shall increase, and their joy shall be in the Lord'. “the poor among men shall rejoice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:19.
provenance.significance: A transitive verb has been made intransitive and the object turned into a new clause, so that the meek increase in number rather than in joy, and the joy is predicated separately. That is a reading of an ambiguous English sentence rather than a slip: the KJV's 'shall increase their joy' can be parsed as it stands, but 'the meek shall increase' is the more natural English if the words are heard rather than construed. The second half of the verse, 'the poor among men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel', is verbatim.

links.note: One of the small syntactic departures that a mechanical collation would report as a word-order variant and that is in fact a change of meaning. The Book of Mormon's version has the meek multiplying, which fits the chapter's restoration theme and does not fit Isaiah's clause.
links.text: The meek also shall increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.

pericopes.text: For assuredly as the Lord liveth, they shall see that the terrible one is brought to nought, and the scorner is consumed, and all that watch for iniquity are cut off:

provenance.other: Isaiah 29:20's three clauses — the terrible one brought to nought, the scorner consumed, all that watch for iniquity cut off — stand verbatim. Isaiah's opening 'For' is replaced by fourteen words of the Book of Mormon's own: 'For assuredly as the Lord liveth, they shall see that'. “the scorner is consumed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:20.
provenance.significance: The inserted oath does two things. It converts Isaiah's assertion into something promised to witnesses — 'they shall see that' — which continues the chapter's preoccupation with seeing, from the closed eyes of 27:5 to the opened eyes of 27:29 to the three witnesses who 'shall behold it' at 27:12. And 'as the Lord liveth' is the oath formula that 2 Nephi 25:20 borrowed from Jeremiah 16:14, two chapters earlier and in the same writer's exposition.

links.note: Isaiah's 'the terrible one' is singular here and the same chapter's 'the terrible ones' plural at 29:5 went to 2 Nephi 26:18 with the pronoun changed. Both survive unaltered in number, which is a small check that the two halves of Isaiah 29 were handled independently rather than harmonised.
links.text: For the terrible one is brought to nought, and the scorner is consumed, and all that watch for iniquity are cut off:

pericopes.text: and they that make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought.

provenance.other: Isaiah 29:21 stands entire and word for word: 'That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought.' The Book of Mormon's only change is 'and they that make' for 'That make', supplying the relative's antecedent. The machine's longest run in the chapter, thirty words, is here. “an offender for a word” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:21.
provenance.significance: A verse with no departure at all is evidence in its own right. It shows that where the expansion leaves Isaiah alone it leaves him completely alone, which is what makes the departures elsewhere — the agency reversal at 27:5, the speech tag at 27:27, the intransitive verb at 27:30 — legible as choices rather than as the noise of loose recollection.

links.note: Reproduced verbatim across thirty words, so this passage is above Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; it is not among his 36 and nothing here should be taken to imply that it is. Recorded chiefly as the control case for the chapter's other rows.
links.text: That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought.

pericopes.text: Therefore thus saith the Lord, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale.

provenance.other: Isaiah 29:22 stands entire, with 'the LORD' rendered 'the Lord' and 'thus saith' retained: 'Therefore thus saith the Lord, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale.' “neither shall his face now wax pale” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:22.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's phrase 'who redeemed Abraham' is one of the Old Testament's few references to a redemption of Abraham himself, and the Book of Mormon keeps it without comment — as it keeps 'wax pale', a KJV idiom for shame that no modern version retains. Where 2 Nephi 27 has an argument to make it makes it; where Isaiah is simply concluding, the expansion goes silent and copies.

links.note: Verbatim. This verse and the two that follow close the chapter as a plain transcription of Isaiah 29:22-24, which is the reverse of how the chapter opened — 27:1 is wholly non-biblical and 27:7-14 has no Isaiah at all. The expansion is front-loaded, and the finding is that the additions cluster precisely around the sealed book.
links.text: Therefore thus saith the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale.

pericopes.text: But when he seeth his children, the work of my hands, in the midst of him, they shall sanctify my name, and sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel.

provenance.other: “the work of mine hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:23. The Book of Mormon reads 'the work of my hands', substituting the possessive that stands before a consonant for the KJV's pre-vocalic 'mine'.
provenance.significance: The my/mine alternation is a live feature of early modern English that the King James translators observe by rule — 'mine hands' before a vowel or h, 'my hands' elsewhere — and the 1830 Book of Mormon does not observe it here. That is a small but real datum about the route: the borrowing has passed through a nineteenth-century hand for which the rule is no longer productive, which is exactly what CONVENTIONS §8 says the first edition is evidence for.

links.note: Otherwise verbatim, including 'sanctify the Holy One of Jacob' — a title the KJV uses only here — and 'shall fear the God of Israel'. The row is graded certain on the wording and the note carries the orthographic observation, which is worth having across the corpus and is not by itself an argument about anything larger.
links.text: But when he seeth his children, the work of mine hands, in the midst of him, they shall sanctify my name, and sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel.

pericopes.text: They also that erred in spirit shall come to understandding, and they that murmured shall learn doctrine.

provenance.other: “erred in spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:24. The Book of Mormon reproduces the verse entire, with the 1830 misprint 'understandding'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29 ends on instruction: those who erred come to understanding, those who murmured learn doctrine. Placed at the end of 2 Nephi 27 it closes the arc the chapter opened at 27:5, where the people had closed their own eyes and rejected the prophets — the last word of the expansion is that the erring are taught, which is what the sealed book was for.

links.note: Verbatim, and the chapter's last verse. With 27:32, 27:33 and 27:34 it forms an unbroken transcription of Isaiah 29:21-24 running to the end of both chapters, so the expansion and its source finish together.
links.text: They also that erred in spirit shall come to understanding, and they that murmured shall learn doctrine.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, my brethren, I have spoken unto you, according as the spirit hath constrained me; wherefore, I know that they must surely come to pass.
The things which shall be written out of the book shall be of great worth unto the children of men, and especially unto our seed, which are a remnant of the House of Israel.

For it shall come to pass in that day, that the churches which are built up, and not unto the Lord, when the one shall say unto the other, Behold, I, I am the Lord’s; and the other shall say, I, I am the Lord’s. And thus shall every one say, that hath built up churches, and not unto the Lord;

links.text: One shall say, I am the LORD’s; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the LORD, and surname himself by the name of Israel.

provenance.other: “I am the LORD’s” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 44:5, and Isaiah 44 is not among the chapters this book transcribes. The construction is reproduced with its syntax intact: Isaiah's “One shall say… and another shall call himself” becomes “the one shall say unto the other… and the other shall say”.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis inverts the source. In Isaiah 44 the sentence is a promise of blessing on Jacob's seed — the outpoured Spirit makes people claim the LORD by name, subscribe with the hand, surname themselves Israel — and it is the happy outcome of the chapter. 2 Nephi 28 gives the identical sentence to rival churches “built up, and not unto the Lord”, so that the KJV's one verse for freely claiming God's name becomes the formula of sectarian contention. The 1830's doubled “Behold, I, I am the Lord's” is not in Isaiah; it is the stammer of the claim being made twice at once by two parties, which is the whole point of the verse.

links.note: The distinctive element is a KJV singleton and it is quoted exactly. What the verse does with it is the finding: Isaiah 44:5 describes people gladly avowing the LORD, and 28:3 puts the avowal in the mouths of churches the verse has just said are not built unto Him. Nothing in Isaiah 44 licenses that reading, and the Book of Mormon has not supplied a bridge — it has simply taken the sentence and turned it. Note that the run “for it shall come to pass in that day” which the n-gram stream ranked first here is Jeremiah 30:8's connective boilerplate and is excluded.

pericopes.text: and they shall contend one with another; and their priests shall contend one with another; and they shall teach with their learning, and deny the Holy Ghost, which giveth utterance.

links.text: And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.

provenance.other: “gave them utterance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:4. “Utterance” at all is a rare KJV word and in every other instance it is something asked for or given to a preacher (Ephesians 6:19, Colossians 4:3, 1 Corinthians 1:5, 2 Corinthians 8:7); Acts 2:4 is the only verse where the Spirit is its subject in this construction.
provenance.significance: Nephi's charge is that the priests “teach with their learning, and deny the Holy Ghost, which giveth utterance”. Recover the source and the antithesis is exact: Pentecost is the one scene in the Bible where men speak without their learning because the Spirit gives the utterance, and the crowd's charge against them is that they are unlearned Galileans. To teach with learning and deny the Spirit's utterance is, in the terms of Acts 2, to be the mockers rather than the apostles. The chapter returns to the same page of Acts at 28:26, where what is denied is “the gift of the Holy Ghost” (Acts 2:38).

links.note: Three words carry this, but they are the KJV's only three of their kind, and they arrive attached to the Holy Ghost in a clause about teaching — which is Acts 2's subject exactly. Nephi has taken the participial tag that identifies the Spirit at Pentecost and used it as an appositive definition: the Holy Ghost is “the Holy Ghost, which giveth utterance”, as though naming the office these teachers deny. The link is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is catalogued as an allusion accordingly.

pericopes.text: And they deny the power of God, the Holy One of Israel; and they say unto the people, Hearken unto us, and hear ye our precept: for behold, there is no God to-day, for the Lord and the Redeemer hath done his work, and he hath given his power unto men.

links.text: Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.

provenance.other: “denying the power” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 3:5. No KJV verse reads “deny the power” in any inflection other than this one.
provenance.significance: 2 Timothy 3:1-5 is the KJV's set-piece catalogue of last-days corruption, and 2 Nephi 28 is a catalogue of the same shape: Paul's “lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud… heady, highminded” against Nephi's pride, puffed-up hearts, fine sanctuaries and fine clothing. Paul's list ends with the very charge Nephi makes here, and Paul's frame — “in the last days perilous times shall come” — is the frame 28:3 has already set with “in that day”. Recovering the source therefore supplies not one phrase but the genre of the whole chapter: the reader who hears 2 Timothy 3 behind 28:5 is being asked to read verses 12-15 as its expansion.

links.note: “They deny the power of God” reproduces the KJV's one occurrence of the phrase, and does so where Paul does — at the end of a list of last-days sins whose members Nephi has been reciting since verse 3. The form-of-godliness half is not quoted, but 28:3's churches “built up, and not unto the Lord” is what it describes. The verse then goes further than Paul in a way worth recording: Paul's men keep the form and deny the power; Nephi's say outright “there is no God to-day”, which is the position of the fool in Psalm 14:1 — the psalm the chapter will quote at verse 11, though it will quote it in Romans's words rather than the psalm's.

pericopes.text: Behold, hearken ye unto my precept: if they shall say there is a miracle wrought, by the hand of the Lord, believe it not; for this day he is not a God of miracles: he hath done his work.
Yea, and there shall be many which shall say, eat, drink, and be merry, for to-morrow we die; and it shall be well with us.

links.text: And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.

provenance.other: “eat, drink, and be merry” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 12:19. Isaiah 22:13 and 1 Corinthians 15:32 both read “let us eat and drink”, without the merriment; Ecclesiastes 8:15 has “to eat, and to drink, and to be merry”, which is a different construction. The Book of Mormon has Luke's three imperatives in Luke's order and Luke's punctuation.
provenance.significance: The rich fool is the point. Luke 12:19 is spoken by a man whose barns are full and who is dead by verse 20 — “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee” — and Luke's application is “so is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God”. That is precisely Nephi's indictment two verses later: fine sanctuaries, fine clothing, robbing the poor. The chapter then draws on the same chapter of Luke again at 28:8 (Luke 12:48's few stripes), so the two sayings the false teachers use to excuse themselves are both taken from the one Lucan discourse that exists to condemn them.

links.note: The saying is usually traced to Isaiah 22:13, and Isaiah is indeed behind it — but not for these words. “Eat, drink, and be merry” is the rich fool's sentence and no one else's in the KJV; Isaiah's people say “let us eat and drink”. The second half of the verse comes from elsewhere again: see the 1 Corinthians 15:32 link, where the mediation is decided. What 28:7 has done is fuse the Lucan parable's clause with the Pauline clause, which is why the composite reads more fluently than either source.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 2 Ne 28.7 (Isaiah 22:13, Ecclesiastes 8:15, Luke 12:19, 1 Corinthians 15:32)
