links.text: If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantageth it me, if the dead rise not? let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die.

provenance.route: Isaiah 22:13 → 1 Corinthians 15:32 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “for to morrow we die” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:32. “for to morrow we shall die” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 22:13. The two differ by a single auxiliary and the Book of Mormon has Paul's form, without “shall”.
provenance.significance: Paul quotes Isaiah 22:13 as the slogan of people who do not believe in resurrection — “if the dead rise not, let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die” — and Nephi's speakers add the clause Paul's do not: “and it shall be well with us.” Recover Paul's context and the addition is the joke. 1 Corinthians 15 is the resurrection chapter; the sentence Nephi's easy believers borrow is the one Paul frames as what you would say only if there were no resurrection at all. Their “it shall be well with us” is thus staked on the very thing their slogan denies.

links.note: This is the chapter's cleanest mediation result. Isaiah 22:13 and 1 Corinthians 15:32 differ at exactly one word — Isaiah's “shall” — and the Book of Mormon lacks it, which is Paul's form. `mediation-check.py` returned no decisive divergence on this pair, for two reasons worth recording: the 1830 prints “to-morrow” hyphenated against the KJV's two words, so the tool's alignment breaks at that token, and “shall” is a common word the tool suppresses to avoid false positives (ADJUDICATING §4). The comparison is therefore made by eye, and it is not close. Nephi's speakers say Paul's sentence, not Isaiah's.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 2 Ne 28.7 (Isaiah 22:13, Ecclesiastes 8:15, Luke 12:19, 1 Corinthians 15:32)

pericopes.text: And there shall also be many which shall say, eat, drink, and be merry; nevertheless, fear God, he will justify in committing a little sin; yea, lie a little, take the advantage of one because of his words, dig a pit for thy neighbor; there is no harm in this. And do all these things, for to-morrow we die; and if it so be that we are guilty, God will beat us with a few stripes, and at last we shall be saved in the Kingdom of God.

links.text: But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more.

provenance.other: “beaten with few stripes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 12:48; its companion “beaten with many stripes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 12:47. No other KJV passage counts stripes.
provenance.significance: The two sayings this verse and the last put in the mouths of the wicked come from one chapter of Luke, twenty-nine verses apart: the rich fool's “eat, drink, and be merry” (12:19) and the unfaithful steward's few stripes (12:48). That is not two borrowings but one, from a single discourse whose subject is exactly the security these speakers are claiming — Luke 12 runs from the barns to the thief in the night to the servant beaten at his lord's return. And Luke 12:48's punchline is the sentence Nephi's speakers have carefully not quoted: “unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.” The false doctrine is built by stopping the verse one clause early.

links.note: “God will beat us with a few stripes, and at last we shall be saved” is Luke 12:48 turned into a doctrine of limited liability. In Luke the few stripes are the lighter of two sentences on servants who are both beaten; the point of the pair is that ignorance mitigates but does not acquit. Nephi's speakers hear it as an assurance. That the verse also supplies “beat” and “stripes” as a collocation found nowhere else in the KJV is what makes this a verbal borrowing and not a shared idea. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the argument here lives in the half of Luke 12:48 that has been suppressed.

links.text: That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought.

provenance.other: Isaiah 29:21 is transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 27:32, where its wording is identical to the KJV's. The clause here is a paraphrase rather than a quotation and no rarity count supports it on its own.
provenance.significance: The chapter is an exposition of Isaiah 29 and it uses the source twice over: paraphrased into the sins it catalogues at verse 8, and quoted outright at verse 16. Read that way, “take the advantage of one because of his words” is Isaiah's “make a man an offender for a word” restated as a maxim of the wicked instead of a charge against them — the same move the chapter makes at 28:3 with Isaiah 44:5.

links.note: “Take the advantage of one because of his words” has no KJV wording behind it, but it restates Isaiah 29:21's first clause exactly in sense, and Isaiah 29:21 is demonstrably in view eight verses later where it is quoted verbatim. The link is offered as the paraphrase half of that quotation, not as independent evidence; a reader who declines it loses nothing at 28:16.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is a paraphrase and nothing more — no shared distinctive word survives. If 28:16 did not quote Isaiah 29:21 outright this row would not be worth writing, and it should be read as a pointer to that verse rather than as a link standing on its own evidence.

pericopes.text: Yea, and there shall be many which shall teach after this manner, false, and vain, and foolish doctrines, and shall be puffed up in their hearts, and shall seek deep to hide their counsels from the Lord; and their works shall be in the dark;

links.text: Woe unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the LORD, and their works are in the dark, and they say, Who seeth us? and who knoweth us?

provenance.route: Isaiah 29:15 → KJV → Book of Mormon (this book's own transcription of the verse is at 2 Nephi 27:27)
provenance.other: “seek deep to hide” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:15, and “their works are in the dark” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Both are reproduced here, the second with tense adjusted to the prophecy's future: “their works shall be in the dark”.
provenance.significance: This is the shape the whole of Nephi's exposition takes, and it is worth stating once here. 2 Nephi 27 has just transcribed Isaiah 29 at length; 2 Nephi 28 then preaches from it, and the borrowed clauses arrive without quotation formula, as Nephi's own words about the churches of the last days. Isaiah's target was Jerusalem's counsellors hiding policy from the LORD; Nephi's is teachers hiding counsel from Him while claiming His name. The recovered context supplies the taunt the Book of Mormon does not repeat — “Who seeth us? and who knoweth us?” — which is the unspoken premise of the “no God to-day” of verse 5.

links.note: Two KJV singletons in one clause, in the source's order, with only the verb tense moved. There is no question of dependence. The interest is entirely in the route: the verse Nephi is quoting has already been given in full four chapters earlier at 2 Nephi 27:27, and the 27 text reads “seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord. And their works are in the dark” — so the plural “counsels” here is the expositor's own, not the transcription's and not the KJV's. That single letter is the only thing separating Nephi's sermon from his scripture, which is a fair emblem of how this chapter works.

pericopes.text: and the blood of the Saints shall cry from the ground against them.

links.text: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.

provenance.route: Genesis 4:10 + Revelation 17:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “crieth unto me from the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 4:10; “from the ground” in the sense of blood crying occurs nowhere else (its three other KJV occurrences are Ezekiel's temple measurements). “the blood of the saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 17:6.
provenance.significance: The verse fuses the Bible's first murder with its last, and the fusion is set up by the chapter itself. Revelation 17:6's blood of the saints belongs to “the woman drunken with the blood of the saints” — the great whore — and eight verses later 28:18 names “the whore of all the earth”. So the blood that cries from Abel's ground in verse 10 is, by verse 18, in the cup of Revelation's harlot. Neither source says this. Reading 28:10 and 28:18 as one sentence says it, and that is the argument for taking the composite seriously rather than treating the two phrases as unrelated borrowings.

links.note: A ten-word verse resting on two KJV singletons pulled from opposite ends of the canon. Genesis supplies the crying blood and the ground; Revelation supplies whose blood it is. The Book of Mormon's own contribution is “against them”, which Genesis leaves implicit and which turns a cry into an accusation — and which is what makes the clause a prophecy of judgment rather than a lament. Hebrews 12:24, where Christ's blood “speaketh better things than that of Abel”, is the passage the New Testament usually reaches for here and is conspicuously not in view: this verse wants Abel's cry unanswered.

pericopes.text: Yea, they have all gone out of the way; they have become corrupted.

links.text: They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one.

provenance.route: Psalm 14:3 → Romans 3:12 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Psalm 14:3 הַכֹּל סָר, 'the whole has turned aside' — which is what the KJV renders 'all gone aside'.
provenance.lxx: Psalm 13:3 LXX πάντες ἐξέκλιναν, quoted at Romans 3:12; the KJV renders the Greek 'all gone out of the way' and the Hebrew 'all gone aside'.
provenance.other: “all gone out of the way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 3:12. “all gone aside” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 14:3. The Book of Mormon has Romans's.
provenance.significance: Romans 3:10-18 is Paul's chain of Old Testament indictments, and Psalm 14:1 — “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God” — is its opening text. 2 Nephi 28 has been working the same psalm since verse 5, where the false teachers say “there is no God to-day”; at verse 11 it reaches the psalm's third verse and takes it in Paul's English rather than the psalm's. What the reader recovers is that the chapter's charge is Romans 3's charge: not that some are wicked but that all have gone out of the way, which is why verse 14 has to except “a few, which are the humble followers of Christ”.

links.note: The chapter's decisive mediation result and one of the clearest in the book. `mediation-check.py` on Psalm 14:3 against Romans 3:12 reports one decisive point: the Book of Mormon reads “out of the way”, which is Romans's rendering of the Greek, and not “aside”, which is the KJV's rendering of the Hebrew at the psalm the verse is otherwise following. Psalm 53:3, the doublet psalm, reads “every one of them is gone back” and is likewise excluded. The second clause confirms it structurally without confirming it verbally: Psalm 14:3 has “become filthy”, Romans 3:12 “become unprofitable”, and the Book of Mormon has “become corrupted”, which is neither — a paraphrase of Paul's abstraction rather than the psalm's concrete word.

pericopes.text: Because of pride, and because of false teachers, and false doctrine, their churches have become corrupted; and their churches are lifted up; because of pride, they are puffed up.

They rob the poor, because of their fine sanctuaries; they rob the poor, because of their fine clothing; and they persecute the meek, and the poor in heart; because in their pride, they are puffed up.

links.text: Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate:

provenance.other: “Rob not the poor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 22:22; no other KJV verse joins the verb 'rob' to 'the poor' in any inflection. “The wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 10:2, and is the only KJV verse holding pride, persecution and the poor together.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon supplies the reason Proverbs withholds. Proverbs 22:22 forbids robbing the poor “because he is poor”; 28:13 says these rob the poor “because of their fine sanctuaries… because of their fine clothing”, so the causal clause is kept and its content replaced, turning a prohibition into an account of motive. Psalm 10:2 then supplies the frame the verse ends on — the wicked persecuting the poor out of pride — which is why “because in their pride, they are puffed up” closes a sentence that began with robbery.

links.note: “They rob the poor” twice, with a causal clause each time, against the KJV's one verse that says exactly “Rob not the poor, because…”. The inversion of the imperative into an indictment is the borrowing's whole method, and it is the method of 28:3 and 28:9 as well. The Psalm 10:2 half is weaker verbally but supplies the two elements Proverbs lacks and 28:13 has: persecution, and pride as its motive. Confidence is held at moderate because both sources are proverbial denunciations of a very common biblical kind, and a reader who prefers to call this the shared idiom of prophetic social criticism rather than a borrowing has a case.

pericopes.text: They wear stiff necks, and high heads; yea, and because of pride, and wickedness, and abominations, and whoredoms, they have all gone astray, save it be a few, which are the humble followers of Christ; nevertheless, they are led, that in many instances they do err, because they are taught by the precepts of men.

links.text: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.

provenance.other: “have gone astray” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 119:176 and Isaiah 53:6; only Isaiah 53:6 has it of a whole people, and only there is it 'all'. Isaiah 53 is not among the chapters transcribed in this book.
provenance.significance: The recovered context does the work. Isaiah 53:6 is the verse where the general straying is answered — “the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all” — so the sentence Nephi borrows to say the churches have all gone astray is the sentence that says the straying has been carried by the Servant. The exception clause follows immediately: “save it be a few, which are the humble followers of Christ.” Isaiah's 'all' admits no exception and Nephi's does, which is the one substantive change, and it is made in favour of the very figure Isaiah 53:6 introduces.

links.note: Four words, but they are the four that open the most quoted verse of Isaiah 53 and they are used of the same subject: a whole people gone astray, each in his own way. The Book of Mormon drops Isaiah's simile — no sheep here — which is why this is catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation, and why confidence is moderate rather than high. Note also the pairing with the second link on this verse: 28:14 reaches Isaiah 53 and Isaiah 29 in one sentence, which is a fair description of what the chapter is doing throughout.

links.text: Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:

provenance.other: “taught by the precept of men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:13, and the KJV's noun there is singular. This book's own transcription of the verse, at 2 Nephi 27:25, reads “taught by the precepts of men” — plural. 28:14, 28:26 and 28:31 all read the plural.
provenance.significance: This is the mediation the book has been promising since CONVENTIONS §7 predicted it: not OT-via-NT but OT-via-earlier-Book-of-Mormon. The proximate model for 28:14 is not the KJV's Isaiah 29:13 but 2 Nephi 27:25, which had already pluralised the precept, and the plural then propagates through the sermon — 28:26 and 28:31 both have 'precepts of men', and so does the false teachers' invitation at 28:5, “hear ye our precept”, which is the singular restored to the mouths of the men doing the teaching. A reader who recovers the context recovers the mechanism: the expositor is quoting his own scripture, and quoting it in the form his book gave it.

links.note: A KJV singleton quoted exactly except in number, and the number is the finding. The KJV has 'precept', 2 Nephi 27:25 has 'precepts', and every occurrence in this chapter has 'precepts' — which locates the proximate source inside the Book of Mormon rather than in the Bible. That is a small thing to hang a mediation call on, and it is the only evidence there is, so it is stated rather than assumed: nothing else in 28:14 distinguishes the two possible routes. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:13 at this verse and at 28:26; the transcription he would send a reader to is at 27:25.

pericopes.text: O the wise, and the learned, and the rich, that are puffed up in the pride of their hearts, and all they that preach false doctrines, and all they that commit whoredoms, and pervert the right way of the Lord; wo, wo, wo be unto them, saith the Lord God Almighty, for they shall be thrust down to hell.

links.text: And thou, Capernaum, which art exalted to heaven, shalt be thrust down to hell.

provenance.other: “thrust down to hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 10:15. “brought down to hell” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 14:15 and Matthew 11:23 — Matthew's being the synoptic parallel to Luke 10:15 and Isaiah's being the taunt over Lucifer which this book transcribes at 2 Nephi 24:15.
provenance.significance: The discrimination is threefold and it all falls one way. Of the three KJV sentences that send someone down to hell, the Book of Mormon has the one that says 'thrust' — not Matthew's 'brought', and not Isaiah 14:15's 'brought', although Isaiah 14:15 stands transcribed in this same book eight chapters earlier at 2 Nephi 24:15 and was therefore the nearest form to hand. Recover Luke 10:15 and the reason is visible: Capernaum is condemned for being 'exalted to heaven', which is the sin of 28:15 exactly — the wise, the learned and the rich 'puffed up in the pride of their hearts'. Exaltation is what makes the thrusting apt, and Isaiah 14:15's proud king would have served the theme but not the syntax.

links.note: Five words, a KJV singleton, and a real choice made between three near-identical candidates one of which is inside this book. That is what makes the row worth more than its length. The verse's other distinctive feature, the triple “wo, wo, wo”, is not from Luke: it belongs with Revelation 8:13's threefold woe on the inhabiters of the earth, which 28:16 goes on to name — but the wording there is too slight to catalogue and it is registered as an exclusion rather than a link.

pericopes.text: Wo unto them that turn aside the just for a thing of nought and revile against that which is good, and say that it is of no worth: for the day shall come that the Lord God will speedily visit the inhabitants of the earth; and in that day that they are fully ripe in iniquity, they shall perish.

links.text: That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought.

provenance.route: Isaiah 29:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon (transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 27:32)
provenance.other: “turn aside the just for a thing of nought” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:21, and is reproduced here word for word, in the 1830's spelling 'nought' which 1920 modernised to 'naught'. 2 Nephi 27:32's transcription of the same verse is identical to the KJV, so — unlike 28:14 — nothing here distinguishes the biblical route from the internal one.
provenance.significance: The clause is turned from a participle into a woe. Isaiah 29:21 is the tail of a list describing 'all that watch for iniquity'; Nephi makes it the subject of “Wo unto them that…”, which is the formula of Isaiah 29:15 that he has already borrowed at 28:9. So the exposition reassembles Isaiah 29 out of order: 29:15's woe-formula at verse 9, 29:21's offence at verse 16, 29:13's precepts at verse 14. What a reader recovers is that 2 Nephi 28 is not commenting on Isaiah 29 verse by verse but preaching from it, taking its clauses as they serve.

links.note: Nine words verbatim from a KJV singleton, which by any measure is a quotation. The verse then adds “and revile against that which is good, and say that it is of no worth”, restating Isaiah's 'thing of nought' as a valuation the wicked make rather than a price they accept — a gloss, and the kind of gloss the brief expects where an expositor handles a text his book has transcribed. The n-gram stream also offered Jeremiah 14:14 for 'a thing of nought'; it is excluded in favour of Isaiah 29:21, whose whole clause is here.

links.text: And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.

provenance.other: “fully ripe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:18. The Book of Mormon uses 'ripe in iniquity' as a standing formula elsewhere; the intensifier 'fully' is what points at Revelation.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:18-20 is the vintage of wrath: the grapes fully ripe are gathered and trodden in the winepress outside the city. 28:16's sentence has the same two movements in the same order — the Lord 'will speedily visit the inhabitants of the earth', and 'in that day that they are fully ripe in iniquity, they shall perish'. Ripeness in Revelation is not a metaphor for wickedness but the signal that the harvest may begin, and that is the logic of Nephi's clause: the destruction waits on the ripening, which is also why 28:17 can offer the escape of repentance.

links.note: Two words, and it would not be worth a row except that they are the KJV's only two of their kind and they arrive attached to the same idea — a judgment held until a crop is ready. 'Fully ripe in iniquity' is a Book of Mormon formula rather than a biblical phrase, so what is being catalogued is where the formula got its intensifier, not a quotation. Confidence is moderate and the reader who prefers to treat 'fully ripe' as ordinary English rather than a borrowing should.

pericopes.text: But behold, if the inhabitants of the earth shall repent of their wickedness and abominations, they shall not be destroyed, saith the Lord of Hosts.
But behold, that great and abominable church, the whore of all the earth, must tumble to the earth; and great must be the fall thereof:

links.text: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it.

provenance.other: “great was the fall of it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:27; Luke's parallel at 6:49 reads 'the ruin of that house was great', which is a different sentence. The clause was adjudicated at its first Book of Mormon occurrence, 1 Nephi 11:36.
provenance.significance: The phrase re-enters here in a new hand and with a new referent. At 1 Nephi 11:36 the great and spacious building falls; here it is 'that great and abominable church, the whore of all the earth' that must tumble, and ten verses later 28:28 returns to the same parable from the other end — the house on the rock and the house on the sandy foundation. So the chapter opens and closes its account of the false church with the two halves of Matthew 7:24-27, the fall first and the foundations after. Recovering Matthew's context supplies the criterion Nephi's verse withholds: what distinguishes the two houses is not what they profess but whether they do the sayings.

links.note: Across a book boundary the link is written rather than excluded (ADJUDICATING §4): a reader of 2 Nephi shown nothing at 28:18 has been told there is no borrowing here. The argument for the KJV singleton was made at 1 Nephi 11:36 and is not restated. What is new at 28:18 is the object — the whore of all the earth, whose blood-drunkenness at Revelation 17:6 has already been drawn on eight verses earlier at 28:10 — and the modal, 'great must be the fall thereof', which converts Matthew's narrative past into prophetic necessity.

pericopes.text: for the kingdom of the Devil must shake, and they which belong to it must needs be stirred up unto repentance, or the Devil will grasp them with his everlasting chains, and they be stirred up to anger and perish:

links.text: And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.

provenance.other: “everlasting chains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jude 1:6. 2 Peter 2:4's parallel reads 'chains of darkness', which is a different phrase; no other KJV verse binds anyone in chains that are everlasting.
provenance.significance: In Jude the everlasting chains hold the fallen angels, and the devil is not the jailer but a fellow prisoner — reserved, like them, unto the judgment of the great day. 28:19 hands him the chains: 'the Devil will grasp them with his everlasting chains', and 28:22 repeats the grasp with 'his awful chains'. The metalepsis is a reversal of role rather than of sense. What Jude says is being kept for the devil's own judgment becomes, in Nephi's sentence, the instrument he uses on others — which is why 28:23 can put 'the Devil, and all that have been seized therewith' in one dock together before the throne of God. Jude's arrangement is restored at the end of the paragraph.

links.note: The possessive is the whole finding: Jude's chains belong to the judgment and Nephi's belong to the devil. A borrowing that changes the owner of the rarest phrase in its source is doing something, and what it is doing here is set right three verses later, where the chained devil stands before the throne with those he chained. The 'kingdom of the Devil' that opens the verse has no KJV wording behind it — the KJV's nearest is Matthew 12:26's 'how shall then his kingdom stand' — and is not catalogued.

pericopes.text: for behold, at that day shall he rage in the hearts of the children of men, and stir them up to anger against that which is good;

and others will he pacify, and lull them away into carnal security, that they will say, All is well in Zion; yea, Zion prospereth, all is well; and thus the Devil cheateth their souls, and leadeth them away carefully down to hell.

And behold, others he flattereth away, and telleth them there is no hell; and he saith unto them, I am no Devil, for there is none: and thus he whispereth in their ears, until he grasps them with his awful chains, from whence there is no deliverance.

Yea, they are grasped with death, and hell; and death, and hell, and the Devil, and all that have been seized therewith, must stand before the Throne of God, and be judged according to their works, from whence they must go into the place prepared for them, even a lake of fire and brimstone, which is endless torment.

links.text: And the sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works.

provenance.other: “judged every man according to their works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:13. “death and hell” occurs in exactly two, Revelation 20:13 and 20:14. “lake of fire and brimstone” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 20:10. The trailing relative clause 'which is endless torment' answers Revelation 21:8's 'which is the second death', the only other KJV sentence that closes a lake-of-fire with a 'which is' gloss.
provenance.significance: The verse walks Revelation 20:10-15 in Revelation's order and compresses six verses into one: the devil cast into the lake of fire and brimstone (20:10), the dead standing before God (20:12), death and hell delivering up their dead and every man judged according to his works (20:13), death and hell themselves cast into the lake (20:14). Nephi's addition is to make the seized share the sentence of the seizer — 'death, and hell, and the Devil, and all that have been seized therewith' stand in one rank — which collapses Revelation's careful sequence of separate judgments into a single arraignment. The 'which is endless torment' that replaces 'which is the second death' is the one place the verse declines its source's word, and it declines the word that would have made the torment finite.

links.note: Four Revelation verses in one sentence, three of them identifiable by KJV singletons, in the source's sequence. This is the densest borrowing in the chapter and the most nearly mechanical: the only substantive rearrangement is the merging of Revelation 20:13's judged dead with 20:14's condemned death-and-hell, so that the personified powers are judged alongside the people. The n-gram stream found the lake of fire from both Revelation 20:10 and 21:8 and could not order them; the ordering is supplied by the phrase 'judged according to their works', which is 20:13's and fixes the passage.

pericopes.text: Therefore, wo be unto him that is at ease in Zion.

links.text: Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!

provenance.other: “at ease in Zion” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Amos 6:1, and the whole woe-formula is reproduced with only the number changed from plural to singular: 'Woe to them that are at ease in Zion' becomes 'wo be unto him that is at ease in Zion'.
provenance.significance: Amos 6 is the oracle against complacency, and its next verses are an inventory of luxury — beds of ivory, lambs out of the flock, wine in bowls, chief ointments — 'but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph'. 2 Nephi 28 has already made that inventory its own at verse 13, with the fine sanctuaries and fine clothing, and has already put the complacent slogan in the mouth at verse 21: 'All is well in Zion; yea, Zion prospereth, all is well.' So the woe at verse 24 is not a new thought but the naming of the source the sermon has been drawing on for a dozen verses. Recover Amos 6 and the phrase 'at ease in Zion' brings the whole indictment of a prosperous religion with it.

links.note: A KJV singleton reproduced entire, with the person shifted from plural to singular because the run of woes at 28:24-29 addresses individuals. The verse is nine words long and every one of them is Amos's. Worth recording that the n-gram stream's proposal here was Job 12:5's 'him that is at ease', which shares the idiom and nothing else — Job's phrase describes the comfortable man who despises the slipping, and the excluded entry says so; Amos's is the only KJV verse that puts the ease in Zion, which is the word 28:21 and 28:25 both need.

pericopes.text: Wo be unto him that crieth, All is well;

links.text: They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.

provenance.other: “Peace, peace; when there is no peace” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 6:14 and 8:11, in both cases as the cry of prophets and priests who deal falsely. No word of it survives in 2 Nephi 28:25; what survives is the form — a false reassurance quoted in order to be cursed.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah's is the Bible's model of the sentence 28:25 is written to condemn: a slogan of well-being, put in the mouth of the religious professionals, quoted by the prophet as evidence against them. 'Wo be unto him that crieth, All is well' is that sentence with the slogan translated. What recovering Jeremiah 6:14 supplies is the object of the cry — the hurt of the daughter of my people, healed slightly — which is exactly the injury 28:13 named and 28:21 said the devil uses to lull.

links.note: There is no verbal contact and the row is written as an echo on that understanding. The case for it is that 'All is well' occupies, in Nephi's sermon, the precise structural position 'Peace, peace' occupies in Jeremiah's — the quoted lie of the leaders — and that the surrounding verses have been quoting Amos and Isaiah for the same purpose. A reader who declines it loses nothing else in the chapter.
links.whyNot: Not one word is shared. 'All is well' is ordinary English and needs no source; the Book of Mormon may simply have coined the slogan it wanted. The link is a claim about a rhetorical convention, not about wording, and is filed at moderate for that reason rather than being urged.

pericopes.text: yea, wo be unto him that hearkeneth unto the precepts of men, and denieth the power of God and the gift of the Holy Ghost.

links.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “the gift of the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 2:38 and Acts 10:45, both in Luke's account of Pentecost and its extension to the Gentiles. Acts 2:38 is the promise; Acts 10:45 is the astonishment that it reached the uncircumcised.
provenance.significance: The chapter began its indictment at 28:4 with the Holy Ghost 'which giveth utterance', which is Acts 2:4, and ends it here with 'the gift of the Holy Ghost', which is Acts 2:38 — the opening and the close of the one Pentecost sermon. Recover that and what the false teachers are denying is not an abstraction but a specific offer: Peter's, made to the men who had just crucified Christ, on the terms 28:32 restates almost exactly — repent and come unto me, and I will be merciful. Acts 10:45's Gentiles are the other half of the frame, and 28:32's woe is pronounced on the Gentiles.

links.note: A four-word KJV phrase confined to two verses of one book, paired in the same clause with 'the power of God', and set opposite the same chapter's Acts 2:4 allusion at verse 4. Confidence is moderate rather than high because 'the gift of the Holy Ghost' had become a fixed theological term long before 1830 and need not be quoted from Acts to be used; the argument for the link is the pairing with 28:4, not the phrase alone. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:13 at this verse for 'the precepts of men'; that clause is adjudicated at 28:14, where the plural first appears, and the register sends a reader there.

pericopes.text: Yea, wo be unto him that saith, We have received, and we need no more.

And in fine, wo unto all they that tremble, and are angry because of the truth of God. For behold, he that is built upon the rock, receiveth it with gladness; and he that is built upon a sandy foundation, trembleth, lest he shall fall.

links.text: Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:

provenance.route: Matthew 7:24-27 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Luke 6:49 supplying the foundation
provenance.other: “built his house upon a rock” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:24. “upon the sand” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 7:26 and Revelation 13:1. The Book of Mormon's 'sandy foundation' is in no KJV verse at all — 'sandy' does not occur in the KJV — and fuses Matthew's sand with Luke 6:49's house built 'without a foundation'.
provenance.significance: The two houses are made to turn on hearing rather than on building. In Matthew the wise man is the one who hears the sayings and does them; in 28:28 the man on the rock 'receiveth it with gladness' and the man on the sandy foundation 'trembleth, lest he shall fall'. That substitution — doing replaced by receiving — is what the verse is for, since the whole run of woes from 28:27 concerns people who say 'we have received, and we need no more'. Recovering Matthew 7 supplies the criterion these speakers have exempted themselves from, and 28:30's 'unto him that receiveth, I will give more' answers it in Matthew's own economy of increase.

links.note: The parable is the chapter's frame — 28:18 took its collapse and 28:28 takes its foundations — and the coinage 'sandy foundation' is the evidence that it is being handled rather than quoted: the word 'sandy' is nowhere in the KJV, so the phrase is a fusion of Matthew's 'upon the sand' with Luke's 'without a foundation'. Written as a link rather than excluded because this is a different book from 1 Nephi 8:26, where the parable's foolish builder was first adjudicated (ADJUDICATING §4); the argument for the KJV singleton was made there.

pericopes.text: Wo be unto him that shall say, We have received the word of God, and we need no more of the word of God, for we have enough.

For behold, thus saith the Lord God: I will give unto the children of men line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little and there a little; and blessed are they that hearken unto my precepts, and lend an ear unto my counsel, for they shall learn wisdom: for unto him that receiveth, I will give more; and them that shall say, We have enough, from them shall be taken away even that which they have.—

links.text: For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little:

provenance.route: Isaiah 28:10 and 28:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “line upon line” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 28:10 and 28:13; “precept upon precept” occurs in exactly two, the same pair; “here a little, and there a little” occurs in exactly two, the same pair again. Isaiah 28 is not among the chapters transcribed in this book — 2 Nephi 12-24 covers Isaiah 2-14 — so this is the KJV direct.
provenance.significance: The order is reversed and the polarity with it. Both KJV verses put precept first and line second; the Book of Mormon puts line first, and drops the doubling that makes Isaiah's phrase a taunt. That matters because in Isaiah the words are mockery — the drunkards of Ephraim jeering at the prophet's babbling, and at 28:13 the LORD giving them exactly that, 'that they might go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken'. 2 Nephi 28:30 takes the mocked stammer and makes it the method of revelation itself, blessed rather than punitive: 'blessed are they that hearken unto my precepts.' A reader who recovers Isaiah 28 finds a verse of judgment converted into a promise, which is the largest single reversal in the chapter.

links.note: Three of the KJV's rarest formulae, each confined to the same two verses, reproduced together — dependence is not deniable. Two things are the Book of Mormon's own: the reversal of line and precept, and the removal of Isaiah's repetitions, which flattens 'precept upon precept, precept upon precept' into a single measured pair. The result reads as an orderly pedagogy rather than a drunken jeer. Note that the chapter has used 'precepts of men' three times as a term of abuse (28:14, 26, 31) before arriving here at 'my precepts' as the Lord's own word — the same noun turned, which is the sermon's closing move.

links.text: For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath.

provenance.route: Matthew 25:29 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Matthew 13:12 fused
provenance.other: “shall be taken away even that which he hath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:29. “taken away even that he hath” — without the relative — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:12. The Book of Mormon reads 'taken away even that which they have', which is 25:29's relative construction; but 'I will give more' answers 13:12's 'he shall have more abundance', where 25:29 has only 'abundance'.
provenance.significance: The saying arrives immediately after Isaiah 28:10, and the join is the point. Isaiah's line-upon-line is a method of giving revelation in instalments; Matthew's logion is the rule governing who receives instalments at all. Put together they answer the boast of 28:29 — 'we have received the word of God, and we need no more' — with the parable's arithmetic: the servant who declines increase loses the principal. Recover Matthew 25 and the man who says he has enough is the servant who buried the talent, whose defence was that he already had what he was given.

links.note: `mediation-check.py` on Matthew 13:12 against Matthew 25:29 returns no decisive divergence, because the words that separate them — 'which', 'more' — are the common words the tool suppresses. Decided by eye, and the answer is a fusion rather than a choice: the long clause is 25:29's, relative pronoun included, and the short one before it ('I will give more') is 13:12's. That is honest to the evidence and it is the reason both are recorded, with 25:29 as the source because the singleton is longer and exact. The verse also ends with an 1830 dash that 1920 removed, marking the seam where Nephi stops quoting and the chapter turns to its final curse.

pericopes.text: Cursed is he that putteth his trust in man, or maketh flesh his arm, or shall hearken unto the precepts of men, save their precepts shall be given by the power of the Holy Ghost.

Wo be unto the Gentiles, saith the Lord God of Hosts: for notwithstanding I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them from day to day, they will deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, saith the Lord God, if they will repent and come unto me: for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts.

links.text: I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts;

provenance.route: Isaiah 65:2, possibly via Romans 10:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “spread out my hands all the day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 65:2; Romans 10:21 quotes it as 'All day long I have stretched forth my hands'. The Book of Mormon has neither verb — it reads 'lengthen out mine arm' and 'mine arm is lengthened out all the day long' — and 'all the day long' occurs in thirteen KJV verses, so it cannot discriminate.
provenance.significance: Both source and quotation are addressed to a people who will not have the offer: Isaiah's 'rebellious', Paul's 'disobedient and gainsaying'. 28:32's Gentiles 'will deny me' and the arm is lengthened out to them anyway. What makes the echo worth recording despite its weak wording is that Romans 10:21 stands at the end of Paul's argument about Israel and the Gentiles, which is the argument the next chapter of 2 Nephi will take up outright — so a reader who hears Romans 10 here is being prepared for 2 Nephi 29.

links.note: This is the chapter's one undecided mediation. `mediation-check.py` on Isaiah 65:2 against Romans 10:21 reports no decisive divergence, and correctly: the Book of Mormon reproduces neither candidate's verb and neither candidate's object, keeping only the posture of an outstretched limb held out all day to people who refuse. 'Mine arm' rather than 'my hands' may point instead at the refrain of Isaiah 9-10, 'his hand is stretched out still', which this book transcribes at 2 Nephi 19:12, 19:17, 19:21 and 20:4 — but that phrase is a threat of continuing judgment, not an offer of mercy, and the sense here is Isaiah 65:2's. Recorded as an echo at moderate, mediation left uncertain rather than guessed.
links.whyNot: No distinctive wording is shared with either candidate. The only phrase in common with anything, 'all the day long', is in thirteen KJV verses and settles nothing. The row rests on the situation — a limb held out all day to a refusing people — which is a real and rare configuration in the KJV but is not a verbal borrowing, and a reader may reasonably decline it.

pericopes.text: But behold, there shall be many at that day, when I shall proceed to do a marvellous work among them, that I may remember my covenants which I have made unto the children of men, that I may set my hand again the second time to recover my people, which are of the House of Israel;

links.text: Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, even a marvellous work and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid.

provenance.route: Isaiah 29:14 → KJV → Book of Mormon (transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 27:26)
provenance.other: “proceed to do a marvellous work” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:14. 'Marvellous work' alone occurs in five, four of them Chronicles and Psalms in the plural 'marvellous works'; only Isaiah 29:14 has the singular with 'proceed to do'. The Book of Mormon's own transcription at 2 Nephi 27:26 keeps the KJV's 'among this people'; 29:1 changes it to 'among them'.
provenance.significance: Chapter 29 is spoken in the Lord's voice and opens by quoting the verse that has been its warrant since chapter 27: the marvellous work of Isaiah 29:14 is, in this book's reading, the coming forth of the record. What the source supplies and the quotation withholds is the rest of the sentence — 'the wisdom of their wise men shall perish' — which 2 Nephi 27:26 does give in full, and which is the judgment 29:3's Gentiles are about to earn by saying there cannot be any more Bible. The oracle they are standing under is the one about wisdom perishing.

links.note: The opening clause reproduces a KJV singleton exactly except for its object, and the object is the change worth noting: Isaiah's work is done 'among this people' — Jerusalem — while 29:1's is done 'among them', the many at that day, which the rest of the verse identifies as the house of Israel scattered. This is the Lord resuming, in his own voice, the text his prophet has just transcribed. The pairing with Isaiah 11:11 in the same sentence is treated as a separate link.

links.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon (transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 21:11)
provenance.other: “set his hand again the second time” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11, and “recover the remnant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. 2 Nephi 21:11's transcription is verbally identical to the KJV at both points, so nothing here distinguishes the biblical route from the internal one.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 11:11 is the verse this whole chapter is an argument about. Its second recovery gathers the remnant from eight named places ending 'from the islands of the sea', and 29:7 and 29:11 will both press that ending: if the Lord recovers people from the islands of the sea, he has people there, and if he has people there he has spoken to them. The Gentile objection at 29:3 is answered out of the geography of a verse the book has already transcribed. Recover Isaiah 11 and one sees why the chapter cites it twice and closes on Abraham's seed: 11:12's ensign gathers 'the outcasts of Israel' and 'the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth', which is 29:11-14's east, west, north, south and gathering home.

links.note: Two KJV singletons in one clause. The Book of Mormon's change is 'my people, which are of the House of Israel' for Isaiah's 'the remnant of his people, which shall be left' — first person for third, since the Lord is speaking, and the standing Book of Mormon formula for the house of Israel in place of Isaiah's remnant. Isaiah 11 stands transcribed in this book eight chapters earlier at 2 Nephi 21, and that transcription reads exactly as the KJV here, so the mediation cannot be decided from the wording and is recorded as direct-OT rather than guessed at OT-via-earlier-BoM. Compare 29:14 at 28:14, where the same test did yield an answer.

pericopes.text: and also, that I may remember the promises which I have made unto thee, Nephi, and also unto thy father, That I would remember your seed; and that the words of your seed should proceed forth out of my mouth unto your seed. And my words shall hiss forth unto the ends of the earth, for a standard unto my people, which are of the House of Israel.

links.text: And he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far, and will hiss unto them from the end of the earth: and, behold, they shall come with speed swiftly:

provenance.route: Isaiah 5:26 + Isaiah 49:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon; both verses stand transcribed or quoted earlier in this book, at 2 Nephi 15:26 and 2 Nephi 6:6
provenance.other: The KJV hisses in exactly two verses, Isaiah 5:26 and Zechariah 10:8, and only Isaiah 5:26 hisses toward the end of the earth. “set up my standard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 49:22; 'standard' as a signal raised for a people occurs otherwise only at Isaiah 59:19 and 62:10.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis reverses the direction of the summons. In Isaiah 5:26 the hissing calls a distant army down on Judah — it is the last verse before the invaders arrive with speed swiftly — and in 29:2 it is the Lord's words that hiss forth to the ends of the earth, so that the sound which summoned destroyers now summons readers. Isaiah 49:22's standard is set up to gather the exiles' sons and daughters, and Jacob has already quoted that verse in this book at 2 Nephi 6:6 for exactly that purpose. 29:2 fuses the two signals: the hiss from Isaiah 5 and the standard from Isaiah 49, both aimed at the same house of Israel.

links.note: Two Isaiah signals joined in a sentence about a book. 'Hiss' is the rarer and the odder — a modern reader hears derision where the KJV means a whistle for attention — and its appearance here, with 'unto the ends of the earth', places Isaiah 5:26 rather than Zechariah 10:8. What makes the row more than a phrase-match is that both source verses are already inside this book: Isaiah 5:26 transcribed at 2 Nephi 15:26 with the same wording, and Isaiah 49:22 quoted by Jacob at 2 Nephi 6:6. The mediation is left direct-OT because neither internal text differs from the KJV at the words 29:2 uses.

pericopes.text: And because my words shall hiss forth, many of the Gentiles shall say, A Bible, a Bible, we have got a Bible, and there cannot be any more Bible.

But thus saith the Lord God: O fools, they shall have a Bible; and it shall proceed forth from the Jews, mine ancient covenant people. And what thank they the Jews for the Bible which they receive from them? Yea, what do the Gentiles mean? Do they remember the travels, and the labors, and the pains of the Jews, and their diligence unto me, in bringing forth salvation unto the Gentiles?

links.text: Then he said unto them, O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken:

provenance.other: “O fools, and slow of heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:25, and the bare vocative 'O fools' is that verse's alone as well (Proverbs 13:19's 'abomination to fools' is not a vocative and is addressed to no one). The singular 'Thou fool' at 29:6 occurs in four KJV verses, of which Luke 12:20's is the rich fool this book has already drawn on at 2 Nephi 28:7.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest recovered context. Luke 24:25 is the risen Christ on the road to Emmaus rebuking two disciples who have the scriptures and cannot read them — 'slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken' — and the rebuke is followed immediately by his expounding 'in all the scriptures the things concerning himself'. 2 Nephi 29:4 addresses the identical fault: Gentiles who possess the Bible and conclude from possessing it that there cannot be any more. Luke's fools are told they have not read what they hold; Nephi's are told they have not asked where they got it. The insult is the same insult, and it comes with the same remedy attached.

links.note: Two words, and a rare vocative, doing more work than their length. The case rests on the situation matching as exactly as the wording: in the KJV only Luke 24:25 says 'O fools', and only Luke 24:25 says it to people whose fault is what they do with scripture. Confidence is held at moderate because the vocative is a natural thing for a rebuke to reach for, and because the second half of Luke's sentence is not quoted. The verse's other pressure — 'what thank they the Jews' — is registered separately as a Lucan echo at Luke 6:32.

links.text: For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.

provenance.other: “what thank have ye” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Luke 6:32, 6:33 and 6:34, all in one paragraph of the Sermon on the Plain, and nowhere else in the KJV is 'thank' used as a bare noun in a rhetorical question.
provenance.significance: Luke's triple question asks what credit there is in returning good for good; 29:4 asks the inverse — what thanks the Gentiles have given the Jews for a benefit they never returned. Read against Luke 6, the Gentiles fail a test easier than the one Christ sets: they have not even loved those that loved them.

links.note: 'What thank they the Jews for the Bible which they receive from them?' turns the KJV's one idiom for this question inside out — Luke's speaker asks what thank the doer has earned, Nephi's asks what thank the receiver has paid. The syntax 'what thank' plus a rhetorical frame is confined to three adjacent verses of Luke, which is what makes it worth recording at all.
links.whyNot: The construction is inverted and the noun is the only shared content word; 'thank' as a noun was ordinary in 1611 and not confined to Luke in period English, so the KJV's monopoly on the idiom may be an accident of the KJV rather than evidence of borrowing. Filed at low, and the reader who takes 29:4's question as free composition is not obviously wrong.

pericopes.text: O ye Gentiles, have ye remembered the Jews, mine ancient covenant people? Nay; but ye have cursed them, and have hated them, and have not sought to recover them. But behold, I will return all these things upon your own heads: for I the Lord, hath not forgotten my people.

links.text: Behold, I will raise them out of the place whither ye have sold them, and will return your recompence upon your own head:

provenance.other: “upon your own head” (singular “head”) occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Joel 3:4 and 3:7, where the Lord returns the recompence of Tyre and Zidon on their own head for selling the children of Judah. Acts 18:6 is close in idea — Paul shakes his raiment at the synagogue and says 'Your blood be upon your own heads' before turning to the Gentiles — but its noun is plural, a different phrase, not a third instance of this one.
provenance.significance: Joel 3 is the oracle against the nations that trafficked in Judah, and its charge is precisely 29:5's: 'ye have cursed them, and have hated them, and have not sought to recover them.' Joel's Tyre and Zidon sold the children of Judah to the Grecians and are told their recompence returns on their own head; Nephi's Gentiles received the scriptures from the Jews and cursed them for it. The Acts 18:6 half is the same phrase pointed the other way — there the blood is on the Jews' own heads and Paul departs to the Gentiles — so that the KJV's three occurrences of the idiom hold both halves of the quarrel 2 Nephi 29 is adjudicating. Whether the Book of Mormon intends that symmetry cannot be shown; that the symmetry is there is a fact about the three verses.

links.note: 'I will return all these things upon your own heads' has Joel's verb, Joel's preposition and Joel's noun, with 'all these things' standing where Joel has 'your recompence' — a generalisation, since the things being returned are the cursing and hating just listed rather than a price. The verse ends 'for I the Lord, hath not forgotten my people', which answers Isaiah 49:14-15's 'the LORD hath forsaken me… yet will I not forget thee' — a passage Jacob quotes in this book at 2 Nephi 7-8's neighbourhood and which is too diffuse here to catalogue. Confidence moderate: the idiom is a standard prophetic recompense-formula and only its exact KJV wording, confined to three verses, argues for Joel specifically.

pericopes.text: Thou fool, that shall say, A Bible, we have got a Bible, and we need no more Bible. Have ye obtained a Bible, save it were by the Jews?

Know ye not that there are more nations than one? Know ye not that I the Lord your God, have created all men, and that I remember they which are upon the isles of the sea; and that I rule in the heavens above, and in the earth beneath; and I bring forth my word unto the children of men, yea, even upon all the nations of the earth?

links.text: Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.

provenance.other: “isles of the sea” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Esther 10:1 and Isaiah 24:15; only Isaiah's are a place where the LORD is glorified. “islands of the sea” — a different phrase — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11. 29:7 has 'the isles of the sea' and 29:11 has 'the islands of the sea', four verses apart.
provenance.significance: The pair is the finding. The KJV distinguishes two phrases that mean the same thing, and 2 Nephi 29 uses each once, each in the setting its own source supplies: at verse 7 the isles are where the Lord remembers people who are already his, which is Isaiah 24:15's islands glorifying his name, and at verse 11 the islands are the last item in a list of directions from which a scattered people is recovered, which is Isaiah 11:11's. Neither verse could be swapped for the other without losing its source. Isaiah 24 is not among the chapters this book transcribes — 2 Nephi 12-24 covers Isaiah 2-14 — so unlike almost every other borrowing in the chapter this one is reached in the Bible directly.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 24:15 at this verse, and the discrimination against Isaiah 11:11 is what makes the row worth writing: an author reaching loosely for a formula would not switch spellings between verse 7 and verse 11 in a way that tracks two different KJV verses. Esther 10:1's isles, a tribute-list, are ruled out by sense. The rest of 29:7 — 'I rule in the heavens above, and in the earth beneath' — is treated as a separate link.

links.text: Know therefore this day, and consider it in thine heart, that the LORD he is God in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath: there is none else.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 4:39, with Exodus 20:4's preposition → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “in the earth beneath” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Exodus 20:4, Deuteronomy 5:8 and Acts 2:19 — and Deuteronomy 4:39, whose sense 29:7 has, reads 'upon the earth beneath'. The Book of Mormon has Deuteronomy 4:39's claim in the second commandment's preposition, so no single verse accounts for it.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 4:39 is the KJV's flat statement that the LORD's rule has no geographical limit — 'in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath: there is none else' — and that is the premise 29:7 needs. The Gentile position under attack is territorial: one people, one book, one revelation. The answer is the Shema's neighbourhood, and the question that frames it, 'Know ye not that there are more nations than one?', is Deuteronomy's 'Know therefore this day' turned into a rebuke.

links.note: The wording is a fusion and is recorded as such: the sense and the sentence-shape are Deuteronomy 4:39's, the preposition is the second commandment's. Confidence is moderate and `kjvSpecific` uncertain, because 'heaven above and earth beneath' is a formula the KJV repeats in several settings (Joshua 2:11, 1 Kings 8:23) and no one of them is decisively in view. What is not in doubt is that 29:7 is arguing from the universality claim these verses make.

pericopes.text: Wherefore murmur ye, because that ye shall receive more of my word? Know ye not that the testimony of two nations is a witness unto you that I am God, that I remember one nation like unto another? wherefore, I speak the same words unto one nation like unto another. And when the two nations shall run together, the testimony of the two nations shall run together also.

links.text: It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 19:15 / 17:6 → John 8:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the testimony of two” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:17, and 2 Nephi 29:8 uses the phrase twice — 'the testimony of two nations is a witness unto you' and 'the testimony of the two nations shall run together'. Deuteronomy 19:15 and 17:6, the underlying law, have neither 'testimony' nor 'two' in this construction: the KJV renders them 'at the mouth of two witnesses'. The Book of Mormon has John's noun, not Moses's.
provenance.significance: John 8:17 is Christ invoking the two-witness law in an argument about whether a single testimony can establish anything — the Pharisees have just said 'Thou bearest record of thyself; thy record is not true', and he answers by adding the Father as the second witness. 2 Nephi 29:8 runs that argument about books rather than persons: one record cannot establish the matter, two can, and the second is supplied by the same God who gave the first. Recover John 8 and the parallel is structural, not decorative. The objectors in both scenes hold the law and use their possession of it to rule out further testimony; in both, the answer is that the law they hold requires a second witness they have refused to hear. The Gentiles of 29:3 say 'we have got a Bible, and there cannot be any more Bible'; John's Pharisees say the same thing about a witness.

links.note: A KJV singleton, used twice in one verse, and it settles the mediation cleanly. The two-witness rule is Deuteronomy's, but Deuteronomy's KJV wording is 'at the mouth of two witnesses… shall the matter be established' — no 'testimony', no 'the testimony of two'. That phrase exists in exactly one English verse and it is John's, so the Book of Mormon reaches Deuteronomy through the Gospel rather than directly. Note what the substitution costs and gains: John's two witnesses are persons and 29:8's are nations, which is why the verse has to add the guarantee that the Lord 'speaks the same words unto one nation like unto another' — two witnesses only corroborate if their testimony agrees, and nations, unlike the Father and the Son, might not.

pericopes.text: And I do this that I may prove unto many, that I am the same yesterday, to-day, and forever; and that I speak forth my words according to mine own pleasure. And because that I have spoken one word, ye need not suppose that I cannot speak another: for my work is not yet finished; neither shall it be, until the end of man; neither from that time henceforth and forever.
Wherefore, because that ye have a Bible, ye need not suppose that it contains all my words; neither need ye suppose that I have not caused more to be written:

for I command all men, both in the east, and in the west, and in the north, and in the south, and in the islands of the sea, that they shall write the words which I speak unto them: for out of the books which shall be written, I will judge the world, every man according to their works, according to that which is written.—

links.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “judged out of those things which were written” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:12, and it is the KJV's only judgment conducted out of the contents of books. “judged every man according to their works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:13, which 2 Nephi 28:23 has already used.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's argument closed with a hard consequence, and Revelation supplies the mechanism. 29:11's claim is that the Lord commands all men in every quarter to write, 'for out of the books which shall be written, I will judge the world' — which is Revelation 20:12's assize with the plurality of books made the point rather than an incidental detail. If the world is judged out of books, then whose books there are is not a matter of preference. The recovered context also explains why the verse ends 'according to that which is written': in Revelation the written record is what the dead are measured by, so a nation whose record was never made or never received would be judged out of somebody else's books.

links.note: Two Revelation 20 verses again, ten chapters after 2 Nephi 28:23 used the same pair for the same assize — there for the fate of the damned, here for the standing of the records. The borrowing is unmistakable at 'judged… according to… works' plus 'out of the books which shall be written', and the Book of Mormon's one substantive change is tense: Revelation's books are already written and opened, and 29:11's are still to be written. That change is the whole chapter in miniature.

links.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:11-12 → KJV → Book of Mormon (transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 21:11-12)
provenance.other: “islands of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11, and is the last item in its list of places from which the remnant is recovered — which is exactly where 29:11 puts it, after east, west, north and south. 2 Nephi 21:11's transcription reads 'islands of the sea' identically. The four quarters themselves are Psalm 107:3's 'from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south', one of exactly two KJV verses with that sequence, the other being Luke 13:29.
provenance.significance: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 11:11 here, and the reason is visible once the two phrases in this chapter are set side by side: 29:7's 'isles of the sea' is Isaiah 24:15's and 29:11's 'islands of the sea' is Isaiah 11:11's, and each sits in the argument its own source fits. Here the point is enumerative — the Lord commands men to write in every direction, and the list ends where Isaiah's list of recovery ends. So the geography of the second gathering becomes the geography of the second scripture. The chapter's whole case is that these are the same map.

links.note: Three words, a KJV singleton, and placed at the end of a list of quarters exactly as in the source. The row is written separately from the Isaiah 11:11 quotation at 29:1 because it is a different clause of the source verse doing different work: 29:1 takes the second-time recovery, 29:11 takes the islands. Isaiah 11 stands transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 21 with no departure at either point, so the mediation cannot be told from the wording and is not guessed.

pericopes.text: For behold, I shall speak unto the Jews, and they shall write it; and I shall also speak unto the Nephites, and they shall write it; and I shall also speak unto the other tribes of the House of Israel, which I have led away, and they shall write it; and I shall also speak unto all the nations of the earth, and they shall write it.

And it shall come to pass that the Jews shall have the words of the Nephites, and the Nephites shall have the words of the Jews; and the Nephites and the Jews shall have the words of the lost tribes of Israel; and the lost tribes of Israel shall have the words of the Nephites and the Jews.

And it shall come to pass that my people which are of the House of Israel, shall be gathered home unto the lands of their possessions; and my word also shall be gathered in one. And I will shew unto them that fight against my word and against my people, which are of the House of Israel, that I am God, and that I covenanted with Abraham that I would remember his seed forever.

links.text: And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.

provenance.other: 'Everlasting covenant' occurs in fifteen KJV verses and 'thy seed after thee' in a dozen more, so no rarity count supports this row; what supports it is that Genesis 17:7 is the only verse where the covenant with Abraham is made perpetual to his seed, which is the exact claim 29:14 closes on.
provenance.significance: The chapter ends where it must. Its argument has been that the Lord speaks to more nations than one; its danger is that this dissolves the covenant into a general benevolence. Genesis 17:7 is the guard: the covenant is with Abraham 'and thy seed after thee', in perpetuity, so a Lord who speaks to all the nations of the earth has still not stopped being the God of one particular family. That is why 'I covenanted with Abraham that I would remember his seed forever' is the last clause of the chapter and not an appendix to it.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Genesis 17:7 here and the reference is sound at the level of substance while carrying almost no wording — 'covenanted with Abraham', 'his seed', 'forever' against Genesis's 'establish my covenant… thy seed after thee… everlasting covenant'. It is written as a moderate allusion rather than either inflated to a quotation or discharged as thematic: the covenant formula is genuinely Genesis 17's and is genuinely being invoked, but nothing in the phrasing could distinguish the KJV from another English Bible, which is why `kjvSpecific` is 'no'.

links.text: And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.

provenance.other: “gather together in one” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 11:52 and Ephesians 1:10. John's gathers the scattered children of God, Ephesians' gathers all things in Christ; 29:14 gathers a people to their lands and a word into one, which is John's object rather than Paul's.
provenance.significance: The two halves of 29:14 are the two halves of John 11:52. John's sentence is the evangelist's gloss on Caiaphas — that Jesus would die 'not for that nation only, but… gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad' — which is a statement about one nation's scripture becoming more than one nation's, in a verse about a nation and the others beyond it. That is the subject of 2 Nephi 29 entire. And the neighbouring verse of the same oracle, John 11:50, stands behind 1 Nephi 4:13, where Nephi kills Laban with Caiaphas's sentence; the book returns to the same three verses of John at the moment it argues that its own record belongs with the Jews'.

links.note: A two-verse KJV phrase, and the object matches John's rather than Ephesians': what is gathered is a scattered people and their word, not all things in Christ. The row is filed as an echo at moderate because 'gathered in one' is only three words and the Book of Mormon uses gathering language constantly without needing a source for it. What lifts it above coincidence is the recurrence: this book has been in John 11 before, at 1 Nephi 4:13, and the Caiaphas oracle is the New Testament's one passage about a nation's benefit extending past that nation — which is the thesis 29:14 is closing.
links.whyNot: Three words, and 'gather in one' is a natural English collocation the KJV happens to use twice. The link is a claim about which of two KJV verses is nearer, made where a third possibility — no source at all — is entirely live.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you: for I, Nephi, would not suffer that ye should suppose that ye are more righteous than the Gentiles shall be. For behold, except ye shall keep the commandments of God, ye shall all likewise perish; and because of the words which have been spoken, ye need not suppose that the Gentiles are utterly destroyed.

links.text: I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.

provenance.other: “ye shall all likewise perish” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 13:3 and Luke 13:5, which are the same sentence said twice in one paragraph. The construction occurs nowhere else in the Bible.
provenance.significance: The whole paragraph is here, not the clause. Luke 13:1-5 is Christ's answer to people who assume that those who died — the Galilaeans whose blood Pilate mingled, the eighteen killed by the tower of Siloam — must have been worse sinners: 'Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.' 2 Nephi 30:1 opens with exactly that supposition, in Luke's own verb: 'I… would not suffer that ye should suppose that ye are more righteous than the Gentiles shall be… ye shall all likewise perish.' Nephi has just spent two chapters prophesying the destruction of the Gentiles, and he opens the next by refusing his own audience the inference Luke's hearers drew. The metalepsis supplies the reason — not that the Gentiles are innocent, but that judgment on others licenses no conclusion about oneself.

links.note: Five words from the KJV's one construction, with 'suppose' — Luke 13:2's verb, and the hinge of the passage — arriving in the same sentence. The condition attached to the threat is changed and the change is worth recording: Luke's is 'except ye repent', Nephi's 'except ye shall keep the commandments of God', which converts a call to repentance into a standard of conduct. The verse then repeats 'ye need not suppose' a second time about a different inference, so the Lucan verb is doing structural work in the paragraph rather than appearing once.

pericopes.text: For behold, I say unto you, as many of the Gentiles as will repent, are the covenant people of the Lord; and as many of the Jews as will not repent, shall be cast off: for the Lord covenanteth with none, save it be with them that repent and believe in his Son, which is the Holy One of Israel.

And now, I would prophesy somewhat more concerning the Jews and the Gentiles. For after the book of which I have spoken shall come forth, and be written unto the Gentiles, and sealed up again unto the Lord, there shall be many which shall believe the words which are written; and they shall carry them forth unto the remnant of our seed.
And then shall the remnant of our seed know concerning us, how that we came out from Jerusalem, and that they are a descendant of the Jews.

And the Gospel of Jesus Christ shall be declared among them; wherefore, they shall be restored unto the knowledge of their fathers, and also to the knowledge of Jesus Christ, which was had among their fathers.

links.text: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God;

provenance.other: “the gospel of Jesus Christ” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 1:1. The New Testament elsewhere has 'the gospel of Christ' (a dozen times), 'the gospel of God', 'the gospel of his Son' and 'the gospel of the kingdom', but the full name appears in this construction only at the head of Mark.
provenance.significance: Mark 1:1 is not a sentence but a title — the opening words of a book, naming what the book is. 2 Nephi 30:5 uses it of something being declared to the remnant of Nephi's seed after a book has come forth and been carried to them, which is the same relation: a written record whose subject is named by this phrase. Recovering the source therefore supplies a genre claim the verse does not make explicitly. What is to be declared among them is not a message in general but a gospel of the kind that comes in a book with a beginning.

links.note: Four words and a KJV singleton, in a verse about a record being brought to a people. Confidence is moderate rather than high because 'the gospel of Jesus Christ' had long since become standard devotional English independent of Mark, and the Book of Mormon uses it freely elsewhere; the argument for Mark specifically is the rarity count and the fact that 30:3-5 is describing the transmission of a book. A reader who treats the phrase as ordinary usage rather than a borrowing is not refuted by anything here.

pericopes.text: And then shall they rejoice: for they shall know that it is a blessing unto them from the hand of God; and their scales of darkness shall begin to fall from their eyes; and many generations shall not pass away among them, save they shall be a white and a delightsome people.

links.text: And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized.

provenance.other: “fell from his eyes as it had been scales” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:18. 'Scales' occurs in nine KJV verses altogether and the other eight are fish scales or Leviathan's; Acts 9:18 is the only verse in the Bible where scales fall from anyone's eyes, and the KJV never calls them 'scales of darkness' — that phrase is the Book of Mormon's own.
provenance.significance: Paul's blindness is the model of a particular kind of conversion: not a sinner reformed but a zealot who was wrong about the scriptures he knew best, struck blind on the road and given sight by a man he had come to arrest. 2 Nephi 30:6 applies it to the remnant of Nephi's seed learning 'that they are a descendant of the Jews' — a recovery of identity, not merely of belief, which is what Acts 9 is about. The added genitive, 'scales of darkness', names what the KJV leaves as a simile ('as it had been scales'), and in doing so it makes Luke's medical detail into a figure for ignorance. That is the Book of Mormon reading Acts, and the reading has since become the ordinary English idiom.

links.note: The KJV's one falling-scales verse, quoted in its distinctive elements — scales, eyes, falling — with the simile hardened into a metaphor. Note what changes: in Acts the scales fall at once ('immediately… forthwith') and in 30:6 they 'shall begin to fall', with 'many generations shall not pass away' before the process completes. A sudden miracle has been made a gradual one, which is the difference between a conversion narrative and a prophecy about a people.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass that the Jews which are scattered, also shall begin to believe in Christ; and they shall begin to gather in upon the face of the land; and as many as shall believe in Christ, shall also become a delightsome people.
And it shall come to pass that the Lord God shall commence his work, among all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people, to bring about the restoration of his people upon the earth.

links.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: Revelation gives its four-fold list of humanity seven times and in seven different orders. “nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:6, and it is the Book of Mormon's order here — 'all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people' — pluralised throughout.
