Revelation 7:9's order is nations, kindreds, people, tongues; Revelation 13:7's is kindreds, tongues, nations; Revelation 5:9's is kindred, tongue, people, nation.
provenance.significance: The order is the evidence, and the verse it selects is the right one. Revelation 14:6's angel carries 'the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth', which is precisely 30:8's subject — the Lord commencing his work among all nations to bring about the restoration of his people. Of the seven Revelation lists this is the only one attached to a gospel going out rather than to a multitude gathered, a beast's dominion, or a people redeemed. Nephi has taken the list from the one occurrence whose sentence matches his own, which is not what an author reaching for a remembered formula would be expected to do.

links.note: A four-item list is weak evidence and a four-item list in one of seven possible orders, matching the one verse whose subject is the same, is strong evidence. The pluralisation is uniform and is the Book of Mormon's standing form of the phrase. Recorded as an allusion rather than a quotation because the list is lifted out of Revelation's sentence and set in Nephi's; the borrowed material is a series, not a clause.

pericopes.text: And with righteousness shall the Lord God judge the poor, and reprove with equity, for the meek of the earth. And he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked:

links.text: But with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth: with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon; whether by way of this book's own transcription at 2 Nephi 21:4 cannot be determined — see the collation in the note
provenance.other: “reprove with equity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:4, and “breath of his lips” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. 2 Nephi 21:4's transcription of the verse reproduces the KJV word for word. 2 Nephi 30:9 departs from both at exactly two points, and both are at the seam: 'And' for 'But', and 'the Lord God' for 'he'.
provenance.significance: This is the second Book of Mormon witness to Isaiah 11 and the point of collating it is to see whether the book's two copies of one chapter are the same text. They are. The two changes here are not textual but framing: 'But' becomes 'And' because the sentence now follows Nephi's verse 8 instead of Isaiah's verse 3, and Isaiah's 'he' — whose antecedent in Isaiah 11:1-3 is the rod out of the stem of Jesse — becomes 'the Lord God', because the quotation has been lifted out of the context that supplied its subject and needs one. An expositor quoting from memory or from a manuscript would be expected to leave traces of a different text; what 30:9 leaves are traces of a different sentence.

links.note: The chapter's centrepiece and the reason it was kept as a hand chapter. Collating 2 Nephi 30:9-15 against both the KJV and 2 Nephi 21:4-9 gives a clean and largely negative result, which is worth stating plainly because the test could have gone the other way (compare 2 Nephi 6:16 against 1 Nephi 21:24, where the two Book of Mormon witnesses genuinely diverge and the verdict had to be recorded as divided). Here: 2 Nephi 21:4-9 agrees with the KJV at every word; 2 Nephi 30:9-15 agrees with both at every word except the two connective adjustments in this verse, one more at 30:12, and the possessive apostrophe at 30:14. Every substantive difference between the two Book of Mormon witnesses is a join, and every join is where Nephi's own prose meets the quotation. The mediation is therefore recorded as uncertain rather than guessed: with the two candidate sources verbally identical, no reading in this verse can tell them apart.

pericopes.text: for the time speedily cometh, that the Lord God shall cause a great division among the people; and the wicked will he destroy; and he will spare his people, yea, even if it so be that he must destroy the wicked by fire.

links.text: The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy.

provenance.other: “the wicked will he destroy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 145:20, and the inversion — object, auxiliary, subject, verb — is preserved intact in 2 Nephi 30:10. Both of the psalm verse's halves are present: 'the wicked will he destroy' and, for 'The LORD preserveth all them that love him', 'he will spare his people'.
provenance.significance: The placement is what makes this row matter. 2 Nephi 30:10 is the one verse Nephi inserts into his quotation of Isaiah 11 — the block runs 11:4 at verse 9, then this, then 11:5 at verse 11 — and it is inserted precisely where Isaiah has said the Messiah shall 'slay the wicked'. So the gloss on Isaiah's slaying is built out of a psalm, and out of the psalm's own antithesis: destruction of the wicked set against preservation of those who love God. Nephi has answered Isaiah with the Psalter rather than with his own words, at the single point where he interrupts. Note that Psalm 145 has been used at the head of this record before: 145:9's 'tender mercies… over all' stands behind 1 Nephi 1:20, a link the machine streams could not see and which the pilot found by reading.

links.note: A KJV singleton with its unusual word order kept, and its companion clause paraphrased in the next breath — 'the wicked will he destroy; and he will spare his people' against 'The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy.' The Book of Mormon reverses the psalm's order, putting the destruction first, because the verse is glossing Isaiah 11:4's slaying and has to begin there. The closing clause, 'even if it so be that he must destroy the wicked by fire', is Nephi's own and has no source; it is the specification the psalm does not give and Isaiah does not give either.

pericopes.text: And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins.

links.text: And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon; not distinguishable from a route through 2 Nephi 21:5
provenance.other: “girdle of his loins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:5. 2 Nephi 30:11, 2 Nephi 21:5 and the KJV are identical here at every word and every mark of punctuation — the only verse of the six where all three witnesses agree completely.
provenance.significance: The verse's position is the finding rather than its wording. Isaiah 11:5 follows 11:4 immediately; in 2 Nephi 30 the two are separated by verse 10, thirty-eight words of Nephi's own prophecy about a great division and the wicked destroyed by fire. So the expositor has opened Isaiah's oracle at the point where it says the Messiah shall 'slay the wicked', paused to say what that will look like, and then resumed at the girdle of righteousness. The interpolation is a gloss placed inside the quotation, which is a different technique from the one 2 Nephi 27 used on Isaiah 29, where the additions are woven into the verses themselves.

links.note: Verbatim, at nine words, on a KJV singleton. It is recorded as a link rather than passed over because a reader of 2 Nephi 30 should be able to see where the quotation resumes after verse 10's interruption, and because the perfect three-way agreement is itself a datum in the collation argued at 30:9.

pericopes.text: And then shall the wolf dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf, and the young lion, and the fatling, together; and a little child shall lead them.

links.text: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon; not distinguishable from a route through 2 Nephi 21:6
provenance.other: “the fatling” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:6 — a genuine singleton, not the better of two: 2 Samuel 6:13 has “fatlings” (plural, and no article), a different noun form, not a second instance. 2 Nephi 21:6 reproduces the KJV word for word. 30:12 departs from both by one substitution: 'And then shall the wolf dwell' for 'The wolf also shall dwell'.
provenance.significance: The second and last substantive departure in the block, and it is the same kind of thing as 30:9's: a connective. Isaiah's 'also' links his verse 6 to his verse 5; Nephi's 'and then' links it to his own verse 11 and, through it, to the sequence of events he has been narrating since verse 8 — the Lord commencing his work, the division, the burning, and then the peaceable kingdom. Isaiah's 'also' is additive and Nephi's 'and then' is chronological, which converts a description into a timetable. That is what an exposition does to an oracle, and it is the only interpretive pressure the six quoted verses show.

links.note: Thirty-one consecutive words shared with the source once the opening connective is set aside. The 1830 also adds commas to Isaiah's unpunctuated series — 'the calf, and the young lion, and the fatling, together' against both the KJV's and 2 Nephi 21:6's 'the calf and the young lion and the fatling together' — which is the one point in the block where 30 differs from 21 in a way that is not a join. It is recorded rather than argued from: 1830 punctuation is the compositor's before it is the author's, and a comma cannot bear a mediation claim.

pericopes.text: And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.

links.text: And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon; not distinguishable from a route through 2 Nephi 21:7
provenance.other: “straw like the ox” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:7. Isaiah 65:25, the oracle's later reprise, reads 'the lion shall eat straw like the bullock' — a different animal — and it also compresses the whole of 11:6-7 into one clause, 'The wolf and the lamb shall feed together'. 30:13 has Isaiah 11:7's ox and Isaiah 11:7's full sequence, at every word.
provenance.significance: The discrimination against Isaiah 65:25 is worth having because 65:25 is the passage a writer working from memory would be most likely to conflate with this one: it is the same vision, in the same book, using the same animals, and it ends with the same 'they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain'. The n-gram stream duly proposed it here and again at 30:15. The Book of Mormon does not conflate them. It has the ox and not the bullock, and it keeps the cow, the bear and their young ones, which Isaiah 65:25 drops.

links.note: Verbatim at every word. The one difference from the KJV is a semicolon for a colon, and 2 Nephi 21:7 has the semicolon too — an agreement of 30 with 21 against the KJV that is worth exactly as much as the punctuation of a first edition is worth, which is to say it is noted in the collation at 30:9 and not argued from.

pericopes.text: And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice’s den.

links.text: And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice’ den.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:8 → 2 Nephi 21:8 → 2 Nephi 30:14, on one orthographic datum only
provenance.other: “hole of the asp” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:8, and 'cockatrice' occurs in exactly four KJV verses, of which this is the only one with a den. The KJV prints the possessive as 'the cockatrice’ den', with a bare apostrophe and no s; 2 Nephi 21:8 prints 'the cockatrice’s den' and so does 2 Nephi 30:14. This is the only reading anywhere in the six quoted verses where both Book of Mormon witnesses stand together against the KJV.
provenance.significance: It is the whole positive result of the collation, and it is very small. If the two Book of Mormon copies of Isaiah 11 descend from one another rather than independently from the KJV, this apostrophe is the only surviving trace of it. The honest weight to put on that is close to none: a compositor setting 'cockatrice’ den' from copy would regularise it to 'cockatrice’s' without thinking, and would do so twice as readily as once, so the agreement of 21:8 and 30:14 may be two independent normalisations rather than one inherited reading. The mediation field records it because CONVENTIONS §7 asks for a decision and this is the only evidence there is; the note says how thin it is.

links.note: Verbatim except for the possessive. The mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM on a single apostrophe, which is stated here so that no reader mistakes the field for a stronger claim than the evidence supports — this row is the one place in the chapter where the catalogue has taken a position it could lose. Set beside 2 Nephi 6:16, where the same test on Isaiah 49:24 produced two readings pointing opposite ways and the verdict had to be recorded as divided, the result here is different in kind: not a conflict of evidence but an absence of it, with one orthographical straw on the scale.
links.whyNot: The sole basis for preferring an internal route over the KJV directly is the possessive 's' in 'cockatrice’s', which is a printing-house normalisation of an archaic form and could have been made twice independently. Every other word of Isaiah 11:4-9 is identical in all three witnesses, so the mediation claim rests on one apostrophe and should be withdrawn if the 1830 compositor is shown to have regularised bare possessive apostrophes elsewhere as a matter of course.

pericopes.text: They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.

links.text: They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon; not distinguishable from a route through 2 Nephi 21:9
provenance.other: “hurt nor destroy” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 11:9 and Isaiah 65:25, and “as the waters cover the sea” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 11:9 and Habakkuk 2:14. 30:15 is verbatim from Isaiah 11:9 and agrees with neither competitor where they differ: Habakkuk reads 'the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD', with 'filled' for 'full' and an added 'glory of'.
provenance.significance: Two rival verses, each sharing one of this verse's two rare phrases, and the Book of Mormon has Isaiah 11:9's form of both. That is the last confirmation the collation needs: whatever 2 Nephi 30's proximate copy was, it was a copy of Isaiah 11 and not a memory of the several places where the peaceable kingdom is described. The vision then closes the quotation and the chapter turns, at verse 16, to what the earth being full of the knowledge of the Lord will mean in practice — everything made known, nothing sealed.

links.note: Twenty-nine consecutive words, verbatim, ending the block. The n-gram stream ranked Isaiah 65:25 and Habakkuk 2:14 behind Isaiah 11:9 here and both are excluded on their divergent readings rather than on rank; the register gives the reason. The mediation is uncertain for the same reason as at 30:9: 2 Nephi 21:9 and the KJV are identical, so there is nothing to choose between them.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, the things of all nations shall be made known; yea, all things shall be made known unto the children of men.

There is nothing which is secret, save it shall be revealed; there is no works of darkness, save it shall be made manifest in the light; and there is nothing which is sealed upon the earth, save it shall be loosed.

links.text: For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.

provenance.route: Luke 8:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Ephesians 5:11-13 supplying the second clause
provenance.other: “nothing is secret” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 8:17, and both of the Book of Mormon's verbs are Luke's: 'secret' paired with 'made manifest'. The synoptic parallels do not have this pairing — Mark 4:22 reads 'nothing hid, which shall not be manifested; neither was any thing kept secret', with the terms crossed, and Matthew 10:26 reads 'nothing covered, that shall not be revealed'. “works of darkness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 13:12 and Ephesians 5:11, and Ephesians 5:13 continues 'all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light'.
provenance.significance: The verse is a chain of three sayings and each has its own source, which is what makes it a good specimen of how this writer composes. Luke supplies the secret that shall be revealed; Ephesians 5:11-13 supplies the works of darkness made manifest by light, in the one KJV passage that puts those two ideas in one sentence; and the third clause — 'nothing which is sealed upon the earth, save it shall be loosed' — has no biblical source at all, because it is about the sealed book of 2 Nephi 27, which is this book's own subject. So the verse moves from quoted scripture to quoted scripture to the Book of Mormon's own contribution, and the reader who recovers the first two hears the third claimed on their authority.

links.note: Luke 8:17 rather than Mark 4:22 or Matthew 10:26, and the discrimination is clean: the Book of Mormon has 'secret' governed by revelation and 'made manifest' as its verb, which is Luke's arrangement; Mark crosses the terms and Matthew has neither. The Ephesians half is fused rather than quoted — the KJV has works of darkness at 5:11 and 'made manifest by the light' at 5:13, and 30:17 compresses them into 'no works of darkness, save it shall be made manifest in the light', with 'in' for Paul's 'by'. Recorded as an allusion on that account, and because none of the three clauses reproduces a whole KJV clause.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, all things which have been revealed unto the children of men, shall at that day be revealed; and Satan shall have power over the hearts of the children of men no more, for a long time. And now, my beloved brethren, I must make an end of my sayings.

links.text: And cast him into the bottomless pit, and shut him up, and set a seal upon him, that he should deceive the nations no more, till the thousand years should be fulfilled: and after that he must be loosed a little season.

provenance.other: “deceive the nations no more” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:3, and it is the KJV's only sentence in which Satan's power over people is suspended for a stated term. The Book of Mormon's 'for a long time' stands where Revelation has 'till the thousand years should be fulfilled'.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Revelation 20:3 binds Satan for a thousand years and then — 'after that he must be loosed a little season' — releases him; 30:18 gives him no power over the hearts of the children of men 'no more, for a long time', which keeps the release and declines the number. That is a deliberate imprecision in a verse whose source is famously precise, and it leaves the millennium's length an open question in a book that has just insisted the Lord's word is not finished. Recovering Revelation 20 also completes a pattern: 2 Nephi 28:23 took verses 10-14 for the lake of fire, 2 Nephi 29:11 took verse 12 for the judgment out of books, and 30:18 takes verses 2-3 for the binding — three chapters of Nephi's closing exposition drawing on one chapter of Revelation, and drawing on it backwards.

links.note: A five-word KJV singleton, with Revelation's temporal clause replaced by a vaguer one that keeps its logic: a bounded suspension, not an abolition. 'For a long time' is not scriptural English and is the 1830's reading; it is what makes the borrowing visible as an adaptation rather than a quotation. Note the two other Revelation 20 rows in this dispatch, at 2 Nephi 28:23 and 29:11 — taken together they show the chapter-ending sermon working through Revelation 20 from its end to its beginning, which is not how a writer recalling a familiar passage would be expected to move.

pericopes.text: And now I, Nephi, make an end of my prophesying unto you, my beloved brethren. And I cannot write but a few things, which I know must surely come to pass; neither can I write but a few of the words of my brother Jacob.

Wherefore, the things which I have written, sufficeth me, save it be a few words which I must speak, concerning the doctrine of Christ; wherefore, I shall speak unto you plainly, according to the plainness of my prophesying.

For my soul delighteth in plainness: for after this manner doth the Lord God work among the children of men. For the Lord God giveth light unto the understanding: for he speaketh unto men according to their language, unto their understanding.

links.text: And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever.

provenance.other: “the Lord God giveth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 22:5. The collocation is otherwise unattested: elsewhere God gives light by a verb of shining or by a luminary, not by this construction.
provenance.significance: Nephi's account of how revelation works — God condescends to human language and human understanding — is phrased in the words of the last verse but one of the Christian canon, where the light that replaces sun and candle is God himself. If the borrowing is real, the metalepsis is that the accommodation Nephi describes as a pedagogy is, in its source, the eschatological end of all mediation.

links.note: “For the Lord God giveth light unto the understanding: for he speaketh unto men according to their language, unto their understanding.” The subject-verb pair is a KJV singleton and the object in both places is light, but Revelation's light is the New Jerusalem's illumination and Nephi's is intellectual. That gap is why this is an echo at moderate and not an allusion: the wording is distinctive, the sense is transferred. Recorded because the string is rare enough that a reader who finds it will want to know we saw it and what we made of it.
links.whyNot: Four words, one of them the divine title Nephi uses constantly, and the sense of “light” is metaphorical here and literal there. A reader could reasonably call this coincidence of a common theological idiom.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, I would that ye should remember that I have spoken unto you, concerning that Prophet which the Lord showed unto me, that should baptize the Lamb of God, which should take away the sins of the world.

links.text: The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.

provenance.other: “taketh away the sin of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:29. The Book of Mormon pluralizes to “sins”, which is the one departure; “Lamb of God” is John's title, occurring only at John 1:29 and 1:36 in the whole Bible.
provenance.significance: The whole verse is built out of John 1 and out of nothing else. “That Prophet” is the Baptist's interrogators' phrase at John 1:21 and 1:25 — the only place in the KJV where the definite Prophet is put as a question — but John there DENIES being that prophet, and Nephi assigns him the title anyway. The baptizer who says “I am not” in the source is “that Prophet which the Lord showed unto me” in the borrowing, which is a small, deliberate-looking correction of the Fourth Gospel by the book that quotes it.

links.note: The verse names three things that all come from one chapter: the prophet who baptizes, the Lamb of God, and the taking away of the world's sin. John 1:29 supplies the last two in a single clause and is the only KJV verse that does. The pluralizing of “sin” to “sins” is the sort of variation that recurs across the corpus and does not weaken the identification — the six-word run around it is exact. Hardy cross-references John 1:29 at this verse.

pericopes.text: And now, if the Lamb of God, he being holy, should have need to be baptized by water, to fulfil all righteousness, O then, how much more need have we, being unholy, to be baptized, yea, even by water.

links.text: And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him.

provenance.other: “fulfil all righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:15; “have need to be baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:14. Both are absent from Mark, Luke and John, which report the baptism without the exchange.
provenance.significance: This is the mediation decision the chapter turns on, and it is settled by two singletons a verse apart. All four Gospels report the baptism; only Matthew reports the argument about it, and Nephi's argument is Matthew's argument run backwards. In Matthew the Baptist protests that HE has need to be baptized of Jesus; in 2 Nephi it is the reader who has need, “how much more … being unholy”. The a fortiori is Nephi's own, but the two clauses he reasons from are the only two clauses in the Bible where anyone discusses whether Jesus should be baptized at all.

links.note: “Should have need to be baptized by water, to fulfil all righteousness.” Two KJV singletons, from consecutive verses of one Gospel, in one sentence. Both fall well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and neither is one of his 36 quoted passages; taken together they are nevertheless a quotation in this catalogue's sense, because a phrase that occurs once in the Bible and appears here in its source's grammatical form is not a coincidence of common diction. The chapter then presses “fulfil all righteousness” again at 31:6 as the question it will answer for the next twelve verses, which is a use of the phrase Matthew does not make. Hardy cross-references Matthew 3:15 here.

pericopes.text: And now, I would ask of you, my beloved brethren, wherein the Lamb of God did fulfil all righteousness in being baptized by water?

Know ye not that he was holy? But notwithstanding he being holy, he showeth unto the children of men, that according to the flesh, he humbleth himself before the Father, and witnesseth unto the Father that he would be obedient unto him in keeping his commandments;

links.text: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.

provenance.other: “he humbled himself” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 12:12 and Philippians 2:8; only the second has a subject who humbles himself and is thereby obedient. The pairing of self-humbling with obedience, in that order, is Philippians 2:8's alone.
provenance.significance: Nephi's answer to his own question at 31:6 — in what did the baptism fulfil all righteousness? — is the Philippians hymn. “According to the flesh, he humbleth himself before the Father, and witnesseth unto the Father that he would be obedient.” Paul's sequence is being found in fashion as a man, then humbling, then obedience; Nephi's is according to the flesh, then humbling, then obedience. Recover Philippians 2 and the obedience in question is obedience unto death: the baptism is being read as a rehearsal of the crucifixion, which is exactly what the descent “down into the water” at 31:13 will make explicit.

links.note: The three elements are Paul's and they arrive in Paul's order. What makes the link more than a shared commonplace is that the tense is wrong for a commonplace: Nephi puts it in the present (“he humbleth himself”, “witnesseth”), which is the tense of an exposition of a text rather than of a narration of an event. He is not telling the story of the baptism, he is reading it, and the grid he reads it on is the kenosis of Philippians 2. Frederick does not treat this verse.

pericopes.text: wherefore, after that he was baptized with water, the Holy Ghost descended upon him in the form of a dove.

links.text: And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased.

provenance.other: “the Holy Ghost descended” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 3:22. The other three accounts name the agent differently — Matthew 3:16 “the Spirit of God descending”, Mark 1:10 “the Spirit like a dove descending”, John 1:32 “the Spirit descending from heaven” — so the noun alone decides between them.
provenance.significance: Hardy's apparatus offers all four Gospels here, which is right for a study edition and leaves the interesting question unasked. The wording answers it: the Book of Mormon has Luke's noun and Luke's word order, subject then verb then the manner then “upon him”, where Matthew and Mark both put the participle before the dove. And Luke is the only account in which a voice from heaven follows in the same verse, which is the account this chapter needs, because from 31:11 onward it is going to give the Father and the Son speaking voices of their own.

links.note: “After that he was baptized with water, the Holy Ghost descended upon him in the form of a dove.” The four accounts diverge and the choice is decidable. “Holy Ghost” is Luke's; Matthew, Mark and John all read “Spirit”. The one departure is “in the form of a dove” for Luke's “in a bodily shape like a dove”, which flattens Luke's oddest phrase into an idiom no Gospel uses — a simplification, not a different source. Note the 1830 “after that he was baptized”, with the conjunction 1920 deleted, which is the KJV's own construction and is one of several places in this chapter where the first edition preserves a Jacobean joint that the modern text has smoothed away.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 2 Ne 31.8 (Matthew 3:16, Mark 1:10, Luke 3:22, John 1:32)

pericopes.text: And again: It sheweth unto the children of men the straightness of the path, and the narrowness of the gate, by which they should enter, he having set the example before them.

links.text: Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:

provenance.other: “Enter ye in at the strait gate” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:13; “strait is the gate” and “narrow is the way” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:14. Luke 13:24's parallel reads “Strive to enter in at the strait gate” and lacks the narrow way altogether.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon does not merely borrow Matthew's pair of images, it swaps the adjectives between them. Matthew has a STRAIT gate and a NARROW way; 2 Nephi 31:9 has “the straightness of the path, and the narrowness of the gate”. The two epithets have changed places. That is worth recording because it is precisely the mistake a writer makes when reciting a familiar text from memory rather than copying it, and because it feeds the chapter's later and more consequential slide: 1830 spells the path “straight” at 31:18 and 31:19, not KJV “strait”, so the constricted gate of Matthew has become a path that is not crooked. A homophone has changed the doctrine.

links.note: Matthew 7:13-14 is the only KJV passage that holds gate, way, narrowness and entering together, and the chapter returns to it four times (31:9, 31:17, 31:18, and again in Nephi's farewell at 33:9). The adjectives are transposed at every occurrence, consistently — this is Nephi's own settled form of the saying, not a slip at one verse. The 1830 orthography carries the argument here and is the reason this catalogue runs on the first edition: “straightness of the path” in 1830, against the KJV's “strait is the gate”, is visible evidence of how the saying was heard.

pericopes.text: And he saith unto the children of men, Follow thou me. Wherefore, my beloved brethren, can we follow Jesus, save we shall be willing to keep the commandments of the Father?

links.text: Jesus saith unto him, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me.

provenance.other: “follow thou me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 21:22. The bare “Follow me” is common — Matthew 4:19, 8:22, 9:9, 19:21, Mark 2:14, Luke 5:27, John 1:43, 21:19 — but the emphatic pronoun is John's, once.
provenance.significance: Nephi introduces the words with the same present tense he used at 31:7 — 1830 “he saith unto the children of men”, which 1920 changed to “said”. He is quoting a living voice, not reporting a past one. And the source is the last command in the Fourth Gospel, spoken to Peter after the resurrection and immediately after Peter has been told how he will die: “follow thou me” is, in John, an instruction to follow as far as a martyr's death. Nephi's next clause — “save we shall be willing to keep the commandments of the Father” — makes willingness the test, which is the Johannine sense of the phrase and not the Synoptic one.

links.note: Three words, and a KJV singleton. Everything about the setting supports the identification: the chapter has just used John 1 at 31:4, the pronoun is emphatic in exactly the way John's is, and the demand that follows is a demand about the will. The 1830 present tense (“saith”, corrected to “said” in 1920) is worth noting on its own — the first edition presents this as speech continuing into the reader's present, which the modern text closes off.

pericopes.text: And the Father saith, Repent ye, repent ye, and be baptized in the name of my beloved Son.

links.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: Acts 2:38 is the only KJV verse that puts repentance, baptism, a name, and the receiving of the Holy Ghost in one sentence in that order. Acts 10:48 and 19:5 have baptism in a name without the repentance; Mark 1:4 has repentance and baptism without the Spirit.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:38 is the formula Nephi is expounding for the whole chapter, and 31:11-12 splits it in two and gives each half a speaker. The Father says the first half — “Repent ye, repent ye, and be baptized” — and the Son says the second — “to him will the Father give the Holy Ghost”. Peter's single sentence at Pentecost has been dramatized into a dialogue between two persons of the Godhead. Then 31:17 reassembles it: “the gate … is repentance, and baptism by water; and then cometh a remission of your sins by fire, and by the Holy Ghost”, which restores even Peter's “remission of sins”, the one element the dialogue had dropped.

links.note: The chapter's structural debt, not merely a verbal one. Every clause of Acts 2:38 appears in 2 Nephi 31 and the sequence is never disturbed: repent, be baptized, in a name, receive the Holy Ghost, remission of sins. What the Book of Mormon adds is the substitution of “my beloved Son” for Peter's “Jesus Christ”, which is the voice of the Father speaking and could not have said the name any other way — a coherence the borrowing did not have to have.

pericopes.text: And also, the voice of the Son came unto me, saying, He that is baptized in my name, to him will the Father give the Holy Ghost, like unto me; wherefore, follow me, and do the things which ye have seen me do.

links.text: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.

provenance.other: John 14:26 is the KJV's one verse in which the Son speaks, in the first person, of the Father giving the Holy Ghost in the Son's name. Luke 11:13's “give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him” has the Father giving but not the name and not the Spirit as Ghost.
provenance.significance: The link matters because of what Nephi does with it two chapters later. John 14:26's Comforter “shall teach you all things”; 2 Nephi 32:5 promises that if you receive the Holy Ghost “it will shew unto you all things what ye should do”. The Son's speech at 31:12 sets up the pneumatology that chapter 32 exists to defend, and both ends of it are John 14.

links.note: “He that is baptized in my name, to him will the Father give the Holy Ghost, like unto me.” Three elements of John 14:26 — the Father as giver, the Holy Ghost as gift, the Son's name as the channel — with the Book of Mormon's own addition, “like unto me”, which glosses the Greek Paraclete's sense of another of the same kind without using the word Comforter. Moderate rather than high because no run of KJV wording is reproduced: the case rests on the configuration of the clause, not its diction.
links.whyNot: Every content word here is common. A reader who thinks Acts 2:38's “ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost” accounts for the whole verse has a simpler explanation, and the Acts link is already made at 31:11.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, I know that if ye shall follow the Son, with full purpose of heart, acting no hypocrisy and no deception before God, but with real intent, repenting of your sins, witnessing unto the Father that ye are willing to take upon you the name of Christ, by baptism; yea, by following your Lord and Saviour down into the water, according to his word; behold, then shall ye receive the Holy Ghost; yea, then cometh the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost; and then can ye speak with the tongue of Angels, and shout praises unto the Holy One of Israel.

links.text: Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.

provenance.other: “with the tongues of men and of angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:1. Angelic speech appears nowhere else in the Bible as a tongue that a human being might speak.
provenance.significance: Paul names the tongue of angels in order to dismiss it — it is the first and highest of the gifts he says are nothing without charity. Nephi takes it as the promised outcome of baptism and builds two chapters on it: 31:14 has it again as “a new tongue”, and 2 Nephi 32:2-3 makes it the engine of the whole argument, since angels speak by the Holy Ghost and therefore speak the words of Christ. Recover 1 Corinthians 13 and the rhetorical direction is exactly reversed. What Paul offers as the most impressive thing a Christian could have and still be nothing, Nephi offers as evidence that something has happened. Nephi's own answer to Paul arrives, unremarked, at 33:7-9, where he says three times over that he has charity.

links.note: “Then can ye speak with the tongue of Angels.” The singular for Paul's plural and the dropping of “of men” are the only changes; the phrase has no other biblical home. The verse also carries “with full purpose of heart”, where “purpose of heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 11:23, and the sense there — Barnabas exhorting converts that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord — is the sense here. Note that the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost in this verse inverts the order of both Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, which read Holy Ghost first and fire second; the inversion holds at 31:14 and 31:17 as well, so it is Nephi's form of the phrase.

pericopes.text: But behold, my beloved brethren, thus came the voice of the Son unto me, saying, After that ye have repented of your sins, and witnessed unto the Father that ye are willing to keep my commandments, by the baptism of water, and have received the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost, and can speak with a new tongue, yea, even with the tongue of Angels, and after this, should deny me, it would have been better for you, that ye had not known me.

links.text: For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them.

provenance.other: “better for them not to have known” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 2:21. Mark 14:21's “good were it for that man if he had never been born” is the nearest competitor and shares neither the construction nor the verb of knowing.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 2:21 is about apostates who have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of Christ and are again entangled — precisely the case Nephi is putting, of one who has received the baptism of fire and then denies. The source supplies not only the sentence but the situation, and it supplies the escape clause too: Peter's apostate turns “from the holy commandment”, which is why Nephi's condition is stated as having “witnessed unto the Father that ye are willing to keep my commandments”. The whole of 31:14 is 2 Peter 2:20-21 with baptism written into it.

links.note: “And after this, should deny me, it would have been better for you, that ye had not known me.” The construction is the KJV's exactly — the counterfactual comparative, the perfect infinitive of knowing — with Peter's third person changed to the second because the Son is speaking directly. Peter's object is “the way of righteousness”; Nephi's is the person, “me”, which is a compression appropriate to a speaker who is himself that way. The 1830 “after that ye have repented” at the head of the verse again keeps the conjunction 1920 dropped.

pericopes.text: And I heard a voice from the Father, saying, Yea, the words of my beloved, are true and faithful. He that endureth to the end, the same shall be saved.

links.text: But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.

provenance.route: Matthew 10:22 + Matthew 24:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “endureth to the end” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:22. “the same shall be saved” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13, both of which read “he that shall endure unto the end”. No KJV verse reads as 2 Nephi 31:15 does.
provenance.significance: The most instructive single sentence in the chapter, because the Book of Mormon's form of it exists nowhere in the Bible. “He that endureth to the end, the same shall be saved” fuses Matthew 10:22's protasis with Matthew 24:13's apodosis. Two verses of one Gospel, sixteen chapters apart, joined at the comma. This is the signature of a text recalled rather than transcribed — the memory holds the shorter and more idiomatic half of each — and it is a cleaner instance of conflation than anything the mediation tests in 1 Nephi produced, because both halves are checkable KJV rarities and the seam between them is visible. That the Father is the speaker makes it sharper still: the voice from heaven quotes the Son, in a form the Son is never recorded as using.

links.note: The catalogue's decision to name Matthew 24:13 as the source rather than Mark 13:13 is a coin toss on the wording alone, since the two are identical in the shared clause; Matthew is preferred only because the other half of the conflation is unambiguously Matthew's, at 10:22, and because the chapter has already used Matthew 3 twice and Matthew 7 once. Mark 13:13 is carried in the composite and a reader is entitled to prefer it. What is not a coin toss is that neither Gospel supplies the whole sentence.

pericopes.text: And now, my beloved brethren, I know by this, that unless a man shall endure to the end, in following the example of the Son of the living God, he cannot be saved;

links.text: And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.

provenance.other: “the Son of the living God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 16:16 and John 6:69. Both are confessions by Peter; the title is used by no one else in the Bible.
provenance.significance: Nephi's argument at 31:16 is that endurance means “following the example of the Son of the living God”, and the two KJV verses that supply the title are both moments where Peter identifies who Jesus is. Matthew's is followed at once by the first passion prediction and by Peter being told that if any man will come after Christ he must take up his cross and follow — which is the doctrine of 31:16, in its source, three verses later.

links.note: A title, not a clause, so this is recorded as an echo. It earns a row because the title is genuinely restricted — two verses, one speaker — and because the phrase arrives in this chapter at the exact point where following the Son's example is being made the condition of salvation. Between Matthew 16:16 and John 6:69 there is nothing in the wording to choose; Matthew is named because 2 Nephi 31 is otherwise a Matthean chapter.
links.whyNot: Six words of confessional formula, and the Book of Mormon uses divine titles freely and often without a source. If the chapter did not lean on Matthew elsewhere this would be an exclusion.

pericopes.text: wherefore, do the things which I have told you that I have seen, that your Lord and your Redeemer should do: for, for this cause have they been shown unto me, that ye might know the gate by which ye should enter. For the gate by which ye should enter, is repentance, and baptism by water; and then cometh a remission of your sins by fire, and by the Holy Ghost.

And then are ye in this straight and narrow path which leads to eternal life; yea, ye have entered in by the gate: ye have done according to the commandments of the Father and the Son; and ye have received the Holy Ghost, which witness of the Father and the Son, unto the fulfilling of the promise which he hath made, That if ye entered in by the way, ye should receive.

And now, my beloved brethren, after that ye have got into this straight and narrow path, I would ask, If all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far, save it were by the word of Christ, with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of Him who is mighty to save;

links.text: Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.

provenance.other: “mighty to save” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 63:1. Zephaniah 3:17's “he is mighty; he will save” is the nearest thing to a rival and is not the same phrase.
provenance.significance: The one place in the King James Bible where God is called mighty to save is the opening of the winepress oracle, where the figure comes from Edom in dyed garments because he has trodden the peoples in his anger and his raiment is stained with their blood. Nephi, urging his readers to rely wholly on the merits of Him who is mighty to save, has reached for a title whose context is judgment rather than mercy — and the same book will make the connection explicit later, at Doctrine and Covenants 133's expansion of the same oracle. Whether the resonance is intended or not, it is the sort of thing metalepsis is a name for: the epithet promises salvation and its home verse describes what salvation costs those on the other side of it.

links.note: Three words, one KJV verse, and they arrive in a sentence about relying on merits, which is where the chapter's argument moves from what a convert does to what Christ has done. Isaiah 63 is not otherwise used in 2 Nephi's non-transcribed chapters, so this is not the residue of a nearby block quotation. Note also the 1830 “after that ye have got into this straight and narrow path” — 1830 “got”, 1920 “gotten”, and 1830 “straight” for the KJV's “strait”, on which see 31:9.

pericopes.text: wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.

links.text: I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

provenance.other: “press toward” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 3:14, and the KJV has no instance of “press forward” at all. The verb of pressing on toward a goal is Paul's and, in the King James Bible, only Paul's.
provenance.significance: If the echo stands, it stands with 31:7's Philippians 2:8: the chapter would be reaching into Philippians for both its Christology and its ethic of perseverance, taking the humbling from chapter 2 and the pressing on from chapter 3. Paul's context is his own incompleteness — “not as though I had already attained” — which is precisely the question Nephi has just asked at 31:19, “I would ask, If all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay.”

links.note: Recorded at low confidence because the case is a real one and the wording will not quite carry it. Nephi's question at 31:19 and Paul's disclaimer at Philippians 3:13 are the same move, and the verb that answers both is a pressing forward; but “press forward” is not the KJV's phrase, and an author who wanted Paul's idiom had it available and did not use it.
links.whyNot: The preposition is wrong and it is the only word that would have made this decidable. “Press forward” is ordinary nineteenth-century English and needs no source; the thematic parallel with Philippians 3:13 is the whole of the argument, and thematic parallels of this kind are cheap.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, my beloved brethren, this is the way; and there is none other way nor name given under heaven, whereby man can be saved in the Kingdom of God. And now, behold, this is the doctrine of Christ, and the only and true doctrine of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, which is one God, without end. Amen.

links.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.

provenance.other: “none other name under heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 4:12. The whole construction — a negated existential, a name, “under heaven”, and a relative clause of being saved — has no other biblical occurrence.
provenance.significance: The chapter that began by expounding Peter's Pentecost sermon ends by quoting Peter before the Sanhedrin, and the two Acts sermons are consecutive: Acts 2:38 at 31:11 and Acts 4:12 at 31:21. Peter's speech in Acts 4 is a defence of having healed in a name, delivered under interrogation; Nephi's is a summary of a doctrine, delivered as a farewell. What both share is that the name is the only thing at issue. Nephi's one addition is “way” — “there is none other way nor name” — which reaches back to Matthew 7's way at 31:9 and forward to “this is the way” in the same sentence, welding Peter's exclusive name to Matthew's narrow road.

links.note: Ten words in sequence, one departure. Acts 4:12 reads “given among men, whereby we must be saved”; 2 Nephi 31:21 reads “given under heaven, whereby man can be saved in the Kingdom of God”. The Book of Mormon relocates “under heaven” from its adjectival position after “name” and drops “among men”, but keeps the negated existential, the name, the relative clause and the passive of salvation. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his 36; catalogued as a quotation for the reasons in CONVENTIONS §2.

links.text: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:

provenance.other: “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 28:19 — twelve consecutive words with one biblical home.
provenance.significance: The chapter's last sentence closes the frame it opened at 31:5. It began with Matthew 3, the baptism of Jesus, and it ends with Matthew 28, the command to baptize everyone else; the first and last words about baptism in the First Gospel are the first and last words about baptism in Nephi's exposition of the doctrine of Christ. And the triadic formula is what lets Nephi's final clause do its work: having named the three, he adds “which is one God, without end”, a gloss Matthew does not offer and which turns a baptismal formula into a creedal statement.

links.note: Twelve words verbatim, and this one clears Skousen's sixteen-word threshold only if the surrounding clause is counted, so it is worth saying plainly that on his measure it does not — the run is twelve. It is nonetheless the longest exact KJV run in the chapter and the identification is not disputable. The interest is in the appended “which is one God, without end”: the modalist-sounding gloss is the Book of Mormon's own, and the 1830 text has it with no punctuation to soften it.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, my beloved brethren, I suppose that ye ponder somewhat in your hearts, concerning that which ye should do, after that ye have entered in by the way. But behold, why do ye ponder these things in your hearts?

links.text: And immediately when Jesus perceived in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, he said unto them, Why reason ye these things in your hearts?

provenance.other: “these things in your hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 2:8. Luke 5:22, the parallel, reads “What reason ye in your hearts?” and Matthew 9:4 reads “Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?” — neither has the demonstrative, and the mediation is therefore decidable on a single word.
provenance.significance: The verse borrows more than the question; it borrows the situation. In Mark, Jesus knows what the scribes are reasoning without being told, and the rhetorical question is the proof that he knows. Nephi opens chapter 32 by claiming exactly that knowledge — “I suppose that ye ponder somewhat in your hearts, concerning that which ye should do” — and then asks the Markan question of his readers. Nine verses later the whole short chapter turns on the same claim, at 32:8: “I perceive that ye ponder still in your hearts.” Mark's “perceived in his spirit” has become Nephi's warrant for addressing objections nobody has voiced, which is the rhetorical engine of the entire chapter.

links.note: Nephi's substitution is “ponder” for “reason”, which is Luke's verb elsewhere (Luke 2:19, “Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart”) and softens the rebuke into an invitation. Everything else is Mark's, including the demonstrative that separates Mark from both Synoptic parallels. The frame recurs at 32:8 and is registered there rather than given a second row.

pericopes.text: Do ye not remember that I said unto you, that after ye had received the Holy Ghost, ye could speak with the tongue of Angels? And now, how could ye speak with the tongue of Angels, save it were by the Holy Ghost?

Angels speak by the power of the Holy Ghost; wherefore, they speak the words of Christ.— Wherefore, I said unto you, feast upon the words of Christ: for behold, the words of Christ will tell you all things what ye should do.

Wherefore, now after that I have spoken these words, if ye cannot understand them, it will be because ye ask not, neither do ye knock; wherefore, ye are not brought into the light, but must perish in the dark.

links.text: Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.

provenance.route: James 4:2 + Matthew 7:7-8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “because ye ask not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:2 — and the Book of Mormon reproduces the causal conjunction with it: “it will be because ye ask not”. The knocking that follows is Matthew 7:7-8's, the only KJV passage where asking and knocking are paired as conditions of receiving.
provenance.significance: Two sources are fused in six words, and each brings something the other lacks. Matthew 7:7 supplies the pairing of ask and knock; James 4:2 supplies the diagnosis, that the failure is the petitioner's own. The fusion is what makes the sentence work as a rebuke rather than an invitation: Matthew alone would have promised, James alone would have accused, and Nephi needs both because he is explaining why his own writing has not been understood. Recover James 4 and the accusation is sharper still — James's non-askers do not ask because they are at war with each other, and Nephi's chapter is about a people he has just called unbelieving, wicked, ignorant and stiffnecked at 32:7.

links.note: “It will be because ye ask not, neither do ye knock; wherefore, ye are not brought into the light, but must perish in the dark.” The James singleton is exact and carries its conjunction; the knocking has no other biblical source than Matthew 7:7-8, where “knock, and it shall be opened unto you” stands with “ask, and it shall be given you” in a single sentence. Note that Nephi has inverted the sequence — Matthew and Luke 11:9 both run ask, seek, knock, and Nephi drops the seeking, which is the middle term and the one his argument has no use for.

pericopes.text: For behold, again I say unto you, that if ye will enter in by the way, and receive the Holy Ghost, it will shew unto you all things what ye should do.

links.text: Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.

provenance.other: “he will shew you things to come” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 16:13, and “guide you into all truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. John 14:26's “he shall teach you all things” is the companion promise and stands behind 2 Nephi 31:12; this verse has John 16's verb, not John 14's.
provenance.significance: The two Johannine Paraclete promises are used at two different points and not confused. At 31:12 the Father gives the Holy Ghost and the emphasis is on teaching, which is John 14:26; here the Holy Ghost, once received, will shew, which is John 16:13. Nephi's addition is the object: John's Spirit shews things to come, Nephi's shews “all things what ye should do”. Prophecy has been converted into practical guidance, and that conversion is the answer chapter 32 exists to give — the question at 32:1 was concerning that which ye should do.

links.note: The decisive evidence is a spelling the modern text no longer has. 1830 reads “it will shew unto you all things”; the 1920 edition changed “shew” to “show”, and with it went the only surface trace of John 16:13's verb, which the KJV also spells “shew”. This is the case CONVENTIONS §8 describes exactly: the first edition displays a borrowing that the current text conceals. Confidence is high rather than certain because the shared run is short and the collocation of Spirit with shewing is not unique to John; what carries it is that this chapter has already used John 14:26 one chapter earlier and is plainly working through the Farewell Discourse.

pericopes.text: Behold, this is the doctrine of Christ; and there will be no more doctrine given, until after that he shall manifest himself unto you in the flesh. And when he shall manifest himself unto you in the flesh, the things which he shall say unto you, shall ye observe to do.

links.text: All the commandments which I command thee this day shall ye observe to do, that ye may live, and multiply, and go in and possess the land which the LORD sware unto your fathers.

provenance.other: “shall ye observe to do” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 8:1. The bare “observe to do” is a Deuteronomic formula and appears a dozen times (5:32, 6:3, 12:32, 24:8 among them), but always with a different subject placement; the inverted clause with the postposed subject pronoun is Deuteronomy 8:1's alone.
provenance.significance: The frame matters more than the words. Deuteronomy 8:1 makes what Moses commands this day the thing to be observed; 2 Nephi 32:6 makes what Christ shall say when he manifests himself in the flesh the thing to be observed, and says in the same breath that “there will be no more doctrine given” until then. A Deuteronomic sentence about the sufficiency of the law delivered at Horeb has been rewritten as a statement about a doctrine that is closed until a future appearance. If the echo is real, the canon-closing move is being made in the words of the canon-closing chapter of the Pentateuch's own farewell discourse.

links.note: Five words in the same inverted order, from a single KJV verse. Kept at moderate and typed as an echo because “observe to do” is genuinely formulaic in Deuteronomy and a nineteenth-century writer steeped in the KJV could produce the inversion without Deuteronomy 8 in view. It earns its row because the sentence it stands in is the chapter's doctrinal hinge and because the frame — a body of commandment declared complete — is Deuteronomy's, not just its phrasing.
links.whyNot: A Deuteronomic idiom used dozens of times in the book it comes from, and the identification of Deuteronomy 8:1 in particular rests on word order rather than on distinctive vocabulary. Nothing else in 2 Nephi 32 touches Deuteronomy.

pericopes.text: And now I, Nephi, cannot say more: the spirit stoppeth mine utterance, and I am left to mourn because of the unbelief, and the wickedness, and the ignorance, and the stiff-neckedness of men: for they will not search knowledge, nor understand great knowledge, when it is given unto them in plainness, even as plain as word can be.

And now my beloved brethren, I perceive that ye ponder still in your hearts; and it grieveth me that I must speak concerning this thing. For if ye would hearken unto the spirit which teacheth a man to pray, ye would know that ye must pray: for the evil spirit teacheth not a man to pray, but teacheth him that he must not pray.

links.text: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.

provenance.other: “the Spirit itself maketh intercession” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:26. It is the Bible's only statement that the Spirit's office is to supply what human prayer lacks, which is the proposition 2 Nephi 32:8 needs.
provenance.significance: Nephi's claim is that the disposition to pray is itself diagnostic — the Spirit teaches a man to pray, the evil spirit teaches him that he must not. That claim has one biblical foundation and this is it: Romans 8:26 is the only place where the Spirit is said to be involved in the act of praying rather than in its answer. Note also what Nephi does not take. Paul's Spirit intercedes with groanings which cannot be uttered, and Nephi has just said at 32:7 that “the spirit stoppeth mine utterance”. The unutterable is on both sides of the borrowing, but Paul's is the Spirit's speech and Nephi's is his own silence.

links.note: No KJV run is reproduced, so this is conceptual and moderate: the argument is that the doctrine has a single biblical home and that Nephi is standing in it. Romans 8:26 supplies the Spirit as the agent of prayer; 2 Nephi 32:8 turns that agency into a test of spirits, which is a step Paul does not take and which owes something to 1 John 4:1-3. `kjvSpecific` is 'uncertain' by design — there is no phrasing here to test against any English version.
links.whyNot: A conceptual link with no verbal contact at all beyond the pairing of spirit and prayer, which is common ground in any Christian devotional writing of the period. A reader who declines it loses nothing from the chapter's other links.

pericopes.text: But behold, I say unto you, that ye must pray always, and not faint; that ye must not perform any thing unto the Lord, save in the first place ye shall pray unto the Father in the name of Christ, that he will consecrate thy performance unto thee, that thy performance may be for the welfare of thy soul.

links.text: And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;

provenance.other: “always to pray” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 18:1, and “pray, and not to faint” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The pairing of continual prayer with fainting is unique to it: 1 Thessalonians 5:17's “Pray without ceasing” has the continuity and not the fainting, and Galatians 6:9's “let us not be weary in well doing” has neither.
provenance.significance: Nephi's one change is grammatical and it changes the force entirely. Luke's sentence is descriptive and third-person — Jesus spoke a parable to the end that MEN OUGHT always to pray. Nephi's is imperative and second-person: “ye must pray always, and not faint.” An observation about what is fitting has become a commandment, and the modal has moved from ought to must, which is the same move the chapter makes at 32:6 with Deuteronomy's “shall ye observe to do” and at 33:15 with “I must obey”. The verse then adds the manner from John 16:23 — pray to the Father in the name of Christ — so that the last instruction in Nephi's writing is Luke's persistence performed by John's route.

links.note: Seven of nine words in sequence, from the single KJV verse that holds them, with the word order of “always to pray” reversed to “pray always” — a reversal the Book of Mormon makes consistently and which does not weaken the identification, since the two rare collocations of the verse are both present. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his 36. The remainder of the verse takes “ye shall pray unto the Father in the name of Christ” from John 16:23, where “ask the Father in my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the substitution of praying for asking is Nephi's, and it is the substitution the whole chapter has been arguing for since 32:4.

pericopes.text: And now I, Nephi, cannot write all the things which were taught among my people; neither am I mighty in writing, like unto speaking: for when a man speaketh by the power of the Holy Ghost, the power of the Holy Ghost carrieth it unto the hearts of the children of men.

But behold, there are many that harden their hearts against the Holy Spirit, that it hath no place in them; wherefore, they cast many things away which are written, and esteem them as things of nought.

links.text: I know that ye are Abraham’s seed; but ye seek to kill me, because my word hath no place in you.

provenance.other: “hath no place in” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:37. The idiom of a word or spirit having no place in a person is unattested elsewhere in the Bible.
provenance.significance: The source is one of the sharpest exchanges in the Fourth Gospel, and Nephi has taken the accusation and changed its subject. In John, what has no place is Christ's word, and the hearers are Abraham's seed who nevertheless seek to kill him; in 2 Nephi 33:2, what has no place is the Holy Spirit, and the hearers are those who cast away what is written. Recover John 8 and the charge Nephi is making against the rejectors of his book is the charge Jesus made against the children of Abraham — that descent from the right father is no protection when the word finds no room. Which is precisely the argument Nephi will make in his own person six verses later, at 33:8: “I have charity for the Jew; I say Jew, because I mean them from whence I came.”

links.note: Four words, one KJV verse, and the construction is reproduced intact including the preposition and the pronoun object. The single change — Christ's word becomes the Holy Spirit — is the change the colophon needs, because Nephi's subject is not his own words' rejection but the Spirit's. The 1830 spelling “nought” at the end of the verse, which 1920 modernized to “naught”, keeps the KJV's own orthography.

pericopes.text: But I, Nephi, have written what I have written; and I esteem it as of great worth, and especially unto my people. For I pray continually for them by day, and mine eyes water my pillow by night, because of them; and I cry unto my God in faith, and I know that he will hear my cry;

links.text: Pilate answered, What I have written I have written.

provenance.other: “what I have written” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 19:22, and the doubled perfect — the clause repeated verbatim as its own predicate — occurs nowhere else in the Bible in any form.
provenance.significance: This is the find of the chapter and it is uncomfortable. Nephi's assertion of his own authority as a writer — “I, Nephi, have written what I have written” — is, word for word, Pilate's refusal to amend the title on the cross. The chief priests ask him to write that the man SAID he was King of the Jews; Pilate declines, and the sentence is the Gospel's image of a text that stands whatever its readers think of it. That is exactly what Nephi wants to claim, and the fact that the one biblical voice claiming it is the man who condemned Christ is not something the borrowing acknowledges. Metalepsis cuts both ways here: recover the context and the colophon's confidence acquires an author it would not have chosen. The task brief was right that colophon formulae often look biblical and are not; this one is, and the surrounding formulae in the same verse are not.

links.note: Six words in a doubled construction with a single biblical home. Confidence is high rather than certain only because the sentence is so natural a thing for any writer to say that independent coinage cannot be formally excluded — but the KJV has no other instance, and the Book of Mormon is a text that quotes John constantly, including three chapters earlier at 2 Nephi 31:4 and 31:10. The rest of 33:3 is not biblical in the same way: “I esteem it as of great worth” and “I cry unto my God in faith” have no identifiable source, and Nephi's own earlier colophons at 1 Nephi 6 and Jacob 7 were adjudicated without one.

links.text: I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.

provenance.other: “water my couch” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 6:6, and it is the Bible's only instance of tears as the verb of watering a place of sleep. Job 16:20's “mine eye poureth out tears unto God” and Jeremiah 9:1's “fountain of tears” share the grief and not the image.
provenance.significance: The transferred epithet is the whole of it. Psalm 6:6 waters a couch; 2 Nephi 33:3 waters a pillow, and the substitution is the sort a writer makes who has the image by heart and not the verse in front of him. The Psalm is the first of the penitential psalms and its speaker weeps for himself under God's chastening; Nephi's weeping is intercessory, “for them by day … because of them”. The borrowed image has been turned outward, which is the same turn the chapter makes at 33:7-9 with charity.

links.note: “Mine eyes water my pillow by night, because of them.” The verb, the object-as-place, and the nocturnal setting are all Psalm 6:6's; Nephi supplies the eyes as the grammatical subject, which the Psalm does not, and swaps couch for pillow. Note that the KJV's “all the night” becomes “by night”, paired with Nephi's “continually for them by day” — the Psalm's single nocturnal image has been opened into a day-and-night antithesis that Psalm 6 does not have. Below any reasonable quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion accordingly.

pericopes.text: and I know that the Lord God will consecrate my prayers, for the gain of my people. And the things which I have written in weakness, will be made strong unto them: for it persuadeth them to do good; it maketh known unto them of their fathers; and it speaketh of Jesus, and persuadeth men to believe in him, and to endure to the end, which is life eternal.

links.text: Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

provenance.other: “out of weakness were made strong” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:34. 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 is the passage a reader expects here — “my strength is made perfect in weakness”, “when I am weak, then am I strong” — but neither verse contains the phrase, and neither has weakness made strong as a completed passive.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has been reading Hebrews 11 since its second chapter. 1 Nephi 2 built the departure from Jerusalem out of Hebrews 11:8-9, 1 Nephi 4:2 built the Red Sea exhortation out of Hebrews 11:29, and here, at the last page Nephi writes, the promise for his own book comes from Hebrews 11:34. The catalogue's note at 1 Nephi 4:2 proposed that the Book of Mormon works through Hebrews 11 in order and uses it as an index to the Old Testament. This verse is the strongest confirmation of that reading available, because it is the furthest point in the chapter and the furthest point in Nephi's writing, and because the borrowing is no longer about an Israelite hero at all — it is about a manuscript. Hebrews 11's roll of those made strong out of weakness ends, in Nephi's hands, with a book.

links.note: “The things which I have written in weakness, will be made strong unto them.” The KJV's exact collocation, with weakness as the source-state and strength as the passive outcome, and with Nephi's own writing put in the place Hebrews gives to Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthae. Note the 1830 “things”, which 1920 changed to “words” — the first edition's noun is the vaguer one, and the later editors' correction moves the sentence toward a claim about the text and away from a claim about its contents. The verse's closing “endure to the end, which is life eternal” is Nephi's own formula from 2 Nephi 31:15 and is registered there, not here.

pericopes.text: And it speaketh harsh against sin, according to the plainness of the truth; wherefore, no man will be angry at the words which I have written, save he shall be of the spirit of the Devil.
I glory in plainness; I glory in truth; I glory in my Jesus, for he hath redeemed my soul from hell.

links.text: For great is thy mercy toward me: and thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell.

provenance.route: Psalm 86:13 + Psalm 49:15 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “delivered my soul from the lowest hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 86:13, and it is the Bible's only first-person statement of a soul brought out of hell. “Redeem my soul” is the Psalter's other half of the idea — Psalm 49:15, “God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave” — and the Book of Mormon has the verb of the second with the object of the first.
provenance.significance: “He hath redeemed my soul from hell” is a conflation of the Psalter's two statements about a soul retrieved from below, taking Psalm 49:15's redeeming and Psalm 86:13's hell. Neither psalm says both. The interest is that this is the same kind of seam as 2 Nephi 31:15, where Matthew 10:22's protasis was welded to Matthew 24:13's apodosis: two verses of one book, joined at the point where the memory holds the more idiomatic half of each. Two such conflations in three chapters is a small but real datum about how this text handles its sources.

links.note: Recorded at moderate because no single KJV verse supplies the clause and the reconstruction is therefore an argument rather than an identification. What makes it worth having is the pairing: the Psalter contains exactly two verses about a soul brought up from the place of the dead, and 2 Nephi 33:6 contains exactly the elements of both and nothing else. The three-fold “I glory” that opens the verse has no biblical model — Paul glories in tribulations, in infirmities, in the cross, but never in a series of three, and never in plainness.
links.whyNot: A conflation argued from two verses neither of which is reproduced. A reader may reasonably hold that “redeemed my soul from hell” is ordinary devotional English of the period requiring no source at all, and the phrase does recur in the Book of Mormon.

pericopes.text: I have charity for my people, and great faith in Christ, that I shall meet many souls spotless at his judgment seat.

links.text: But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.

provenance.other: “judgment seat of Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10. Nothing in Nephi's wording separates them; Romans is named because it also carries “set at nought”, the idiom the chapter used five verses earlier at 33:2, and the two verses stand a page apart in Nephi's text.
provenance.significance: The tribunal is Paul's and so is the reason for mentioning it. Romans 14:10 invokes the judgment seat to stop Christians despising one another; 2 Nephi 33:7-9 invokes it to declare charity for three groups in turn — my people, the Jew, the Gentiles — which is the same argument put positively. And the pairing of a judgment seat with charity is not accidental in a chapter that has been standing on 1 Corinthians 13 since 2 Nephi 31:13: Nephi, who took the tongue of angels from a passage that says it is nothing without charity, closes by claiming the charity.

links.note: A shared technical phrase and a shared argument, without a reproduced run, so this is an echo at moderate. “That I shall meet many souls spotless at his judgment seat” — “spotless” is not a KJV word at all, which is worth saying plainly, since a reader will expect 1 Peter 1:19's “without blemish and without spot” or 2 Peter 3:14's “without spot” behind it and the wording is not there. Only the tribunal is biblical.
links.whyNot: Four words of a fixed New Testament phrase and no way to choose between its two occurrences. The verse's other distinctive terms — charity, spotless — either belong to Nephi or belong to a chapter of Paul already linked elsewhere.

pericopes.text: I have charity for the Jew; I say Jew, because I mean them from whence I came.

I also have charity for the Gentiles.— But behold, for none of these I cannot hope, except they shall be reconciled unto Christ, and enter into the narrow gate, and walk in the straight path, which leads to life, and continue in the path until the end of the day of probation.

And now, my beloved brethren, and also Jew, and all ye ends of the earth, hearken unto these words, and believe in Christ; and if ye believe not in these words, believe in Christ. And if ye shall believe in Christ, ye will believe in these words: for they are the words of Christ, and he hath given them unto me; and they teach all men that they should do good.

links.text: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.

provenance.other: “all the ends of the earth” occurs in seven KJV verses and is on its own too common to identify a source. What narrows it is the grammar: Isaiah 45:22 is the only one of the seven in which the ends of the earth are ADDRESSED — a vocative followed by an imperative of turning and being saved. The other six speak about them in the third person.
provenance.significance: Nephi's peroration reproduces the one biblical construction that matches what he is doing. “All ye ends of the earth, hearken unto these words, and believe in Christ” is Isaiah 45:22's vocative plus imperative plus promise of salvation, with looking replaced by believing and the exclusive claim (“I am God, and there is none else”) transposed into the exclusive claim already made at 2 Nephi 31:21 out of Acts 4:12. The address recurs at 33:13, where it is joined to the house of Israel — so the last two summonses in Nephi's book are both Isaiah 45:22's, and both are aimed past his own people.
