links.note: The link is to a construction rather than to a run of words, hence conceptual and moderate. It is worth a row because the vocative is genuinely restricted — one of seven — and because the salvation clause travels with it in both places. Note that Nephi's argument here is circular and openly so (“if ye believe not in these words, believe in Christ. And if ye shall believe in Christ, ye will believe in these words”), which is a structure Isaiah 45 does not supply; only the address does.
links.whyNot: The phrase itself is common and the identification rests on syntax. A reader who takes “all ye ends of the earth” as a general biblicism rather than a citation of Isaiah 45:22 has not made an error, only a different judgment.

pericopes.text: And if they are not the words of Christ, judge ye: for Christ will shew unto you, with power and great glory, that they are his words, at the last day; and you and I shall stand face to face before his bar; and ye shall know that I have been commanded of him to write these things, notwithstanding my weakness:

links.text: And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.

provenance.other: “with power and great glory” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:30 and Luke 21:27, and both are the same saying in the same discourse. Mark 13:26 reads “with great power and glory”, which is a different word order and is therefore excluded by the Book of Mormon's phrasing.
provenance.significance: Mark is ruled out and Matthew and Luke are not separable, which is a small mediation result but a real one: the Book of Mormon has the Matthew-Luke form of the phrase and not Mark's. What Nephi does with it is the interesting part. In all three Gospels the power and great glory attend the Son of man's coming; in 2 Nephi 33:11 they attend a demonstration about a document — “Christ will shew unto you, with power and great glory, that they are his words”. The parousia has been made the occasion of a textual attestation, with Nephi and his reader standing face to face at the bar. It is the boldest claim in the colophon and it is made in borrowed words.

links.note: Four words in sequence, in the word order that separates Matthew and Luke from Mark. The 1830 “Christ will shew unto you” again preserves the KJV spelling that 1920 modernized to “show” — the third such case in these three chapters, after 31:9 and 32:5. “Face to face” in the same verse is a KJV idiom but a widely distributed one, and 1 Corinthians 13:12 is not proposed as a source for it.

pericopes.text: and I pray the Father in the name of Christ, that many of us, if not all, may be saved in his kingdom, at that great and last day.

And now, my beloved brethren, all they which are of the House of Israel, and all ye ends of the earth, I speak unto you, as the voice of one crying from the dust: farewell until that great day shall come;

links.text: For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

provenance.route: Isaiah 40:3 via Matthew 3:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon, fused with Isaiah 29:4
provenance.mt: Isaiah 40:3 reads “The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness”.
provenance.other: “the voice of one crying” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4, John 1:23 — and in none of them is it the Old Testament. Isaiah 40:3, which all four quote, reads “the voice of him that crieth”. The mediation is therefore decided by the pronoun, and mediation-check.py returns it as the one decisive divergence.
provenance.significance: Nephi's last self-description is a fusion of two Isaiah passages, and only one of them reaches him through Isaiah. “The voice of one crying” is the New Testament's form of Isaiah 40:3, not Isaiah's own — every Gospel has “one crying”, the prophet has “him that crieth” — so the phrase enters by way of John the Baptist. “From the dust” is Isaiah 29:4, which Nephi has already expounded twice in this book, at 26:16 (“their speech shall be low out of the dust”) and in the expansion of Isaiah 29 at chapter 27. The result is that Nephi signs off as the Baptist speaking from the grave: the forerunner's title, applied to a dead man's book, out of the dust of the buried record. And the frame closes exactly — 2 Nephi 31:4, the first verse of this final sequence, is about “that Prophet which should baptize”; 2 Nephi 33:13, the last but two, takes that prophet's own words for Nephi himself.

links.note: Five words verbatim in the NT form, with Isaiah's own wording available and not used. This is the mediation finding of the three chapters and it is decidable on a single pronoun, in the manner of the sixteen such rows the 1 Nephi pilot produced. The fusion with Isaiah 29:4 is not a second borrowing but Nephi's own established idiom, argued at 26:16 and at 27, and pointed to here rather than restated.

pericopes.text: and you that will not partake of the goodness of God, and respect the words of the Jews, and also my words, and the words which shall proceed forth out of the mouth of the Lamb of God, behold, I bid you an everlasting farewell, for these words shall condemn you at the last day:

links.text: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 8:3 and/or Matthew 4:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 8:3 reads “every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD”.
provenance.other: “proceedeth out of the mouth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4, which are the same saying: Matthew quotes Deuteronomy in the wilderness temptation. They differ in one word, the divine name — the LORD in Deuteronomy, God in Matthew.
provenance.significance: This is the mediation case in these three chapters that will not resolve, and it is worth saying why rather than guessing. The test is normally the divine name, and here the name has been replaced: 2 Nephi 33:14 reads “out of the mouth of the Lamb of God”, which is neither the LORD nor God but John's title, already used in this sequence at 31:4 and 31:5. mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence, correctly. The word “God” is present, which is Matthew's noun and not Deuteronomy's, but it is present as part of a Johannine title that Nephi would have written whichever source he had in view, so it decides nothing. Recorded as uncertain and flagged in the report.

links.note: Four words of a saying that exists in the KJV in two forms, with the one discriminating word overwritten by the Book of Mormon's own christology. The echo is worth recording because 33:14 is building a hierarchy of words — the words of the Jews, my words, the words of the Lamb — and the third term is described in the Bible's one formula for words that come from God's mouth. Note that Deuteronomy 8:1 is separately linked at 2 Nephi 32:6, two verses above this one in its own chapter, which is a mild argument for Deuteronomy 8 being in view here as well; it is not strong enough to settle the mediation and it is not treated as if it were.
links.whyNot: Four words, no decisive divergence between the two candidates, and the phrase is common enough in devotional English that a source need not be posited at all. Kept because the mediation question it raises is itself the finding.

pericopes.text: for what I seal on earth, shall be brought against you at the judgment bar; for thus hath the Lord commanded me, and I must obey. Amen.

links.text: And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.

provenance.other: “bind on earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 16:19 and Matthew 18:18, and they are the same formula. The KJV never uses “seal” in this sense at all — sealing in the KJV is the closing of a book (Isaiah 29:11, Daniel 12:4) or the marking of the elect (Revelation 7:3), never the ratification of an earthly act in heaven.
provenance.significance: If the echo stands, the interest is entirely in the substituted verb. Nephi's “what I seal on earth, shall be brought against you at the judgment bar” has the shape of Matthew's binding formula — an indefinite relative, an act on earth, a consequence above — with a verb the KJV does not supply for it. And the verb Nephi chooses is the one Isaiah 29:11 uses for a sealed book, which this book has expounded at 2 Nephi 27:7-11. The formula for ecclesiastical authority and the image of the sealed record have been welded together in the last sentence Nephi writes.

links.note: Recorded at low because the argument is about a construction whose one distinctive word has been replaced, which is close to the definition of an undemonstrable link. It earns the row rather than an exclusion because 33:15 is the final verse of Nephi's writing and the reader who feels Matthew 16:19 behind it deserves to be told what the catalogue made of that feeling: the shape is Matthew's, the vocabulary is not, and the sealing comes from Isaiah 29 by way of this book's own chapter 27. The closing “thus hath the Lord commanded me, and I must obey” has no biblical source — Acts 5:29's “We ought to obey God rather than men” is the verse a reader will reach for and it shares only the verb.
links.whyNot: The one word that would make the link decidable is absent, and it is absent by substitution rather than by paraphrase. Two words of contact (“on earth”, plus an indefinite relative) cannot carry a source, and the sealing image is fully accounted for within the Book of Mormon itself.
